name: .NET
shortDescription: The cross-platform runtime, SDK, libraries, and tooling behind modern C# applications.
overview: .NET is the open-source, cross-platform platform that combines runtimes, SDKs, languages, libraries, build tooling, package management, diagnostics, and deployment models for modern applications.
detail: A production .NET system is shaped by distinct choices: the SDK and MSBuild produce assets, the target framework defines compile-time APIs, NuGet resolves dependencies, the runtime loads managed assemblies and executes them through JIT or ahead-of-time compilation, and the publish model decides what ships. Teams must service those layers deliberately, keep builds reproducible, validate configuration, test the published artifact on its target OS and architecture, and use runtime diagnostics before optimizing.
learningObjectives: Distinguish the SDK, CLI, target framework, runtime, host, shared framework, and base class libraries.
Explain restore, compilation to IL and metadata, assembly loading, JIT execution, garbage collection, and native AOT tradeoffs.
Create repeatable repositories with global.json, Directory.Build.props, central package management, analyzers, and CI checks.
Choose framework-dependent, self-contained, single-file, trimmed, native AOT, or container deployment based on operational needs.
Use configuration, dependency injection, logging, cancellation, async I/O, and diagnostics as platform capabilities.
Verify package risk, compatibility, publish output, target runtime identifiers, startup, shutdown, and production telemetry.
prerequisites: Basic C# syntax and familiarity with projects, solutions, files, processes, and command-line tools.
The .NET 10 SDK and a terminal; the dedicated sample has no database or external-service dependency.
Basic awareness of operating systems, CPU architectures, environment variables, and application deployment.

use: Cross-platform web, cloud, worker, desktop, mobile, data, tooling, and service applications that benefit from one managed runtime ecosystem.
Teams that value strong tooling, mature libraries, built-in diagnostics, long-term-support releases, and multiple deployment models.
Systems that need productive managed code with selective native interop, runtime compilation, trimming, or native AOT options.
avoid: A constrained environment where supported .NET runtime or native AOT output cannot meet memory, startup, OS, or architecture limits.
A platform-mandated codebase whose required native ecosystem, runtime, or ownership makes another stack the safer operational choice.
Choosing .NET only from synthetic benchmarks without validating expertise, dependencies, deployment, observability, and lifecycle needs.

concepts.title: SDK, CLI, and MSBuild
concepts.description: The SDK supplies compilers, templates, targets, and the dotnet CLI; MSBuild evaluates project files and executes restore, build, test, pack, and publish targets.

concepts.title: Target frameworks
concepts.description: A target such as net10.0 selects the compile-time reference API surface; compatibility rules govern referenced projects and packages.

concepts.title: Runtime, host, and shared frameworks
concepts.description: The host selects a compatible runtime, the CLR loads assemblies and manages execution, and shared frameworks provide commonly installed libraries.

concepts.title: IL, JIT, and native AOT
concepts.description: Compilers emit intermediate language and metadata; the runtime normally JIT-compiles methods, while native AOT moves more work to publish time.

concepts.title: Managed memory and GC
concepts.description: The garbage collector reclaims managed objects by generation, while IDisposable and await using define deterministic ownership for scarce resources.

concepts.title: NuGet dependency graphs
concepts.description: Restore resolves direct and transitive packages; central versions, source mapping, lock policy, and audits improve control.

concepts.title: Generic Host and extensions
concepts.description: Configuration, logging, dependency injection, options, lifetime, HTTP clients, caching, and telemetry provide common composition primitives.

concepts.title: Publishing and runtime identifiers
concepts.description: Framework-dependent, self-contained, single-file, trimmed, AOT, and container outputs have different size, patching, startup, and compatibility implications.

architecture.description: The SDK restores packages and uses MSBuild plus language compilers to produce assemblies. Publish combines assemblies with configuration and optional runtime assets. The .NET host selects the runtime, the CLR loads and executes code, and operating-system resources remain explicitly owned.

implementationIntroduction: Create a repeatable repository first, then prove the built and published application on the runtime environment that will own it.

implementationSteps.title: Select and record the toolchain
implementationSteps.description: Choose a supported target framework, record SDK/runtime details, and use global.json when the repository needs deliberate SDK roll-forward behavior.

implementationSteps.title: Centralize repository policy
implementationSteps.description: Use Directory.Build.props for nullable analysis, analyzers, warnings, and build settings, and Directory.Packages.props for reviewed package versions.

implementationSteps.title: Design the project graph
implementationSteps.description: Keep executable entry points, libraries, and tests explicit; enforce dependency direction through project or package references.

implementationSteps.title: Make restore reproducible
implementationSteps.description: Control package sources, centralize versions, use lock policy where needed, cache safely, and fail CI on vulnerable dependencies.

implementationSteps.title: Compose platform services
implementationSteps.description: Load configuration by environment, validate typed options, register owned services, use structured logging, and propagate cancellation.

implementationSteps.title: Choose a publish model
implementationSteps.description: Decide who services the runtime and whether the target requires self-contained, single-file, trimming, AOT, a runtime identifier, or containers.

implementationSteps.title: Verify the artifact
implementationSteps.description: Test Release output, publish from a clean restore, run on each target OS and architecture, exercise shutdown, scan dependencies, and capture diagnostics.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: The dedicated sample combines Generic Host configuration, validated options, dependency injection, logging, and a cancellation-aware application boundary.

testing.introduction: Test source behavior and the produced artifact because Debug builds on a developer machine do not prove restore, publish, platform, trimming, or runtime compatibility.
items: Run unit and integration tests in Release with the same SDK selection, warning policy, and package graph used by CI.
Use deterministic seams such as TimeProvider and isolated temporary storage instead of sleep-based or machine-dependent tests.
Publish from a clean restore and run smoke tests against the output directory rather than only using dotnet run.
Test every supported OS, architecture, runtime identifier, globalization mode, and deployment model in an appropriate runner or container.
Enable trimming or native AOT analyzers early and test reflection, serialization, configuration binding, native libraries, and dynamic loading.

security.introduction: The platform boundary includes source feeds, build agents, packages, runtime servicing, configuration, native dependencies, and published artifacts.
items: Use trusted NuGet sources, package source mapping where appropriate, dependency review, vulnerability auditing, and controlled private-feed credentials.
Centrally manage direct packages, review transitive changes, and produce an inventory or SBOM for released artifacts.
Keep secrets out of project files, appsettings, logs, command histories, and images; use an approved runtime secret provider.
Patch installed runtimes or rebuild self-contained artifacts promptly when runtime servicing updates are published.
Use least-privilege OS identities, writable directories, network access, native libraries, and container capabilities.

performance.introduction: Measure the real workload with runtime diagnostics; allocation, GC, JIT, thread pool, I/O, networking, and dependencies interact.
items: Baseline latency, throughput, CPU, working set, allocation, GC pauses, exceptions, thread-pool behavior, and startup before tuning.
Use dotnet-counters for live signals, dotnet-trace for traces, dotnet-gcdump for managed heaps, and dotnet-dump for failures.
Prefer asynchronous APIs for concurrent I/O, propagate cancellation, pool expensive connections through supported clients, and dispose scarce resources.
Benchmark isolated hot paths with representative inputs and Release settings, then confirm gains end to end.
Evaluate ReadyToRun, tiered compilation, dynamic PGO, trimming, single-file, and native AOT against startup, throughput, size, diagnostics, and compatibility.

deployment.introduction: The deployment model decides artifact contents, compatible targets, runtime servicing ownership, and rollback behavior.
items: Framework-dependent deployment uses a compatible installed runtime; self-contained deployment ships one and makes releases responsible for runtime patches.
Specify and test runtime identifiers only for platform-specific assets; win-x64 output does not run on Linux or Arm64.
Treat single-file, trimming, ReadyToRun, and native AOT as independent choices with analyzer and runtime verification requirements.
Build immutable artifacts once, attach provenance and dependency metadata, promote the same artifact, and keep environment configuration external.
Verify startup, readiness, graceful shutdown, logs, dumps, roll-forward policy, rollback, and runtime version in the target host or container.

troubleshooting.symptom: The repository builds locally but fails in CI.
troubleshooting.cause: SDK selection, workload versions, package sources, cached assets, OS behavior, or warning policy differs.
troubleshooting.fix: Compare dotnet --info, global.json resolution, restore sources, environment variables, and a clean bin/obj-free restore using the CI command.

troubleshooting.symptom: The published application reports that a framework is missing.
troubleshooting.cause: Framework-dependent output reached a host without a compatible shared framework or roll-forward policy.
troubleshooting.fix: Install and service the required runtime, set deliberate roll-forward behavior, or publish self-contained and accept patch ownership.

troubleshooting.symptom: A trimmed, single-file, or AOT build fails after publishing.
troubleshooting.cause: Reflection, dynamic loading, serializers, configuration binding, or native assets were not visible to analysis or packaging.
troubleshooting.fix: Enable publish analyzers, use source generation or annotations, inspect warnings and bundle contents, and add artifact tests.

troubleshooting.symptom: Memory remains high after work completes.
troubleshooting.cause: Live references, caches, large objects, pinned buffers, native memory, or GC policy may retain memory.
troubleshooting.fix: Correlate counters with GC dumps and process metrics, identify retention paths or native owners, then change the measured cause.

troubleshooting.symptom: Restore resolves an unexpected package or version.
troubleshooting.cause: A transitive dependency, central override, floating version, source ordering, cache, or conditional property changed the graph.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect transitive packages, generated assets, central props, sources, and lock policy; make the intended dependency explicit.

productionChecklist: The target framework is supported, SDK selection and roll-forward behavior are deliberate, and dotnet --info is captured in CI diagnostics.
Nullable analysis, analyzers, warnings, deterministic builds, package versions, sources, and vulnerability audits are centrally enforced.
Release tests and published-artifact smoke tests cover every supported OS, architecture, runtime identifier, and deployment model.
Configuration is validated at startup, secrets remain external, logs are structured, and cancellation plus graceful shutdown are tested.
Runtime servicing ownership is explicit for framework-dependent, self-contained, and container deployments.
Diagnostics can capture counters, traces, dumps, and build/runtime metadata without exposing sensitive data.
Artifacts are immutable, inventoried, promotable across environments, and covered by rollback procedures.
bestPractices: Treat SDK, target framework, runtime, host, and deployment mode as separate versioned decisions.
Centralize nullable, analyzer, warning, deterministic-build, and package policy.
Keep restore sources trusted and explicit; audit direct and transitive dependencies.
Use validated options, structured logging, async I/O, cancellation, and deterministic disposal.
Publish once and test the Release artifact on every supported OS and architecture.
Choose deployment mode based on runtime servicing ownership, not convenience alone.
Enable trimming and AOT analyzers before adopting those modes and verify dynamic features.
Measure with counters, traces, dumps, and representative benchmarks before tuning.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the .NET SDK, target framework, and runtime?
interviewQuestions.answer: The SDK builds applications, the target framework selects compile-time APIs and compatibility rules, and the runtime executes the application. One SDK can target multiple frameworks and a framework-dependent app needs a compatible host runtime.

interviewQuestions.question: What does managed code mean?
interviewQuestions.answer: Managed assemblies execute under the CLR, which provides type loading, exceptions, garbage collection, JIT compilation, diagnostics, and other services; unmanaged resources still require explicit ownership.

interviewQuestions.question: Framework-dependent or self-contained deployment?
interviewQuestions.answer: Framework-dependent output is smaller and relies on a serviced host runtime. Self-contained output includes a runtime but enlarges artifacts and requires application releases for runtime security patches.

interviewQuestions.question: How do JIT, ReadyToRun, and native AOT differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: JIT compiles IL during execution, ReadyToRun precompiles portions while retaining the runtime, and native AOT creates native output at publish time with stricter limits for dynamic code and reflection.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use global.json?
interviewQuestions.answer: It controls SDK selection and roll-forward when a repository needs predictable tool behavior. It does not choose the deployed runtime and must be maintained rather than pinned indefinitely.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you investigate high memory in .NET?
interviewQuestions.answer: Start with process and runtime counters, distinguish managed heap from native and committed memory, capture a GC dump or dump, inspect retention and allocation, then validate the fix under the real workload.

note: The SDK used to build, target framework used to compile, and runtime used to execute are related but distinct; capture all three when diagnosing differences.
tip: Run the published DLL or executable from a clean output directory in CI so missing content, native assets, configuration, and runtime assumptions fail before deployment.
warning: A successful dotnet run on a developer workstation does not prove restore reproducibility, published-artifact completeness, runtime compatibility, trimming safety, or target-platform support.
latestNote: Gold-standard platform guide with a dedicated runnable sample

name: C#
shortDescription: A strongly typed language for explicit domain models, safe composition, asynchronous workflows, and high-performance .NET software.
overview: C# is the primary general-purpose language of .NET. It combines static typing, managed memory, object-oriented and functional techniques, expressive data modeling, asynchronous control flow, and access to the full .NET library ecosystem.
detail: Production C# is less about using every syntax feature and more about making contracts, ownership, state changes, failure modes, and concurrency visible. Types should prevent invalid states where practical; nullable annotations should match runtime truth; exceptions should represent exceptional failure; async code must propagate cancellation; LINQ must be understood as an execution pipeline; and newer language features should improve clarity without hiding cost. C# 14 on .NET 10 adds extension members, field-backed properties, null-conditional assignment, and improved Span conversions, while the durable fundamentals remain types, generics, patterns, delegates, resource ownership, and testable boundaries.
learningObjectives: Distinguish value types, reference types, identity, value equality, boxing, copying, and nullable intent.
Design domain contracts with classes, records, record structs, interfaces, generics, and constrained type parameters.
Use pattern matching, expressions, delegates, lambdas, and LINQ while keeping control flow and execution cost visible.
Build asynchronous and streaming workflows with Task, ValueTask, IAsyncEnumerable, cancellation, and exception propagation.
Own managed and unmanaged resources with IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable, using, and clear lifetime boundaries.
Apply analyzers, tests, benchmarks, and API-compatibility discipline to evolve production C# safely.
prerequisites: Basic programming concepts such as variables, conditions, loops, methods, collections, and exceptions.
The .NET 10 SDK and a terminal; the dedicated sample has no database or external-service dependency.
Familiarity with projects, namespaces, packages, build warnings, and automated tests is helpful.

use: Web, cloud, desktop, mobile, data, tooling, games, and services that run on .NET and benefit from strong tooling and static analysis.
Domains where expressive types, generics, records, pattern matching, and nullable contracts can make rules reviewable and testable.
Concurrent I/O-heavy systems that benefit from Task-based APIs, async streams, cancellation, and mature runtime diagnostics.
avoid: A host where neither the .NET runtime nor an appropriate native AOT artifact can meet platform, startup, memory, or deployment constraints.
A team or ecosystem whose required libraries, operational tooling, or platform ownership strongly favors another supported language.
Using dynamic or reflection-heavy C# to imitate an untyped language when compile-time contracts would be clearer and safer.

concepts.title: Types, identity, and equality
concepts.description: Value types contain their data and are copied by value; reference types carry object references. Equality semantics, mutability, allocation, and boxing should match the domain.

concepts.title: Nullable reference analysis
concepts.description: Annotations such as string and string? express intent while flow analysis warns when maybe-null values are assigned or dereferenced; runtime representation is unchanged.

concepts.title: Classes, records, and structs
concepts.description: Classes suit identity and behavior, records provide value-oriented equality and with expressions, and small readonly structs can model allocation-free values when copying is cheap.

concepts.title: Generics and constraints
concepts.description: Generic types and methods preserve compile-time information and avoid casts; constraints describe the members, construction, nullability, or value/reference behavior an algorithm requires.

concepts.title: Patterns and expressions
concepts.description: Type, property, relational, list, logical, and recursive patterns make branching over shape and state explicit; guards handle rules not expressible as patterns alone.

concepts.title: Delegates, lambdas, and LINQ
concepts.description: Delegates model executable behavior, lambdas create it concisely, and LINQ composes transformations whose deferred or provider-specific execution must remain understood.

concepts.title: Tasks, async streams, and cancellation
concepts.description: Task represents eventual completion, async and await preserve readable control flow, IAsyncEnumerable streams results, and CancellationToken carries cooperative cancellation.

concepts.title: Resource and failure ownership
concepts.description: Exceptions communicate exceptional failure, result types can model expected alternatives, and using or await using defines deterministic cleanup for scarce resources.

architecture.description: External data is parsed and validated into typed boundary contracts. Application workflows coordinate domain behavior through interfaces and explicit results. Infrastructure owns I/O and resources, while output contracts prevent internal mutable state from leaking.

implementationIntroduction: Start with the domain language and failure boundaries, then select C# features that make those decisions obvious to callers and verifiable in tests.

implementationSteps.title: Enable compiler guardrails
implementationSteps.description: Select the supported language version, enable nullable analysis and analyzers, treat reviewed warnings as errors, and centralize repository policy.

implementationSteps.title: Model valid domain states
implementationSteps.description: Choose classes for identity, records for value-oriented contracts, and small readonly structs for cheap values; validate construction and expose only required mutation.

implementationSteps.title: Define boundaries and variance
implementationSteps.description: Use interfaces and generics at real substitution points, apply the narrowest useful constraints, and avoid abstraction that only renames a concrete type.

implementationSteps.title: Express decisions clearly
implementationSteps.description: Use pattern matching, switch expressions, guard clauses, and named methods so business branches are exhaustive, ordered, and easy to review.

implementationSteps.title: Compose data deliberately
implementationSteps.description: Use LINQ for readable transformations, distinguish IEnumerable from IQueryable, know when execution is deferred, and materialize once at ownership boundaries.

implementationSteps.title: Design asynchronous flow
implementationSteps.description: Return Task or ValueTask deliberately, avoid blocking waits, propagate CancellationToken, stream large results with IAsyncEnumerable, and preserve exception context.

implementationSteps.title: Test contracts and costs
implementationSteps.description: Test equality, nullability assumptions, patterns, cancellation, disposal, enumeration, serialization, public API compatibility, and measured hot paths.

code.label: OrderProcessor.cs
code.introduction: The dedicated sample combines records, a readonly value object, C# 14 extension members, property patterns, LINQ, async streams, and cancellation in one typed workflow.

testing.introduction: Test semantics that syntax can obscure: equality, copying, null-state assumptions, enumeration timing, cancellation, exceptions, resource cleanup, and concurrency.
items: Write focused unit tests for domain construction, record equality, value-object operators, generic algorithms, pattern branches, and exhaustive fallbacks.
Test async methods by awaiting them; use controllable fakes or TaskCompletionSource instead of sleeps, and assert cancellation separately from failure.
Enumerate deferred LINQ queries intentionally and test for multiple enumeration, ordering, provider translation, and mutation of the underlying source.
Exercise IDisposable and IAsyncDisposable ownership on success, failure, and cancellation; verify resources are not captured beyond their intended lifetime.
Run analyzers and nullable warnings in CI, add integration tests at serialization and I/O boundaries, and benchmark only measured hot paths.

security.introduction: Language safety reduces classes of defects but does not validate untrusted data, authorize actions, erase secrets, or make unsafe/native boundaries harmless.
items: Validate length, range, format, encoding, and allowed values at trust boundaries; do not treat a successful parse or non-null annotation as authorization.
Avoid logging secrets and sensitive object graphs; remember strings are immutable and cannot be reliably cleared from memory.
Use checked arithmetic where overflow changes security or money decisions, bound collection growth, and reject attacker-controlled recursion or allocation sizes.
Treat reflection, dynamic loading, expression compilation, unsafe code, native interop, and deserialization as explicit reviewed trust boundaries.
Preserve exception context internally but return safe external errors; do not expose stack traces, filesystem paths, connection details, or secret-bearing values.

performance.introduction: C# syntax maps to allocations, copies, dispatch, enumeration, state machines, and runtime calls. Measure the complete workload before trading clarity for lower-level constructs.
items: Use BenchmarkDotNet or representative application telemetry to measure CPU, allocation, throughput, latency, and generated code in Release builds.
Avoid accidental boxing, closure captures, repeated enumeration, intermediate collections, string concatenation in loops, and large mutable struct copies.
Use arrays, spans, pooling, ref-like types, or stack allocation only when profiling identifies a hot path and lifetime rules stay clear.
Choose Task by default; consider ValueTask only for measured frequently synchronous paths where callers obey its consumption constraints.
Keep LINQ when it is clear and fast enough; replace a pipeline with loops only when measurements justify the maintenance cost.

deployment.introduction: C# source is compiled under a selected language version into .NET assemblies; runtime and publish choices can change reflection, trimming, serialization, and dynamic-code behavior.
items: Record the SDK and language version, compile Release with the same nullable and analyzer policy in CI, and avoid relying on a developer IDE's implicit settings.
Publish and smoke-test the actual artifact; source-level success does not prove content files, native assets, dynamic loading, or runtime compatibility.
Enable trimming and native AOT analyzers early when those modes are targets; test reflection, serializers, dependency injection, and expression generation.
Version public contracts deliberately, use API compatibility checks for libraries, and account for record constructor or required-member changes in consumers and serializers.
Capture symbols and source metadata for diagnostics, keep secrets external, and ensure cancellation plus graceful shutdown reach asynchronous application boundaries.

troubleshooting.symptom: A nullable warning is silenced but a NullReferenceException still occurs.
troubleshooting.cause: The null-forgiving operator changed compiler analysis, not runtime data, or an external boundary violated its annotation.
troubleshooting.fix: Trace the actual source, correct annotations and validation, add appropriate nullable attributes, and reserve ! for invariants the code truly proves.

troubleshooting.symptom: An async workflow hangs or loses throughput.
troubleshooting.cause: Code blocks on Result or Wait, holds scarce resources across awaits, ignores cancellation, or starts unbounded concurrent work.
troubleshooting.fix: Await end to end, propagate tokens, bound concurrency, shorten resource ownership, and inspect task, thread-pool, and dependency telemetry.

troubleshooting.symptom: A LINQ query runs repeatedly or changes after it was created.
troubleshooting.cause: Deferred execution re-enumerates a mutable source, or IQueryable delegates behavior to a provider.
troubleshooting.fix: Identify the execution boundary, materialize once where ownership changes, inspect generated provider queries, and avoid hidden side effects.

troubleshooting.symptom: Record equality or dictionary lookup behaves unexpectedly.
troubleshooting.cause: Generated value equality includes different members than intended, mutable members changed a key, or reference equality was required.
troubleshooting.fix: Choose identity versus value semantics explicitly, keep keys immutable, customize equality only with a complete contract, and test hash behavior.

troubleshooting.symptom: Code works normally but fails after trimming or native AOT publishing.
troubleshooting.cause: Reflection, dynamic code, serializers, or plugins depend on members the compiler cannot discover statically.
troubleshooting.fix: Act on analyzer warnings, prefer source generation and explicit registrations, annotate unavoidable reflection, and test the published artifact.

productionChecklist: The supported SDK and C# language version are recorded; nullable analysis, analyzers, formatting, and warning policy run in CI.
Public types make identity, equality, nullability, mutation, ownership, and failure behavior explicit.
Inputs are validated at trust boundaries and sensitive values are excluded from logs, exceptions, and serialized output.
Async APIs are awaited end to end, cancellation is propagated, concurrency is bounded, and async void is limited to event handlers.
LINQ execution, materialization, provider translation, ordering, and multiple enumeration are understood and tested.
Disposable and async-disposable resources have clear owners on success, exception, and cancellation paths.
Release tests cover public contracts and published artifacts; performance changes are measured and trimming or AOT warnings are resolved.
bestPractices: Enable nullable reference analysis and correct the contract instead of routinely suppressing warnings.
Choose class, record, record struct, or readonly struct from identity, equality, mutation, copying, and allocation needs.
Make invalid states difficult to construct and validate untrusted data at the boundary.
Use generics and interfaces where they preserve meaningful type information or substitution, not as ceremony.
Keep pattern matches exhaustive and ordered from specific to general; name complex guards.
Understand deferred execution and materialize LINQ results once at clear ownership boundaries.
Await asynchronous work end to end, propagate cancellation, and bound parallelism.
Give scarce resources deterministic owners and preserve exception context when adding useful domain information.
Measure before applying spans, pooling, ValueTask, unsafe code, or allocation-avoiding complexity.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a class, record, and record struct?
interviewQuestions.answer: A class is a reference type with reference equality by default. A record class is still a reference type but synthesizes value-oriented equality and nondestructive mutation. A record struct is a value type, so assignments copy its data and size matters.

interviewQuestions.question: Do nullable reference types prevent null at runtime?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. They add annotations and flow-analysis warnings at compile time without changing runtime representation. External data and oblivious code still require validation.

interviewQuestions.question: What does deferred execution mean in LINQ?
interviewQuestions.answer: Many operators build a pipeline that executes only when enumerated. Re-enumeration can repeat work and observe changed source data; IQueryable may translate the expression for another provider.

interviewQuestions.question: Task or ValueTask?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use Task by default because it is simple and safely awaitable multiple times. Consider ValueTask only for measured, often-synchronous hot paths and document its stricter consumption rules.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should async void usually be avoided?
interviewQuestions.answer: It cannot be awaited or composed and its exceptions follow the synchronization context rather than a returned task. It is mainly appropriate for event handlers.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you use a generic constraint?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use a constraint when an algorithm genuinely requires capabilities such as an interface, base type, value/reference semantics, construction, unmanaged representation, or a static abstract member.

interviewQuestions.question: How do IEnumerable and IQueryable differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: IEnumerable composes delegates executed by .NET over objects. IQueryable builds expression trees that a provider translates, so supported operations, execution location, and performance depend on that provider.

note: The newest syntax is optional. A feature earns its place when it makes contracts or ownership clearer to the next reader and survives the project's supported toolchain.
tip: Model domain values such as Money, EmailAddress, or OrderId as focused types when they carry validation, equality, formatting, or behavior beyond a primitive.
warning: Do not hide uncertain nulls with !, block asynchronous work with Result or Wait, or assume a deferred LINQ pipeline has already executed; each removes evidence the compiler or runtime could give you.

name: Dependency Injection
shortDescription: Compose .NET applications from explicit services with correct lifetimes, validated configuration, and container-owned disposal.
overview: Dependency injection is the application-composition technique built into modern .NET hosting. It makes required collaborators explicit, centralizes object construction, manages reuse and disposal, and lets application code depend on stable contracts at meaningful boundaries.
detail: The built-in .NET dependency-injection container turns service registrations into object graphs at a composition root. Constructor injection declares required collaborators, while singleton, scoped, and transient lifetimes express how long instances are reused and who disposes them. ASP.NET Core creates a scope for each request; workers, console applications, queues, and scheduled jobs must create scopes for their own logical operations. Production design also includes validated options, feature-level registration extensions, keyed services for named implementations, container validation, and tests that prove lifetime behavior. DI improves replaceability and ownership only when dependencies remain explicit: resolving services from a global provider, capturing scoped instances in singletons, injecting factories everywhere, or adding interfaces without a real boundary simply moves coupling into harder-to-see runtime configuration.
learningObjectives: Explain inversion of control, dependency inversion, dependency injection, and the composition root without treating them as synonyms.
Choose singleton, scoped, and transient lifetimes from ownership, thread-safety, state, and disposal requirements.
Organize registrations by feature while keeping application services free of service-location calls.
Create and dispose explicit scopes for workers, message handlers, console tools, and scheduled operations.
Use validated options, keyed services, factories, and multiple implementations only where each solves a concrete composition problem.
Validate, test, diagnose, and observe object graphs before lifetime defects reach production.
prerequisites: Comfort with C# classes, interfaces, constructors, generics, IDisposable, and async disposal.
Basic familiarity with .NET hosting, configuration, logging, and application startup.
An understanding that database contexts, HTTP handlers, caches, and other resources have different ownership and concurrency rules.

use: Applications with a composition root where framework entry points need services assembled from configuration, infrastructure, and application policy.
Components with meaningful replacement boundaries, multiple implementations, environment-specific adapters, or focused test doubles.
Hosted workloads that benefit from container-owned lifetime, disposal, options, logging, and framework integrations.
avoid: Using the container inside domain entities, value objects, or static helpers; construct simple objects directly and keep dependencies explicit.
Creating an interface for every class when there is no substitution, boundary, or testing need; concrete constructor injection is valid.
Treating DI as a substitute for modular design: a container can construct a tightly coupled graph but cannot make its responsibilities coherent.

concepts.title: Inversion of control
concepts.description: Framework or host code controls application activation and supplies collaborators instead of each service constructing its own dependencies.

concepts.title: Composition root
concepts.description: A small startup boundary selects implementations, binds configuration, and assembles features; business code should not know how the container is configured.

concepts.title: Constructor injection
concepts.description: Required collaborators appear in the constructor, making object contracts reviewable and allowing incomplete instances to be rejected at creation.

concepts.title: Singleton lifetime
concepts.description: One instance is reused by the root provider and all scopes. The service must be thread-safe and may depend only on singleton-safe collaborators.

concepts.title: Scoped lifetime
concepts.description: One instance is reused inside a logical operation. Web requests get scopes automatically; background operations must create and dispose them explicitly.

concepts.title: Transient lifetime
concepts.description: A new instance is produced for each resolution. Transient does not mean free: disposable transients are retained for disposal by the resolving scope.

concepts.title: Disposal ownership
concepts.description: The provider disposes instances it creates when their owning scope or root provider ends; callers should not dispose container-owned services independently.

concepts.title: Options and validation
concepts.description: Typed options separate configuration from behavior and can fail startup when required values or ranges are invalid.

concepts.title: Keyed and multiple services
concepts.description: Keyed registrations select named strategies, while IEnumerable<T> composes all implementations; both should preserve explicit application dependencies.

concepts.title: Container validation
concepts.description: ValidateOnBuild and ValidateScopes detect constructability and common captive dependencies, but runtime-created branches and semantic mistakes still require tests.

architecture.description: The host builds a validated root provider. Each entry point opens or receives an operation scope, and the container constructs application services plus their infrastructure adapters within that ownership boundary.

implementationIntroduction: Design the ownership model before choosing registration methods. Start with the entry point and logical operation, then register a graph whose lifetimes can only flow from shorter-lived consumers toward equally long or longer-lived dependencies.

implementationSteps.title: Identify the composition root
implementationSteps.description: Keep host creation and top-level feature registration in startup code. Move cohesive registrations into AddFeature extension methods without hiding runtime service resolution.

implementationSteps.title: Define real dependency boundaries
implementationSteps.description: Inject concrete classes by default and introduce interfaces for external adapters, multiple strategies, stable module contracts, or focused test substitution.

implementationSteps.title: Choose lifetimes from ownership
implementationSteps.description: Use singleton for thread-safe process-wide state, scoped for one request or operation, and transient for lightweight independent collaborators; include everything each service captures.

implementationSteps.title: Bind and validate configuration
implementationSteps.description: Register typed options, validate ranges and allowed values, and use ValidateOnStart when the process cannot work correctly with invalid configuration.

implementationSteps.title: Compose variants explicitly
implementationSteps.description: Use IEnumerable<T> for ordered pipelines, keyed services for named strategies, and factories when selection needs runtime data or controlled object creation.

implementationSteps.title: Create non-web scopes
implementationSteps.description: Inject IServiceScopeFactory into the worker or runner, open one async scope per message, job, batch, or command, resolve the scoped entry point, and dispose the scope.

implementationSteps.title: Validate and exercise the graph
implementationSteps.description: Enable ValidateOnBuild and ValidateScopes in development and tests, then resolve real entry points and test configuration, identity, disposal, and all keyed branches.

code.label: FulfillmentServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
code.introduction: The dedicated sample groups feature registrations, validates options, makes three lifetimes explicit, and registers named notification strategies with keyed services.

testing.introduction: Test the composition contract as well as individual service behavior. A unit test with manually constructed objects cannot prove registration completeness, keyed selection, scope isolation, or disposal.
items: Build a ServiceProvider with ValidateOnBuild and ValidateScopes enabled, then resolve each application entry point inside its intended scope.
Assert singleton identity across scopes, scoped identity within and across operations, and transient identity across resolutions.
Exercise every keyed service or IEnumerable<T> pipeline branch so missing registrations and wrong keys fail before production.
Verify option validation with missing, malformed, boundary, and valid values; start a Host when ValidateOnStart behavior is the contract.
Track disposal of scoped and transient resources on success, exception, and cancellation, and add integration tests where framework-created scopes matter.

security.introduction: DI controls construction, not trust. Registrations can accidentally broaden access, retain sensitive state, or select privileged implementations, so security boundaries must remain explicit and testable.
items: Do not inject a root IServiceProvider or broad service locator into domain and application code; it hides capabilities and makes authorization paths difficult to review.
Never store request identity, tokens, tenant data, or mutable user state in singleton services unless the data is isolated, bounded, and concurrency-safe.
Keep secrets in dedicated providers or options with restricted logging; avoid dumping option objects or complete service graphs into diagnostics.
Treat keyed or factory-selected implementations as policy decisions when variants have different privileges, networks, or data access, and test unauthorized selections.

Register authorization handlers and infrastructure clients with the documented framework lifetimes, but enforce authorization at the operation boundary rather than assuming injection grants permission.

performance.introduction: Resolution is normally small compared with I/O, but oversized graphs, expensive constructors, disposable transient capture, and unnecessary scopes can add startup time, allocation, memory retention, and contention.
items: Keep constructors cheap and side-effect free; defer network calls, database access, and expensive initialization to explicit asynchronous operations.
Do not register a service as singleton merely to avoid allocation; first prove thread safety, captured lifetime compatibility, state bounds, and measured value.
Watch for large numbers of disposable transient objects resolved from the root because the provider retains them until shutdown.
Prefer direct constructor dependencies over repeated provider lookups, reflection-driven activation, or nested factories in hot paths; measure with representative graphs.
Keep scopes aligned to meaningful operations rather than individual helper calls, and observe resolution failures, allocations, startup duration, and retained objects when diagnosing costs.

deployment.introduction: The graph can vary by environment, configuration, trimming, and hosting model. Validate the same registrations and published artifact that production will execute.
items: Run graph-validation and composition tests for each supported environment or feature combination; development-only registrations can hide production failures.
Fail deployment startup for invalid required options and expose readiness only after mandatory dependencies and initialization are usable.
Test reflection-based registration scanning under trimming or native AOT, heed analyzer warnings, and prefer explicit or source-generated registrations when discovery is fragile.
Ensure graceful shutdown disposes the root provider after hosted operations stop, and allow scoped asynchronous resources to finish or cancel within the shutdown budget.
Record ownership for externally managed clients, pools, and handles; avoid disposing objects that the container or a framework factory owns.

troubleshooting.symptom: A scoped service behaves like a singleton or leaks one user's state into another operation.
troubleshooting.cause: A singleton captured the scoped instance, the service was resolved from the root provider, or a background loop reused one scope.
troubleshooting.fix: Enable ValidateScopes, inject IServiceScopeFactory into the worker, create one scope per operation, and remove mutable request state from singletons.

troubleshooting.symptom: No service for type X has been registered or a constructor cannot be activated.
troubleshooting.cause: A feature registration was omitted, an implementation is inaccessible, or multiple constructors make activation ambiguous.
troubleshooting.fix: Resolve the real entry point in a ValidateOnBuild test, call the feature registration at the composition root, and keep one unambiguous public constructor.

troubleshooting.symptom: Configuration errors appear only on the first request.
troubleshooting.cause: Options were bound without validation or validation was deferred until IOptions.Value was first accessed.
troubleshooting.fix: Add semantic validators and ValidateOnStart, then test host startup with production-shaped configuration.

troubleshooting.symptom: Memory grows even though transient services should be short lived.
troubleshooting.cause: Disposable transients were resolved from the root, scopes were not disposed, or a singleton retained transient instances or unbounded state.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect ownership and heap roots, resolve disposable services in bounded scopes, dispose every scope, and replace accidental root resolution.

troubleshooting.symptom: The wrong keyed implementation is used or a runtime key fails.
troubleshooting.cause: String keys drifted between registration and resolution or selection policy was scattered across callers.
troubleshooting.fix: Centralize keys and selection, prefer typed enums or a focused dispatcher at the application boundary, and test every supported variant.

troubleshooting.symptom: A singleton fails intermittently under load.
troubleshooting.cause: The instance or one of its captured dependencies contains mutable non-thread-safe state.
troubleshooting.fix: Make shared state immutable or synchronized, change the lifetime to match ownership, and add concurrent tests plus runtime telemetry.

productionChecklist: The composition root is small, feature registrations are discoverable, and application or domain code does not use a global service locator.
Every service lifetime is justified by state, thread-safety, disposal, and the lifetimes of all captured dependencies.
Web requests use framework scopes and every worker, message, job, or console operation creates and disposes an explicit scope.
Required options are strongly typed, semantically validated, and fail startup when the application cannot operate safely.
All entry points, keyed services, multiple implementations, and environment-specific registration branches are covered by graph tests.
Container and framework-owned services have clear disposal ownership; disposable transients are not accumulated in the root provider.
Singletons contain no unbounded tenant or request state and are safe for concurrent use.
Published builds verify trimming or AOT assumptions, graceful shutdown, readiness, startup failure, and production configuration.
bestPractices: Keep one visible composition root and group cohesive registrations with feature-named extension methods.
Use constructor injection for required collaborators and avoid provider lookups in business code.
Inject abstractions at real replacement or infrastructure boundaries, not an interface for every class.
Choose lifetimes from ownership and thread-safety, including every dependency captured by the service.
Validate options on startup when invalid values make the application unsafe or unusable.
Create and dispose one scope per logical background operation; never reuse a request scope across concurrent work.
Enable provider validation in development and composition tests, then resolve real entry points and every variant.
Keep constructors cheap, avoid async work during resolution, and let the container dispose the objects it creates.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a captive dependency?
interviewQuestions.answer: It occurs when a longer-lived service, commonly a singleton, captures a shorter-lived dependency such as a scoped service and unintentionally extends its lifetime.

interviewQuestions.question: How do singleton, scoped, and transient lifetimes differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: Singleton reuses one root-owned instance, scoped reuses one instance per logical scope, and transient creates an instance for each resolution; disposal still follows the provider or scope that created it.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should a background worker create scopes?
interviewQuestions.answer: Hosted services are normally singleton, while operation services such as DbContext are scoped. One explicit scope per message or job preserves isolation and ensures timely disposal.

interviewQuestions.question: Is dependency injection the same as the dependency inversion principle?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. DI is a composition technique; dependency inversion is a design principle that high-level policy should depend on abstractions rather than low-level details.

interviewQuestions.question: When are keyed services appropriate?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use them when several implementations share a contract and selection is based on a stable key such as channel or tenant tier; centralize selection and test every supported key.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is injecting IServiceProvider often a smell?
interviewQuestions.answer: It hides required dependencies, defers failures to runtime, encourages service location, complicates tests, and can resolve services from the wrong ownership scope.

interviewQuestions.question: What does ValidateOnBuild not guarantee?
interviewQuestions.answer: It checks constructability for services it can validate, but it cannot prove semantic correctness, every runtime key or factory branch, thread safety, or production configuration.

note: The container is an application assembly mechanism and lifetime owner, not a global registry for domain code to query.
tip: Test the graph with ValidateOnBuild and ValidateScopes, then assert actual instance identity across two scopes; the dedicated sample makes those rules executable.
warning: Never inject a scoped service into a singleton or resolve it from the root provider. Create and dispose a scope for each well-defined background operation.
latestNote: Gold-standard DI guide with a dedicated lifetime and composition sample

name: ASP.NET Core
shortDescription: A high-performance, cross-platform framework for APIs, web apps, real-time systems, and services.
overview: ASP.NET Core is the cross-platform .NET framework for HTTP APIs, server-rendered applications, real-time systems, background-enabled web services, and cloud-native workloads.
detail: An ASP.NET Core application is a hosted process with configuration, logging, dependency injection, and an ordered HTTP middleware pipeline. Kestrel accepts a request, middleware applies cross-cutting behavior, routing selects an endpoint, and the endpoint coordinates application services before the response travels back through the pipeline. The framework supplies primitives for authentication, authorization, validation, problem details, rate limiting, caching, health checks, graceful shutdown, and telemetry, but teams must still choose clear boundaries and verify the complete runtime path.
learningObjectives: Explain how Kestrel, middleware, routing, endpoints, dependency injection, and application services collaborate for one HTTP request.
Build a small API that returns consistent success and problem-detail responses.
Place exception handling, correlation, rate limiting, and endpoint execution in an intentional order.
Separate liveness from readiness and propagate request cancellation to downstream work.
Verify routing, serialization, validation, middleware, and headers through end-to-end tests.
prerequisites: Comfort with C# types, records, asynchronous methods, and cancellation tokens.
The .NET 10 SDK and an editor or terminal capable of sending HTTP requests.
Basic HTTP knowledge: methods, routes, headers, status codes, and JSON bodies.

use: HTTP APIs, web applications, real-time hubs, backend-for-frontend services, and cloud-hosted .NET workloads.
Systems that benefit from built-in dependency injection, configuration, logging, security middleware, health checks, and test hosting.
Teams that want one programming model from a small minimal API to a structured controller-based application.
avoid: A simple scheduled or queue-driven process with no HTTP surface; use a Worker Service instead.
Static content that can be served directly from object storage or a CDN without an application process.
A requirement to hide unclear domain boundaries inside controllers or endpoint handlers; design the application model first.

concepts.title: Hosting and Kestrel
concepts.description: WebApplication composes configuration, logging, services, server startup, and lifetime while Kestrel accepts HTTP connections.

concepts.title: Middleware pipeline
concepts.description: Ordered components can inspect, enrich, reject, short-circuit, or pass requests to the next component and then observe the response.

concepts.title: Routing and endpoints
concepts.description: Endpoint routing matches method, path, constraints, and metadata to minimal API handlers, controllers, Razor pages, hubs, or health checks.

concepts.title: Dependency injection
concepts.description: The built-in container creates endpoint and service dependencies with singleton, scoped, or transient ownership.

concepts.title: HTTP contracts
concepts.description: Status codes, headers, JSON shapes, validation responses, and problem details form the observable contract clients depend on.

concepts.title: Operational middleware
concepts.description: Exception handling, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, caching, health checks, and telemetry belong in the runtime design, not as afterthoughts.

architecture.description: A request enters Kestrel, receives cross-cutting policy in middleware, is matched by routing, reaches a feature endpoint, and coordinates an application boundary before the response returns through the same pipeline.

implementationSteps.title: Create the host
implementationSteps.description: Use WebApplication.CreateBuilder to load configuration, logging, environment information, and the dependency-injection container.

implementationSteps.title: Register capabilities
implementationSteps.description: Add problem details, repositories, health checks, rate limiting, options, and other dependencies before building the application.

implementationSteps.title: Compose middleware
implementationSteps.description: Order exception handling, correlation, security, rate limiting, caching, and routing based on which requests and responses each component must observe.

implementationSteps.title: Map feature endpoints
implementationSteps.description: Group related routes, attach metadata and policies, validate boundary input, call application services, and translate outcomes into HTTP responses.

implementationSteps.title: Propagate cancellation
implementationSteps.description: Pass the request CancellationToken into database, messaging, and outbound HTTP work so disconnected requests do not waste resources.

implementationSteps.title: Expose health signals
implementationSteps.description: Keep liveness focused on the process and readiness focused on dependencies required to serve traffic.

implementationSteps.title: Test through HTTP
implementationSteps.description: Use WebApplicationFactory to exercise the real middleware, routing, serialization, validation, and response contract.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: The dedicated sample keeps startup readable while registering problem details, health checks, rate limiting, correlation, and a feature-oriented product endpoint group.

testing.introduction: Unit tests are useful for domain rules, but an HTTP application also needs integration tests that prove framework configuration works together.
items: Create the application with WebApplicationFactory so tests use the real service registrations and middleware pipeline.
Test successful and failed routes, JSON serialization, validation problem details, headers, and status codes.
Avoid assertions that depend on test execution order or shared mutable state.
Keep live external-service tests behind an explicit opt-in flag; normal tests should remain deterministic.

security.introduction: Security depends on middleware order, endpoint metadata, trusted proxy configuration, and safe boundary handling.
items: Authenticate before authorization and require policies on route groups or endpoints instead of relying on UI visibility.
Validate and normalize all boundary input; never bind persistence entities directly as public contracts.
Configure forwarded headers only for known proxies and do not trust arbitrary client identity headers.
Limit request sizes, protect secrets with environment-specific providers, and return safe problem details without stack traces.

performance.introduction: ASP.NET Core is efficient by default, but application throughput is usually constrained by blocking I/O, unbounded work, serialization, databases, or downstream services.
items: Use asynchronous APIs for I/O and pass cancellation tokens throughout the call chain.
Bound request bodies, query results, queues, concurrency, retries, and outbound timeouts.
Measure with metrics and traces before optimizing allocations or switching serializers.
Use output caching only for responses whose identity, authorization, and invalidation rules are explicit.

deployment.introduction: A deployable API needs more than a successful local build.
items: Publish for the target OS and architecture, run containers as non-root, and scan dependencies and images in CI.
Terminate TLS at a trusted boundary and configure reverse-proxy headers, host filtering, and HTTPS behavior consistently.
Export structured logs, metrics, and traces with correlation across inbound and outbound calls.
Handle graceful shutdown, readiness changes, configuration validation, and database migrations as deliberate operational workflows.

troubleshooting.cause: The route, HTTP method, constraint, base path, or endpoint registration does not match the request.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the mapped endpoint pattern and test the exact URL and method through WebApplicationFactory or an HTTP file.

troubleshooting.cause: Authentication did not establish an identity, a policy requirement failed, or middleware is ordered incorrectly.
troubleshooting.fix: Separate authentication from authorization, inspect claims, and integration-test the endpoint metadata and middleware order.

troubleshooting.cause: Blocking calls, missing timeouts, unbounded concurrency, thread-pool starvation, or a slow downstream dependency is consuming request capacity.
troubleshooting.fix: Capture traces and runtime metrics, remove sync-over-async calls, add timeouts and bounds, and load-test the real dependency path.

troubleshooting.symptom: The service is healthy but cannot serve traffic.
troubleshooting.cause: A single health endpoint reports process health without checking required dependencies.
troubleshooting.fix: Use separate liveness and readiness checks and make readiness fail when a required dependency is unavailable.

bestPractices: Keep the composition root readable and registrations close to their feature boundaries.
Keep middleware order explicit and cover security-sensitive ordering with integration tests.
Return consistent problem details for failures instead of ad hoc error shapes.
Propagate request cancellation to database and outbound HTTP operations.
Expose separate liveness and readiness checks when orchestration depends on them.
Keep business rules outside HttpContext-dependent code so they remain fast to test.
productionChecklist: Configuration is validated on startup and secrets are not stored in source control.
Authentication, authorization, CORS, forwarded headers, and rate limits match the deployment boundary.
Errors use safe problem details and logs contain correlation without sensitive payloads.
Liveness and readiness have distinct meanings and are tested during dependency failure.
Outbound calls have timeouts, resilience policies, cancellation, and telemetry.
Integration tests cover critical routes and the published artifact is smoke-tested in CI.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does middleware order matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each middleware wraps the next component. Ordering changes which requests it sees and whether authentication, authorization, exceptions, and endpoints behave correctly.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Kestrel?
interviewQuestions.answer: Kestrel is ASP.NET Core's cross-platform web server. It can be internet-facing or run behind a reverse proxy depending on the deployment.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose controllers over minimal APIs?
interviewQuestions.answer: Controllers are useful when conventions, filters, model-binding customization, and a structured large API surface outweigh minimal APIs' compact vertical-slice style.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between liveness and readiness?
interviewQuestions.answer: Liveness answers whether the process should be restarted. Readiness answers whether this instance currently has the dependencies and state required to receive traffic.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use WebApplicationFactory instead of testing handlers directly?
interviewQuestions.answer: Handler tests do not prove route matching, middleware order, dependency registration, serialization, filters, or headers. WebApplicationFactory exercises those behaviors through the in-memory HTTP server.

note: Treat the HTTP layer as an adapter. Business rules should remain testable without constructing HTTP contexts.
tip: Use WebApplicationFactory integration tests to verify routing, filters, serialization, authentication, and middleware together.
warning: A health endpoint that always returns success can cause an orchestrator to route traffic to an application that cannot serve real requests.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated runnable sample

name: Entity Framework Core
shortDescription: An object-relational mapper for expressive data access, change tracking, migrations, and transactions.
overview: Entity Framework Core is the modern .NET object-relational mapper for translating LINQ into database commands, mapping domain state to relational schemas, coordinating units of work, and evolving schemas through reviewed migrations.
detail: Entity Framework Core sits between application code and a database provider, but it does not remove the need to understand relational design or SQL. A short-lived DbContext holds model metadata, a database connection strategy, query composition, change tracking, transactions, and SaveChanges behavior. Providers translate expression trees into database-specific SQL, so the same LINQ can behave differently across SQLite, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or another provider. Production-ready use requires intentional mappings and constraints, bounded projections, query inspection, optimistic concurrency, migration discipline, provider-realistic tests, and operational ownership of schema deployment.
learningObjectives: Explain the roles of DbContext, the model, providers, change tracking, SaveChanges, and the underlying database.
Map aggregates with keys, relationships, owned types, conversions, indexes, constraints, and concurrency tokens.
Shape efficient read models with projection, AsNoTracking, bounded pagination, query tags, and generated-SQL inspection.
Coordinate atomic writes with transactions while allowing database constraints to protect invariants.
Create, review, test, script, and deploy migrations as versioned production artifacts.
Test important behavior against SQLite and the real production provider without relying on EF Core's in-memory substitute.
prerequisites: Comfort with C#, LINQ, asynchronous methods, cancellation tokens, and dependency injection.
Basic relational concepts including tables, primary and foreign keys, indexes, joins, constraints, and transactions.
The .NET 10 SDK; Docker Desktop is optional for the PostgreSQL/Testcontainers verification path.

use: Transactional .NET applications that benefit from strongly typed LINQ, unit-of-work change tracking, relationship mapping, and managed schema evolution.
Teams that want most CRUD and aggregate persistence expressed in C# while retaining access to SQL, transactions, interceptors, and provider-specific features.
Workloads where developers will inspect generated SQL, measure important queries, and treat migrations and database constraints as first-class engineering artifacts.
avoid: A read-heavy path requiring tightly controlled hand-written SQL or specialized database features for nearly every query; Dapper or the provider API may be clearer.
Bulk ingestion, analytical processing, or set-based maintenance where database-native commands and bulk tooling are the primary abstraction.
A design that assumes one LINQ query is portable and equally efficient across all providers without provider-specific verification.

concepts.title: DbContext lifetime
concepts.description: A DbContext is a short-lived unit of work that coordinates queries, tracked state, transactions, and persistence; it is not thread-safe.

concepts.title: Model and Fluent API
concepts.description: Entity configuration maps CLR types to keys, columns, conversions, relationships, owned values, indexes, constraints, and concurrency behavior.

concepts.title: Query translation
concepts.description: The provider translates a composable LINQ expression tree into database-specific commands; translation and performance must be verified.

concepts.title: Change tracking
concepts.description: Snapshots and entity states let SaveChanges calculate inserts, updates, and deletes, while no-tracking queries avoid that cost for read models.

concepts.title: Transactions and constraints
concepts.description: SaveChanges is transactional for one batch, explicit transactions span multiple operations, and database constraints remain the final consistency boundary.

concepts.title: Optimistic concurrency
concepts.description: A concurrency token participates in an update predicate so stale writers fail instead of silently overwriting newer state.

concepts.title: Migrations
concepts.description: Versioned schema operations capture model changes for review, testing, scripting, deployment, and rollback planning.

concepts.title: Provider behavior
concepts.description: SQLite, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and other providers differ in types, SQL translation, locking, migrations, functions, and operational capabilities.

architecture.description: Application commands and queries use a short-lived DbContext. EF Core applies model metadata and provider translation to execute parameterized SQL inside database transactions, then materializes results or reconciles tracked changes.

implementationSteps.title: Choose the provider deliberately
implementationSteps.description: Install the provider for the production database and keep provider versions compatible with the EF Core runtime.

implementationSteps.title: Define aggregate boundaries
implementationSteps.description: Model entities and value objects around business invariants before persistence configuration leaks into every domain type.

implementationSteps.title: Configure the relational model
implementationSteps.description: Use IEntityTypeConfiguration classes for keys, relationships, owned types, lengths, precision, conversions, indexes, constraints, and delete behavior.

implementationSteps.title: Shape read queries
implementationSteps.description: Filter, order, project, and bound results in the database; use AsNoTracking when the unit of work will not modify returned entities.

implementationSteps.title: Protect write workflows
implementationSteps.description: Use database constraints, explicit transactions when one SaveChanges is insufficient, and concurrency tokens for competing writers.

implementationSteps.title: Create and review migrations
implementationSteps.description: Generate a migration, inspect every operation, test it on representative data, and create an idempotent script or migration bundle for deployment.

implementationSteps.title: Verify real providers
implementationSteps.description: Use fast relational tests locally and container-backed tests for behaviors whose types, SQL, locking, or migrations depend on the production provider.

code.label: OrderQueries.cs
code.introduction: The dedicated sample projects a bounded read model in SQL, disables tracking, tags the query for diagnostics, and keeps cancellation explicit.
code.code:
return await db.Orders
    .TagWith("Open order summaries")
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(order => order.Status == OrderStatus.Placed)
    .OrderByDescending(order => order.CreatedAtUtc)
    .ThenBy(order => order.Id)
    .Select(order => new OrderSummary(
        order.Id,
        order.CreatedAtUtc,
        order.Customer.Name,
        order.Items.Count,
        order.Items.Sum(item => item.UnitPrice * item.Quantity)))
    .Skip(page * pageSize)
    .Take(pageSize)
    .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);

testing.introduction: EF Core tests should prove relational behavior, not just exercise LINQ against an in-memory collection.
items: Use SQLite or another relational provider for fast tests that need migrations, foreign keys, unique constraints, transactions, and concurrency behavior.
Avoid the EF Core in-memory provider when relational translation or constraints are part of the requirement.
Run focused Testcontainers tests against the production provider for provider-specific SQL, types, locking, migrations, and functions.
Assert observable outcomes and important SQL shape without coupling every test to incidental generated text.
Keep external provider tests explicit and deterministic so a missing Docker engine is reported honestly rather than causing mysterious failures.

security.introduction: An ORM reduces repetitive SQL construction but does not make data access automatically safe.
items: Prefer LINQ parameters, ExecuteSqlInterpolated, or provider parameters; never concatenate untrusted values into raw SQL.
Store connection strings in environment-specific secret providers and use a least-privilege database identity per workload.
Do not enable sensitive-data logging in production because parameter values and personal data can enter logs.
Bound queries and command timeouts to reduce resource-exhaustion risk, and authorize access before constructing tenant or resource queries.
Review migration permissions separately from runtime permissions; an application account rarely needs schema-owner rights.

performance.introduction: The dominant EF Core cost is usually database work and data shape, not the ORM call itself.
items: Project only required columns, bound every list, and choose pagination that remains efficient at the expected depth.
Use AsNoTracking for read-only materialization and compiled queries only after measurement shows compilation overhead matters.
Prevent N+1 queries by projecting related values or loading relationships intentionally; do not add Include automatically.
Inspect ToQueryString output, database query plans, row counts, round trips, indexes, and telemetry for critical paths.
Batch writes where appropriate and use provider-native bulk operations when change tracking is the wrong tool for the volume.

deployment.introduction: Schema evolution is an operational workflow with availability, compatibility, backup, and rollback consequences.
items: Review generated migrations and test them against production-like schema size and data before release.
Deploy provider-supported scripts or migration bundles from one controlled job rather than racing migrations across application instances.
Use expand-and-contract changes when old and new application versions may run concurrently during rollout.
Back up data, define rollback or forward-fix procedures, monitor locks and duration, and separate provider-specific migration sets when supporting multiple databases.
Pin and audit EF Core, provider, native database, and migration-tool dependencies as one compatible release set.

troubleshooting.symptom: A LINQ query throws a translation exception.
troubleshooting.cause: The expression contains a .NET method or shape the selected provider cannot translate.
troubleshooting.fix: Rewrite the query using supported expressions, split database and in-memory work at an intentional bounded point, and inspect generated SQL.

troubleshooting.symptom: A page is slow or sends many database commands.
troubleshooting.cause: The query loads too many columns or rows, uses offset pagination deeply, lacks an index, or triggers N+1 relationship loading.
troubleshooting.fix: Capture command telemetry, project the exact read model, bound results, inspect the plan, add the right index, and remove accidental per-row queries.

troubleshooting.cause: Another writer changed or deleted a row after this context loaded its concurrency token.
troubleshooting.fix: Reload current values and apply a documented retry, merge, or conflict response; do not blindly overwrite the winner.

troubleshooting.symptom: A migration works locally but fails in production.
troubleshooting.cause: Production has different provider behavior, data volume, locks, permissions, schema history, or incompatible application versions.
troubleshooting.fix: Test the generated artifact on a production-like copy, use expand-and-contract changes, validate migration history, and deploy from a controlled identity.

troubleshooting.symptom: A DbContext reports disposed or concurrent-operation errors.
troubleshooting.cause: The context escaped its unit of work, was shared across threads, or a query was not awaited before another operation started.
troubleshooting.fix: Create one short-lived context per unit of work, await each operation, and use IDbContextFactory for parallel or background flows.

bestPractices: Keep DbContext short-lived and never share one instance across concurrent operations.
Use explicit Fluent API mappings and database constraints for important invariants.
Project bounded read models and use AsNoTracking when updates are not required.
Inspect generated SQL and database plans for critical queries instead of reasoning from LINQ alone.
Use concurrency tokens and handle conflicts as an application outcome.
Review and test migrations as production code, deploying them through one controlled workflow.
Test provider-specific behavior against the real provider and keep separate migrations when providers diverge.
Pass cancellation tokens and configure realistic command timeouts for database work.
productionChecklist: EF Core runtime, database provider, native dependencies, and migration tool are pinned to compatible audited versions.
Connection strings come from a secret provider and runtime identities have least-privilege permissions.
Critical mappings include deliberate lengths, precision, indexes, constraints, delete behavior, and concurrency tokens.
Important queries are projected, bounded, observable, cancellation-aware, and verified with generated SQL and query plans.
N+1 risks, deep pagination, large writes, transaction boundaries, retries, and command timeouts are tested under realistic load.
Migrations are reviewed, tested on representative data, backed by recovery procedures, and deployed once through a controlled job.
Provider-realistic integration tests cover schema, constraints, translation, and concurrency without depending on shared developer databases.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the recommended DbContext lifetime in a web application?
interviewQuestions.answer: Scoped is the common default because it aligns a context with one request or unit of work. A context is not thread-safe and should not be shared across concurrent operations.

interviewQuestions.question: What causes the N+1 query problem?
interviewQuestions.answer: The application first loads a set of parent rows and then issues another query for each parent's related data, often through repeated explicit or lazy loading.

interviewQuestions.question: When should AsNoTracking be used?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use it for read-only materialization when entities will not be changed in the current unit of work. Projection to a DTO often avoids entity tracking entirely.

interviewQuestions.question: How does optimistic concurrency work in EF Core?
interviewQuestions.answer: A configured token is included in the update or delete predicate. If no row matches the original token, EF Core throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException so the application can resolve the conflict.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should migrations not automatically run from every production application instance?
interviewQuestions.answer: Concurrent instances can race, application identities gain excessive schema permissions, and long migrations can block startup or traffic. A controlled deployment job provides clearer ownership and recovery.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can the same LINQ query behave differently across providers?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each provider owns translation, type mapping, functions, SQL generation, and database capabilities. Portability must be verified rather than assumed.

note: LINQ is an expression for a provider to translate. Code that looks cheap in C# can still produce expensive SQL, excessive rows, or unsupported operations.
tip: Use TagWith and ToQueryString during investigation, then correlate the command with database plans, row counts, duration, and application traces.
warning: Do not share a DbContext across threads or allow every production instance to race schema migrations during startup.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated relational sample

name: Blazor
shortDescription: Build accessible component-based web applications with Razor, C#, and deliberate static, server, or WebAssembly rendering.
