overview: Blazor is the ASP.NET Core component framework for building web interfaces with Razor markup, C#, dependency injection, routing, forms, validation, and browser integration.
detail: A modern Blazor Web App can render static HTML on the server, attach interactive components through a server-side SignalR circuit, download a WebAssembly runtime for client execution, or use automatic mode to move eligible components to the client after the runtime is available. Rendering and interactivity are separate decisions: server-side rendering can produce useful HTML without a persistent circuit, while an interactive component owns event handlers and mutable state after hydration. Production design therefore starts with the user experience and hosting boundary, not with a favorite render mode. Teams must account for first load, network latency, connection loss, browser-visible code and configuration, server memory per circuit, serialization across boundaries, enhanced navigation, accessibility, cancellation, and deployment topology. Components should remain presentation-focused; business rules, data access, and external calls belong in injected services with explicit lifetimes. A reliable application also handles prerendering twice-run lifecycle work, persistent component state, form validation, antiforgery, authorization at the server boundary, JavaScript module disposal, reconnect experiences, observability, and end-to-end testing of the actual selected render mode.
learningObjectives: Explain static server rendering, interactive server, interactive WebAssembly, and automatic render modes and choose between them from measurable constraints.
Build focused Razor components with parameters, events, routing, layouts, lifecycle methods, dependency injection, and accessible markup.
Manage per-user state without leaking data across server circuits or assuming that client state is trusted.
Handle prerendering, reconnection, cancellation, forms, validation, and JavaScript interop across component lifecycle boundaries.
Test services, components, rendered HTTP output, and browser interactivity at the appropriate layers.
Deploy and observe Blazor applications with the capacity, security, caching, and routing requirements of the selected render mode.
prerequisites: Comfort with C#, asynchronous programming, dependency injection, and ASP.NET Core hosting.
Basic HTML, CSS, HTTP, browser security, and accessibility knowledge.
The .NET 10 SDK and a modern browser for running the dedicated sample.

use: Teams want a component model shared with .NET services and can benefit from C# types, validation, dependency injection, and tooling across the UI boundary.
The application needs server-rendered HTML with optional per-component interactivity instead of a mandatory full single-page application download.
Interactive server suits controlled connectivity and fast startup, or WebAssembly suits client execution, offline scenarios, and reduced per-user server UI state.
avoid: A mostly static site needs only HTML and a small amount of progressive JavaScript; static generation may be simpler and cheaper.
The team depends heavily on a JavaScript ecosystem or client platform that has no practical .NET/browser integration path.
Interactive server is being chosen for high-latency or intermittently connected users without capacity tests, reconnect design, and circuit-aware state management.

concepts.title: Razor components
concepts.description: Reusable UI units combine parameters, child content, markup, event callbacks, local state, and lifecycle behavior behind a typed contract.

concepts.title: Static server rendering
concepts.description: The server renders HTML per request without attaching event handlers or retaining a UI circuit, which is ideal for content-first pages and forms.

concepts.title: Interactive server
concepts.description: Component code executes on the server and UI diffs travel over a SignalR circuit, enabling a small download but requiring connectivity and per-circuit capacity.

concepts.title: Interactive WebAssembly
concepts.description: Component assemblies and a .NET runtime execute in the browser, improving client autonomy while increasing download size and exposing all client-delivered code.

concepts.title: Automatic interactivity
concepts.description: Auto mode starts eligible components on the server and uses WebAssembly on later visits after the client bundle is available; both execution locations must be valid.

concepts.title: Prerendering and hydration
concepts.description: Interactive components can first emit server HTML and later become interactive, so initialization may run in different environments or more than once.

concepts.title: Lifecycle and disposal
concepts.description: OnInitialized, OnParametersSet, OnAfterRender, disposal, cancellation, and JS module cleanup define when work and browser access are safe.

concepts.title: State ownership
concepts.description: Local fields, scoped services, persistent component state, URLs, and durable stores serve different lifetimes; client or circuit state never replaces authorization.

concepts.title: Forms and validation
concepts.description: EditForm, EditContext, data annotations, custom validators, antiforgery, and server validation create a complete input boundary.

concepts.title: JavaScript interop
concepts.description: Isolated ES modules bridge browser-only APIs; calls must respect rendering, disconnection, serialization, and disposal constraints.

architecture.description: A request produces server-rendered HTML, then an optional render-mode runtime attaches interactivity. Components coordinate UI state while application services enforce trusted rules and access durable systems.

implementationIntroduction: Start with a useful server-rendered page, then add interactivity only where events or client state improve the experience. Keep trusted behavior behind services and make execution location explicit.

implementationSteps.title: Choose a render boundary
implementationSteps.description: Document first-load, SEO, latency, offline, security, hosting, and capacity needs; select static, server, WebAssembly, or auto per page or component.

implementationSteps.title: Compose the application
implementationSteps.description: Register Razor components, the required interactive render modes, application services, options, authentication, authorization, antiforgery, and telemetry in Program.cs.

implementationSteps.title: Build focused components
implementationSteps.description: Use typed parameters and EventCallback, stable @key values, semantic HTML, keyboard support, clear loading and failure states, and business services outside the component.

implementationSteps.title: Own state deliberately
implementationSteps.description: Keep transient UI state local, use scoped services for circuit or client-session state, persist only what must survive reloads, and never trust state for authorization decisions.

implementationSteps.title: Handle lifecycle boundaries
implementationSteps.description: Make initialization idempotent, persist expensive prerendered state when appropriate, start JS interop after rendering, cancel outstanding work, and dispose subscriptions and modules.

implementationSteps.title: Validate every input
implementationSteps.description: Use EditForm and EditContext for feedback, enforce antiforgery on server form posts, repeat validation and authorization on trusted server endpoints, and display safe errors.

implementationSteps.title: Verify the selected runtime
implementationSteps.description: Unit-test services, component-test rendering and events, integration-test SSR and routes, and browser-test hydration, reconnect, navigation, accessibility, and deployment paths.

code.label: Home.razor
code.introduction: The dedicated sample prerenders an accessible product catalog and adds server interactivity for a scoped per-circuit cart without moving business behavior into the page.

testing.introduction: Blazor needs layered tests because service correctness, rendered markup, component events, server routing, hydration, and browser behavior fail in different ways.
items: Unit-test state containers and application services without a renderer, including isolation, limits, cancellation, and deterministic outcomes.
Use a component test library when event handling, parameters, cascading values, validation messages, or rendered fragments need fast coverage.
Use WebApplicationFactory to verify server-rendered routes, status codes, HTML, security headers, dependency registration, and error handling.
Use Playwright or an equivalent browser runner for actual render-mode startup, enhanced navigation, JS interop, reconnect, keyboard flows, and accessibility checks.

security.introduction: Browser-delivered UI is never a trusted authorization boundary, regardless of whether the component was rendered on the server or in WebAssembly.
items: Enforce authentication and resource authorization in server endpoints and services; AuthorizeView only controls presentation.
Never ship secrets in WebAssembly assemblies, JavaScript, HTML, or public configuration because users can inspect all downloaded assets.
Protect server form posts with antiforgery, validate uploads and inputs, encode output, and avoid rendering untrusted MarkupString content.
Treat circuit state, browser storage, route values, and JS interop results as untrusted input and prevent one user's scoped state from becoming singleton state.

performance.introduction: Performance depends on the selected execution model: server interactivity consumes connection and circuit resources, while WebAssembly pays download and client startup costs.
items: Keep component subtrees small, use @key for changing collections, avoid unnecessary StateHasChanged calls, and virtualize genuinely large lists.
Measure circuit memory, concurrent connections, event latency, reconnect rates, and backplane requirements for interactive server deployments.
For WebAssembly, trim and compress published assets, lazy-load optional assemblies, cache immutable files, and measure startup on realistic devices and networks.
Avoid duplicate prerender and hydration data loads by caching or persisting safe state, and cancel obsolete work when parameters or navigation change.

deployment.introduction: The hosting topology must match the render mode and preserve correct asset, routing, connection, and security behavior.
items: Publish and smoke-test the exact artifact behind its real reverse proxy, base path, HTTPS termination, forwarded headers, compression, and cache policy.
For interactive server, configure WebSocket support, connection timeouts, capacity limits, graceful shutdown, and sticky sessions or a scale-out design where required.
For WebAssembly, serve framework assets with correct content types, compression, immutable caching, integrity expectations, and an API configured for its true origin.
Capture structured logs, traces, circuit events, HTTP metrics, client error signals, and deployment version information without recording sensitive UI data.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page renders but buttons do nothing.
troubleshooting.cause: The component is static SSR, the interactive render mode was not registered, or the Blazor boot script failed to load.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm @rendermode, AddInteractiveServerComponents or AddInteractiveWebAssemblyComponents, endpoint render-mode mapping, and browser console/network output.

troubleshooting.symptom: Initialization or an API call runs twice.
troubleshooting.cause: Prerendering created server HTML and the interactive instance initialized again during hydration.
troubleshooting.fix: Make initialization idempotent, persist safe prerendered state, or disable prerendering only when the user-experience tradeoff is intentional.

troubleshooting.cause: Browser interop was attempted while the component was prerendering or before its element existed.
troubleshooting.fix: Call DOM-dependent interop from OnAfterRenderAsync after checking firstRender and dispose imported modules safely.

troubleshooting.symptom: One user can see another user's UI state.
troubleshooting.cause: Per-user mutable data was placed in a singleton or static object in an interactive server application.
troubleshooting.fix: Move circuit state to a scoped service, remove static mutable state, and enforce authorization again at the server resource boundary.

troubleshooting.symptom: Interactive server users disconnect under load.
troubleshooting.cause: WebSockets, proxy timeouts, server capacity, long-running event handlers, or scale-out routing do not support the circuit workload.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect circuit and SignalR telemetry, test the proxy path, bound work, capacity-test memory and connections, and configure the deployment topology.

troubleshooting.symptom: A WebAssembly publish loads locally but fails in production.
troubleshooting.cause: The base path, fallback routing, content types, compressed assets, cache policy, or API origin differs from local hosting.
troubleshooting.fix: Test the published output behind the real host, verify framework asset responses and base href, and configure fallback routes and CORS intentionally.

bestPractices: Choose render mode per component from user experience, security, connectivity, hosting, and capacity constraints.
Keep components focused and move business rules, persistence, and external I/O into injected application services.
Use semantic HTML, visible focus, labels, live regions, keyboard support, and automated plus manual accessibility testing.
Use stable @key values for changing lists and cancel obsolete asynchronous work when parameters change or components dispose.
Design loading, empty, failure, reconnecting, unauthorized, and offline states as first-class UI.
Keep JS interop small, module-based, asynchronous, lifecycle-aware, and covered by real-browser tests.
Treat browser and circuit state as replaceable UI state, never as proof that a user may access a resource.
Measure the published application on realistic networks and devices before changing rendering or optimization strategy.
productionChecklist: Each page and component has a documented render mode and a reason tied to measurable constraints.
Server authorization protects every resource and no secret is shipped to browser-visible assets or configuration.
Prerendering, hydration, enhanced navigation, direct URL loading, reconnect, and browser refresh are tested.
Forms provide accessible validation, repeat validation on the server, and use antiforgery where required.
Scoped state cannot leak between users; subscriptions, timers, cancellation sources, and JS modules are disposed.
Interactive server capacity, WebSocket/proxy behavior, graceful shutdown, and scale-out assumptions are load-tested.
WebAssembly assets use correct compression, content types, base paths, caching, and API-origin configuration.
Logs, traces, metrics, circuit signals, client errors, health checks, and deployment smoke tests cover the real hosting path.

interviewQuestions.question: How do static SSR and interactive server rendering differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: Static SSR produces HTML per request without retaining component event state. Interactive server keeps component state on the server and sends UI events and render diffs over a SignalR circuit.

interviewQuestions.question: How do server and WebAssembly interactivity differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: Server interactivity executes component code on the server with a small initial client but depends on a live circuit. WebAssembly downloads runtime and application assets and executes components in the browser.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can initialization run twice?
interviewQuestions.answer: An interactive component may run once to prerender HTML on the server and again when the interactive instance starts. Initialization must be idempotent or use persistent state.

interviewQuestions.question: What triggers a component render?
interviewQuestions.answer: Parameter updates, handled events, cascading value changes, and explicit StateHasChanged calls can schedule a render; the renderer computes and applies a UI diff.

interviewQuestions.question: What does scoped lifetime mean in interactive server Blazor?
interviewQuestions.answer: A scoped service normally lives for the user's circuit rather than for one HTTP request. Mutable user state belongs there, never in a singleton shared across circuits.

interviewQuestions.question: Is AuthorizeView an authorization control?
interviewQuestions.answer: It controls which UI fragment is shown but does not secure the underlying resource. The server API or application service must enforce authorization.

interviewQuestions.question: When is JavaScript interop appropriate?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use it for browser capabilities or JavaScript libraries without a practical .NET abstraction, keeping the boundary small, asynchronous, module-isolated, lifecycle-aware, and disposable.

note: Rendering and interactivity are separate decisions. A page can return useful server-rendered HTML without owning a server circuit or downloading a WebAssembly runtime.
tip: Test direct navigation, hydration, reconnect, refresh, slow networks, and browser back/forward behavior through the same proxy path users will reach.
warning: Never rely on hidden UI or browser-held state for authorization, and never place trusted secrets in WebAssembly code or browser-delivered configuration.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated interactive catalog sample

name: Minimal APIs
shortDescription: Design production HTTP APIs with explicit routes, binding, typed results, filters, OpenAPI, security, tests, and operational limits.
overview: Minimal APIs are ASP.NET Core's streamlined model for HTTP APIs. They remove controller ceremony while retaining the full hosting, routing, dependency injection, configuration, authentication, authorization, diagnostics, rate limiting, OpenAPI, and testing stack.
detail: A Minimal API is minimal in syntax, not in engineering responsibility. Route handlers combine an HTTP method and route pattern with parameter binding and a return contract. The framework can bind values from routes, query strings, headers, JSON bodies, forms, services, and custom binders, while route constraints decide which endpoint is eligible before binding occurs. Route groups let a feature share a prefix, tags, authorization, filters, and rate limits without repeating metadata. TypedResults and Results<T1, T2> make success and failure shapes visible to the compiler and OpenAPI generator. Endpoint filters can validate, observe, or short-circuit selected handlers, but cross-cutting behavior that applies to the whole request pipeline still belongs in middleware. A production design keeps handlers thin, uses dedicated request and response contracts, validates every untrusted boundary, attaches stable endpoint names and metadata, enforces authorization on the server, bounds expensive work, emits safe Problem Details, and verifies behavior through the real HTTP pipeline. Minimal APIs can support large systems when features own their endpoint mapping and application logic; a single growing Program.cs file is an organization failure, not a framework limit.
learningObjectives: Choose Minimal APIs or controllers from API requirements, team conventions, and extension needs rather than endpoint count alone.
Understand route matching, parameter binding precedence, constraints, services, cancellation, and malformed-input behavior.
Organize endpoints by cohesive feature with route groups, endpoint names, tags, policies, filters, and rate limits.
Model explicit success and failure contracts with TypedResults, Results unions, Problem Details, and OpenAPI metadata.
Keep validation, authorization, persistence, and business rules at the correct boundary instead of accumulating logic in handlers.
Test handlers where useful and integration-test routing, JSON, metadata, authentication, authorization, and errors through HTTP.
Deploy Minimal APIs with bounded resources, observability, secure proxy configuration, dependency auditing, and graceful shutdown.
prerequisites: Comfort with C# records, nullable reference types, asynchronous code, and cancellation tokens.
Basic HTTP knowledge: methods, routes, headers, status codes, content types, caching, and idempotency.
Familiarity with ASP.NET Core hosting, dependency injection, configuration, logging, and middleware.
A .NET 10 SDK for running the dedicated sample and its tests.
Awareness that authentication proves identity while authorization decides whether that identity may perform an action.

use: New ASP.NET Core HTTP APIs where concise endpoint definitions and direct control of route metadata are useful.
Vertical-slice or feature-folder designs where each capability maps its own routes and delegates to application services.
Small services, backend-for-frontend APIs, internal APIs, and larger systems whose teams agree on endpoint conventions.
Native AOT or trimming-oriented API workloads after verifying every dependency supports the chosen publishing model.
avoid: A UI-rendering application where Razor Pages, MVC views, or Blazor is the primary interaction model.
A team that depends heavily on controller-specific filters, conventions, model-binding extensions, or existing controller tooling and would gain little from migration.
A design whose domain and application boundaries are still unclear; fewer framework types do not replace use cases, contracts, or ownership.
Protocol requirements better served by gRPC, SignalR, messaging, or a worker without an HTTP endpoint surface.

concepts.title: Route matching and constraints
concepts.description: HTTP method, route pattern, precedence, and constraints select an endpoint. Constraints disambiguate routes; validation explains why a matched value is unacceptable.

concepts.title: Parameter binding
concepts.description: Handler parameters can come from routes, queries, headers, bodies, forms, services, HttpContext, claims, cancellation, or custom TryParse and BindAsync patterns.

concepts.title: Route handlers
concepts.description: Lambdas or named methods receive bound values and collaborators, invoke one use case, and translate its outcome into an HTTP response.

concepts.title: Route groups
concepts.description: MapGroup creates a feature boundary that shares prefixes and metadata such as tags, authorization policies, filters, and rate limits.

concepts.title: Typed results
concepts.description: TypedResults returns concrete HttpResults types, while Results<T1, T2> declares the finite response alternatives and improves compile-time checks and OpenAPI output.

concepts.title: Errors and Problem Details
concepts.description: Expected failures map to deliberate 4xx results; unexpected exceptions flow through centralized handling that returns safe RFC-style problem responses with correlation.

concepts.title: Endpoint filters
concepts.description: Filters wrap selected handlers to inspect arguments, validate input, add feature-level observations, or short-circuit execution; global pipeline concerns remain middleware.

concepts.title: Endpoint metadata and OpenAPI
concepts.description: Stable names, tags, summaries, parameter descriptions, response types, authorization, and exclusion metadata form the contract used by link generation, tooling, and documentation.

concepts.title: Authentication and authorization
concepts.description: Authentication handlers establish a principal; policies attached to groups or endpoints enforce permissions. Hidden documentation or client UI never protects a server resource.

concepts.title: Testing boundaries
concepts.description: Named handlers can be unit-tested, but WebApplicationFactory proves routing, binding, serialization, filters, metadata, middleware, and security work together.

architecture.description: The ASP.NET Core pipeline handles cross-cutting HTTP concerns, routing selects a feature group, binding and filters establish a safe request contract, a thin handler invokes an application capability, and typed results describe the response while telemetry follows the request end to end.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated sample builds an order API as a feature module. Public reads and protected writes share one route group, while validation, authorization, OpenAPI, Problem Details, rate limiting, security headers, storage, and tests each have a clear owner.

implementationSteps.title: Register the platform capabilities
implementationSteps.description: Add Problem Details, first-party OpenAPI generation, authentication, authorization policies, rate limiting, and the feature repository before building the host.

implementationSteps.title: Create one feature route group
implementationSteps.description: Map /api/orders once, attach its tag and rate-limit policy, then add cohesive read and write operations beneath it.

implementationSteps.title: Define boundary contracts
implementationSteps.description: Use separate request and response records so persistence and domain changes cannot silently alter the public JSON schema.

implementationSteps.title: Bind explicit inputs
implementationSteps.description: Let route constraints handle shape, bind optional paging from the query, bind JSON from the body, resolve the repository from DI, and accept cancellation for real I/O.

implementationSteps.title: Validate and authorize before effects
implementationSteps.description: Short-circuit invalid create requests with a validation filter and require a named write policy before the handler mutates state.

implementationSteps.title: Return typed HTTP outcomes
implementationSteps.description: Use Ok, NotFound, BadRequest, CreatedAtRoute, NoContent, and declared result unions so contracts remain visible to code, tests, and OpenAPI.

implementationSteps.title: Test through the complete pipeline
implementationSteps.description: Use WebApplicationFactory to prove a seeded read, unauthorized write, validation response, created-resource location, follow-up read, and generated OpenAPI document.

code.label: OrderEndpoints.cs
code.introduction: This feature group shares tags and rate limiting, makes write authorization explicit, validates before mutation, and exposes stable endpoint names for OpenAPI and location generation.

testing.introduction: Handler unit tests are fast when a named method owns meaningful mapping logic, but only HTTP integration tests prove the endpoint graph and hosting configuration.
items: Use WebApplicationFactory to execute the real routing, binding, JSON options, filters, authentication, authorization, exception handling, and response metadata.
Test malformed routes, invalid query bounds, absent and invalid credentials, missing resources, validation details, content types, and Location headers—not only 200 responses.
Assert the generated OpenAPI document includes stable paths, operation identifiers, schemas, security expectations, and declared response codes.
Keep domain and application rules independently unit-testable; do not require an HTTP server to prove every business permutation.
Use real infrastructure selectively for critical persistence behavior, while keeping the default suite deterministic and independent of execution order.

security.introduction: Minimal APIs use the same ASP.NET Core security system as controllers. Compact syntax does not change the need for trusted identity, server-side policy, safe input, and deliberate exposure.
items: Validate token issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and permitted algorithms with an approved authentication handler; never trust decoded claims without validation.
Attach named authorization policies to route groups or individual endpoints and include negative tests for anonymous, wrong-scope, wrong-tenant, and non-owner callers.
Treat request bodies, route values, queries, headers, files, and custom binders as untrusted; cap sizes and counts before allocation or downstream work.
Expose OpenAPI documents and interactive tooling only to the intended environment or authenticated audience; documentation secrecy is not endpoint security.
Return safe Problem Details without stack traces, secrets, connection strings, or sensitive payloads, and redact logs while preserving correlation.

performance.introduction: Minimal APIs reduce framework ceremony and can work well with trimming and Native AOT, but throughput still depends mainly on I/O, serialization, allocations, downstream latency, and bounded concurrency.
items: Use asynchronous I/O and propagate HttpContext.RequestAborted or the bound CancellationToken into databases, HTTP calls, and messaging operations.
Bound page sizes, body sizes, uploads, queues, rate limits, retries, concurrency, and downstream timeouts so one client cannot consume unlimited work.
Stream only when the client and complete dependency path support backpressure and partial-failure semantics; otherwise return a bounded materialized response.
Measure endpoint latency, allocation rate, serialization cost, database queries, and dependency spans before applying pooling, custom binders, or Native AOT complexity.
Cache only responses with explicit identity, authorization, variation, freshness, and invalidation rules; never let shared caching leak caller-specific data.

deployment.introduction: The deployed artifact must preserve the same routes and policies behind its real proxy, identity provider, configuration source, and observability pipeline.
items: Publish and smoke-test the exact target artifact or container, run as non-root where applicable, and scan SDK, NuGet, OS, and image dependencies in CI.
Validate configuration on startup, obtain secrets from an approved provider, and fail clearly when issuer, audience, database, or other required settings are absent.
Configure forwarded headers only for known proxies, terminate TLS at a trusted boundary, enforce host and request limits, and verify the external base path used by OpenAPI clients.
Emit structured logs, metrics, and distributed traces with route names and correlation, while avoiding high-cardinality identifiers in metric dimensions.
Support graceful shutdown, readiness transitions, safe migrations, rollback, and version-compatible contracts during rolling deployment.

troubleshooting.symptom: A request returns 404 even though a similar route exists.
troubleshooting.cause: The HTTP method, literal segment, route precedence, constraint, base path, or registration does not match the request.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect endpoint metadata, test the exact method and deployed path, and use constraints to disambiguate shape rather than using them as business validation.

troubleshooting.symptom: The handler receives an unexpected value or the request returns 400 before the handler runs.
troubleshooting.cause: Binding inferred a different source, conversion failed, the JSON shape or content type is wrong, or a required value is absent.
troubleshooting.fix: Make ambiguous sources explicit, inspect the Problem Details response, keep request contracts nullable only when absence is valid, and integration-test representative payloads.

troubleshooting.symptom: OpenAPI omits a response or shows a vague schema.
troubleshooting.cause: The handler returns IResult or mixed anonymous shapes without sufficient typed results and metadata.
troubleshooting.fix: Prefer TypedResults and Results unions, use stable endpoint names, declare extra validation or problem responses, and assert the generated document in tests.

troubleshooting.symptom: A protected endpoint returns 401 or 403 unexpectedly.
troubleshooting.cause: Authentication did not establish an identity, the scheme did not challenge correctly, or the authorization policy rejected the caller's claims or resource access.
troubleshooting.fix: Separate identity failure from permission failure, inspect safe authentication diagnostics and claims, and test anonymous, authenticated-but-forbidden, and authorized requests.

troubleshooting.symptom: Endpoint filters run in an unexpected order or miss some requests.
troubleshooting.cause: Filters are scoped to mapped handlers and execute in registration order around the handler; they are not global middleware.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep endpoint-specific validation or observation in filters, move whole-pipeline concerns to middleware, and test short-circuit plus post-handler behavior.

troubleshooting.symptom: The API slows down or exhausts resources under load.
troubleshooting.cause: Synchronous I/O, unbounded queries or bodies, missing timeouts, excessive retries, large serialization work, or a slow dependency is consuming request capacity.
troubleshooting.fix: Use traces and runtime metrics, propagate cancellation, bound inputs and concurrency, add safe timeouts, and load-test the complete deployed dependency path.

productionChecklist: Every route has an intentional method, pattern, constraint, stable name, tag, and documented success and failure contract.
Request and response DTOs are separate from persistence entities, and validation covers all untrusted boundary data and collection bounds.
Authentication configuration is validated and write or sensitive endpoints enforce named authorization policies with negative tests.
Problem Details, correlation, structured logs, metrics, and traces reveal failures without leaking secrets or sensitive payloads.
Request sizes, result sizes, concurrency, rate limits, retries, and outbound timeouts are bounded and based on measured capacity.
OpenAPI output is verified, versioned deliberately, and exposed only to the intended audience; client compatibility is checked before breaking changes.
Integration tests exercise the real pipeline, while persistence and external dependencies have focused contract or infrastructure tests.
The published artifact passes dependency audit, security scan, smoke test, proxy-path test, graceful-shutdown test, and rollback rehearsal.
bestPractices: Group endpoints by cohesive capability, not by HTTP verb, and keep Program.cs as composition rather than a catalog of business logic.
Use named handler methods when signatures or mapping logic become difficult to scan, and delegate business policy to application services.
Use request and response contracts rather than exposing persistence or domain entities directly.
Prefer TypedResults and finite Results unions so code, tests, and OpenAPI share an explicit response contract.
Use route constraints for route selection and validation for user-facing business or range errors.
Attach authorization, rate limits, tags, filters, and shared metadata at the narrowest useful route-group boundary.
Propagate cancellation and bound every client-controlled collection, body, page size, upload, and expensive operation.
Test through WebApplicationFactory before claiming routing, binding, filters, security, serialization, or OpenAPI work together.
Return safe Problem Details and correlate failures; never serialize exception details or log credentials and complete sensitive payloads.
Measure the real deployed path before optimizing or choosing Native AOT, custom serialization, pooling, or streaming complexity.

interviewQuestions.question: Are Minimal APIs only for small applications?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. They can support large systems when endpoints are organized by cohesive feature, conventions are enforced, and handlers delegate to application capabilities. A large Program.cs is an organization problem, not a required Minimal API shape.

interviewQuestions.question: How does parameter binding decide where a value comes from?
interviewQuestions.answer: The framework uses explicit binding attributes when present and otherwise infers from special framework types, route parameters, services, simple TryParse-compatible values, and body-capable complex types. Ambiguous or security-sensitive sources should be explicit.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between route constraints and validation?
interviewQuestions.answer: Constraints help routing select an endpoint based on value shape. Validation runs after selection and returns a useful explanation when a matched request violates range, format, or business rules.

interviewQuestions.question: Why prefer TypedResults and Results<T1, T2>?
interviewQuestions.answer: They expose concrete response alternatives to the compiler, make direct handler assertions easier, and allow OpenAPI generation to infer more of the contract without manual metadata.

interviewQuestions.question: When should endpoint filters be used instead of middleware?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use filters for behavior tied to selected handlers and their bound arguments, such as feature validation. Use middleware for concerns that must surround broad pipeline traffic, such as global exception handling or correlation.

interviewQuestions.question: How should a Minimal API be tested?
interviewQuestions.answer: Unit-test domain and application rules directly, optionally test named handler mapping, and use WebApplicationFactory for the critical HTTP paths so routing, binding, JSON, filters, middleware, authentication, authorization, and metadata are proven together.

interviewQuestions.question: When would controllers be a better choice?
interviewQuestions.answer: Controllers can be better when a team relies on controller conventions, action filters, complex model-binding extensions, MVC-specific tooling, or an established controller codebase whose migration cost has no clear payoff.

note: Minimal syntax does not mean minimal design. Contracts, validation, authorization, observability, operational bounds, and failure semantics still matter.
tip: Use route groups as the feature boundary for shared prefixes and metadata, then integration-test the final endpoint graph rather than assuming fluent calls composed as intended.
warning: Avoid returning database entities directly or trusting client-side visibility as authorization; both can leak data even when the handler itself looks small.

name: Authentication & Authorization
shortDescription: Establish identity, enforce policy, protect credentials, and design secure application boundaries.
overview: Authentication establishes who a principal is; authorization decides what that principal may do in a specific context.
detail: ASP.NET Core authentication handlers validate credentials such as cookies or bearer tokens and construct a ClaimsPrincipal. A scheme selects the handler that authenticates, challenges an anonymous caller, or forbids an authenticated caller. APIs should accept OAuth access tokens from a trusted authorization server and validate signature, issuer, audience, lifetime, and algorithms before trusting claims; ID tokens are for clients and are not API access tokens. Authorization then evaluates roles, claims, scopes, named policies, custom requirements, and the actual resource. Declarative policies work for decisions known before a record is loaded, while ownership and tenant decisions require imperative resource authorization. Production design also includes deny-by-default fallback policy, cookie protections, token and key rotation, revocation expectations, multiple schemes, least privilege, 401 versus 403 semantics, deliberate non-disclosure, and negative tests. A valid identity never proves permission to every function or object, and client-side visibility is never a server authorization boundary.
learningObjectives: Separate authenticate, challenge, forbid, sign-in, sign-out, and authorization responsibilities.
Choose cookies, bearer access tokens, or multiple schemes from client and trust-boundary requirements.
Validate access tokens and distinguish them from ID tokens, refresh tokens, and application sessions.
Model permissions with policies, requirements, handlers, roles, scopes, and claims.
Apply resource and tenant authorization after loading the target object.
Return deliberate 401, 403, and non-disclosing 404 responses and test negative paths.
Operate identity safely through key rotation, token lifetime, telemetry, and incident response.
prerequisites: HTTP status codes, headers, cookies, TLS, and browser versus API behavior.
ASP.NET Core dependency injection, middleware, routing, and configuration.
Basic familiarity with claims, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, JWT structure, and signatures.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the dedicated document-authorization sample.

use: Use secure cookies when a server-rendered browser application owns the session and can enforce antiforgery controls.
Use validated OAuth access tokens for APIs called by native, browser, service, or delegated clients.
Use named policies for reusable permission rules and resource handlers for ownership, tenant, or state decisions.
Use a fallback policy when authenticated access should be the default.
avoid: Do not invent production token formats when a standards-based identity platform is available.
Do not use an ID token as authorization to call an API.
Do not encode rapidly changing object permissions into long-lived tokens when request-time checks are required.
Do not rely on CORS, hidden buttons, gateway-only checks, or possession of any valid token as authorization.

concepts.title: Schemes and handlers
concepts.description: A scheme selects the handler that authenticates, challenges, or forbids a request.

concepts.title: Claims principal
concepts.description: One or more identities and their claims represent the authenticated caller.

concepts.title: Policy authorization
concepts.description: Named policies combine reusable requirements that handlers evaluate against user and resource.

concepts.title: Token lifecycle
concepts.description: Issuance, audience, expiry, rotation, revocation, and key management shape token safety.

concepts.title: OAuth and OpenID Connect
concepts.description: OAuth delegates API access; OpenID Connect adds authentication and ID tokens for the client. Token type and audience must not be confused.

concepts.title: Resource authorization
concepts.description: Ownership, tenant, operation, and resource state are evaluated after loading the target record.

concepts.title: Fallback policy
concepts.description: A fallback policy protects endpoints without explicit authorization metadata; genuinely public endpoints opt out deliberately.

concepts.title: Challenge and forbid
concepts.description: Unauthenticated callers receive 401 and a challenge, while authenticated callers without permission receive 403; selected lookups may return 404 to avoid disclosure.

architecture.description: A client obtains credentials from a trusted identity provider. The application validates them, builds a principal, evaluates endpoint policy, loads the target resource, and performs resource authorization before returning minimum permitted data.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated sample uses a local-only test scheme so every outcome is runnable without external infrastructure. It requires identity by default, applies a scope policy for creation, and uses an ownership-or-administrator handler for document reads.

implementationSteps.title: Choose the trust model
implementationSteps.description: Identify clients, token issuer, audience, credential type, session boundary, and TLS termination.

implementationSteps.title: Register schemes
implementationSteps.description: Configure cookie, JWT bearer, certificate, or approved handlers with explicit defaults and strict validation.

implementationSteps.title: Define policies
implementationSteps.description: Express business permissions through named policies and requirements instead of scattered strings.

implementationSteps.title: Protect by default
implementationSteps.description: Apply fallback or group policy and mark genuinely public endpoints explicitly.

implementationSteps.title: Authorize resources
implementationSteps.description: Load within the tenant boundary and authorize the user-resource-operation tuple.

implementationSteps.title: Map failures
implementationSteps.description: Return 401 for unacceptable identity, 403 for insufficient permission, and deliberate 404 only to prevent disclosure.

implementationSteps.title: Test denials
implementationSteps.description: Cover anonymous, invalid, missing-scope, wrong-role, wrong-tenant, non-owner, owner, and administrator paths.

code.introduction: A policy expresses business permission as a named requirement instead of scattering claim checks through endpoints.

testing.introduction: Security tests must prove denied paths as carefully as allowed paths.
items: Use WebApplicationFactory with deterministic test identities without bypassing authorization middleware.
Test 401, 403, and non-disclosing inaccessible-resource behavior.
Cover wrong scope, role, tenant, owner, operation, and resource state.
Test wrong token issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and algorithm where bearer tokens are used.
Assert responses and logs do not reveal tokens, secrets, claims, or protected object existence.

security.introduction: Identity configuration, keys, redirects, cookies, claims, and logs all belong to the security boundary.
items: Use a trusted standards-based provider and validate token signature, issuer, audience, lifetime, and algorithms.
Use short-lived access tokens and protect refresh tokens with rotation, reuse detection, and revocation procedures.
For cookies, use Secure, HttpOnly, appropriate SameSite, antiforgery protection, and protected shared data keys.
Minimize claims and never log authorization headers, cookies, token bodies, or unnecessary personal data.
Perform object and tenant authorization on the server even when gateways and UI layers restrict access.

performance.introduction: Identity checks run on every protected request, but caching must not extend permissions beyond the accepted security window.
items: Use supported metadata and signing-key caches and test rollover.
Keep claims compact to limit header, proxy, logging, and serialization cost.
Bound remote introspection with timeouts and fail closed.
Cache authorization decisions only with subject, tenant, resource, operation, policy version, and safe TTL in the key.
Measure handler and policy latency without recording token data.

deployment.introduction: External URLs, proxy headers, key persistence, clocks, and issuer settings affect production identity behavior.
items: Validate authority, audience, callback paths, redirects, and external scheme against the real HTTPS hostname.
Persist and isolate data-protection keys for shared cookie deployments.
Synchronize clocks and rehearse signing-key rollover and provider degradation.
Use managed identity or workload federation for service credentials where supported.
Deploy authorization changes with audit telemetry, compatibility tests, and rollback.

troubleshooting.cause: No scheme authenticated the request or token validation failed.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect safe diagnostics, scheme selection, issuer, audience, keys, lifetime, and challenge headers without logging the token.

troubleshooting.cause: A policy requirement or resource handler did not succeed.
troubleshooting.fix: Verify the principal, policy, failed requirement, and exact user-resource-operation tuple.

troubleshooting.symptom: Changing an ID exposes another tenant.
troubleshooting.cause: The endpoint authenticated but did not scope loading and authorize the resource.
troubleshooting.fix: Filter by tenant, authorize the loaded object, and add cross-tenant tests.

troubleshooting.symptom: Cookie login loops behind a proxy.
troubleshooting.cause: Forwarded headers, HTTPS detection, callback paths, SameSite, or data keys are misconfigured.
troubleshooting.fix: Trust known proxies only and verify external URL, cookie attributes, and shared key storage.

troubleshooting.cause: Key metadata is stale or rollover overlap is insufficient.
troubleshooting.fix: Use supported refresh, retain overlapping valid keys, monitor rollover, and test it.

troubleshooting.cause: A token or decision cache still contains the permission.
troubleshooting.fix: Shorten lifetime or use introspection/revocation when immediate removal is required.

productionChecklist: Issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, algorithms, metadata endpoint, and clock skew are explicit.
Schemes, defaults, fallback policy, and every anonymous endpoint are reviewed.
Policies model business permissions and object or tenant checks authorize resources.
Cookies, refresh tokens, signing keys, client secrets, and data keys have protected storage and rotation.
401, 403, and non-disclosing behavior is covered by negative tests.
Logs and telemetry exclude tokens, cookies, secrets, and unnecessary claims.
Rollover, provider outage, revoked access, emergency access, and compromise have runbooks.
The real proxy, HTTPS hostname, callbacks, cookies, and shared keys are smoke-tested.
bestPractices: Validate issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and algorithms for bearer access tokens.
Prefer policy and resource-based authorization over inline role checks.
Protect endpoints by default and review anonymous access.
Authorize the subject-resource-operation tuple within the tenant boundary.
Keep identity credentials and keys out of source and logs and rotate them.
Return deliberate 401, 403, or non-disclosing 404 outcomes.
Keep access tokens short-lived and claims minimal.
Test anonymous, invalid, wrong-scope, wrong-role, wrong-tenant, and non-owner callers.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
interviewQuestions.answer: Authentication verifies identity. Authorization evaluates whether that identity is permitted to perform an action on a resource.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are refresh tokens treated differently from access tokens?
interviewQuestions.answer: Refresh tokens are longer-lived credentials used to obtain access tokens, so they require stronger storage, rotation, reuse detection, and revocation controls.

interviewQuestions.question: What is resource-based authorization?
interviewQuestions.answer: It evaluates access using both the principal and the actual resource instance—for example, whether the current user owns a document.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
interviewQuestions.answer: 401 means acceptable authentication is missing; 403 means an authenticated caller lacks permission.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is an ID token not an API access token?
interviewQuestions.answer: It describes authentication to a client and is intended for that client, while an access token targets an API audience.

interviewQuestions.question: When should a fallback policy be used?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use it when endpoints should be private unless explicitly marked anonymous.

interviewQuestions.question: Can JWT access be revoked immediately?
interviewQuestions.answer: Self-contained tokens normally remain valid until expiry unless the system adds revocation or introspection, so lifetime must match the accepted window.

note: CORS is a browser cross-origin policy; it is not authentication or authorization and does not protect server-to-server calls.
tip: Write negative authorization tests—anonymous, wrong role, missing claim, wrong tenant, and non-owner—not only the happy path.
warning: Do not decode a JWT and trust its claims without cryptographically validating the token and its intended issuer and audience.

name: Azure for .NET
shortDescription: Run, integrate, observe, and secure .NET workloads using Azure-managed services and identity.
overview: Azure gives .NET workloads managed compute, data, messaging, identity, secrets, networking, delivery, and observability building blocks. A production design maps workload requirements to those capabilities, keeps authentication secret-free with managed identity, treats service limits and transient failure as architecture inputs, and proves security, reliability, performance, recovery, and cost through automation and telemetry.
detail: A sound Azure design begins with workload requirements rather than a service catalog. Record critical flows, data classification, latency and availability objectives, recovery targets, scale shape, residency, integrations, and team responsibilities before selecting services. Choose compute by execution and control needs; choose data by access, consistency, partition, backup, and recovery needs; add messaging when buffering or temporal decoupling is valuable. In .NET, reuse Azure SDK clients and credential instances, use a convenient developer credential chain locally, and select ManagedIdentityCredential deterministically in hosted production. Assign only required data-plane roles. Bound timeouts and retries, make replayed effects idempotent, control concurrency before dependencies saturate, and carry cancellation and trace context throughout the call path. Infrastructure, private networking and DNS, immutable delivery, observability, quotas, budgets, backup, restore, regional recovery, and incident ownership are parts of the application architecture rather than work postponed until release.

concepts.title: Workload and service selection
concepts.description: Map latency, execution model, scale, network, recovery, compliance, and team-operating needs to services; do not begin from a favorite product.

concepts.title: Azure SDK client lifecycle
concepts.description: Register thread-safe Azure SDK clients once, reuse credential and transport state, configure bounded retries, and pass cancellation to every asynchronous operation.

concepts.title: Identity and authorization
concepts.description: Use developer credentials locally, a deterministic managed identity in Azure, and least-privilege data-plane RBAC at the narrowest practical scope.

concepts.title: Configuration and secrets
concepts.description: Keep endpoints and non-secret settings in typed configuration; reference secrets from Key Vault and rotate rather than embedding keys or connection strings.

concepts.title: Compute selection
concepts.description: App Service, Container Apps, Functions, and AKS trade platform control for operational responsibility, scale behavior, networking capabilities, and cost shape.

concepts.title: Data and messaging
concepts.description: Choose data stores from access and consistency requirements, and use Service Bus or Event Hubs when buffering, temporal decoupling, or stream ingestion is required.

concepts.title: Resilience and idempotency
concepts.description: Bound attempts with timeouts, retry only transient and safe operations, control concurrency, and make side effects idempotent before replay.

concepts.title: Observability and governance
concepts.description: Correlate traces, metrics, logs, deployments, cost, security posture, quotas, backup, and recovery evidence around workload service-level objectives.

architecture.description: A managed entry point routes traffic to .NET compute, which uses identity-based access to data and messaging while emitting correlated telemetry.

code.label: AzureClient.cs
code.introduction: DefaultAzureCredential supports local developer identity and managed identity in Azure without changing application code.

bestPractices: Choose Azure services from documented workload requirements and explicit responsibility boundaries.
Use DefaultAzureCredential for local development and a specific ManagedIdentityCredential in hosted production.
Reuse Azure SDK clients and credentials; do not create them for each request.
Assign minimal data-plane RBAC and separate application, deployment, and human identities.
Configure timeouts and bounded retry policies from operation semantics and downstream capacity.
Use private networking only with a complete DNS, egress, observability, and operational design.
Deploy immutable artifacts and infrastructure as code with staged validation and post-deployment smoke checks.
Define SLOs, alerts, budgets, quotas, backup, restore, and regional recovery before production traffic.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use deterministic credentials in production?
interviewQuestions.answer: A fixed ManagedIdentityCredential prevents an unexpected credential in a chain from succeeding after configuration drift and makes the application identity auditable.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should Azure SDK clients be reused?
interviewQuestions.answer: They are designed to be thread-safe and reuse transports and token caches; per-request construction adds connections, authentication calls, latency, and resource pressure.

interviewQuestions.question: When does messaging improve an Azure design?
interviewQuestions.answer: When producers need buffering, independent scaling, retry isolation, fan-out, temporal decoupling, or durable acceptance before slower processing.

interviewQuestions.question: What does a private endpoint not solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: It does not by itself solve DNS, outbound control, identity, authorization, data exfiltration, monitoring, high availability, or application-layer security.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose between system and user-assigned identity?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use system-assigned for lifecycle-coupled simplicity; use user-assigned when identity must survive resource replacement or be shared deliberately across instances.

interviewQuestions.question: How should Azure service limits influence architecture?
interviewQuestions.answer: Treat quotas, throttles, connection limits, scale units, and regional availability as design inputs, test near expected peaks, and automate quota monitoring.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the safe response to a regional dependency outage?
interviewQuestions.answer: Follow a tested recovery design with idempotent failover, replicated or restorable data, controlled traffic movement, dependency validation, and clear consistency trade-offs.

note: Cloud-native is an operating model as much as a hosting location: automated delivery, observability, resiliency, and ownership all matter.
tip: Use the same credential abstraction locally and in Azure, but verify exactly which credential wins in each environment.
warning: Retries can amplify an outage or duplicate effects. Bound them, add jitter, and make write operations idempotent before retrying.
