name: Design Patterns
shortDescription: A vocabulary of reusable design structures for recurring collaboration and change problems.
overview: Design patterns describe proven arrangements of responsibilities and collaborations for recurring software design problems.
detail: Design patterns are named arrangements of responsibilities that help teams discuss recurring construction, composition, collaboration, and state-change problems. They are neither frameworks nor goals: each moves complexity and is justified only by a concrete force such as interchangeable policy, incompatible integration, layered behavior, controlled creation, notification fan-out, or lifecycle transitions. Modern C# records, delegates, pattern matching, generics, dependency injection, middleware, and first-class functions often express the same intent with less ceremony than classic class diagrams. A good implementation keeps selection and composition visible, preserves substitution, owns failure and concurrency semantics, and is tested through behavior rather than participant names. Patterns can combine—such as a factory composing strategies and decorators around an adapter—but excessive abstraction, speculative extension points, service location, and generic repositories can make simple changes harder. Refactor toward a pattern after the pressure becomes clear and remove it when it no longer earns its cost.

concepts.title: Creational patterns
concepts.description: Factories, builders, and prototypes separate construction decisions from consumers.

concepts.title: Structural patterns
concepts.description: Adapters, decorators, composites, and facades shape how objects and systems fit together.

concepts.title: Behavioral patterns
concepts.description: Strategies, observers, commands, and mediators organize algorithms and collaboration.

concepts.title: Pattern trade-offs
concepts.description: Each pattern shifts complexity; the benefit must outweigh indirection, objects, and conventions.

concepts.title: Strategy and policy
concepts.description: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms while keeping selection rules visible at composition.

concepts.title: Adapter and boundary translation
concepts.description: Adapter converts an external or legacy contract into an application-owned interface and contains semantic mismatch.

concepts.title: Decorator and pipelines
concepts.description: Decorator adds ordered behavior around a stable contract without changing the wrapped implementation.

concepts.title: Factory and composition
concepts.description: Factories centralize nontrivial construction and selection without becoming global service locators.

architecture.description: A caller depends on a stable strategy contract while the composition root selects a behavior suited to current policy.

code.label: PricingStrategy.cs
code.introduction: Strategy replaces branching that changes for different pricing policies with a focused, selectable behavior.

learningObjectives: Classify creational, structural, and behavioral patterns by the pressure they address.
Implement Strategy, Adapter, Decorator, and Factory using modern C# composition.
Distinguish similar patterns by intent rather than diagram shape.
Select language or framework features when they express the intent more simply.
Test substitutability, ordering, translation, failure, and composition.
Recognize and remove speculative or misleading pattern use.
prerequisites: C# interfaces, records, delegates, generics, dependency injection, and testing.
SOLID principles, composition, coupling, cohesion, and application boundaries.
Ability to describe a real change pressure before choosing a structure.

use: Two or more policies must vary behind one stable contract.
An external contract must be translated at a boundary.
Ordered cross-cutting behavior must wrap a capability.
Construction or lifecycle rules are complex enough to centralize.
avoid: A direct method, switch, delegate, or framework feature is clearer.
Variation is speculative and has only one stable implementation.
The abstraction hides ownership or turns dependencies into runtime lookup.

implementationIntroduction: The pricing sample combines Strategy for discounts, Adapter for a legacy tax gateway, Decorator for a safety limit, and Factory for explicit composition, with one focused test per pressure.

implementationSteps.title: Name the force
implementationSteps.description: Describe what varies, what must remain stable, and which dependency or responsibility causes pain.

implementationSteps.title: Choose the smallest intent
implementationSteps.description: Compare direct code, a language feature, framework middleware, and the candidate pattern.

implementationSteps.title: Define the contract
implementationSteps.description: Express only behavior consumers need and preserve substitutability.

implementationSteps.title: Implement participants
implementationSteps.description: Keep each strategy, adapter, decorator, or creator cohesive and side effects explicit.

implementationSteps.title: Compose visibly
implementationSteps.description: Select implementations in a composition root or focused factory, not hidden service location.

implementationSteps.title: Test semantics
implementationSteps.description: Verify alternatives, translation, ordering, errors, concurrency, and boundary cases.

implementationSteps.title: Reassess cost
implementationSteps.description: Measure comprehension and change impact and simplify when the pattern no longer earns its indirection.

testing.introduction: Test the behavioral promise and trade-off of a pattern, not merely class existence.
items: Run the same contract tests against every strategy implementation.
Test adapter units, rounding, missing fields, timeouts, and error translation.
Verify decorator ordering, short-circuiting, and exception behavior.
Test factory selection and unsupported configuration.
Exercise observer duplication, ordering, and failure isolation where used.
Add concurrency tests for shared or stateful participants.

security.introduction: Patterns can centralize security policy or hide it, so trust boundaries and ordering must remain explicit.
items: Do not use a decorator as the only resource-authorization check when callers can bypass it.
Validate and normalize data inside adapters at external boundaries.
Keep factories from becoming unrestricted service locators.
Redact sensitive inputs in logging decorators.
Fail closed when a security policy participant is missing or fails.

performance.introduction: Virtual dispatch is usually small; allocation, reflection, network work, and long decorator chains matter more and must be measured.
items: Profile the real composed path before optimizing dispatch.
Keep hot strategies allocation-conscious.
Avoid repeated serialization or mapping between decorators.
Cache immutable factory products only with correct lifetimes.
Measure chain depth, latency contribution, and failure amplification.

deployment.introduction: Selection rules and external adapters are configuration-sensitive production behavior.
items: Validate factory configuration at startup.
Version application-owned adapter contracts.
Roll out new strategies behind explicit flags when outcomes change.
Trace concrete participant names and timing without leaking data.
Smoke-test the production composition, not isolated defaults.

troubleshooting.cause: A pattern was applied without real variation.
troubleshooting.fix: Inline participants or use delegates and direct composition.

troubleshooting.symptom: A new strategy requires changing callers.
troubleshooting.cause: Selection leaked outside composition.
troubleshooting.fix: Centralize selection in one factory or root.

troubleshooting.cause: Pipeline semantics are undocumented.
troubleshooting.fix: Define and test explicit ordering.

troubleshooting.cause: Translation stops at the boundary.
troubleshooting.fix: Map inputs, outputs, errors, and units into owned contracts.

troubleshooting.cause: It became a service locator.
troubleshooting.fix: Inject explicit dependencies and return a focused product.

troubleshooting.cause: Failure, concurrency, and lifecycle semantics are missing.
troubleshooting.fix: Document and test operational behavior.

productionChecklist: A concrete force and expected benefit justify every pattern.
Contracts are minimal and substitutable.
Selection and composition are visible.
Adapters own complete semantic translation.
Decorator order and bypass rules are tested.
Factories do not hide arbitrary dependency lookup.
Failure, security, concurrency, and lifetime behavior are explicit.
The design is simpler than the branching or coupling it replaces.
bestPractices: Name the design pressure before naming a pattern.
Prefer language features and simple composition when they solve the problem clearly.
Keep pattern participants cohesive and make selection rules visible.
Document trade-offs when a pattern introduces meaningful indirection.
Test all implementations against the same behavioral contract.
Keep boundary translation complete inside adapters.
Make decorator order and short-circuit behavior explicit.
Refactor away patterns that no longer reduce change cost.

interviewQuestions.question: How do Strategy and State differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: They have similar structure, but Strategy selects an interchangeable algorithm while State models behavior that changes with an object's internal state transitions.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between Adapter and Facade?
interviewQuestions.answer: Adapter changes an interface so a client can use it. Facade provides a simpler entry point over a subsystem without necessarily adapting an incompatible contract.

interviewQuestions.question: When is a pattern over-engineering?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the predicted variation is unlikely, the simpler design is already easy to change, or the added abstractions make ownership and behavior harder to understand.

interviewQuestions.question: Decorator or middleware?
interviewQuestions.answer: Both form ordered pipelines; decorators wrap an application contract, while middleware usually surrounds a framework request pipeline.

interviewQuestions.question: Factory or dependency injection container?
interviewQuestions.answer: A factory owns focused runtime construction or selection. A container composes the object graph and should not be resolved from business code.

interviewQuestions.question: When is a delegate better than Strategy?
interviewQuestions.answer: When behavior has little state or lifecycle and a named function clearly expresses the variation with less ceremony.

interviewQuestions.question: How should an Adapter handle failures?
interviewQuestions.answer: Translate vendor errors, units, nullability, retries, and cancellation into the application-owned contract rather than leaking them.

note: Patterns give teams names for trade-offs. They do not remove the need to understand the forces in a specific design.
tip: Study a pattern beside the refactoring pressure that leads to it, not as an isolated class diagram.
warning: Do not force every class into a GoF pattern; unnecessary abstraction makes simple changes expensive.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated multi-pattern pricing sample

name: Docker
shortDescription: Package .NET applications and runtime dependencies into repeatable, portable container images.
overview: Docker packages an application, its runtime, and filesystem dependencies into an immutable image executed as isolated containers.
detail: For .NET, multi-stage builds separate SDK compilation from the smaller ASP.NET or runtime image, keeping source code and compilers out of production. Layer ordering and .dockerignore determine cache efficiency and accidental build inputs. A running container should be replaceable: durable state belongs in external services or deliberate volumes, configuration arrives at runtime, and logs flow to stdout. Production images should run as a non-root user, expose meaningful health signals, honor graceful termination, and be rebuilt, scanned, identified, and promoted immutably whenever application or base-image dependencies change.

concepts.title: Images and layers
concepts.description: Immutable layers describe a filesystem and startup configuration, enabling caching and content-addressed distribution.

concepts.title: Containers
concepts.description: Running image instances isolate processes and files while sharing the host kernel.

concepts.title: Multi-stage builds
concepts.description: A build stage compiles with the SDK and a final stage carries only publish output and runtime dependencies.

concepts.title: Compose
concepts.description: A declarative local topology coordinates services, networks, volumes, environment, and health dependencies.

concepts.title: Registries and identity
concepts.description: Registries distribute images while tags, digests, signatures, and provenance identify exactly what was built and approved.

concepts.title: Runtime boundaries
concepts.description: Ports, networks, mounts, resource limits, users, capabilities, and signals define how an isolated process interacts with its host and dependencies.

concepts.title: Configuration and secrets
concepts.description: Runtime configuration keeps one image portable while secret mounts or external providers prevent sensitive values from entering layers.

concepts.title: Lifecycle and observability
concepts.description: Health signals, stdout logs, metrics, traces, and graceful termination make a short-lived container operable.

architecture.description: Source is compiled in an SDK stage, copied into a minimal runtime image, and executed as a replaceable container connected to external state.

code.label: Dockerfile
code.introduction: A multi-stage Dockerfile restores deterministically, publishes once, and runs the final image without root privileges.
code.code:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["Portal.Api.csproj", "."]
RUN dotnet restore "Portal.Api.csproj"
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish "Portal.Api.csproj" -c Release -o /app --no-restore

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0 AS final
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app .
USER $APP_UID
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Portal.Api.dll"]

bestPractices: Use multi-stage builds and a minimal trusted runtime base image.
Copy project files before source to preserve dependency restore caching.
Run as a non-root user and scan both dependencies and the final image.
Keep secrets out of layers, build arguments, and committed Compose files.
Externalize durable state and make container replacement routine.
Publish immutable versions or digests and keep a tested rollback image.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an image and a container?
interviewQuestions.answer: An image is an immutable package definition; a container is a running instance with a writable layer and runtime configuration.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use a multi-stage build?
interviewQuestions.answer: It keeps compilers, source, and build caches out of the runtime image, reducing size and attack surface.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should container state be externalized?
interviewQuestions.answer: Containers are replaceable. External databases, object stores, or volumes preserve durable state across restarts, rescheduling, and scaling.

interviewQuestions.question: What belongs in .dockerignore?
interviewQuestions.answer: Exclude build outputs, source-control metadata, editor state, test results, credentials, and any file the image build does not require so contexts stay small and safe.

interviewQuestions.question: Why deploy an image digest instead of only a tag?
interviewQuestions.answer: A digest is content-addressed and immutable, so it proves which exact image was deployed even if a human-readable tag later moves.

interviewQuestions.question: How do Docker volumes differ from bind mounts?
interviewQuestions.answer: Docker manages named-volume storage and lifecycle, while a bind mount exposes a specific host path and therefore couples the container more closely to that host.

interviewQuestions.question: What should a container write to stdout?
interviewQuestions.answer: Write structured application and access logs without secrets; the runtime platform should collect, retain, route, and query them.

note: A successful image build proves packaging, not that the application starts correctly with real dependencies and configuration.
tip: Build from the repository root when project references or shared files live outside the API project folder.
warning: Never bake production secrets into an image; image layers remain inspectable even after a later layer removes a file.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated hardened container sample
learningObjectives: Explain images, layers, containers, registries, networks, volumes, and Compose.
Build a cache-efficient multi-stage .NET image.
Run ASP.NET Core as a non-root process with a constrained filesystem.
Separate build-time inputs from runtime configuration and secrets.
Design container health, logging, shutdown, and external state correctly.
Test, scan, publish, and operate immutable images safely.
prerequisites: Basic ASP.NET Core publishing and configuration knowledge.
Docker Desktop or another Docker Engine for the container exercises.
Familiarity with ports, HTTP health endpoints, and command-line workflows.

use: Portable packaging across developer, CI, and runtime environments.
Repeatable service dependencies with Compose for local integration.
Immutable deployment units for orchestrators and managed container platforms.
avoid: Treating a container as a durable server with important local state.
Baking secrets or environment-specific settings into image layers.
Adding containers when a simple process deployment already meets the operational need.

implementationIntroduction: The Docker Orders API packages a small ASP.NET Core service with a cache-aware multi-stage build, non-root runtime, explicit health endpoints, read-only Compose filesystem, and focused behavior tests.

implementationSteps.title: Choose the build context
implementationSteps.description: Build from the narrowest directory that still contains every project reference, shared props file, and lock file required by restore.

implementationSteps.title: Order layers for caching
implementationSteps.description: Copy project metadata first, restore dependencies, then copy changing source so ordinary code edits can reuse the restore layer.

implementationSteps.title: Publish in an SDK stage
implementationSteps.description: Restore and publish with a pinned SDK family, Release configuration, and no redundant restore during publish.

implementationSteps.title: Create the runtime stage
implementationSteps.description: Copy only publish output into the ASP.NET runtime image, set the working directory and port, and use exec-form ENTRYPOINT.

implementationSteps.title: Reduce privileges
implementationSteps.description: Run with the .NET image APP_UID, remove unneeded capabilities, prevent privilege escalation, and prefer a read-only root filesystem.

implementationSteps.title: Inject runtime configuration
implementationSteps.description: Supply settings through environment variables or mounted configuration and retrieve secrets from an approved runtime secret store.

implementationSteps.title: Expose operational signals
implementationSteps.description: Write structured logs to stdout, implement distinct health semantics, and handle termination so in-flight work can finish.

implementationSteps.title: Verify and distribute
implementationSteps.description: Test the running image, scan dependencies and layers, generate provenance or an SBOM, tag immutably, and push to a controlled registry.

testing.introduction: Test the artifact that will run, not only the project that produced it.
items: Build with an empty cache periodically to reveal hidden inputs.
Start the image with production-like configuration and query health and business endpoints.
Assert the runtime user is non-root and the intended port is reachable.
Run with a read-only filesystem to expose accidental local writes.
Verify graceful stop behavior and bounded termination.
Inspect image history and scan the final stage for secrets and vulnerabilities.

security.introduction: A smaller, immutable, least-privileged image narrows risk but still needs supply-chain controls.
items: Use trusted base images and patch by rebuilding regularly.
Pin important production inputs by digest and record provenance.
Run as non-root with dropped capabilities and no new privileges.
Keep credentials out of Dockerfiles, build arguments, layers, and Compose source.
Scan OS and application dependencies and define remediation policy.
Sign or attest release images where the delivery platform supports verification.

performance.introduction: Optimize build feedback and runtime behavior independently.
items: Use deterministic layer ordering and a focused .dockerignore.
Keep the runtime stage free of SDK and source files.
Measure startup, memory, CPU, and request latency under container limits.
Set ASP.NET Core thread, GC, and memory behavior from observed workload needs.
Avoid writing high-volume data into the container writable layer.

deployment.introduction: Promote one verified image digest and vary only runtime configuration.
items: Publish immutable version and commit tags, then deploy by digest for strong identity.
Store images in a private registry with retention and access policy.
Inject environment configuration and secrets at runtime.
Run pre-deployment smoke and post-deployment health checks.
Retain the previous known-good digest for rollback.
Rebuild when base-image security updates arrive even if application code is unchanged.

troubleshooting.symptom: Restore reruns after every code change.
troubleshooting.cause: Source was copied before project metadata and restore.
troubleshooting.fix: Copy solution and project files first, restore, then copy source.

troubleshooting.symptom: The app works locally but the container port is unreachable.
troubleshooting.cause: The app listens on another interface or port, or no host port is published.
troubleshooting.fix: Set ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS, expose the container port, and publish the host mapping.

troubleshooting.cause: The entry point is wrong or the foreground process failed.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect container logs, run the image interactively, and verify publish output and ENTRYPOINT.

troubleshooting.symptom: A non-root container cannot write a file.
troubleshooting.cause: The path is owned by root or the filesystem is read-only.
troubleshooting.fix: Write only to an explicit mounted writable path with correct ownership, or externalize the data.

troubleshooting.symptom: A secret remains visible after deletion.
troubleshooting.cause: It was added in an earlier immutable layer.
troubleshooting.fix: Rotate the secret, remove it from build inputs, and rebuild from a clean history.

troubleshooting.symptom: Compose starts the API before its dependency is usable.
troubleshooting.cause: Process start was mistaken for readiness.
troubleshooting.fix: Add a dependency health check and gate startup or make the application retry safely.

productionChecklist: Multi-stage build copies only publish output.
Restore layers are cache-friendly and deterministic.
Runtime process is non-root and minimally privileged.
Secrets never enter image layers.
State is external or mounted deliberately.
Health, logs, and graceful termination are verified.
Final image and dependencies pass vulnerability policy.
Immutable digest, provenance, and rollback are recorded.

name: Kubernetes
shortDescription: Orchestrate containerized workloads with declarative scheduling, service discovery, rollout, and recovery.
overview: Kubernetes continuously reconciles declared workload state with running containers across a cluster.
detail: Kubernetes runs a control plane that stores declared resources and controllers that reconcile actual cluster state toward them. Pods are the scheduling unit; Deployments manage replaceable replicas and rollout; Services and EndpointSlices provide stable discovery over changing pods; and Gateway or Ingress resources control external routes. Startup, readiness, liveness, requests, limits, disruption budgets, autoscaling, and graceful termination must agree with real application behavior. Configuration, secrets, workload identity, policy, and telemetry stay separate from immutable images so the same artifact can move safely through environments.

concepts.title: Desired state
concepts.description: Controllers watch resources and repeatedly reconcile observed state toward the declared specification.

concepts.title: Pods and deployments
concepts.description: Pods are scheduling units; Deployments manage replica sets, updates, rollback, and availability.

concepts.title: Services and ingress
concepts.description: Services provide stable internal discovery while ingress or gateways expose controlled external routes.

concepts.title: Probes and resources
concepts.description: Startup, readiness, liveness, requests, and limits inform safe scheduling and traffic decisions.

concepts.title: Configuration and identity
concepts.description: ConfigMaps, Secrets, service accounts, and workload identity provide environment data and controlled access without rebuilding images.

concepts.title: Disruption and autoscaling
concepts.description: Rollout strategy, termination, disruption budgets, replica scaling, and capacity policy keep availability and demand response coordinated.

concepts.title: Storage and state
concepts.description: PersistentVolumes, claims, StatefulSets, operators, and managed services provide different ownership models for data that outlives pods.

concepts.title: Policy and observability
concepts.description: Admission policy, RBAC, network controls, events, logs, metrics, and traces make declared workloads governable and diagnosable.

architecture.description: External traffic enters a gateway and Service, which selects ready .NET pods managed by a Deployment and connected to managed state.

code.label: deployment.yaml
code.introduction: Readiness controls traffic while liveness detects a stuck process; resource requests give the scheduler useful information.
code.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/orders-api:1.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 8080 }
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }

bestPractices: Set realistic resource requests using observed workload data.
Use separate startup, readiness, and liveness semantics.
Deploy immutable image tags or digests and record configuration provenance.
Plan disruption budgets, graceful shutdown, rollout safety, and rollback together.
Apply least-privilege workload identity, pod security, and network policy.
Use managed control planes where appropriate and continuously test cluster upgrades.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between readiness and liveness probes?
interviewQuestions.answer: Readiness decides whether a pod should receive traffic. Liveness decides whether Kubernetes should restart the container.

interviewQuestions.question: What does a Kubernetes Service provide?
interviewQuestions.answer: It gives a stable virtual address and discovery name over a changing set of selected pods.

interviewQuestions.question: Why set resource requests?
interviewQuestions.answer: The scheduler uses requests to place pods, and autoscaling or capacity decisions depend on having meaningful resource expectations.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a Deployment and StatefulSet?
interviewQuestions.answer: A Deployment manages interchangeable replicas; a StatefulSet adds stable identity and ordered storage or lifecycle semantics for workloads that truly require them.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a PodDisruptionBudget not a full availability guarantee?
interviewQuestions.answer: It limits certain voluntary disruptions, but it cannot prevent node failure, application crashes, capacity shortages, or unsafe rollouts.

interviewQuestions.question: What happens during Deployment rollout?
interviewQuestions.answer: The controller creates a new ReplicaSet and scales old and new sets according to surge and unavailable limits while pod readiness determines usable capacity.

interviewQuestions.question: When should an application use a startup probe?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use it when legitimate initialization may exceed the liveness window; it prevents liveness and readiness checks from taking effect until startup succeeds.

note: Kubernetes automates declared operations; it does not make an application stateless, resilient, or observable by itself.
tip: Make the application stop accepting new work before termination and finish in-flight requests within the grace period.
warning: A liveness probe that depends on a downstream database can restart every healthy app instance during a database outage.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with dedicated workload and manifest sample
learningObjectives: Explain clusters, nodes, Pods, controllers, Services, and configuration resources.
Deploy a .NET workload with safe rollout and rollback behavior.
Design startup, readiness, and liveness probes with distinct meanings.
Set resource requests, limits, disruption protection, and autoscaling deliberately.
Apply pod security, secret, networking, and identity controls.
Operate deployments using events, logs, metrics, traces, and declarative change history.
prerequisites: Working knowledge of container images and registries.
Basic YAML, HTTP, DNS, and ASP.NET Core health behavior.
kubectl and access to a development cluster for deployment exercises.

use: Multiple containerized services need consistent scheduling, discovery, rollout, policy, and recovery.
Teams can operate a platform or use a managed Kubernetes service responsibly.
Workloads benefit from declarative scaling and portable orchestration APIs.
avoid: A small workload is simpler and cheaper on a managed application or container service.
The team cannot fund cluster security, upgrades, observability, and on-call ownership.
Using Kubernetes only to copy a virtual-machine deployment model without container readiness.

implementationIntroduction: The Kubernetes Inventory API separates liveness from readiness in application code and ships manifests for a safe Deployment, stable Service, disruption budget, pod security, resources, and horizontal autoscaling.

implementationSteps.title: Define workload ownership
implementationSteps.description: Choose a Deployment for replaceable stateless replicas and use StatefulSet or Job only when their ordering or completion semantics are required.

implementationSteps.title: Label and select consistently
implementationSteps.description: Use stable recommended labels and ensure the Deployment selector and Service selector match the pod template exactly.

implementationSteps.title: Configure the container
implementationSteps.description: Deploy an immutable image, named port, environment-neutral command, external configuration, and explicit security context.

implementationSteps.title: Model lifecycle signals
implementationSteps.description: Use startup for slow initialization, readiness for traffic eligibility, and liveness only for process states a restart can repair.

implementationSteps.title: Budget resources
implementationSteps.description: Set requests from measured steady demand, limits with runtime behavior in mind, and namespace quotas to protect shared capacity.

implementationSteps.title: Make rollout safe
implementationSteps.description: Coordinate readiness, max unavailable, surge, termination grace, pre-stop behavior, and a PodDisruptionBudget.

implementationSteps.title: Expose and scale
implementationSteps.description: Use a Service for stable discovery, Gateway or Ingress for controlled external traffic, and scale on a meaningful constrained signal.

implementationSteps.title: Secure and observe
implementationSteps.description: Apply workload identity, least-privilege RBAC, secret delivery, network policy, admission rules, structured telemetry, and actionable alerts.

testing.introduction: Validate application lifecycle behavior, rendered manifests, and real rollout behavior.
items: Unit-test readiness state transitions and cancellation.
Validate manifests against schemas and organization policy.
Deploy to an ephemeral namespace and wait for rollout completion.
Query Service endpoints rather than only port-forwarding a Pod.
Delete pods and drain a node to observe recovery and disruption behavior.
Run rollback and configuration failure drills before production.

security.introduction: Cluster defaults are not a complete workload security boundary.
items: Run as non-root with seccomp RuntimeDefault, no privilege escalation, and dropped capabilities.
Use a read-only root filesystem and explicit writable volumes.
Grant the service account only required API permissions.
Use workload identity and an external secret provider instead of long-lived credentials.
Restrict ingress and egress using network policy where the network implementation enforces it.
Enforce image provenance, approved registries, and pod standards at admission.

performance.introduction: Scheduling and autoscaling work only when requests and signals represent reality.
items: Load-test under configured CPU and memory limits.
Size requests from observed percentiles rather than guesses.
Understand .NET GC behavior under container memory limits.
Scale on latency, queue depth, concurrency, or another demand signal when CPU is insufficient.
Set stabilization and rate policies to avoid scaling oscillation.
Protect dependencies from a replica surge.

deployment.introduction: Declarative delivery should make every change observable and reversible.
items: Render and review manifests before apply.
Deploy immutable image digests and record source provenance.
Wait for rollout status and run a Service-level smoke test.
Use progressive traffic for high-risk changes.
Pause or roll back when service-level indicators regress.
Keep cluster and API-version upgrade compatibility under continuous test.

troubleshooting.cause: No node satisfies resource, affinity, taint, volume, or policy requirements.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect pod events and compare requests and scheduling constraints with node capacity.

troubleshooting.cause: The process exits, configuration is invalid, or liveness kills startup.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect previous container logs, events, exit code, and startup probe settings.

troubleshooting.symptom: Pods run but receive no Service traffic.
troubleshooting.cause: Labels, selector, target port, or readiness do not match.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect EndpointSlices, pod labels, named ports, and readiness results.

troubleshooting.cause: New pods never become ready or capacity cannot satisfy surge requests.
troubleshooting.fix: Describe the rollout and pods, correct readiness or capacity, then resume or roll back.

troubleshooting.symptom: Healthy pods restart during a database outage.
troubleshooting.cause: Liveness incorrectly depends on the database.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep liveness local to process health and place dependency state in readiness with bounded checks.

troubleshooting.cause: Requests or metric targets are missing or unrelated to demand.
troubleshooting.fix: Correct resource requests, inspect metric availability, and add stabilization behavior.

productionChecklist: Controller and service selectors are correct.
Immutable image identity and provenance are recorded.
Startup, readiness, and liveness semantics are distinct.
Requests, limits, and autoscaling are load-tested.
Graceful termination and disruption budgets are verified.
Pod security, RBAC, identity, secrets, and network policy are enforced.
Rollout, smoke, rollback, and disaster drills are automated.
Events, logs, metrics, traces, and service objectives are actionable.

name: Testing
shortDescription: Build confidence through focused unit, integration, contract, and end-to-end feedback loops.
overview: Testing provides layered evidence that units, integrations, contracts, and complete user flows behave as intended.
detail: A production test strategy allocates evidence according to risk. Unit tests give fast, deterministic feedback on policy and edge cases; integration tests exercise real framework, serialization, persistence, and authentication boundaries; contract tests protect the shape and meaning exchanged between independently changing components; and a deliberately small set of end-to-end tests proves critical user outcomes in a deployed environment. Test doubles belong at narrow controllable boundaries, not around every class. Reliable suites control time, randomness, identifiers, concurrency, data, and asynchronous completion. They report the violated behavior clearly, run independently in any order, and fail for one diagnosable reason. Coverage is a gap-finding signal rather than a quality target. Teams should define test ownership, quarantine rules, retry policy, fixtures, data reset, and CI lanes, then track flake rate and time-to-diagnosis alongside pass rate.

concepts.title: Risk-based strategy
concepts.description: Choose evidence from failure impact and uncertainty instead of enforcing a fixed pyramid quota.

concepts.title: Unit tests
concepts.description: Exercise deterministic policy and edge cases quickly without infrastructure or process boundaries.

concepts.title: Integration tests
concepts.description: Verify real framework, database, HTTP, serialization, identity, or broker behavior at selected boundaries.

concepts.title: Contract tests
concepts.description: Protect request, response, event, and error compatibility between producers and consumers.

concepts.title: End-to-end journeys
concepts.description: Prove a few business-critical outcomes through the deployed surface and its real integrations.

concepts.title: Test doubles
concepts.description: Use fakes, stubs, or mocks at narrow outbound seams when control or observation is valuable.

concepts.title: Determinism and isolation
concepts.description: Control time, randomness, concurrency, and data so tests can run independently in any order.

concepts.title: Suite operations
concepts.description: Flake ownership, diagnostics, parallel lanes, and failure triage determine whether tests remain trusted.

architecture.description: A balanced suite gives broad, fast domain feedback and progressively narrower but higher-fidelity checks at system boundaries.

code.label: OrderTests.cs
code.introduction: A useful test names the behavior, arranges only relevant state, and asserts an externally meaningful outcome.

bestPractices: Test observable behavior.
Choose levels from risk.
Control time and randomness.
Use real providers where semantics matter.
Keep fixtures isolated.
Treat flakes as defects.
Capture useful failure evidence.
Delete redundant slow tests.

interviewQuestions.question: What should be mocked?
interviewQuestions.answer: Mock narrow outbound boundaries when controlling behavior is valuable; keep domain collaborators concrete.

interviewQuestions.question: Unit versus integration test?
interviewQuestions.answer: A unit test isolates deterministic policy; an integration test verifies collaboration with a real framework or provider boundary.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a contract test?
interviewQuestions.answer: It verifies the shape and meaning one component promises another without requiring the entire deployed journey.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you reduce flakes?
interviewQuestions.answer: Control time, concurrency, data, ports, and async completion, then assign ownership instead of retrying blindly.

interviewQuestions.question: Why not maximize code coverage?
interviewQuestions.answer: Coverage shows executed lines, not meaningful assertions, missing risks, or production compatibility.

interviewQuestions.question: When is an end-to-end test justified?
interviewQuestions.answer: For a small business-critical journey whose value depends on the deployed components working together.

interviewQuestions.question: How should CI tests be layered?
interviewQuestions.answer: Fast deterministic checks first, provider and contract evidence before merge, and deployment smoke journeys after release.

note: Coverage is a map of executed code, not proof that the right behaviors and failure cases were asserted.
tip: Write a regression test that fails for the reported defect before changing production code.
warning: An in-memory database substitute may not reproduce relational constraints, transactions, collation, or SQL translation.
latestNote: Gold-standard strategy with unit, HTTP integration, contract, and journey tests
learningObjectives: Map test levels to concrete product risks.
Write deterministic behavior-focused unit tests.
Exercise the real ASP.NET Core HTTP pipeline.
Protect success and error contracts.
Control fixtures, time, data, and concurrency.
Operate a fast and trusted CI suite.
prerequisites: C# async code, dependency injection, HTTP, and JSON fundamentals.
A list of critical journeys and expensive failure modes.
Basic xUnit or equivalent test-runner experience.

use: Unit tests for dense deterministic policy.
Integration tests where framework or provider behavior matters.
End-to-end tests for a small set of critical journeys.
avoid: Mocking every internal collaborator.
Using one test level for every risk.
Retrying failures until a flaky suite looks green.

implementationIntroduction: The sample separates deterministic order policy tests from real ASP.NET Core HTTP integration, validation-contract checks, and a create-then-read journey.

implementationSteps.title: List risks
implementationSteps.description: Rank critical outcomes, complex policy, integration uncertainty, and costly regressions.

implementationSteps.title: Assign evidence
implementationSteps.description: Select the cheapest test level that can reveal each important failure.

implementationSteps.title: Create deterministic seams
implementationSteps.description: Inject time and external boundaries while keeping domain objects concrete.

implementationSteps.title: Test policy
implementationSteps.description: Cover nominal behavior, boundaries, invalid input, and invariants with fast unit tests.

implementationSteps.title: Test integrations
implementationSteps.description: Run the actual HTTP pipeline, serialization, middleware, and provider where behavior differs.

implementationSteps.title: Protect contracts
implementationSteps.description: Assert stable success, validation, error, and event shapes without overspecifying internals.

implementationSteps.title: Operate the suite
implementationSteps.description: Parallelize safe tests, capture diagnostics, measure flakes, and remove redundant slow checks.

testing.introduction: The testing system itself needs tests and operational rules.
items: Prove tests fail when the behavior is deliberately broken.
Run in random order and in parallel.
Repeat timing-sensitive tests under stress.
Validate fixtures clean up after cancellation.
Track runtime and flake rate per lane.
Review contract changes as API changes.

security.introduction: Tests must verify authorization boundaries without turning secrets or personal data into fixtures.
items: Include negative authorization tests.
Use synthetic non-sensitive data.
Keep secrets outside source and test output.
Redact captured requests and snapshots.
Test abuse limits and validation.

performance.introduction: Fast feedback is a product feature of the suite.
items: Keep policy tests in the fastest lane.
Share expensive immutable fixtures safely.
Parallelize isolated tests.
Move only critical journeys to end-to-end.
Profile slow tests before adding retries.

deployment.introduction: Different evidence runs at different release stages.
items: Run unit and focused integration tests on every change.
Run provider and contract tests before merge.
Run smoke tests after deployment.
Gate promotion on critical journeys.
Retain artifacts and diagnostics for failures.

troubleshooting.symptom: A test passes alone but fails in suite.
troubleshooting.cause: State, port, clock, or data is shared.
troubleshooting.fix: Give each test isolated state and remove ordering assumptions.

troubleshooting.cause: Work is not awaited or cancellation is ignored.
troubleshooting.fix: Await completion, apply a timeout, and propagate cancellation.

troubleshooting.cause: Tests specify internal collaboration.
troubleshooting.fix: Assert observable outcomes and mock only stable boundaries.

troubleshooting.cause: A substitute does not match the real provider.
troubleshooting.fix: Use provider-real infrastructure for provider behavior.

troubleshooting.cause: Retry hides nondeterminism.
troubleshooting.fix: Quarantine with ownership and fix the uncontrolled input.

troubleshooting.cause: Assertions and captured context are vague.
troubleshooting.fix: Name behavior, keep assertions focused, and attach diagnostics.

productionChecklist: Critical risks map to test evidence.
Unit tests are deterministic and fast.
Real boundaries have integration coverage.
Success and error contracts are protected.
Authorization has negative tests.
Fixtures isolate data and clean up.
Flake rate and duration are owned.
Post-deploy smoke evidence is retained.

name: Performance
shortDescription: Measure latency, throughput, allocation, and saturation before optimizing the system bottleneck.
overview: Performance engineering turns user and capacity goals into measurable budgets, diagnoses bottlenecks, and validates improvements under realistic load.
detail: Performance engineering begins with a user, business, or capacity objective and an explicit budget for latency percentiles, throughput, errors, resource use, and cost. Always-on metrics reveal saturation and regressions; distributed traces locate critical-path time; profiles identify CPU and allocation hotspots; database plans expose I/O; BenchmarkDotNet isolates repeatable code paths; and production-shaped load tests show queuing, contention, dependency limits, and failure behavior. The highest-value improvements usually eliminate unnecessary network or database work, bound concurrency and queues, reduce payloads, batch calls, choose appropriate caching, and remove allocations only from proven hot paths. Release builds, realistic inputs, steady-state warmup, multiple runs, confidence intervals, and environmental notes keep evidence honest. An optimization is incomplete until correctness, tail latency, memory, throughput, cost, rollback, and post-deployment telemetry show improvement without shifting the bottleneck or weakening reliability.
learningObjectives: Translate user and capacity goals into latency, throughput, error, resource, and cost budgets.
Choose metrics, traces, profiles, benchmarks, and load tests for distinct questions.
Diagnose queuing, saturation, I/O, contention, allocation, GC, and thread-pool problems.
Build statistically useful BenchmarkDotNet experiments with realistic inputs and release settings.
Optimize the measured constraint while preserving correctness and reliability.
Verify performance in production-shaped deployment and prevent regressions.
prerequisites: Asynchronous .NET, HTTP and database I/O, memory allocation, and concurrency basics.
Metrics, traces, logs, release builds, and automated tests.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the telemetry parser benchmarks.

use: Use production telemetry to locate the user-visible or capacity constraint before creating a benchmark.
Use BenchmarkDotNet for isolated repeatable code paths and load tests for end-to-end concurrency.
Use profiles when you need evidence of where CPU time, allocation, locks, or I/O is spent.
avoid: Do not optimize from intuition, averages, debug builds, or one stopwatch result.
Do not trade correctness, security, maintainability, or resilience for an unmeasured micro-gain.
Do not use a microbenchmark to claim whole-system scalability.
Do not leave caches, queues, concurrency, payloads, or cardinality unbounded.

concepts.title: Latency and percentiles
concepts.description: Median describes typical response while tail percentiles reveal slow experiences hidden by averages.

concepts.title: Throughput and saturation
concepts.description: Work per interval must be understood beside queues, CPU, memory, connections, and dependency capacity.

concepts.title: Allocation and GC
concepts.description: Allocation rate and object lifetime influence collection frequency, pauses, and memory footprint.

concepts.title: Measurement
concepts.description: Benchmarks isolate code; load tests evaluate systems; profiles locate time and allocation in realistic paths.

concepts.title: Critical path
concepts.description: End-to-end latency follows dependent work, so optimizing parallel or non-critical work may not change the user outcome.

concepts.title: Queuing and contention
concepts.description: Locks, pools, thread starvation, and arrival rates can create nonlinear tail latency before CPU reaches 100 percent.

concepts.title: Benchmark validity
concepts.description: Warmup, release compilation, realistic data, consumed results, isolated noise, and statistical distributions make measurements credible.

concepts.title: Performance budgets
concepts.description: A measurable SLO and resource envelope turns optimization into an acceptance decision rather than an endless activity.

architecture.description: A request budget is consumed across edge, application, cache, database, and network calls, all observed through correlated telemetry.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated sample starts with an allocation-heavy string-splitting parser, preserves its contract in tests, introduces a span-based implementation, and measures both through BenchmarkDotNet with MemoryDiagnoser. On the measured machine the span path was about 0.69 times the mean latency and eliminated the baseline's 208-byte allocation, but the sample records that results are environment-specific.

implementationSteps.title: Define the objective
implementationSteps.description: Choose the user journey, percentile, throughput, resource, error, and cost target.

implementationSteps.title: Capture a baseline
implementationSteps.description: Record representative production telemetry, environment, workload, and current result before editing code.

implementationSteps.title: Locate the constraint
implementationSteps.description: Follow traces and profiles through queues, application code, database, cache, network, and downstream dependencies.

implementationSteps.title: Protect correctness
implementationSteps.description: Add parity and edge-case tests so an optimization cannot silently change behavior.

implementationSteps.title: Create the experiment
implementationSteps.description: Use BenchmarkDotNet or a production-shaped load test with realistic inputs and controlled variables.

implementationSteps.title: Evaluate tradeoffs
implementationSteps.description: Compare distribution, allocation, throughput, saturation, error, readability, and operational cost.

implementationSteps.title: Deploy and guard
implementationSteps.description: Roll out safely, compare real telemetry, retain rollback, and add a regression budget.

testing.introduction: Performance evidence sits beside functional tests; it never replaces them.
items: Prove baseline and optimized implementations return identical results for representative and invalid inputs.
Run BenchmarkDotNet in Release without a debugger and consume return values.
Use several iterations and report distribution, runtime, hardware, GC mode, and allocations.
Load-test concurrency, ramp, steady state, burst, dependency slowdown, and recovery.
Set regression thresholds only after understanding environment noise and statistical variance.
Re-run production telemetry after deployment to confirm the end-to-end objective.

security.introduction: Performance controls are also availability controls and must not expose sensitive diagnostic data.
items: Bound requests, concurrency, queues, caches, result sets, fan-out, and expensive operations.
Authorize diagnostic endpoints and protect dumps, traces, profiles, query plans, and benchmark inputs.
Do not remove validation, cryptography, tenant isolation, or audit evidence for speed.
Redact secrets and personal data from profiling artifacts and high-cardinality labels.
Threat-model cache poisoning, algorithmic complexity, decompression, regex, and resource-exhaustion paths.

performance.introduction: Optimize in descending order of measured end-to-end impact.
items: Eliminate unnecessary work and round trips before micro-optimizing syntax.
Batch or parallelize only independent work within downstream capacity and cancellation bounds.
Use pooling and spans only where profiles show allocation or copying is material.
Tune GC, thread pool, connection pools, and server limits only with workload evidence.
Track P50, P95, P99, throughput, errors, saturation, allocation rate, heap, GC pauses, and queue time together.

deployment.introduction: Hardware, runtime, containers, proxies, databases, and neighboring workloads change performance behavior.
items: Match architecture, runtime, GC mode, CPU and memory limits, database scale, and network path to production.
Warm caches and JIT deliberately or include cold behavior in the objective.
Use canary or staged rollout and compare the same metrics against a baseline cohort.
Set alerts on user SLOs and saturation rather than one host metric.
Keep benchmark reports, load models, dashboards, rollback, and capacity assumptions versioned.

troubleshooting.symptom: Average latency is healthy but users time out.
troubleshooting.cause: Tail percentiles or a subset of operations are slow.
troubleshooting.fix: Segment normalized operations and inspect P95 and P99 traces plus queue time.

troubleshooting.symptom: CPU is low while latency rises.
troubleshooting.cause: The service is waiting on I/O, locks, pools, queues, or thread starvation.
troubleshooting.fix: Correlate traces, counters, thread stacks, connection pools, and dependency latency.

troubleshooting.symptom: A benchmark changes dramatically between runs.
troubleshooting.cause: Debugging, thermal or power state, background load, JIT, input, or insufficient iterations differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Use BenchmarkDotNet, stable release conditions, multiple runs, and report variance.

troubleshooting.cause: An unbounded cache or queue, retained object graph, or slow consumer accumulates work.
troubleshooting.fix: Capture counters and a memory profile, then bound and backpressure the owning structure.

troubleshooting.symptom: An optimization improves benchmark time but not the API.
troubleshooting.cause: The optimized code is not the end-to-end constraint.
troubleshooting.fix: Return to the critical-path trace and target database, network, queue, or dominant work.

troubleshooting.cause: A finite dependency, pool, CPU, lock, or quota has saturated.
troubleshooting.fix: Find the first saturated resource, apply admission control, and scale or reduce work there.

productionChecklist: User and capacity objectives define percentile, throughput, error, resource, and cost budgets.
Representative baseline telemetry and workload are captured.
Critical-path traces and profiles identify the actual constraint.
Correctness and security parity tests protect every optimization.
Benchmarks use Release, realistic inputs, warmup, consumed results, allocations, and reported environment.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are percentiles better than average latency alone?
interviewQuestions.answer: Averages hide the distribution. P95 or P99 reveal tail experiences that often dominate timeouts and user dissatisfaction.

interviewQuestions.question: When can caching make a system worse?
interviewQuestions.answer: It adds invalidation, staleness, memory, stampede, and consistency concerns; low reuse or oversized keys can cost more than the saved work.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a benchmark and a load test?
interviewQuestions.answer: A benchmark isolates a code path under controlled conditions. A load test exercises a system under concurrency and dependency constraints.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can low CPU coexist with high latency?
interviewQuestions.answer: Requests may be waiting on database or network I/O, locks, queues, thread-pool work, or exhausted connection pools rather than executing on CPU.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes a microbenchmark trustworthy?
interviewQuestions.answer: Release compilation, warmup, representative inputs, consumed outputs, isolated conditions, multiple measurements, allocation evidence, and a recorded runtime and machine.

interviewQuestions.question: What is coordinated omission in load testing?
interviewQuestions.answer: A load generator waits for slow responses and therefore sends less work during stalls, undercounting the latency users would experience at the intended arrival rate.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you know an optimization succeeded?
interviewQuestions.answer: Correctness remains intact and production-shaped evidence improves the target budget without unacceptable regressions in tails, errors, resources, cost, or maintainability.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a performance budget?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is an explicit acceptable limit for a user or capacity outcome such as P95 latency, throughput, memory, CPU, allocation, database calls, payload size, or cost.

note: Optimize the constraint that limits the user or capacity objective, not the code that merely looks inefficient.
tip: Capture a trace for a slow request and follow the critical path before opening a microbenchmark project.
warning: Unbounded caches and queues can convert a latency problem into memory exhaustion during sustained load.

name: Background & Hosted Services
shortDescription: Run recurring, queued, and long-lived work outside the request path with hosted services and job schedulers.
overview: Background processing lets an application do meaningful work—emails, media pipelines, cleanup, retries—without blocking a request or depending on a client staying connected.
detail: The .NET Generic Host starts registered IHostedService instances, coordinates BackgroundService execution, propagates cancellation, and gives each service a bounded graceful-shutdown window. In-process workers suit lifecycle-bound loops, polling, telemetry, and best-effort local queues; they do not make accepted work durable. A bounded Channel can separate producers and consumers while applying backpressure, but pending items disappear when the process fails. Durable schedulers, databases, or brokers are required for work that must survive restart, coordinate replicas, run once according to a business schedule, or support operator replay. Hosted services are singletons, so each item creates and disposes its own dependency-injection scope. Production loops avoid overlapping timers, propagate cancellation, isolate item failures, bound retries and concurrency, make effects idempotent, expose progress and oldest-work age, stop admission before drain, and checkpoint unfinished durable work before the shutdown deadline.

concepts.title: Hosted services

concepts.title: Durable job scheduling

concepts.title: Idempotent processing
concepts.description: A retried or redelivered job must produce the same outcome as a single successful run, usually enforced with a processed-work record.

concepts.title: Claim-based concurrency
concepts.description: Database-native locking—unique constraints and a LockedUntil column—lets multiple workers pick up jobs safely without an in-app mutex.

architecture.description: A producer enqueues durable job records; one or more workers claim and process them, writing results back to the same store they were claimed from.

bestPractices: Make every job handler idempotent; assume at-least-once delivery and possible redelivery.

Emit structured logs and metrics per job run so stuck or slow jobs are visible before they become an incident.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between IHostedService and a job scheduler like Hangfire?
interviewQuestions.answer: IHostedService is an in-process, code-driven worker tied to the application's own lifetime; a scheduler like Hangfire persists job state externally, so scheduling, retries, and visibility survive restarts and can be distributed across workers.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does at-least-once delivery matter for background jobs?
interviewQuestions.answer: Most schedulers retry on failure or after a crash, so a handler can run more than once for the same logical job; without idempotency this can double-charge, double-send, or corrupt state.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you stop two worker instances from processing the same job?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use the job store's own concurrency control—row-level locking, a unique claim constraint, or a LockedUntil column—rather than an in-memory lock, since workers may run in separate processes or machines.

name: Observability & OpenTelemetry
shortDescription: Connect traces, metrics, and logs across services so production behavior is diagnosable, not guessed at.
overview: Observability means being able to ask new questions about a running system without shipping new code—usually by combining correlated traces, metrics, and structured logs.
detail: Observability is the ability to explain unfamiliar production behavior from emitted evidence. OpenTelemetry gives .NET applications vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs, semantic conventions, context propagation, sampling, processing, and exporters for traces, metrics, and logs. Traces connect causally related spans, metrics summarize rate and distributions, and structured logs capture event detail; correlation turns them into one investigation path. Instrument service boundaries first, then add business spans and low-cardinality measurements that answer operational questions. Propagate W3C trace context across HTTP and message metadata, preserve baggage carefully, and never place secrets or unbounded identifiers in metric dimensions. Sampling and processors control cost but must preserve useful errors and exemplars. Collectors decouple applications from backends, add batching and routing, and become part of capacity planning. Define service-level indicators before dashboards, test telemetry shape, and alert on user-visible symptoms.

concepts.description: Receivers, processors, and exporters batch, enrich, filter, and route signals independently of application code.

code.introduction: Registering OpenTelemetry once at startup instruments ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, and EF Core without touching business code.
code.code:
builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .ConfigureResource(resource => resource.AddService("orders-api"))
    .WithTracing(tracing => tracing
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddHttpClientInstrumentation()
        .AddEntityFrameworkCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter())
    .WithMetrics(metrics => metrics
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddRuntimeInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter());

interviewQuestions.question: Why are logs alone insufficient for distributed requests?
interviewQuestions.answer: They lack a causal operation graph unless trace context consistently correlates events across services.

interviewQuestions.question: Counter versus histogram?
interviewQuestions.answer: A counter totals occurrences; a histogram records a value distribution such as duration or payload size.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is metric cardinality dangerous?
interviewQuestions.answer: Every unique dimension combination creates a time series and can overwhelm cost and query capacity.

interviewQuestions.question: What does the collector provide?
interviewQuestions.answer: A vendor-neutral place to batch, enrich, filter, route, and export telemetry.

interviewQuestions.question: Head versus tail sampling?
interviewQuestions.answer: Head sampling decides near trace start; tail sampling decides after observing more of the completed trace.

interviewQuestions.question: What belongs in resource attributes?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stable producer identity such as service name, version, environment, and instance.

interviewQuestions.question: How do traces and logs correlate?
interviewQuestions.answer: Log records include the current trace and span identifiers from the active Activity context.

note: Observability is a property of the system's design, not a dashboard added after an incident.
tip: Pick a small set of golden signals—latency, traffic, errors, saturation—per service and make sure they are wired end to end before adding anything fancier.
warning: Sampling every trace at high volume can be expensive and slow; use head- or tail-based sampling once traffic grows, but keep error traces at full fidelity.

name: CI/CD for .NET
shortDescription: Automate build, test, and deployment so every change is verified and shipped the same way, every time.
overview: A CI/CD pipeline turns ‘it works on my machine’ into a repeatable, observable process: restore, build, test, package, and deploy the same way for every change.
detail: Continuous integration gives every proposed change fast, repeatable evidence through deterministic restore, compilation, tests, analysis, and security checks. Continuous delivery produces a verified release that is always ready to promote; continuous deployment also performs that promotion automatically when policy passes. A trustworthy .NET pipeline pins tools and dependencies, builds one immutable artifact, attaches source and digest metadata, and promotes the identical bytes through protected environments. Least-privilege identity, isolated untrusted code, observable rollout, database compatibility, and tested rollback make deployment automation safe rather than merely fast.

concepts.title: Pipeline stages
concepts.description: Restore, build, test, and publish run in order so a fast failure in an early stage avoids wasting time on later ones.

concepts.title: Artifacts
concepts.description: A pipeline should build one deployable artifact once and promote that same artifact through environments, not rebuild per environment.

concepts.title: Quality gates
concepts.description: Required checks—tests, coverage thresholds, static analysis, vulnerability scans—block a merge or deployment until they pass.

concepts.title: Environments and promotion
concepts.description: Separate environments with their own configuration and approval rules let a change move from validation toward production deliberately.

concepts.title: Identity and permissions
concepts.description: Job-scoped tokens, protected environments, and OIDC federation give each stage only the short-lived access it needs.

concepts.title: Release safety and feedback
concepts.description: Progressive delivery, smoke tests, service indicators, concurrency controls, rollback, and delivery metrics close the operational loop.

concepts.title: Reproducibility and caching
concepts.description: Pinned SDKs, lock files, deterministic commands, isolated runners, and correctly keyed caches keep results explainable.

concepts.title: Provenance and audit
concepts.description: Commit identity, artifact digests, SBOMs, attestations, approvals, and deployment records connect source review to production state.

architecture.description: A commit triggers a pipeline that restores, builds, and tests the change, then packages and promotes one artifact through environments toward production.

code.label: .github/workflows/ci.yml
code.introduction: A focused workflow restores, builds, and tests on every pull request before anything is published.
code.code:
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with:
          dotnet-version: '10.0.x'
      - run: dotnet restore
      - run: dotnet build --no-restore -c Release
      - run: dotnet test --no-build -c Release --logger trx

bestPractices: Fail fast: run restore, build, and unit tests before anything slow like integration tests or container builds.
Build the deployable artifact once and reuse it across every environment instead of rebuilding per stage.
Pin tool and action versions so a pipeline behaves the same today and in six months.
Keep secrets in the platform's secret store, never in workflow files or environment variables checked into source.
Use explicit least-privilege permissions and short-lived federated deployment identity.
Automate smoke evidence and preserve a rehearsed rollback path for every production release.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
interviewQuestions.answer: Continuous delivery means every change is automatically verified and ready to release, with a manual approval to actually deploy; continuous deployment removes that manual gate and ships automatically once checks pass.

interviewQuestions.question: Why build one artifact and promote it, instead of rebuilding for each environment?
interviewQuestions.answer: Rebuilding per environment risks shipping code that differs from what was tested—different dependency versions, timestamps, or compiler output—so promoting one immutable artifact keeps what you tested and what you ship identical.

interviewQuestions.question: How should a pipeline handle a failing quality gate?
interviewQuestions.answer: It should block the merge or deployment, report the specific failure clearly, and leave the previous known-good artifact in place rather than partially deploying a change.

interviewQuestions.question: Why prefer OIDC over a stored cloud credential?
interviewQuestions.answer: OIDC exchanges trusted workflow identity for short-lived scoped access, avoiding a long-lived secret that can leak, be copied, or outlive its intended job.

interviewQuestions.question: How do database changes affect rollback?
interviewQuestions.answer: A binary rollback can fail after a breaking schema migration, so use backward-compatible expand-and-contract changes and verify old and new versions during transition.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a deployment environment?
interviewQuestions.answer: It scopes configuration, protection rules, identity, concurrency, approvals, and audit history for a target such as staging or production.

interviewQuestions.question: Which delivery metrics are most useful?
interviewQuestions.answer: Lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, and recovery time reveal both flow and stability when interpreted with product and reliability context.

note: A pipeline is production code: version it, review changes to it, and test that it still does what you expect.
tip: Cache dependency restores between runs, but invalidate the cache on lockfile changes so a stale cache never hides a real dependency problem.
warning: A pipeline that deploys on green tests but has no rollback plan turns every bad merge into a production incident.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated build-once promotion workflow
learningObjectives: Separate continuous integration, delivery, deployment, and release management.
Design a fast .NET verification pipeline with deterministic inputs.
Build one immutable artifact and promote it through environments.
Apply quality, security, approval, and provenance gates proportionally.
Use short-lived workload identity and least-privilege pipeline permissions.
Operate deployments with progressive exposure, observability, rollback, and measurable delivery performance.
prerequisites: Git branching, pull requests, and basic GitHub Actions concepts.
Ability to restore, build, test, publish, and audit a .NET solution locally.
A target environment with a defined deployment and rollback mechanism.

use: Every merge needs consistent automated verification.
Releases must be traceable from source to artifact to environment.
Teams need repeatable deployment, approval, rollback, and audit evidence.
avoid: Automating an undefined manual process before ownership and rollback are clear.
Giving one pipeline broad permanent credentials across all environments.
Adding slow gates that do not map to a concrete risk or decision.

implementationIntroduction: The CI/CD Release Pipeline verifies a .NET 10 solution, audits dependencies, publishes one release artifact, preserves commit and digest identity, and promotes that artifact through a protected production environment without rebuilding.

implementationSteps.title: Define the release contract
implementationSteps.description: Specify source trigger, version identity, artifact contents, environments, approvals, deployment mechanism, evidence, owner, and rollback.

implementationSteps.title: Make local commands authoritative
implementationSteps.description: Ensure the same restore, build, test, publish, audit, and smoke commands work locally and in CI.

implementationSteps.title: Restore deterministically
implementationSteps.description: Pin the SDK and tools, commit lock files where appropriate, use locked restore, and key caches from dependency inputs.

implementationSteps.title: Fail fast in CI
implementationSteps.description: Run formatting or compilation and fast tests before expensive integration, container, or end-to-end stages.

implementationSteps.title: Create one artifact
implementationSteps.description: Publish once after verification, calculate its digest, attach source and version metadata, generate an SBOM, and retain it immutably.

implementationSteps.title: Promote through environments
implementationSteps.description: Download the same artifact in deployment jobs and vary configuration, identity, and approval policy rather than rebuilding binaries.

implementationSteps.title: Secure the workflow
implementationSteps.description: Minimize token permissions, isolate untrusted pull requests, protect environments, and exchange OIDC identity for short-lived cloud access.

implementationSteps.title: Observe and improve
implementationSteps.description: Record deployment status, run smoke checks, automate rollback signals, and measure lead time, frequency, failure rate, and recovery time.

items: Run unit and focused integration tests on every pull request.
Exercise workflow changes on a safe branch or disposable environment.
Assert artifacts contain expected files and metadata.
Verify artifact digests before deployment.
Run post-deployment smoke and critical-journey checks.
Practice rollback, credential expiry, runner failure, and partial deployment recovery.
