items: Set explicit minimal permissions for every job.
Never expose deployment secrets to untrusted fork workflows.
Prefer OIDC federation and short-lived credentials over stored cloud keys.
Pin dependencies, tools, actions, and reusable workflows to reviewed versions or commits.
Scan dependencies, source, containers, and infrastructure definitions.
Generate provenance and an SBOM and verify policy before promotion.

performance.introduction: Fast trusted feedback improves both developer flow and recovery speed.
items: Measure queue time separately from execution time.
Cache only reproducible dependencies and invalidate from lock inputs.
Parallelize independent test lanes without sharing mutable state.
Use change-aware selection carefully and retain a full verification lane.
Publish test results immediately when a stage fails.
Remove redundant gates after proving they cover the same risk.

deployment.introduction: Release progressively and preserve a clear route back to the last known-good state.
items: Protect production with environment-specific authorization and concurrency control.
Deploy the verified artifact by immutable version or digest.
Apply database changes with backward-compatible expand-and-contract sequencing.
Use rolling, blue-green, or canary exposure based on risk.
Gate progression on health and service-level indicators.
Record who deployed what, where, when, and with which evidence.

troubleshooting.symptom: CI passes locally but fails on the runner.
troubleshooting.cause: SDK, OS, locale, time, file casing, or hidden dependencies differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Pin the environment, remove machine assumptions, and reproduce using the runner image or container.

troubleshooting.cause: The cache key does not include lock or project dependency inputs.
troubleshooting.fix: Key caches from dependency files and treat cache as optimization rather than source of truth.

troubleshooting.symptom: Deployment contains code different from staging.
troubleshooting.cause: The pipeline rebuilt separately for each environment.
troubleshooting.fix: Publish once, store immutably, and promote the identical digest.

troubleshooting.symptom: A secret is printed in logs.
troubleshooting.cause: A command echoed credentials or masking was incomplete.
troubleshooting.fix: Rotate it, remove logging, use secret-safe inputs, and prefer federated identity.

troubleshooting.cause: No environment concurrency policy exists.
troubleshooting.fix: Serialize deployments per environment and define whether newer runs cancel queued or active work.

troubleshooting.symptom: Rollback restores code but the service remains broken.
troubleshooting.cause: Schema or configuration changes were not backward compatible.
troubleshooting.fix: Use expand-and-contract migrations, version configuration, and test full rollback paths.

productionChecklist: SDK, tools, dependencies, and actions are pinned.
Restore, build, test, audit, and publish commands are reproducible locally.
One immutable artifact is promoted without rebuild.
Pipeline permissions and environment identities are least privilege.
Untrusted code cannot access protected credentials.
Artifact digest, provenance, SBOM, and source commit are traceable.
Deployment health, concurrency, approval, and rollback are automated.
Delivery speed, failure rate, and recovery time are measured.

name: .NET Aspire
shortDescription: Orchestrate multi-project .NET applications locally with service discovery, dashboards, and consistent configuration.
overview: Aspire is a code-first orchestration and observability layer for distributed applications, giving teams one application model for services, data stores, queues, containers, executables, and cloud dependencies.
detail: An AppHost declares resources and relationships in C# or TypeScript. Aspire starts the development topology, injects references and endpoints, evaluates health and dependencies, and exposes logs, metrics, traces, commands, and lifecycle state in the dashboard. It supports multi-language workloads, but it is not an application framework, cloud provider, or production runtime; deployment still needs an explicit target and production-grade infrastructure decisions.
learningObjectives: Explain Aspire's application model and what it does not replace.
Model projects, containers, executables, data stores, parameters, and dependencies in an AppHost.
Use resource references and service discovery instead of hardcoded local endpoints.
Apply health checks, telemetry, logs, traces, and metrics through shared service defaults.
Run and debug a multi-resource system through the CLI, dashboard, and IDE tooling.
Test the application model and critical resource journeys in automated pipelines.
Publish or deploy the model while choosing production identity, networking, storage, scaling, and secrets explicitly.
Keep AppHost declarations reviewable, portable, secure, and aligned with the real architecture.
prerequisites: .NET project and dependency-injection fundamentals.
Basic distributed application, container, health-check, and OpenTelemetry concepts.
Docker-compatible container runtime when the model includes container resources.
A .NET 10 SDK and stable Aspire CLI to run the dedicated service-map sample.

use: Use Aspire when developers must coordinate several services or dependencies consistently from one model.
Use it to standardize service discovery, health, telemetry, local resource lifecycle, and onboarding.
Use multi-language resources when one distributed system spans .NET, JavaScript, Python, Java, Go, or other runtimes.
Use its publish and deployment integrations as inputs to an explicit target-platform design.
avoid: Do not present Aspire as a production scheduler, cloud, service mesh, or replacement for Kubernetes or Container Apps.
Do not hide business logic, migrations, or environment-specific provisioning inside a sprawling AppHost.
Do not assume a development container has production durability, security, backups, or scale.
Do not add Aspire to a single-process application unless the application-model and observability benefits justify it.
tradeoffs: One application model reduces setup drift but adds Aspire SDK, CLI, and integration version management.
Automatic references reduce hardcoded configuration while still requiring deliberate naming and secret boundaries.
Rich local observability accelerates diagnosis, but production exporters, retention, access, and costs remain separate decisions.
Deployment integrations speed delivery for supported targets, while portability still depends on avoiding target-specific assumptions in application code.

concepts.title: AppHost
concepts.description: A C# or TypeScript application model declares services, frontends, databases, caches, queues, containers, executables, and their relationships.

concepts.title: Service discovery
concepts.description: Dependent projects receive resolved endpoints for the resources they reference instead of hardcoded URLs or ports.

concepts.title: Integrations
concepts.description: Hosting integrations model resources while client integrations configure health, resilience, telemetry, and provider clients inside workloads.

concepts.title: Dashboard
concepts.description: The dashboard shows resource lifecycle, endpoints, commands, structured logs, traces, and metrics across the running application.

concepts.title: Resource graph
concepts.description: References, wait conditions, parent-child relationships, endpoints, parameters, and annotations form an inspectable dependency graph.

concepts.title: Service defaults
concepts.description: A shared project can apply OpenTelemetry, health checks, service discovery, and HttpClient resilience consistently to .NET services.

concepts.title: Testing
concepts.description: Aspire testing starts the AppHost under test, resolves resource endpoints, waits for readiness, and exercises real cross-resource journeys.

concepts.title: Publishing
concepts.description: The application model can produce deployment artifacts or feed target integrations, but production topology and governance remain explicit choices.

architecture.description: The AppHost starts and wires together each declared resource, injecting configuration and endpoints while the dashboard observes all of them together.

code.label: AppHost.cs
code.introduction: The AppHost project describes resources once; dependent projects reference them by name instead of configuring connection strings manually.

implementationSteps: Install a stable Aspire CLI compatible with the selected AppHost SDK and pin versions through repository policy.
Create an AppHost and add each project, container, executable, datastore, queue, parameter, and external endpoint with stable names.
Express dependencies with typed references, wait conditions, endpoints, environment values, and persistent volumes only where development state should survive.
Apply service defaults and client integrations so health, discovery, resilience, telemetry, and provider clients follow one convention.
Run the complete model, inspect dashboard resource state and traces, and remove hardcoded ports and duplicate startup scripts.
Add model tests and critical journey tests that start the AppHost, wait for readiness, resolve endpoints, and capture diagnostics on failure.
Choose a production target, map development resources to managed equivalents, provision identity and networking with IaC, publish immutable artifacts, and verify the deployed topology.

testing.introduction: Test both the declared resource graph and the behavior of the distributed application it starts.
items: Unit-test custom topology rules, naming, parameter validation, and environment-specific choices.
Use Aspire hosting testing to start the AppHost and wait for named resources to become healthy.
Resolve endpoints from the model and run real HTTP or messaging journeys instead of hardcoding test ports.
Exercise missing dependency, slow readiness, restart, transient failure, and cancellation behavior.
Run container-backed tests in CI with sufficient runtime, port, memory, and diagnostic permissions.
Preserve AppHost logs, dashboard telemetry, resource events, and test traces when startup or readiness fails.

security.introduction: The AppHost handles powerful configuration and process orchestration, so development convenience must not weaken production identity or secret boundaries.
items: Model secrets as parameters or secret references; never commit values or expose them in resource commands and logs.
Use distinct workload identities and least-privilege access for production resources instead of copying development credentials.
Bind development endpoints deliberately and do not expose dashboards, databases, or admin ports to untrusted networks.
Pin and audit Aspire integrations, container images, templates, and CLI versions as supply-chain dependencies.
Protect dashboard access and telemetry because logs, traces, environment metadata, and endpoints can reveal sensitive architecture.
Review generated deployment artifacts, role assignments, ingress, egress, TLS, secret stores, and network policies before release.

performance.introduction: Aspire improves visibility into distributed performance; it does not remove the need for capacity and topology design.
items: Use traces to find fan-out, serialization, dependency, and retry latency across resource boundaries.
Track process and container CPU, memory, restarts, request duration, error rate, queue depth, and datastore saturation.
Avoid starting unnecessary heavyweight resources in every developer loop; use profiles or external resources where appropriate.
Use persistent development volumes deliberately and reset state when deterministic tests require isolation.
Bound dashboard and telemetry retention locally and choose sampled, cost-aware production exporters.
Load-test the target deployment because local AppHost timing and resource limits do not represent production capacity.

deployment.introduction: Treat Aspire's application model as a deployment input, then make target-platform requirements explicit and reviewable.
items: Pin the SDK, CLI, integrations, base images, and workload artifacts used by the model.
Choose a supported deployment integration or generate artifacts that fit the organization's IaC and promotion workflow.
Replace development containers with durable managed services where required; define backups, private networking, identity, and availability separately.
Supply environment parameters and secrets through the deployment system, not AppHost source or committed launch settings.
Deploy immutable versions, validate resource references and health, observe traces, and use canary or staged traffic where supported.
Keep production dashboards, alerts, runbooks, scaling, disaster recovery, and cost controls aligned with each declared resource.

troubleshooting.cause: The process exited, a dependency is unhealthy, the health path is wrong, or the container runtime cannot start the resource.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect resource events, console logs, health details, dependency order, runtime state, ports, and image availability in the dashboard.

troubleshooting.symptom: A service cannot resolve another service
troubleshooting.cause: The AppHost reference is missing, the client used a hardcoded URI, or the resource and client names differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Add the typed reference, use service discovery or the integration client, and compare injected configuration names.

troubleshooting.symptom: The dashboard has logs but no traces
troubleshooting.cause: Service defaults or OpenTelemetry instrumentation is missing, exporters are misconfigured, or no traceable operation ran.
troubleshooting.fix: Verify service-default registration, instrumentation, OTLP endpoint injection, ActivitySource creation, and sampling.

troubleshooting.symptom: The model works locally but deployment fails
troubleshooting.cause: A development-only resource, volume, credential, port, or target integration has no production mapping.
troubleshooting.fix: Review the publish artifact and explicitly map identity, secrets, storage, networking, ingress, scaling, and supported resource types.

troubleshooting.symptom: AppHost startup is slow or flaky
troubleshooting.cause: Too many images restore at once, readiness is inaccurate, stale volumes conflict, or dependency startup exceeds bounds.
troubleshooting.fix: Pin images, pre-pull in CI, improve health checks, use wait conditions, reset only intended state, and capture resource timing.

troubleshooting.symptom: Package or CLI commands disagree with documentation
troubleshooting.cause: The Aspire CLI, AppHost SDK, integrations, or templates are from different release lines.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect pinned versions, upgrade them as one tested set, regenerate only intended files, and verify the migration notes.

productionChecklist: AppHost SDK, CLI, integrations, templates, images, and workload dependencies are pinned and audited.
Every resource has a stable name, owner, reference graph, health definition, and documented production mapping.
Service discovery replaces hardcoded endpoints and environment-specific configuration is injected through controlled parameters.
Secrets are external, identities are least privilege, dashboards are protected, and ingress and egress are reviewed.
Logs, metrics, traces, resource events, readiness, business outcomes, dashboards, alerts, and diagnostic retention are verified.
Model and journey tests start the real topology, wait for health, exercise failure, and preserve diagnostics in CI.
Production IaC defines durable storage, networking, backups, scaling, availability, patching, and disaster recovery.
Published artifacts are reviewed, immutable, promoted safely, and proven against the actual target environment.
bestPractices: Keep the AppHost declarative; let it describe resources and references instead of embedding business logic.
Use the dashboard during development to check traces and logs before reaching for a debugger.
Treat local resource definitions as a starting point, not a production topology; review managed service choices separately.
Reference resources through typed builders instead of hardcoding hostnames, ports, or connection strings.
Pin CLI, SDK, integration, and image versions as one tested compatibility set.
Use stable resource names and small reusable extension methods for repeated platform conventions.
Keep service defaults focused on cross-cutting infrastructure and out of business logic.
Test the resource graph and at least one real distributed journey in CI.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does .NET Aspire solve that Docker Compose does not fully cover?
interviewQuestions.answer: It adds .NET-aware service discovery, typed resource references, and built-in OpenTelemetry wiring across projects, so dependent services and dashboards work with less manual configuration than a generic container definition.

interviewQuestions.question: Is Aspire a hosting platform?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. It is an application model and local orchestration/tooling experience; deployment still targets your chosen hosting platform, using Aspire's manifest to describe the resources needed.

interviewQuestions.question: How does a project get another resource's connection details?
interviewQuestions.answer: Through WithReference in the AppHost, which injects configuration and environment variables that the referencing project's client integration reads automatically.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a hosting and client integration?
interviewQuestions.answer: A hosting integration models and runs a resource in the AppHost. A client integration configures the consuming workload's client, health checks, telemetry, and resilience.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are health checks part of the resource graph?
interviewQuestions.answer: Process start does not mean readiness. Health-aware dependencies let the model and tests wait for a resource that can actually serve work.

interviewQuestions.question: Can Aspire coordinate non-.NET workloads?
interviewQuestions.answer: Yes. The AppHost can be authored in C# or TypeScript and can model projects, executables, containers, and integrations across several languages and runtimes.

note: Aspire's biggest early win is usually local development: one command starts every dependent service with wired-up configuration and a shared dashboard.
tip: Start with the AppHost even for a single API and one database; adding services later is far easier once the pattern is established.
warning: Aspire's local resource definitions are not proof of production durability, security, networking, scaling, backup, or recovery.

name: CQRS & MediatR
shortDescription: Separate the shapes and paths used to change state from the ones used to read it, and route both through a mediator.
overview: Command Query Responsibility Segregation splits an application's write model, optimized for enforcing invariants, from its read model, optimized for the shapes a UI or report actually needs.
detail: CQRS separates intent to change state from requests to read state so each path can use contracts, validation, models, data access, and scaling suited to its job. Logical separation can begin in one process and one database: commands enforce authorization, invariants, idempotency, and transaction boundaries, while queries project only caller-required fields and never mutate. MediatR is an optional in-process dispatcher, not the architecture itself; request handlers improve discovery and pipeline behaviors can apply validation, tracing, transactions, and other cross-cutting policy in a deliberate order. Physical read stores and asynchronous projections add eventual consistency, replay, lag, reconciliation, schema evolution, and operating cost, so they should follow measured needs. CQRS does not imply event sourcing, microservices, separate databases, or one handler per trivial property update.

concepts.title: Commands vs queries
concepts.description: Commands express an intent to change state and stay narrow; queries return data shaped for a specific read need and never mutate anything.

concepts.title: Single handler per request
concepts.description: Each command or query type is matched to exactly one handler, keeping request-to-behavior mapping explicit and easy to locate.

concepts.title: Pipeline behaviors
concepts.description: Cross-cutting concerns—validation, logging, transactions, authorization—wrap every request through a shared pipeline instead of being repeated per handler.

concepts.title: Read models
concepts.description: Query handlers can read from denormalized or differently shaped projections instead of the same model the write side uses.

concepts.title: Logical versus physical separation
concepts.description: Commands and queries can share one store initially; separate stores add operational and consistency cost.

concepts.title: Idempotent commands
concepts.description: A stable request identifier lets repeated delivery return the original outcome without duplicate side effects.

concepts.title: Projection consistency
concepts.description: Synchronous projections are immediately visible; asynchronous projections expose lag and need reconciliation.

concepts.title: Mediator trade-offs
concepts.description: Dispatch improves pipelines and discovery but can hide control flow or add handlers with no useful behavior.

architecture.description: A mediator routes each command or query to its handler; write handlers change the domain model while read handlers return projections shaped for their caller.

code.label: PlaceOrderCommand.cs
code.introduction: A command and its handler stay narrow, returning only what the caller needs to continue.

bestPractices: Keep command handlers focused on one business outcome; split a handler that is doing two unrelated things.
Let query handlers bypass the domain model and read directly from a projection when that projection already exists.
Put validation, logging, and transaction handling in pipeline behaviors instead of repeating them in every handler.
Version read models independently from the write model once their shapes genuinely diverge.
Make commands idempotent wherever clients or transports can retry.
Keep pipeline order explicit and scope transactions around side effects only.
Measure projection lag and provide rebuild and reconciliation paths.
Use direct calls when mediator indirection adds no useful policy boundary.

interviewQuestions.question: What does CQRS require?
interviewQuestions.answer: Separate command and query responsibilities; it does not require separate databases, event sourcing, or microservices.

interviewQuestions.question: What do pipeline behaviors solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: They apply ordered cross-cutting policy such as tracing, validation, authorization, idempotency, and transactions around handlers.

interviewQuestions.question: When is CQRS not worth it?
interviewQuestions.answer: When read and write needs are simple and aligned and separate models add indirection without benefit.

interviewQuestions.question: Does CQRS require MediatR?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. MediatR is an optional dispatcher; CQRS is the responsibility separation.

interviewQuestions.question: How is a command idempotent?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use a stable request key, store the result atomically with state, and return it on duplicate delivery.

interviewQuestions.question: Where should transaction behavior run?
interviewQuestions.answer: Around command side effects after validation and authorization, committing only when the handler succeeds.

interviewQuestions.question: How do read models recover?
interviewQuestions.answer: Track checkpoints, retain replayable events, make updates idempotent, and rehearse rebuild plus reconciliation.

learningObjectives: Separate commands and queries by responsibility and contract.
Design command handlers around invariants, authorization, idempotency, and transactions.
Build read projections shaped for callers without mutating state.
Use MediatR request handlers and ordered pipeline behaviors deliberately.
Choose synchronous or asynchronous projections from consistency needs.
Operate projection lag, rebuilds, reconciliation, and contract evolution.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core, dependency injection, async C#, persistence, and testing.
Transactions, optimistic concurrency, messaging, and eventual consistency basics.
Understanding of domain models and purpose-built read projections.

use: Read and write shapes, rules, or scaling differ materially.
Named requests and pipeline policy improve feature ownership.
Asynchronous projections solve a measured isolation or throughput need.
avoid: Straightforward CRUD has aligned read and write models.
Handlers merely forward every call through extra indirection.
The team cannot operate projection lag, replay, and reconciliation.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated sample uses a small mediator-compatible request/handler abstraction so command/query separation and pipeline ordering stay visible without hiding behavior behind a package.

implementationSteps.title: Separate intent
implementationSteps.description: Name commands as business actions and queries as read needs with explicit results.

implementationSteps.title: Build command handlers
implementationSteps.description: Authenticate context, authorize resources, validate intent, enforce invariants, and commit one outcome.

implementationSteps.title: Build query handlers
implementationSteps.description: Project bounded fields directly into caller-specific read contracts.

implementationSteps.title: Order pipeline behavior
implementationSteps.description: Place tracing, validation, authorization, idempotency, transactions, and exception mapping deliberately.

implementationSteps.title: Choose projection timing
implementationSteps.description: Use synchronous updates for immediate consistency or durable events for asynchronous reads.

implementationSteps.title: Test delivery semantics
implementationSteps.description: Cover duplicates, concurrency, rollback, lag, missing reads, and cancellation.

implementationSteps.title: Operate projections
implementationSteps.description: Measure checkpoints and lag and provide rebuild, replay, and reconciliation tools.

testing.introduction: Test commands for safe state change and queries for accurate bounded projection.
items: Prove validation and authorization fail before side effects.
Test invariants, concurrency, transaction rollback, and cancellation.
Replay the same command identifier and assert one outcome.
Verify query filters, pagination, tenant scope, and no mutation.
Test pipeline ordering explicitly.
Exercise projection lag, replay, rebuild, poison events, and reconciliation.

security.introduction: Request dispatch is not authorization; each handler must apply trusted actor and resource policy.
items: Derive identity and tenant from verified context.
Authorize command and query resources independently.
Do not trust IDs, ownership, or roles in request bodies.
Bound query complexity and returned fields.
Redact request payloads and results from pipeline logs.

performance.introduction: CQRS enables tailored optimization but adds dispatch and consistency overhead.
items: Project only needed columns and paginate reads.
Measure handler latency, allocations, query count, and pipeline cost.
Keep transactions short and avoid remote work inside them.
Track projection throughput, checkpoint, and lag.
Scale stores separately only after evidence.

deployment.introduction: Command contracts, read models, and projection schemas must coexist across rolling deployments.
items: Use additive request and event evolution.
Deploy projection consumers before dependent readers.
Use expand-contract migrations.
Preserve idempotency records across restarts.
Smoke-test command-to-read visibility and rollback.

troubleshooting.cause: Retries lack idempotency.
troubleshooting.fix: Persist a request key and original outcome atomically.

troubleshooting.cause: Projection lag is hidden.
troubleshooting.fix: Expose checkpoints and define freshness behavior.

troubleshooting.cause: Pipeline order or async flow is wrong.
troubleshooting.fix: Test ordering and place commit after the handler succeeds.

troubleshooting.cause: Read and write models remain coupled.
troubleshooting.fix: Use direct bounded projections.

troubleshooting.cause: Too many notifications or pass-through handlers.
troubleshooting.fix: Use named requests only where the boundary adds value.

troubleshooting.cause: Source events or version handling are incomplete.
troubleshooting.fix: Retain replayable inputs and test deterministic rebuilds.

productionChecklist: Commands express business intent and queries never mutate.
Authorization, validation, idempotency, concurrency, and transactions are explicit.
Pipeline order is documented and tested.
Read contracts are bounded and purpose-built.
Projection consistency and freshness are communicated.
Lag, checkpoints, failures, and retries are observable.
Rebuild and reconciliation are rehearsed.
CQRS complexity is justified by measured needs.
note: CQRS is a separation of responsibility, not automatically a separation of databases or an event-sourced write model.
tip: Introduce CQRS at the boundary where reads and writes have genuinely different shapes or scaling needs, not uniformly across every feature.
warning: Splitting commands and queries without addressing how the read side stays in sync just moves the consistency problem instead of solving it.

name: Event-Driven Messaging
shortDescription: Coordinate independently deployed services through durable, asynchronous events instead of synchronous calls.
overview: Event-driven messaging lets services react to what happened elsewhere without a direct, blocking call, trading immediate consistency for looser coupling and better resilience to partial failure.
detail: A publisher records that something happened; a broker such as Service Bus or RabbitMQ delivers that event to one or more subscribers, each processing it independently. Because delivery can be delayed, duplicated, or reordered, the pattern's real difficulty is not publishing—it is designing durable delivery, idempotent handling, and workflows that tolerate partial completion.

Event-driven messaging communicates immutable facts or directed commands through durable asynchronous channels so publishers and consumers need not be available simultaneously. Temporal decoupling introduces duplicates, delay, reordering, poison data, schema evolution, backpressure, retention, and partial completion as normal conditions. A transactional outbox stores outgoing records with business state; a relay publishes later, and idempotent consumers store message identity with side effects. Events should be past-tense bounded facts with stable identity, correlation, causation, occurrence time, version, and ownership. Commands and events have different routing semantics. Sagas make long workflows, timeouts, and compensation explicit. Production needs dead-letter repair, replay, reconciliation, compatibility testing, capacity evidence, security controls, and a business definition of acceptable eventual consistency.

concepts.title: Events vs commands
concepts.description: An event states a fact that already happened and may have many subscribers; a command requests a specific action and expects exactly one handler.

concepts.title: Transactional outbox
concepts.description: Writing a business change and its outgoing event in the same local transaction avoids the dual-write problem of updating a database and publishing separately.

concepts.title: Idempotent consumers
concepts.description: A handler records which message identifiers it has already processed so redelivery does not repeat side effects.

concepts.title: Sagas
concepts.description: A saga coordinates a multi-step workflow across services using events and compensating actions instead of a distributed transaction.

concepts.title: Delivery semantics
concepts.description: At-most-once can lose work; at-least-once redelivers; end-to-end exactly-once depends on idempotent effects.

concepts.title: Event contracts
concepts.description: Identity, type, version, time, correlation, causation, ownership, and bounded payload form a durable contract.

concepts.title: Retries and dead letters
concepts.description: Bounded retries handle transients; poison messages move aside with diagnostics for repair or replay.

concepts.title: Ordering and backpressure
concepts.description: Order is scoped to a key while concurrency must be bounded to protect downstream dependencies.

architecture.description: A service commits a business change and an outbox record in one transaction; a relay publishes the event to a broker, which delivers it to independent, idempotent subscribers.

code.label: OutboxRelay.cs
code.introduction: A background relay publishes outbox rows written in the same transaction as the business change, then marks them sent.

bestPractices: Write the outbox row in the same transaction as the business change it describes, never as a separate call.
Design every consumer to be safe against duplicate delivery before trusting the broker's delivery guarantees.
Version event contracts additively and keep old consumers working through a compatibility window.
Model multi-step workflows as explicit sagas with compensating actions instead of implicit chains of event handlers.
Bound retries and route poison data to controlled dead-letter workflows.
Carry identity, correlation, causation, version, and occurrence time.
Measure end-to-end event age and downstream saturation.
Rehearse replay and reconciliation before incidents.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the dual-write problem and how does the outbox pattern fix it?
interviewQuestions.answer: Dual-write happens when a service updates its database and publishes an event as two separate operations that can fail independently, leaving them out of sync; the outbox pattern writes the event as a row in the same local transaction as the business change, then relays it asynchronously, so the two are always consistent.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can't most message brokers guarantee exactly-once delivery?
interviewQuestions.answer: Coordinating exactly-once delivery across a network requires distributed consensus that most brokers avoid for performance and availability reasons, so they offer at-least-once delivery and expect consumers to handle duplicates.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a saga, and why not just use a distributed transaction?
interviewQuestions.answer: A saga coordinates a multi-step process across services using a sequence of local transactions and compensating actions on failure; distributed transactions need every participant to be available and lock resources together, which does not scale or fit independently deployed services.

interviewQuestions.question: How does an idempotent consumer work?
interviewQuestions.answer: It records a stable message ID in the same transaction as business effects and skips or returns the recorded result on redelivery.

interviewQuestions.question: What belongs in an event envelope?
interviewQuestions.answer: Message ID, type, schema version, occurrence time, correlation and causation IDs, tenant context, and a bounded payload.

interviewQuestions.question: How should poison messages be handled?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use bounded retries for transients, dead-letter permanent failures with diagnostics, then repair and replay through controlled tooling.

interviewQuestions.question: What does exactly-once mean?
interviewQuestions.answer: Broker claims are scoped; end-to-end business exactly-once requires idempotent effects or one constrained transaction boundary.

learningObjectives: Distinguish events, commands, queues, publish-subscribe, streams, and synchronous calls.
Close the dual-write gap with an outbox and idempotent consumer inbox.
Design versioned contracts with identity, correlation, causation, and ownership.
Handle retries, duplicates, poison data, ordering, backpressure, and replay.
Model workflows with saga state, timeouts, and compensation.
Operate lag, throughput, dead letters, reconciliation, and recovery.
prerequisites: Distributed systems, transactions, async C#, workers, and database basics.
Broker, serialization, retry, observability, and eventual-consistency concepts.
A business definition of acceptable delay and recovery.

use: Publisher and consumer need temporal decoupling.
A fact fans out to independent consumers.
Bursts need durable buffering.
avoid: The caller needs an immediate authoritative response.
The workflow cannot tolerate eventual consistency.
A simple in-process call needs no durability or fan-out.

implementationSteps.title: Define semantics
implementationSteps.description: Choose event or command ownership, consistency, ordering key, and failure outcome.

implementationSteps.title: Design the envelope
implementationSteps.description: Add ID, type, version, time, correlation, causation, tenant, and bounded payload.

implementationSteps.title: Write the outbox
implementationSteps.description: Persist business state and outgoing message atomically.

implementationSteps.title: Relay safely
implementationSteps.description: Lease bounded batches, confirm publish, and tolerate duplicate relay.

implementationSteps.title: Consume idempotently
implementationSteps.description: Record identity with side effects before acknowledgement.

implementationSteps.title: Handle failure
implementationSteps.description: Use bounded backoff, dead letters, repair, replay, and reconciliation.

name: Apache Kafka
shortDescription: Build high-throughput, fault-tolerant event streaming pipelines in .NET using Apache Kafka with producers, consumers, consumer groups, and MassTransit.
overview: Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed for high-throughput, durable, ordered message delivery — used for real-time data pipelines, event sourcing at scale, and decoupling services in large systems.
detail: Kafka stores messages as immutable, ordered logs partitioned across a cluster of brokers. Producers append events to topics; consumers read from specific offsets and commit their progress independently, enabling multiple consumer groups to process the same stream at their own pace. Unlike traditional message queues, messages are retained for a configurable period regardless of consumption — allowing replay, late subscribers, and event sourcing. In .NET, Confluent.Kafka provides the low-level client; MassTransit wraps it with familiar consumer and saga patterns. Azure Event Hubs is a fully managed Kafka-compatible service requiring no infrastructure management.

concepts.title: Topics, partitions, and offsets
concepts.description: A topic is a named stream of events divided into partitions for parallelism. Each message has an offset — its position in a partition. Consumers commit offsets to track progress independently, enabling replay from any point.

concepts.title: Consumer groups
concepts.description: A consumer group is a set of consumers that collectively process a topic — each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, balancing load. Multiple groups read the same topic independently at their own pace.

concepts.title: Log compaction and retention
concepts.description: Time-based retention deletes old messages after a configured period. Compaction retains only the latest message per key, enabling Kafka to serve as a durable key-value store or materialised view source.

concepts.title: Exactly-once semantics
concepts.description: Kafka's idempotent producer and transactional API guarantee that a message is written exactly once even on retries, and that a produce-consume-produce cycle is atomic across topics.

concepts.title: Topics, partitions, and offsets
concepts.description: Topics are partitioned append-only logs; offsets identify records and enable independent replay.

concepts.title: Consumer groups
concepts.description: Each partition is assigned to one member per group while different groups consume independently.

concepts.title: Retention and compaction
concepts.description: Time or size retention preserves history; compaction retains the latest record for each key.

concepts.title: Delivery semantics
concepts.description: Offset timing controls loss or replay; transactions cover Kafka read-process-write but not arbitrary external effects.

concepts.title: Keys and ordering
concepts.description: Keys select partitions, and ordering is guaranteed only within a partition.

concepts.title: Replication and acknowledgements
concepts.description: Replication, in-sync replicas, acknowledgements, and leader failover determine durability.

concepts.title: Rebalancing
concepts.description: Membership changes reassign partitions and require safe pause, revocation, commit, and resume behavior.

concepts.title: Schema compatibility
concepts.description: Registries and compatibility policy allow independent producer and consumer evolution.

architecture.description: Producers append events to partitioned topics on the Kafka cluster; each consumer group reads independently at its own offset, enabling multiple downstream services to process the same stream without coordination.

code.label: OrderEventConsumer.cs
code.introduction: MassTransit wraps Confluent.Kafka so Kafka consumers use the same IConsumer interface as Service Bus and RabbitMQ consumers — the infrastructure concern is in registration, not in the handler.

bestPractices: Choose partition count carefully at topic creation — increasing partitions later is possible but rebalances consumer groups; a common starting point is one partition per expected peak consumer instance.
Always commit offsets only after processing succeeds, not before — committing first and then failing means the message is skipped; committing after means it is retried on failure.
Use consumer group IDs that are unique per logical service and environment so dev, staging, and production consumers never share progress state on the same cluster.

Use MassTransit’s Kafka rider when its consumer model fits, but configure delayed redelivery and an error topic explicitly; use Confluent.Kafka directly when the application needs lower-level protocol control.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Kafka differ from a traditional message queue like RabbitMQ or Service Bus?
interviewQuestions.answer: A traditional queue removes a message after it is consumed — one consumer processes each message. Kafka retains messages in an immutable log for a configurable period regardless of consumption, so multiple consumer groups each read the same events independently and consumers can replay from any offset. Kafka is optimised for throughput and stream processing; queues are optimised for task distribution and point-to-point delivery.

interviewQuestions.question: What determines the maximum parallelism of a Kafka consumer group?
interviewQuestions.answer: The number of partitions in the topic. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in a group at a time, so adding more consumers than partitions leaves the extras idle. To increase parallelism, increase the partition count — ideally at topic creation since repartitioning triggers a consumer group rebalance.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between at-least-once and exactly-once delivery in Kafka?
interviewQuestions.answer: At-least-once processing commits the offset after work succeeds, so a crash between the side effect and the commit can cause a replay. Kafka exactly-once semantics use transactions to atomically publish Kafka output records and commit consumed offsets for a read-process-write pipeline; external database or API side effects still require idempotency or an outbox-style design.

note: Kafka is operationally complex — broker sizing, partition leadership, consumer group rebalancing, and schema evolution all require deliberate design. Azure Event Hubs offers Kafka protocol compatibility without the operational overhead for teams that do not need a self-managed cluster.
tip: Use Azure Event Hubs with Kafka protocol compatibility in Azure-hosted workloads — change only the bootstrap server URL and the Confluent.Kafka or MassTransit client connects without code changes, while Azure manages the cluster.
warning: Messages in Kafka are ordered within a partition but not across partitions — if your business logic requires strict global ordering, all related messages must use the same partition key to land in the same partition.

name: RabbitMQ
shortDescription: Route messages reliably between .NET services using RabbitMQ exchanges, queues, bindings, dead-letter handling, and MassTransit for a clean consumer abstraction.
overview: RabbitMQ is a mature, widely deployed open-source message broker that routes messages through exchanges to queues using flexible binding patterns — making it a reliable backbone for microservices communication.
detail: RabbitMQ implements AMQP 0-9-1 and uses a producer-exchange-queue-consumer model. Producers publish to named exchanges rather than directly to queues; exchanges apply routing rules to deliver messages to the correct queues based on binding keys and exchange type — direct, fanout, topic, or headers. Consumer acknowledgements ensure messages are not lost if a consumer crashes before processing. Dead-letter exchanges capture failed or expired messages for inspection. In .NET, MassTransit abstracts RabbitMQ's exchange and queue topology, exposing familiar consumer and saga interfaces so the broker can be swapped with minimal code change.

concepts.title: Exchanges and exchange types
concepts.description: Direct exchanges route by exact routing key match. Fanout exchanges broadcast to all bound queues. Topic exchanges route by wildcard pattern. Headers exchanges route by message header values. Choosing the right exchange type determines the flexibility and complexity of the routing topology.

concepts.title: Queues, bindings, and routing keys
concepts.description: A queue holds messages until a consumer retrieves them. A binding connects an exchange to a queue with an optional routing key pattern. The routing key on the published message is matched against bindings to determine which queues receive a copy.

concepts.title: Acknowledgements and publisher confirms
concepts.description: Consumer acknowledgements tell RabbitMQ the message was processed and can be discarded. Negative acknowledgements requeue or discard failed messages. Publisher confirms tell the producer that RabbitMQ has persisted the message to disk, preventing loss on broker restart.

concepts.title: Dead-letter exchanges
concepts.description: A dead-letter exchange receives messages that are rejected, nacked without requeue, or expired. Dead-lettered messages can be inspected, retried manually, or routed to an error queue for monitoring and alerting.

concepts.title: Exchanges
concepts.description: Direct, fanout, topic, and headers exchanges route publishes to matching bindings.

concepts.title: Queues and bindings
concepts.description: Queues buffer deliveries while bindings declare routing from exchanges.

concepts.title: Acknowledgements
concepts.description: Ack removes a delivery; nack can requeue or reject after processing failure.

concepts.title: Publisher confirms
concepts.description: Confirms tell publishers whether the broker accepted a publish under the configured durability semantics.

concepts.title: Durability and quorum queues
concepts.description: Durable topology, persistent messages, quorum replication, and policies shape survival and availability.

concepts.title: Prefetch and concurrency
concepts.description: Prefetch bounds unacknowledged work and must match consumer and dependency capacity.

concepts.title: Dead lettering
concepts.description: Rejected, expired, or overflowed messages can route to controlled error or retry topology.

concepts.title: Connection recovery
concepts.description: Long-lived connections, channels, heartbeat, topology recovery, and idempotent consumers handle disruption.

architecture.description: A producer publishes to a named exchange with a routing key; the exchange delivers matching copies to bound queues; consumers acknowledge messages after processing; dead-lettered messages are routed to an error exchange for inspection.

code.label: OrderConsumer.cs
code.introduction: MassTransit configures the RabbitMQ topology — exchange, queue, and dead-letter binding — from the consumer type automatically. The consumer itself only handles business logic.

bestPractices: Always acknowledge messages only after processing succeeds — auto-acknowledgement on receipt risks losing messages if the consumer crashes between receipt and processing.
Configure a dead-letter exchange on every queue from the start so failed messages are captured and inspectable rather than silently discarded.

Use MassTransit's retry and redelivery middleware rather than implementing retry loops in consumer code — this keeps retry policy configuration in one place and works consistently across broker types.
Enable publisher confirms for critical message publishing so producers know RabbitMQ has persisted the message before considering the operation complete.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a topic exchange and a fanout exchange in RabbitMQ?
interviewQuestions.answer: A fanout exchange ignores the routing key entirely and delivers every published message to all bound queues — useful for broadcast scenarios. A topic exchange matches the routing key against binding patterns using dot-separated words and wildcard characters (* for one word, # for zero or more), enabling flexible selective routing to multiple queues based on message category.

interviewQuestions.question: What happens to a message when a consumer throws an exception in MassTransit with RabbitMQ?
interviewQuestions.answer: MassTransit applies any configured in-memory retry policy while the delivery remains locked. If retries are exhausted, the message faults and is moved to the endpoint’s _error queue. Delayed or scheduled redelivery happens only when that middleware is configured separately, so retry and redelivery should not be treated as the same operation.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose RabbitMQ over Azure Service Bus?
interviewQuestions.answer: RabbitMQ is a strong choice for flexible routing topologies — topic and headers exchanges have no direct equivalent in Service Bus — and for workloads that need to run on-premises, in a private cloud, or in any cloud without vendor lock-in. Azure Service Bus is better when deep Azure integration, managed infrastructure, geo-redundancy, and native Azure RBAC are more important than routing flexibility or cross-cloud portability.

note: RabbitMQ's flexibility comes from its exchange-binding model, which can represent almost any routing topology — but that flexibility requires deliberate design of the topology before writing producer and consumer code.
tip: Use the RabbitMQ Management UI at /api/queues to monitor queue depth, unacknowledged message counts, and dead-letter queue growth during development and load testing — catching queue depth growth early prevents memory exhaustion on the broker.
warning: Prefetch controls how many unacknowledged deliveries can be in flight. There is no universal ideal value: too high can increase memory pressure and uneven distribution, while too low limits throughput. Start conservatively and tune with production-like load tests.

interviewQuestions.question: Ack versus publisher confirm?

interviewQuestions.question: Why are messages duplicated?

name: gRPC
shortDescription: Define strongly typed service contracts and exchange compact binary messages over HTTP/2, including streaming.
overview: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers to define a service contract once, generating strongly typed client and server code for fast, compact, binary communication over HTTP/2.
detail: A versioned .proto file describes packages, services, methods, messages, enums, field numbers, and streaming direction; build tooling generates client stubs and server base classes so consumers do not hand-write serialization. ASP.NET Core hosts gRPC over HTTP/2 and integrates it with dependency injection, logging, authentication, authorization, interceptors, health checks, and OpenTelemetry. Unary calls fit request-response work, while server, client, and bidirectional streaming support ordered message sequences with cancellation and flow control. Production reliability depends on deadlines propagated through every downstream call, safe retries only for idempotent operations, bounded message sizes, keepalive and proxy compatibility, channel reuse, load-balancing behavior, status-code mapping, and contract compatibility. Fields may be added additively, but published numbers and wire meanings must never be reused; removed fields should be reserved. Browser, public-partner, and debugging needs may favor JSON HTTP, gRPC-Web, or a transcoding gateway, so protocol choice belongs to the consumer boundary rather than a performance slogan.

avoid: Do not require generated clients from unknown public consumers without an adoption plan.
Do not retry non-idempotent methods blindly or omit deadlines.
Do not change protobuf field numbers, reuse removed numbers, or change an established field's wire meaning.
Do not assume every proxy, ingress, load balancer, or browser supports the required HTTP/2 behavior.

concepts.title: Service contracts

concepts.title: HTTP/2 transport
concepts.description: Multiplexed streams over one connection let gRPC support concurrent calls and native streaming without HTTP/1.1's per-request overhead.

concepts.title: Streaming modes
concepts.description: Server, client, and bidirectional streaming let either side send a sequence of messages over one long-lived call.

concepts.title: Deadlines and cancellation
concepts.description: A caller bounds how long work may take and the server propagates cancellation to databases and downstream RPCs.

concepts.title: Status and metadata
concepts.description: Canonical status codes describe RPC outcomes while headers and trailers carry bounded cross-cutting metadata.

concepts.title: Channels and connection reuse
concepts.description: A long-lived channel multiplexes calls over HTTP/2; creating one per call wastes sockets and handshakes.

concepts.title: Wire compatibility
concepts.description: Additive fields preserve old readers, while reserved numbers prevent removed fields from acquiring conflicting meanings.

architecture.description: A shared .proto contract generates client and server code; the client calls generated stubs, and the server implements the matching generated base class.
