items: Reuse channels and generated clients; do not create a channel per call.
Set send and receive limits and stream incrementally rather than buffering unbounded sequences.
Prefer async I/O, propagate cancellation, and avoid blocking service methods.
Configure keepalive and concurrency only from measured infrastructure requirements.
Measure method latency, status, bytes, active streams, and deadline expiry without high-cardinality labels.

deployment.introduction: HTTP/2 behavior must survive every network hop between generated client and service.
items: Verify TLS, ALPN, HTTP/2, ingress protocol, idle timeout, maximum stream duration, and request size.
Use readiness and graceful shutdown so new streams stop before existing calls drain.
Confirm service discovery and load balancing match long-lived channel behavior.
Deploy compatible servers before clients send newly added fields or call new methods.
Smoke-test unary, streaming, authentication, deadline, and status behavior through the real route.

troubleshooting.cause: The endpoint, TLS, DNS, proxy, HTTP/2 route, or readiness is unavailable.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect channel and server telemetry and test the exact deployed HTTP/2 path.

troubleshooting.symptom: Calls hang much longer than expected.
troubleshooting.cause: No deadline was set or cancellation was not propagated.
troubleshooting.fix: Set a caller deadline and pass ServerCallContext.CancellationToken through all work.

troubleshooting.symptom: A browser cannot call the endpoint.
troubleshooting.cause: Browsers do not expose framing required by native gRPC.
troubleshooting.fix: Use gRPC-Web, JSON transcoding, or a browser-facing gateway.

troubleshooting.cause: A field number or wire type was reused or semantics changed.
troubleshooting.fix: Restore compatible meaning, reserve removed numbers, and enforce compatibility checks.

troubleshooting.cause: Messages or the whole stream are buffered without limits.
troubleshooting.fix: Bound message size, process incrementally, observe flow control, and cancel abandoned streams.

troubleshooting.cause: Metadata was stripped or TLS and credential forwarding differ from local hosting.
troubleshooting.fix: Verify approved forwarding and use standard bearer, certificate, or workload identity.

productionChecklist: The versioned .proto package and ownership are documented.
Published field numbers and meanings are stable and removed fields are reserved.
Every call has deadline, cancellation, idempotency, retry, and status policy.
Channels are reused and message, metadata, and stream work are bounded.
TLS, authentication, method and resource authorization, and secret handling are reviewed.
Unary, streaming, negative, deadline, and compatibility tests run in CI.
HTTP/2, ingress, load balancing, health, graceful shutdown, and observability are verified.
Reflection, detailed errors, and production discovery follow an explicit policy.

code.label: OrderGrpcService.cs
code.introduction: A generated base class exposes strongly typed request and response messages, so the implementation stays focused on behavior.

bestPractices: Version .proto contracts additively—add new fields and methods rather than reusing or removing field numbers.
Keep gRPC for controlled service boundaries where consumers can share the generated contract.
Set and propagate deadlines and cancellation on every remote call.
Retry only transient statuses for operations proven idempotent.
Reuse channels and bound messages, metadata, concurrency, and stream duration.
Map domain outcomes to canonical statuses without revealing internal details.
Secure methods with TLS, authentication, authorization, and redacted telemetry.
Test protobuf compatibility and the deployed HTTP/2 route, not only service classes.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is gRPC often faster than a typical JSON REST API?
interviewQuestions.answer: It uses Protocol Buffers, a compact binary format, over HTTP/2, which supports multiplexed streams on one connection—together this reduces both payload size and connection overhead compared to text-based JSON over HTTP/1.1.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose REST over gRPC?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the API needs to be broadly consumable by browsers and third parties without generated clients, or when human-readable payloads and simple tooling matter more than raw performance.

interviewQuestions.question: What are the three streaming modes gRPC supports beyond unary calls?
interviewQuestions.answer: Server streaming, where the server sends multiple responses to one request; client streaming, where the client sends multiple requests for one response; and bidirectional streaming, where both sides send messages independently over the same call.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should a gRPC client set a deadline?
interviewQuestions.answer: A deadline bounds caller resources and propagates cancellation to the server instead of allowing a remote call to wait indefinitely.

interviewQuestions.question: How do protobuf contracts evolve compatibly?
interviewQuestions.answer: Add fields with new numbers, preserve existing meanings, tolerate unknown fields, and reserve removed names and numbers.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should channels be reused?
interviewQuestions.answer: A channel owns reusable HTTP/2 connections and multiplexes calls; recreating it per call adds handshake cost and risks socket exhaustion.

interviewQuestions.question: How should a gRPC service report domain failures?
interviewQuestions.answer: Map them to canonical status codes such as InvalidArgument, NotFound, FailedPrecondition, or PermissionDenied, with safe bounded detail for clients.

note: A .proto file is a contract between teams as much as a code-generation input; treat changes to it with the same care as a public API.
tip: Generate client and server code as part of the build so the contract and the implementation can never silently drift apart.
warning: Browsers cannot call raw gRPC directly; use grpc-web or a gateway if browser clients need to reach a gRPC service.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated authenticated streaming sample

name: SignalR
shortDescription: Push real-time updates from server to client over WebSockets, with automatic fallback and connection management.
overview: SignalR lets a server push messages to connected clients as events happen, instead of clients repeatedly polling for changes.
detail: A hub is a transient server endpoint whose methods receive client invocations and whose typed client contract pushes events to connected callers, users, groups, or all clients. SignalR negotiates WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, or long polling and handles framing and connection management, but an application still owns identity, authorization, group membership, reconnect reconciliation, message compatibility, ordering assumptions, and missed-event recovery. Connections are temporary and a reconnect usually receives a new connection identifier; groups are routing conveniences rather than durable membership or security stores. Multi-instance deployments need Azure SignalR Service or a supported backplane so a message reaches connections on every node, plus sticky-session and transport settings appropriate to the chosen scale path. Production design bounds receive size, invocation concurrency, send rate, connection count, group fan-out, and buffered state, keeps hubs thin, sends compact versioned contracts, and uses a durable source of truth that clients re-fetch after reconnect. WebSockets also require correct proxy upgrades, idle timeouts, origin policy, token handling, observability, and graceful draining.
learningObjectives: Model strongly typed hub and client contracts while keeping business logic outside hubs.
Authenticate connections and authorize each invocation and target resource.
Use caller, user, connection, and server-controlled groups correctly.
Design reconnect and snapshot reconciliation without assuming delivery durability.
Scale across instances with an appropriate managed service or backplane.
Test negotiation, transport, denial, group routing, payload bounds, and deployed proxy behavior.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core authentication and authorization, async C#, and JSON contracts.
Basic WebSocket, proxy, horizontal scaling, and distributed state concepts.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the operations-room sample.

use: Use SignalR for interactive notifications, dashboards, collaboration, or presence where server push materially improves experience.
Use groups for server-authorized routing to a changing subset of connections.
Use a durable API snapshot plus live events when clients must recover after disconnect.
avoid: Do not use SignalR as the only durable event store or guaranteed message bus.
Do not let callers join tenant, user, order, or privileged groups without server authorization.
Do not broadcast large state to every connection when a targeted notification and API refresh will work.
Do not assume reconnect preserves connection ID, group membership, ordering across streams, or missed messages.

concepts.title: Hubs
concepts.description: A hub is a server-side class clients connect to and call methods on; the server can call back to connected clients through the same hub.

concepts.title: Transport negotiation
concepts.description: SignalR automatically selects WebSockets when available and falls back to other transports, so application code does not manage the transport directly.

concepts.title: Groups and users
concepts.description: Connections can be organized into groups or targeted by user identifier, letting the server send updates to exactly the right audience.

concepts.title: Backplane
concepts.description: A backplane such as Redis fans messages out across multiple server instances so clients connected to different servers still receive the same broadcasts.

concepts.title: Connection lifecycle
concepts.description: Negotiation, connect, transient disconnect, reconnect, timeout, and graceful drain are separate states clients and servers must observe.

concepts.title: Typed client contracts
concepts.description: Hub<TClient> turns server-to-client method names and payloads into a compile-time contract for .NET server code.

concepts.title: Reconciliation
concepts.description: A client reloads an authoritative snapshot after reconnect, then applies compact live events without assuming none were missed.

concepts.title: Delivery semantics
concepts.description: SignalR provides live routing to current connections, not durable exactly-once delivery or offline retention.

architecture.description: Clients connect to a hub over a negotiated transport; the server calls back to individual connections, groups, or all clients as events occur.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated operations-room sample authenticates each connection, exposes a strongly typed client contract, validates server-controlled room names, bounds messages and history, sends a snapshot on join, broadcasts only to the room group, and verifies negotiation and WebSocket behavior through the real .NET client.

implementationSteps.title: Define the live use case
implementationSteps.description: Separate transient notifications from durable state, offline delivery, and commands that belong to APIs or messaging.

implementationSteps.title: Design contracts
implementationSteps.description: Create small versionable hub inputs and a strongly typed client interface with explicit event names.

implementationSteps.title: Authenticate early
implementationSteps.description: Configure cookie, bearer, or workload identity before MapHub and derive a stable user identifier.

implementationSteps.title: Authorize routing
implementationSteps.description: Validate every invocation and allow group membership only after tenant and resource checks.

implementationSteps.title: Bound the connection
implementationSteps.description: Set receive size, parallel invocations, timeouts, keepalive, fan-out, rate, and per-connection state limits.

implementationSteps.title: Reconcile reconnects
implementationSteps.description: Have clients rejoin authorized groups and fetch a durable snapshot before resuming event application.

implementationSteps.title: Scale and verify
implementationSteps.description: Choose managed scale or backplane and test real proxy upgrades, multi-node fan-out, drain, and observability.

testing.introduction: Real-time correctness requires a real client connection, not only direct hub method calls.
items: Use the supported client against an in-process server to test negotiate and WebSocket or fallback transport.
Prove anonymous and unauthorized connections or invocations are denied.
Join an authorized group and assert only intended clients receive the typed message.
Test invalid room, payload size, rate, and parallel-invocation limits.
Simulate disconnect and reconnect, then prove group rejoin and snapshot reconciliation.
Run a multi-instance or managed-service test before claiming horizontal fan-out works.

security.introduction: A persistent connection can invoke repeatedly and receive pushed data, so both directions require least privilege.
items: Authenticate the connection and authorize every hub method, group, tenant, and target resource.
Restrict origins deliberately and protect browser token transport, logs, and query-string handling.
Never expose connection IDs as authorization credentials or trust caller-selected group names.
Bound messages, invocation rate, parallel work, connection count, and fan-out to limit abuse.
Send minimum data and avoid detailed production errors or sensitive payload logging.

performance.introduction: Capacity is driven by concurrent connections, fan-out, message rate, payload size, and transport behavior.
items: Send compact events and let clients fetch large authoritative state through cacheable APIs.
Target users or groups rather than broadcasting globally.
Measure active connections, reconnects, send queue, message bytes, hub latency, errors, and backplane lag.
Use MessagePack only after client compatibility and measured bandwidth or CPU benefit.
Load-test connection ramps, steady fan-out, failure recovery, and multi-node scale with production-shaped limits.

deployment.introduction: The entire route must support long-lived upgraded connections and safe multi-instance routing.
items: Verify WebSocket upgrade headers, TLS, origins, proxy buffering, idle timeout, and maximum request size.
Configure Azure SignalR Service or a supported backplane before scaling beyond one node.
Plan sticky sessions only where the selected transport and scale architecture require them.
Drain connections during deployment and make reconnect plus snapshot recovery routine.
Smoke-test authenticated connect, group join, broadcast, disconnect, reconnect, and cross-instance fan-out.

troubleshooting.symptom: WebSockets fail and clients fall back.
troubleshooting.cause: A proxy, load balancer, origin, TLS, or upgrade setting blocks the transport.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect browser and server transport logs and verify the exact deployed upgrade path.

troubleshooting.symptom: Some clients miss broadcasts after scale-out.
troubleshooting.cause: Connections are split across nodes without a backplane or managed service.
troubleshooting.fix: Configure supported scale-out and test a sender and receiver on different instances.

troubleshooting.symptom: A reconnected client stops receiving group messages.
troubleshooting.cause: The new connection did not rejoin authorized groups.
troubleshooting.fix: Re-establish membership and reload the durable snapshot after reconnect.

troubleshooting.symptom: One tenant sees another tenant's update.
troubleshooting.cause: Caller-controlled group membership or missing tenant authorization mixed audiences.
troubleshooting.fix: Derive groups server-side after tenant and resource checks and add negative routing tests.

troubleshooting.cause: Payloads, per-connection state, queues, or invocation concurrency are unbounded.
troubleshooting.fix: Bound each dimension, remove hub state, target fan-out, and load-test retention.

troubleshooting.cause: Idle timeouts, keepalive, token expiry, network instability, or server draining is misaligned.
troubleshooting.fix: Correlate client and server lifecycle telemetry and tune supported timeout and credential refresh behavior.

productionChecklist: The live feature distinguishes transient events from durable source-of-truth state.
Hub and client contracts are small, typed, versioned, and compatibility-tested.
Connections, methods, groups, tenants, and resources are authenticated and authorized.
Message size, rate, parallel invocation, connection count, history, and fan-out are bounded.
Reconnect re-authenticates, rejoins groups, and reconciles an authoritative snapshot.
Managed scale or backplane behavior is tested across instances.
WebSocket, fallback, proxy, TLS, origin, timeout, and drain settings are verified.
Connection, reconnect, error, message, fan-out, and backplane telemetry has alerts.

code.label: OrderStatusHub.cs
code.introduction: A hub method adds a caller to a group; a separate service call notifies just that group when an order's status changes.

bestPractices: Scope broadcasts to server-authorized users or groups instead of all clients.
Add a supported backplane or managed SignalR service before multi-instance scale.
Design reconnect to re-authenticate, rejoin groups, and reload authoritative state.
Keep hubs transient and thin and delegate business rules to application services.
Use typed compact message contracts and evolve them compatibly.
Bound payload, invocation, connection, queue, history, and fan-out work.
Treat groups as routing, not durable membership or authorization storage.
Test negotiation, real transports, denial, multi-node fan-out, and graceful drain.

interviewQuestions.question: How does SignalR decide which transport to use?
interviewQuestions.answer: It negotiates with the client and prefers WebSockets when both the browser and any intermediate proxies support it, falling back to Server-Sent Events or long polling otherwise, without the application needing to choose a transport explicitly.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a backplane needed when scaling SignalR horizontally?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each server instance only knows about the connections it holds directly; a backplane like Redis relays messages between instances so a broadcast reaches clients connected anywhere, not just on the server that triggered it.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a SignalR group used for?
interviewQuestions.answer: It lets the server send a message to a named subset of connections—for example everyone viewing one order—without tracking connection IDs manually in application code.

interviewQuestions.question: Does SignalR guarantee durable delivery?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. It routes live messages to current connections; durable retention, replay, acknowledgement, and offline delivery need another store or broker.

interviewQuestions.question: What should a client do after reconnect?
interviewQuestions.answer: Re-authenticate as needed, rejoin authorized groups, reload an authoritative snapshot, and then resume applying live events.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should group names not be trusted from clients?
interviewQuestions.answer: A caller could select another tenant or resource. The server must authorize the target and derive membership rules before adding the connection.

interviewQuestions.question: What drives SignalR capacity?
interviewQuestions.answer: Concurrent connections, connection churn, message rate and size, fan-out width, serialization, transport, and backplane or managed-service behavior.

note: SignalR handles the transport and connection lifecycle; your application still owns deciding who should receive which message.
tip: Send small, specific payloads over the hub and let the client fetch full detail through a normal API call if needed, rather than pushing large objects.
warning: A dropped connection does not guarantee the client missed nothing or everything; design reconnect logic to reconcile state rather than assume.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated authenticated operations-room sample

name: Resilience & Rate Limiting
shortDescription: Protect a service and its callers from cascading failure with retries, circuit breakers, timeouts, and rate limits.
overview: Resilience policies decide how a call behaves when something downstream is slow or failing; rate limiting decides how much load a service accepts in the first place.
detail: Resilience is controlled failure handling, not a promise that every operation eventually succeeds. Outbound calls need explicit deadlines, bounded retries with jitter, circuit breaking, concurrency limits, and an end-to-end time budget. Inbound rate limiting protects finite capacity and should partition fairly by authenticated client or another trustworthy key. Retry only transient, repeatable operations; use idempotency keys where a repeated write is possible. Choose token bucket for controlled bursts, fixed or sliding windows for quotas, and concurrency limiting for scarce work slots. Emit stable rejection responses and Retry-After guidance, measure attempts and breaker state, and test with deterministic time and injected failures. Layer budgets so retries cannot outlive the caller, and avoid multiplying attempts across clients, gateways, and services.

concepts.title: Failure taxonomy
concepts.description: Classify transient, permanent, overload, cancellation, and timeout outcomes before choosing a response.

concepts.title: Timeout budgets
concepts.description: Bound the whole operation and give each attempt less time than the remaining caller budget.

concepts.title: Retry and jitter
concepts.description: Retry only safe transient failures with bounded exponential delay and randomness that prevents synchronized storms.

concepts.title: Circuit breakers
concepts.description: Stop calls after sustained failure, probe recovery carefully, and expose breaker state to operators.

concepts.title: Concurrency isolation
concepts.description: Limit simultaneous dependency calls so one slow system cannot exhaust every worker or connection.

concepts.title: Rate-limit algorithms
concepts.description: Fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, and concurrency policies offer different burst and fairness behavior.

concepts.title: Partitioning and identity
concepts.description: Partition limits by a trusted tenant, API client, or route instead of attacker-controlled raw input.

concepts.title: Backpressure and signals
concepts.description: Return predictable 429 or 503 responses, Retry-After where useful, and telemetry that explains rejection.

architecture.description: Outbound calls pass through composed resilience policies before reaching a dependency, while inbound requests pass through a rate limiter before reaching application code.

code.label: ResilientClient.cs
code.introduction: A named HttpClient gets a standard resilience pipeline once, so every call through it is protected consistently.

bestPractices: Retry only transient repeatable work.
Budget the entire operation.
Add jitter to delayed retries.
Use breakers with measured thresholds.
Limit dependency concurrency.
Partition admission with trusted identity.
Bound limiter state cardinality.
Tune from telemetry and failure drills.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can retries worsen an outage?
interviewQuestions.answer: They amplify demand while a dependency has reduced capacity, especially when clients retry together.

interviewQuestions.question: Retry versus circuit breaker?
interviewQuestions.answer: Retry repeats one operation; a breaker suppresses new calls after aggregate failure crosses a threshold.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use jitter?
interviewQuestions.answer: It spreads retries over time so callers do not create a synchronized recovery spike.

interviewQuestions.question: Which limiter allows controlled bursts?
interviewQuestions.answer: A token bucket accumulates permits up to a capacity while replenishing at a configured rate.

interviewQuestions.question: When is concurrency limiting useful?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the scarce resource is simultaneous work, such as database connections or expensive requests.

interviewQuestions.question: How should limits be partitioned?
interviewQuestions.answer: By a bounded, trusted identity that matches the fairness boundary, usually tenant or API client.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes retrying a POST safe?
interviewQuestions.answer: An idempotency contract that returns the same outcome and prevents duplicate side effects.

note: Resilience policies manage how you call others; rate limiting manages how others call you—most production APIs need both.
tip: Test resilience policies by actually injecting failures and latency in a lower environment, not just by reading the configuration.
warning: Stacking retries at multiple layers—client, gateway, and service—without coordination can multiply load on a struggling dependency instead of protecting it.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with deterministic retry and token-bucket sample
learningObjectives: Classify failures before applying policies.
Compose timeout, retry, breaker, and concurrency budgets.
Choose an inbound limiter from workload behavior.
Partition admission fairly and securely.
Make repeated writes idempotent.
Test failure and refill behavior deterministically.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core middleware, HttpClient, async cancellation, and dependency injection.
Basic latency, throughput, HTTP status, and idempotency concepts.
A stated capacity and failure budget for the protected operation.

use: A remote dependency has known transient failures.
A service must preserve capacity during bursts.
Clients need predictable overload behavior.
avoid: Retries wrap non-repeatable writes without idempotency.
Every layer independently retries.
Limits use spoofable or unbounded partition keys.

implementationIntroduction: The sample isolates the policy mechanics with a deterministic token bucket and bounded retry policy, making time and failure assertions fast and repeatable.

implementationSteps.title: Define outcomes
implementationSteps.description: Map exceptions and status codes to transient, permanent, timeout, cancellation, or overload.

implementationSteps.title: Set a budget
implementationSteps.description: Choose an end-to-end deadline, per-attempt timeout, and maximum attempts.

implementationSteps.title: Protect repetition
implementationSteps.description: Require idempotency before retrying mutations and add jitter to backoff.

implementationSteps.title: Select admission
implementationSteps.description: Choose token bucket, window, or concurrency limiting from burst and resource behavior.

implementationSteps.title: Partition fairly
implementationSteps.description: Use authenticated client or tenant identity and bound partition count.

implementationSteps.title: Return contracts
implementationSteps.description: Produce stable problem details, 429 or 503 semantics, and Retry-After guidance.

implementationSteps.title: Observe and tune
implementationSteps.description: Measure attempts, latency, rejections, saturation, and breaker transitions under injected failure.

testing.introduction: Test policies as state machines with fake time and scripted outcomes.
items: Prove transient success within the attempt bound.
Prove permanent failure is not retried.
Advance fake time to verify token refill.
Test cancellation and total timeout.
Test partition fairness and eviction.
Load-test rejection before dependency collapse.

security.introduction: Admission controls are also abuse controls, but only when identity and resource accounting are trustworthy.
items: Prefer authenticated client or tenant keys.
Do not reveal internal dependency details.
Bound partition cardinality.
Protect bypass and policy configuration.
Audit repeated abusive rejection patterns.

performance.introduction: Policies consume latency and capacity, so tune the whole call graph rather than isolated defaults.
items: Keep retries inside the caller budget.
Measure retry amplification.
Limit concurrent dependency calls.
Use jitter to smooth recovery.
Benchmark limiter partitions at expected cardinality.

deployment.introduction: Roll policy changes gradually because small threshold changes can reshape traffic.
items: Publish rejection and retry contracts.
Canary threshold changes.
Align gateway and service policies.
Alert on saturation and breaker state.
Rehearse dependency brownouts.

troubleshooting.cause: Retries multiply slow attempts.
troubleshooting.fix: Reduce attempts and enforce an end-to-end timeout.

troubleshooting.cause: Retry storms keep it saturated.
troubleshooting.fix: Add jitter, circuit breaking, and concurrency isolation.

troubleshooting.cause: The chosen algorithm has no burst allowance.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a token bucket or tune queue and replenishment.

troubleshooting.cause: Limits use a global partition.
troubleshooting.fix: Partition by trusted tenant and reserve shared capacity deliberately.

troubleshooting.cause: Partition keys are unbounded.
troubleshooting.fix: Normalize keys and evict idle limiter state.

troubleshooting.cause: Rejections omit useful guidance.
troubleshooting.fix: Return stable 429 responses and a realistic Retry-After value.

productionChecklist: Failure classes are explicit.
Total and per-attempt timeouts are bounded.
Writes are idempotent before retry.
Attempts use backoff and jitter.
Concurrency protects dependencies.
Limiter algorithm and partition key are justified.
Rejections are observable and documented.
Brownout and recovery tests pass.

name: Structured Logging
shortDescription: Emit machine-queryable log events with consistent fields instead of formatted strings that are hard to search.
overview: Structured logging captures each log event as a set of named fields rather than a formatted sentence, making logs searchable, filterable, and aggregable at production scale.
detail: Serilog and similar libraries let you write a log message template with named properties; each property is captured as structured data alongside the rendered text. Enrichers attach context such as a correlation ID or environment to every event, and sinks route events to one or more destinations—console, file, or a centralized platform.

concepts.title: Message templates
concepts.description: A log call captures named properties as structured data, not just an interpolated string, so fields remain queryable after the fact.

concepts.title: Enrichers
concepts.description: Enrichers attach consistent context—correlation ID, environment, version—to every log event without repeating it at each call site.

concepts.title: Log levels
concepts.description: Verbose, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, and Fatal levels let you control noise and route events differently by severity.

concepts.title: Sinks
concepts.description: A sink defines where events go—console, file, or a centralized log platform—and multiple sinks can run at once with different filters.

architecture.description: A log call captures structured properties, enrichers attach shared context, and the pipeline writes the enriched event to one or more sinks.

code.label: LoggingSetup.cs
code.introduction: Structured properties in the message template stay queryable; the enricher attaches a correlation ID to every event automatically.
code.code:
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .Enrich.WithCorrelationId()
    .Enrich.FromLogContext()
    .WriteTo.Console(new CompactJsonFormatter())
    .CreateLogger();

logger.LogInformation(
    "Order {OrderId} placed for {CustomerId} with total {Total}",
    order.Id, order.CustomerId, order.Total);

bestPractices: Log named properties through the message template, not string interpolation, so fields stay structured and queryable.
Attach a correlation ID to every request early and flow it through logs, traces, and outbound calls.
Set log levels deliberately per environment; verbose logging in production is expensive and can leak sensitive detail.
Never log secrets, tokens, or full payloads containing personal data; redact or omit them explicitly.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between structured logging and just writing formatted strings to a file?
interviewQuestions.answer: Structured logging captures each log call's properties as separate, typed fields alongside the message, so a log platform can filter, aggregate, and query on those fields directly instead of parsing free-text strings.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use a message template with named placeholders instead of string interpolation?
interviewQuestions.answer: Named placeholders preserve each value as a distinct property in the structured event; string interpolation collapses everything into one opaque string before logging, losing that structure.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a correlation ID and why does it matter across services?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is an identifier generated at the start of a request and passed through every downstream call and log line, letting you find every log event related to one logical operation across multiple services.

note: Logs are a queryable data source, not just text for a human to scroll through during an incident.
tip: Log at the boundary of a meaningful business event—order placed, payment failed—rather than logging every internal method call.
warning: Logging full request or response bodies by default is a common way secrets and personal data end up in a log platform.
latestNote: New guide on message templates, enrichers, and sinks

name: Architecture Testing
shortDescription: Enforce dependency rules, naming conventions, and layer boundaries automatically in CI using NetArchTest and custom Roslyn analysers.
overview: Architecture tests verify that structural rules — which layers may reference which, how types must be named, what may not depend on what — are enforced automatically rather than relying on code review alone.
detail: Architecture rules decay when they exist only in diagrams and review comments. An architectural fitness function turns an important structural property into executable evidence: domain code has no outward dependency, application code owns ports, modules expose only intended contracts, handlers follow conventions, and adapters remain replaceable. Reflection libraries such as NetArchTest or ArchUnitNET inspect compiled assemblies; Roslyn analyzers provide earlier compiler and IDE feedback; project references and visibility enforce some rules before tests run. Good rules protect consequential boundaries rather than cosmetic preferences, name the violating types, and remain fast enough for every pull request. Existing systems need an explicit baseline and a ratchet that prevents new violations while teams remove old ones incrementally. Rules must evolve with architecture decisions, package or namespace moves, generated code, dynamic loading, and deployment topology, and they complement—not replace—behavior tests and design review.

concepts.title: Fitness functions
concepts.description: Automated checks continuously evaluate a measurable architectural property.

concepts.title: Dependency direction
concepts.description: Inner domain and application assemblies must not reference outer infrastructure or delivery assemblies.

concepts.title: Module boundaries
concepts.description: Only explicit public contracts may cross business-module ownership lines.

concepts.title: Naming and shape
concepts.description: Handlers, ports, adapters, and endpoints can follow searchable conventions when those conventions improve design.

concepts.title: Visibility
concepts.description: Internal types and friend assemblies reduce the surface that other modules can couple to.

concepts.title: Reflection tests
concepts.description: Compiled-assembly inspection is easy to add and works in an ordinary test runner.

concepts.title: Roslyn analyzers
concepts.description: Compiler-integrated rules give immediate feedback and can block builds before test execution.

concepts.title: Baselines and ratchets
concepts.description: Legacy violations are recorded while new violations fail and the permitted set only shrinks.

architecture.description: Architecture tests run alongside unit and integration tests in CI; they inspect compiled assemblies and fail the build when a structural rule is violated, before code reaches main.

code.label: ArchitectureTests.cs
code.introduction: Three focused tests enforce Clean Architecture dependency direction, naming conventions, and module isolation — all failing at CI rather than in a code review comment.

bestPractices: Protect consequential boundaries.
Prefer compile-time enforcement first.
Name rules as sentences.
Report violating types.
Fail on empty scans.
Baseline legacy debt explicitly.
Keep exceptions narrow and owned.
Update rules with ADRs.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an architectural fitness function?
interviewQuestions.answer: An automated check that continuously evaluates a structural or operational architecture property.

interviewQuestions.question: Reflection test versus Roslyn analyzer?
interviewQuestions.answer: Reflection inspects compiled assemblies in a test runner; an analyzer reports during compilation and in the IDE.

interviewQuestions.question: How do project references help?
interviewQuestions.answer: They make coarse dependency direction a compiler-enforced graph rather than a naming convention.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you adopt rules in legacy code?
interviewQuestions.answer: Record existing violations, fail only on growth, and shrink the baseline through owned increments.

interviewQuestions.question: Why fail on an empty type selection?
interviewQuestions.answer: Otherwise a rename can make a rule silently test nothing while remaining green.

interviewQuestions.question: Should every naming convention be tested?
interviewQuestions.answer: No; enforce conventions only when they protect ownership, discovery, safety, or replaceability.

interviewQuestions.question: Do architecture tests replace review?
interviewQuestions.answer: No; they automate observable invariants while review handles tradeoffs and concepts the code graph cannot express.

note: Architecture tests verify structure, not behaviour — they complement unit and integration tests rather than replace them, and they only catch the violations that the rules you write describe.
tip: Start with three rules that match your chosen architecture style: domain does not reference infrastructure, application does not reference web, and infrastructure does not reference web. Those three cover the most common drift patterns in Clean Architecture projects.
warning: Overly granular rules — asserting the exact namespace of every type — make tests brittle and expensive to maintain as the codebase evolves; focus on the boundaries that matter architecturally, not on folder organisation.

name: Testcontainers for .NET
shortDescription: Spin up real PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, and other dependencies as Docker containers inside integration tests — no mocks, no shared test servers.
overview: Testcontainers for .NET starts real infrastructure — databases, message brokers, caches — as short-lived Docker containers for the duration of a test, then tears them down automatically.
detail: Testcontainers for .NET provisions disposable infrastructure from test code so integration evidence runs against the same database, cache, broker, or service implementation used in production. A typed builder pins an image, configures credentials and wait strategy, starts the resource on a random mapped host port, and exposes the runtime connection string. Fixtures choose the lifecycle boundary: per test for maximum isolation, per class or collection for speed, or per assembly with careful reset. Schema migrations run after readiness, while transactions, schema-per-test, database-per-test, or tools such as Respawn restore known state. Tests must require a healthy Docker-compatible runtime, capture container logs on failure, bound startup and cleanup, and budget CPU, memory, disk, and parallelism in CI. Image tags and digests are supply-chain inputs that need review and vulnerability scanning. Testcontainers complements deterministic unit tests; it is valuable specifically where substitute behavior cannot prove SQL translation, constraints, transactions, network protocols, or broker semantics.

interviewQuestions.question: Why not use an in-memory database?
interviewQuestions.answer: It cannot prove provider SQL translation, constraints, locking, transactions, or wire behavior.

interviewQuestions.question: How are port conflicts avoided?
interviewQuestions.answer: Testcontainers maps the container port to a random available host port and exposes it after startup.

interviewQuestions.question: What fixture scope should you use?
interviewQuestions.answer: The narrowest scope affordable for startup cost, with an explicit reset strategy when sharing.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you reset PostgreSQL state?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use rollback, truncation, Respawn, isolated schemas, or databases according to the behavior under test.

interviewQuestions.question: Why pin an image?
interviewQuestions.answer: Floating tags can change engine behavior and supply-chain contents without a code review.

interviewQuestions.question: What does a wait strategy solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: It waits for actual service readiness instead of treating process start as usable infrastructure.

interviewQuestions.question: What must CI provide?
interviewQuestions.answer: A supported container runtime, image access, sufficient resources, bounded parallelism, cleanup, and diagnostic artifacts.

note: Testcontainers tests are slower than unit tests by design — they start real infrastructure. Keep them in a separate test project, run them in CI on every pull request, and treat them as a confidence layer above unit tests rather than a replacement.
tip: Combine Testcontainers with WebApplicationFactory and a custom IAlternateSeed fixture to cover full HTTP request-to-database round trips — this single test type catches the most integration bugs for the least test maintenance.
warning: Testcontainers requires Docker to be running on the build agent; ensure CI runners have Docker available and check that your organisation's container registry policy allows pulling the required images.

name: Semantic Kernel
shortDescription: Microsoft's SDK for building AI-powered .NET applications using LLMs, plugins, memory, and orchestrated agents.
overview: Semantic Kernel is an open-source SDK from Microsoft that lets .NET developers integrate large language models into applications using familiar C# patterns.
detail: Semantic Kernel acts as an orchestration layer between your application and AI services like OpenAI or Azure OpenAI. You define plugins—functions the AI can call—and a kernel routes user intent to the right combination of those plugins. Memory connectors let the AI retrieve relevant context from vector stores, and agents can plan and execute multi-step tasks autonomously.

concepts.title: Kernel and services
concepts.description: The Kernel is the central object that wires together AI services, plugins, and memory, and routes requests through them.

concepts.title: Plugins
concepts.description: C# methods decorated with attributes become tools the LLM can call to read data, call APIs, or trigger business logic.

concepts.title: Memory and embeddings
concepts.description: Text is converted to vector embeddings and stored so the AI can retrieve semantically relevant context before responding.

concepts.title: Agents and planners
concepts.description: Agents reason over a goal and decide which plugins to call and in what order, enabling multi-step autonomous workflows.

architecture.description: A user prompt enters the Kernel, which enriches it with memory context and routes it to the LLM; the model calls plugins as needed before returning a grounded response.

code.label: OrderAssistant.cs
code.introduction: A plugin exposes a C# method as a tool the LLM can call; the kernel wires everything together in one place.

bestPractices: Keep plugins small and focused on one capability so the LLM can choose them reliably.
Store secrets like API keys in Azure Key Vault or environment variables, never in code.
Add memory and retrieval-augmented generation before building agents, as grounded context reduces hallucinations.
Log token usage and latency per kernel invocation so AI costs and performance are visible from the start.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a Semantic Kernel plugin and a prompt template?
interviewQuestions.answer: A plugin is a C# method the LLM can call to perform an action or retrieve data; a prompt template is a structured string passed to the model to guide its text response. Plugins add capabilities; prompt templates shape the conversation.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: LLMs have a fixed training cutoff and no access to private data. RAG retrieves relevant documents from a vector store and injects them into the prompt, grounding the model's response in current, application-specific facts.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you use an agent instead of a single prompt?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the task requires multiple steps, decisions, or tool calls that cannot be predicted upfront—for example, researching a topic and then drafting a summary—an agent can plan and iterate rather than a single prompt producing one fixed response.

note: Semantic Kernel is the orchestration layer, not the model itself. The quality of your plugins and prompts determines how useful the AI actually is.
tip: Start with a single plugin and one well-scoped prompt before adding planners or agents; simpler pipelines are easier to debug and cheaper to run.
warning: Never trust LLM-generated content to drive destructive operations without a human confirmation step or a strict validation layer.
latestNote: New guide on Kernel setup, plugins, and retrieval-augmented generation

name: Domain-Driven Design
shortDescription: Model complex business domains using a shared language, bounded contexts, aggregates, and value objects.
overview: Domain-Driven Design is an approach to software development that puts the business domain at the centre, using a shared language between developers and domain experts to build models that reflect real-world rules.
detail: Domain-Driven Design aligns software boundaries and language with a complex business domain. Strategic design distinguishes core, supporting, and generic subdomains, defines bounded contexts in which one model is consistent, and maps upstream/downstream relationships and translation between contexts. Tactical design uses entities with identity, immutable value objects, small aggregate consistency boundaries, domain services for behavior that belongs to no one entity, repositories for aggregate access, and factories for valid creation. Aggregates protect immediate invariants but should not grow into object graphs; workflows across roots or contexts normally use application coordination and eventual consistency. Domain events record internal facts, while integration events are deliberately mapped, versioned, and delivered through an outbox after state commits. DDD is a continuous collaboration and learning process, not a mandatory folder structure or a reason to add patterns to straightforward CRUD subdomains.

concepts.title: Ubiquitous language
concepts.description: A shared vocabulary used by both developers and domain experts in code, tests, and conversations, so the model and the business stay aligned.

concepts.title: Bounded context
concepts.description: An explicit boundary within which a particular domain model and its language are consistent; different contexts can have different models for the same concept.

concepts.title: Aggregates and entities
concepts.description: An aggregate is a cluster of objects treated as one unit for data changes; the root entity controls access and enforces all invariants.

concepts.title: Value objects and domain events
concepts.description: Value objects model concepts by their attributes rather than identity; domain events record meaningful state changes that other parts of the system can react to.

concepts.title: Subdomains
concepts.description: Core, supporting, and generic subdomains guide where deep modeling and investment create competitive value.

concepts.title: Context mapping
concepts.description: Upstream and downstream relationships, translation, and ownership make dependencies between bounded contexts explicit.

concepts.title: Repositories and factories
concepts.description: Repositories retrieve aggregate roots and factories create valid complex objects without exposing persistence or assembly details.

concepts.title: Domain versus integration events
concepts.description: Domain events coordinate inside a boundary; integration events are stable external contracts published reliably after commit.

architecture.description: Bounded contexts own their models and communicate through well-defined contracts or domain events, keeping each context independently evolvable.

code.label: Order.cs
code.introduction: An aggregate root enforces its own invariants and raises domain events instead of letting callers mutate state directly.

Define bounded contexts and map their upstream and downstream relationships.
Model entities, value objects, aggregates, invariants, services, and repositories deliberately.
Keep aggregate consistency boundaries small and enforce behavior through roots.
Separate domain events from durable integration events and publish safely.

bestPractices: Involve domain experts when naming concepts; code that uses business language is easier to validate and maintain.
Keep aggregates small—an aggregate that owns too much becomes a bottleneck and a source of contention.
Model domain events in past tense to describe what happened, not what should happen.
Map bounded context relationships explicitly using context maps so cross-boundary dependencies are visible and intentional.
Reference other aggregates by identity and coordinate workflows outside one transaction.
Keep domain types free of transport, ORM, and vendor concerns.
Separate internal domain events from stable integration contracts.
Apply tactical DDD depth according to subdomain complexity and value.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an entity and a value object?
interviewQuestions.answer: An entity has a unique identity that persists over time regardless of attribute changes; a value object is defined entirely by its attributes and has no meaningful identity of its own, so two value objects with the same attributes are interchangeable.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should an aggregate be kept small?
interviewQuestions.answer: Aggregates are loaded and saved as a unit and act as a consistency boundary. A large aggregate increases lock contention, load time, and the risk of unrelated operations blocking each other.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a bounded context and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: A bounded context is an explicit boundary within which a domain model is internally consistent. It matters because the same word—like 'customer'—can mean different things in different parts of a business, and mixing those meanings in one model creates confusion and fragile code.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an aggregate consistency boundary?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is the smallest cluster of state that must satisfy invariants atomically through one root; other aggregates are referenced by identity.

interviewQuestions.question: Domain event or integration event?
interviewQuestions.answer: A domain event is an internal model fact. An integration event is a stable external contract mapped and published reliably after commit.

interviewQuestions.question: When should a domain service be used?
interviewQuestions.answer: When domain behavior spans concepts but naturally belongs to no single entity or value object.

interviewQuestions.question: When is DDD unnecessary?
interviewQuestions.answer: When rules are simple, terminology is stable, and CRUD plus basic validation clearly solves the capability.

note: DDD is a design philosophy, not a set of mandatory patterns. Apply aggregates and events where the domain is genuinely complex; simpler areas often need only basic CRUD.
tip: Start with a context map and a glossary before writing any code—shared language problems surface quickly and are cheap to fix on paper.
warning: Avoid anemic domain models where aggregates are just data bags and all logic lives in services; this defeats the purpose of encapsulating business rules in the domain.

name: Vertical Slice Architecture
shortDescription: Organise code by feature instead of by layer, keeping everything a feature needs together and coupling to a minimum.
overview: Vertical Slice Architecture organises an application around features rather than technical layers, so each feature contains its own endpoint, handler, validation, and data access in one place.
detail: Instead of grouping all controllers together, all repositories together, and all services together, Vertical Slice Architecture puts everything a single use case needs into one folder or file. Changes to one feature touch only that slice, reducing the risk of breaking unrelated features. MediatR is a common companion because it lets each slice define its own command or query and handler without a shared service class.

concepts.title: Feature folders
concepts.description: All code for one feature—endpoint, handler, validator, response type—lives in one folder, making the feature easy to find, change, and delete.

concepts.title: Minimal coupling between slices
concepts.description: Slices share as little as possible. Common infrastructure like database access is shared, but business logic stays inside the slice that owns it.

concepts.title: Each slice owns its contract
concepts.description: A slice defines the request and response types it needs, rather than reusing shared DTOs that accumulate properties for many callers.

concepts.title: Contrast with layered architecture
concepts.description: Layers separate concerns horizontally across the whole application; vertical slices separate concerns vertically per feature, favouring cohesion over uniform abstraction.

concepts.title: Behavior boundary
concepts.description: A command or query defines one capability with explicit input, output, validation, authorization, and side effects.

concepts.title: Slice-local data access
concepts.description: Each behavior uses the projection or mutation it needs rather than a universal repository contract.

concepts.title: Cross-cutting pipeline
concepts.description: Validation, tracing, transactions, and idempotency wrap handlers without moving feature rules into middleware.

concepts.title: Independent evolution
concepts.description: High cohesion makes a feature easier to understand, optimize, replace, test, or delete as one unit.

architecture.description: Each feature is a self-contained vertical slice from HTTP endpoint to data access; shared infrastructure sits below all slices but no slice depends on another.

code.label: PlaceOrder/
code.introduction: A single file contains the endpoint, command, handler, and response for the Place Order feature—nothing is shared with other features unless it truly belongs to shared infrastructure.

bestPractices: Co-locate the endpoint, handler, validator, and response type in a single file or folder per feature.
Share only what is genuinely shared—database context, auth helpers, base types—not business logic.
Let each slice define the exact request and response shape it needs instead of inheriting a bloated shared DTO.
Use integration tests per slice to verify the full path from HTTP to database without shared test setup getting in the way.
Keep resource authorization and non-disclosure inside the owning slice.
Prefer purpose-built projections and mutations over universal repositories.
Centralize stable execution policies without centralizing feature rules.
Enforce feature dependency rules automatically.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the main advantage of Vertical Slice Architecture over a traditional layered approach?
interviewQuestions.answer: Changes to one feature touch only that slice, reducing the risk of breaking unrelated features and making it easier to reason about what a change affects. Layered architectures spread one feature across many layers, so a change ripples horizontally.

interviewQuestions.question: Does Vertical Slice Architecture replace Clean Architecture?
interviewQuestions.answer: Not necessarily—they answer different questions. Clean Architecture defines where dependencies point; Vertical Slice Architecture defines how to organise code within a project. You can use feature folders inside a clean architecture structure.

interviewQuestions.question: When is Vertical Slice Architecture a poor fit?
interviewQuestions.answer: When features share significant business logic or domain rules that would be duplicated across slices, a richer shared domain model may be a better fit than pure vertical isolation.

interviewQuestions.question: Does it require MediatR?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. A mediator is an optional dispatch and pipeline mechanism; endpoints may call focused handlers directly.

interviewQuestions.question: What should slices share?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stable infrastructure and genuinely shared domain semantics, not contracts created merely to reduce file count.

interviewQuestions.question: Can slices access a database directly?
interviewQuestions.answer: Yes, when they respect ownership, authorization, transaction, observability, and testing requirements.

interviewQuestions.question: How should duplication be handled?
interviewQuestions.answer: Accept small local duplication and extract only repeated semantics that have proven stable across behaviors.

learningObjectives: Organize behavior by use case instead of technical role.
Design explicit command and query contracts with validation and authorization.
Choose deliberately between slice-local behavior and stable shared infrastructure.
Use purpose-built projections and mutations without leaking persistence models.
Apply cross-cutting policies consistently around handler execution.
Test each slice through its observable behavior boundary.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core, dependency injection, async C#, and automated testing.
Commands, queries, persistence, validation, authorization, and transaction basics.
Understanding of cohesion, coupling, and feature ownership.

use: Layered folders scatter each feature across technical roles.
Commands and queries need tailored contracts and data access.
Teams own capabilities end to end.
avoid: A rich shared domain model would be duplicated.
Slices would copy volatile policy.
The application is too small to benefit.

items: Test valid, invalid, missing, and unauthorized inputs.
Verify endpoint contracts.
Test real-provider translation and transactions.
Prove failures do not mutate state.
Test idempotent retries.
Keep fixtures feature-focused.

security.introduction: Each slice owns resource security.
items: Derive actor and tenant from verified claims.
Authorize resources inside handlers.
Use non-disclosing outcomes.
Bound input and work.
Audit without sensitive content.

performance.introduction: Tailored data access makes work visible.
items: Project needed fields only.
Avoid unnecessary aggregate loading.
Measure queries and latency per slice.
Use pagination and cancellation.
Optimize hot slices independently.

deployment.introduction: Slices deploy together, so evolve contracts safely.
items: Use expand-contract migrations.
Version contracts deliberately.
Trace by slice and outcome.
Smoke-test critical behaviors.
Define rollback and flags.

troubleshooting.cause: Ownership is unclear.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a domain or module contract.

troubleshooting.cause: Stable policy is not shared.
troubleshooting.fix: Centralize identity, not resource rules.

troubleshooting.cause: Behaviors are coupled.
troubleshooting.fix: Use slice-owned contracts.

Contracts are slice-owned.

Data work is bounded and observable.
Dependency rules fail builds.
Contracts evolve safely.
Runbooks identify slice failures.
note: Vertical Slice Architecture is a code organisation strategy, not a silver bullet. The right amount of sharing between slices depends on how much the features genuinely overlap.
tip: Start by grouping existing files into feature folders without changing any logic—the structure alone usually reveals unexpected coupling.
warning: Taken too far, every slice becoming a copy-paste of the last leads to the same duplication problems that layers were meant to solve; shared infrastructure must still be shared.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated support-ticket sample

name: Microsoft.Extensions.AI
shortDescription: Provider-neutral abstractions and middleware for adding generative AI capabilities to .NET applications.
overview: Microsoft.Extensions.AI provides common .NET abstractions for generative AI services so application code can work with chat, embeddings, and related capabilities without being coupled to one provider SDK.
detail: The abstractions package defines exchange types such as IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator, while the higher-level Microsoft.Extensions.AI package adds composable middleware for function invocation, telemetry, caching, and other cross-cutting behavior. Providers implement the interfaces, and applications consume them through dependency injection, which makes provider changes and test doubles much easier to manage.

concepts.title: IChatClient
concepts.description: A common contract for complete and streaming chat responses, messages, tools, and multi-modal content across compatible providers.

concepts.title: IEmbeddingGenerator
concepts.description: A generic abstraction for turning text or other inputs into vector embeddings used by semantic search and retrieval workflows.

concepts.title: Composable middleware
concepts.description: Chat clients can be wrapped with function invocation, caching, telemetry, rate limiting, or custom delegating behavior.

concepts.title: Provider portability
concepts.description: Application services depend on shared abstractions while provider-specific registration remains at the composition root.

architecture.description: Application code calls shared AI abstractions, a middleware pipeline applies cross-cutting behavior, and a provider adapter communicates with the selected model service.

code.label: SupportAssistant.cs
code.introduction: The application service depends only on IChatClient, so provider setup and middleware remain outside the business workflow.

bestPractices: Keep provider-specific construction at the composition root and inject the shared abstractions into application services.
Add telemetry around latency, token use, model identity, and failures without recording sensitive prompt content by default.
Use explicit timeouts, cancellation, retry limits, and rate limits because model calls are remote and comparatively expensive.
Test AI workflows with deterministic fake IChatClient implementations before relying on slower provider integration tests.

interviewQuestions.question: How is Microsoft.Extensions.AI different from Semantic Kernel?
interviewQuestions.answer: Microsoft.Extensions.AI supplies provider-neutral primitives and composable client middleware. Semantic Kernel is a broader orchestration SDK for plugins, agents, prompts, and multi-step AI workflows; the two can be used together.

interviewQuestions.question: Why inject IChatClient instead of a provider SDK client?
interviewQuestions.answer: It keeps application code portable, simplifies tests, and centralizes provider-specific authentication, model selection, and middleware in the composition root.

interviewQuestions.question: What belongs in an AI client middleware pipeline?
interviewQuestions.answer: Cross-cutting concerns such as telemetry, caching, function invocation, rate limiting, safety checks, and resilience belong there when their ordering and failure behavior are explicit.

note: Provider neutrality reduces coupling, but models still differ in supported modalities, tool behavior, context limits, and response quality.
tip: Define one application-level AI use case behind IChatClient first, then add provider selection and middleware only where the use case requires them.
warning: Do not treat provider portability as output equivalence; validate safety, quality, latency, and cost again whenever the model or provider changes.
latestNote: New guide on provider-neutral AI abstractions and middleware

name: .NET MAUI
shortDescription: Build native Android, iOS, macOS, and Windows applications from a shared C# and XAML codebase.
overview: .NET Multi-platform App UI (.NET MAUI) is the .NET framework for creating native mobile and desktop applications with C# and XAML from a shared project.
detail: .NET MAUI provides a single project system, shared controls and layouts, data binding, handlers, app lifecycle APIs, and access to native device capabilities. Shared code targets Android, iOS, macOS through Mac Catalyst, and Windows through WinUI 3. Teams can build native XAML interfaces or host reusable Razor components locally through BlazorWebView, combining web UI reuse with native device access and store packaging.

concepts.title: Single project
concepts.description: One SDK-style project shares code, fonts, images, app metadata, and resources while multi-targeting native platforms.

concepts.title: Handlers
concepts.description: Cross-platform controls map through handlers to native platform views and can be customized globally or per control.

concepts.title: Native and hybrid UI
concepts.description: Use XAML and native controls, or host Razor components locally with BlazorWebView and share them with a Blazor web application through a Razor class library.

concepts.title: Platform integration
concepts.description: Cross-platform APIs cover sensors, connectivity, secure storage, files, and permissions, with direct native APIs available when required.

architecture.description: Shared C# uses native XAML controls or locally hosted Razor components, while MAUI handlers and device services connect the application to each operating system.

code.label: MainPage.xaml.cs
code.introduction: A shared page can call a cross-platform device API while permission and platform details stay behind .NET MAUI abstractions.

bestPractices: Keep business logic and application state in platform-neutral services and view models so they can be unit tested without a device.
Place reusable Razor components in a Razor class library when a Blazor Hybrid app and a Blazor Web App share UI, while isolating host-specific services behind interfaces.
Use handlers or platform folders for genuine native differences instead of scattering platform checks throughout shared code.
Profile startup, memory, rendering, and package size on release builds because debug and emulator behavior can be misleading.

interviewQuestions.question: Does .NET MAUI render one identical UI on every platform?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Shared MAUI controls are mapped to native platform controls through handlers, so behavior and appearance can retain platform conventions while sharing most UI code.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Blazor Hybrid differ from a hosted web app?
interviewQuestions.answer: Blazor Hybrid renders Razor components in a BlazorWebView inside the native MAUI app, with UI assets packaged locally and direct access to .NET and device services; it does not require a browser-hosted WebAssembly application.

interviewQuestions.question: Why must iOS and macOS builds use a Mac?
interviewQuestions.answer: Apple's native toolchain and signing infrastructure are required to compile and package those applications, even when development begins from another operating system.

note: A shared codebase does not remove platform differences; it gives teams one place to share common UI and logic while making native exceptions explicit.
tip: Start with one representative workflow and validate it on physical devices before committing an entire product to a cross-platform UI strategy.
warning: Do not judge production performance from debug builds or emulators alone; measure signed release builds on the oldest supported devices.
latestNote: Blazor Hybrid and shared Razor component guidance added

name: Modular Monolith
shortDescription: Keep one deployable application while enforcing business-module boundaries that can evolve independently.
overview: A modular monolith is a single deployable application divided into strongly encapsulated business modules with explicit contracts and controlled dependencies.
detail: Unlike a traditional monolith organized mainly by technical layers, a modular monolith groups code and data ownership around business capabilities. Modules communicate through public contracts or in-process messages, hide their internal models, and can own separate schemas while still sharing one process and deployment pipeline. It preserves operational simplicity and leaves room to extract a module only when independent scaling or deployment provides proven value.

concepts.title: Business modules
concepts.description: Each module owns a cohesive capability, its application behavior, domain model, persistence, and public contract.

concepts.title: Enforced boundaries
concepts.description: Internal types stay inaccessible and dependency rules prevent modules from reaching into one another's implementation details.

concepts.title: Module communication
concepts.description: Public interfaces, commands, queries, or events make cross-module interactions explicit and replace direct table or class access.

concepts.title: Single deployment
concepts.description: Modules compile and run together, avoiding distributed transactions and network failure while retaining architectural separation.

concepts.title: Data ownership
concepts.description: Each module owns its tables or schema and other modules use contracts or read models instead of direct access.

concepts.title: Integration contracts
concepts.description: Commands, queries, and events carry stable cross-module meaning without exposing internal entities.

concepts.title: Transactional choices
concepts.description: In-process calls can share a transaction when necessary, while outbox delivery supports reliable asynchronous collaboration.

concepts.title: Extraction seam
concepts.description: A well-enforced module can later move behind a network boundary when independent operations justify the cost.

architecture.description: One host composes independently owned modules; modules communicate through contracts while sharing the process and, when appropriate, a database server with isolated schemas.

code.label: OrdersModule.cs
code.introduction: A module exposes only registration and endpoint mapping while keeping handlers, entities, and persistence types internal.

bestPractices: Define modules from business capabilities and bounded contexts, not arbitrary folders or deployment aspirations.
Make module internals inaccessible and enforce dependency rules with architecture tests in continuous integration.
Give each module ownership of its tables or schema; cross-module reads should use contracts or deliberately maintained read models.
Extract a module into a service only when independent deployment, scaling, ownership, or isolation justifies the distributed-system cost.
Keep public module APIs small, business-oriented, versionable, and free of internal entities.
Choose synchronous calls or asynchronous events from consistency and coupling needs.
Use an outbox and idempotent consumers when integration events must survive failure.
Assign module ownership, observability, migrations, and operational runbooks explicitly.

interviewQuestions.question: How does a modular monolith differ from a layered monolith?
interviewQuestions.answer: A layered monolith groups code by technical role across the system, while a modular monolith groups cohesive business capabilities and restricts dependencies across those module boundaries.

interviewQuestions.question: What advantages does it have over microservices?
interviewQuestions.answer: It keeps calls and transactions in process, simplifies deployment and debugging, and avoids network and consistency complexity while still making business boundaries explicit.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you stop module boundaries from eroding?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use internal visibility, small public contracts, separate schemas or contexts, architecture tests, and code ownership rules that fail builds when forbidden dependencies appear.

interviewQuestions.question: Should modules share one database?
interviewQuestions.answer: They may share a server, but each module should own its schema or tables and other modules should not read or write them directly.

interviewQuestions.question: When should modules communicate with events?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use events when the producer should not control downstream work and eventual consistency is acceptable; use direct contracts for an immediate result.

interviewQuestions.question: How are events published reliably?
interviewQuestions.answer: Persist an outbox record with business state, then deliver asynchronously and make consumers idempotent.

interviewQuestions.question: When should a module become a microservice?
interviewQuestions.answer: When independent deployment, scaling, ownership, technology, or fault isolation produces measured value worth the operational cost.

learningObjectives: Identify business-capability module boundaries and ownership.
Design narrow public contracts while hiding internal domain and persistence types.
Choose synchronous calls, queries, events, and read models deliberately.
Enforce dependency and data-ownership rules automatically.
Coordinate transactions, outbox delivery, migrations, and observability.
Decide when service extraction has enough operational value.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core composition, dependency injection, persistence, and automated testing.
DDD bounded-context, transaction, messaging, and deployment fundamentals.
Understanding of coupling, cohesion, consistency, and distributed-system trade-offs.

use: One deployable remains operationally desirable but the domain contains distinct capabilities.
Teams need ownership and controlled dependencies without network failure.
Potential future extraction benefits from proven seams.
avoid: The application is small and module ceremony obscures behavior.
Boundaries cannot be enforced and every module shares the same tables and internals.
Independent deployment or hard isolation is already a non-negotiable requirement.

implementationIntroduction: The storefront sample composes Catalog and Orders in one process. Orders sees only catalog query, inventory command, and event contracts; tests prove success, failure atomicity, and substitutability.

implementationSteps.title: Map capabilities
implementationSteps.description: Use business language, workflows, ownership, and change patterns to propose modules.

implementationSteps.title: Define public APIs
implementationSteps.description: Expose only required commands, queries, events, and registration entry points.

implementationSteps.title: Hide internals
implementationSteps.description: Use projects, internal visibility, and architecture rules to prevent implementation access.

implementationSteps.title: Own data
implementationSteps.description: Assign tables or schemas and prohibit cross-module writes and ad hoc joins.

implementationSteps.title: Choose collaboration
implementationSteps.description: Use direct calls for immediate consistency and events for decoupled propagation.

implementationSteps.title: Test boundaries
implementationSteps.description: Verify contracts, forbidden dependencies, transactions, events, and module workflows.

implementationSteps.title: Operate and evolve
implementationSteps.description: Own migrations, telemetry, capacity, failure handling, and extraction decisions per module.

testing.introduction: Test both module behavior and the boundaries that preserve modularity.
items: Unit-test module domain and application rules.
Contract-test every public command, query, and event.
Integration-test each module against its owned schema.
Fail builds on forbidden project, namespace, and data dependencies.
Test transaction rollback and outbox publication ordering.
Run multi-module workflow tests through the composed host.

security.introduction: A process boundary is not a security boundary; modules must preserve trusted identity and authorize their own resources.
items: Pass a minimal verified actor and tenant context through contracts.
Authorize inside the owning module.
Do not expose internal entities or unrestricted query surfaces.
Protect module data with least-privilege database identities where practical.
Audit cross-module commands and sensitive outcomes without leaking payloads.

performance.introduction: In-process collaboration is fast, but hidden chatty calls and cross-module queries can still dominate latency.
items: Measure calls, queries, payloads, and transaction duration per module.
Use deliberate read models for cross-module reporting.
Avoid serializing in-process messages unnecessarily.
Keep integration events bounded and versioned.
Profile the composed workflow before extracting a service.

deployment.introduction: One artifact simplifies rollout, but module schemas and contracts still need safe evolution.
items: Run module migrations in a controlled order.
Use expand-contract schema changes.
Keep integration events backward compatible.
Expose module-tagged health, traces, metrics, and logs.
Smoke-test critical cross-module workflows and rollback.

troubleshooting.cause: Data ownership is unenforced.
troubleshooting.fix: Introduce a contract or owned read model and block direct access.

troubleshooting.cause: Public contracts expose internal types.
troubleshooting.fix: Shrink and stabilize contract assemblies.

troubleshooting.cause: Publication is not transactional.
troubleshooting.fix: Use an outbox and idempotent consumer.

troubleshooting.cause: Capabilities or shared semantics are misplaced.
troubleshooting.fix: Revisit boundaries or extract a small neutral contract.

troubleshooting.cause: Eager initialization scans or loads excessive state.
troubleshooting.fix: Measure registration and defer bounded work.

troubleshooting.cause: Contracts and data ownership were only conceptual.
troubleshooting.fix: Enforce seams before introducing the network.

productionChecklist: Modules map to business capabilities with named owners.
Public contracts are narrow and versioned.
Internals and forbidden dependencies are build-enforced.
Each module owns data and migrations.
Collaboration and consistency choices are documented.
Outbox and idempotency protect durable events.
Security and observability identify module boundaries.
