Extraction requires measured operational justification.
note: The value comes from enforced modularity, not from putting the word Modules in a folder name.
tip: Start with the business capability that changes most often and define its public contract before reorganizing the rest of the application.
warning: A shared database becomes hidden coupling when modules query or update one another's tables directly.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated contract-isolated storefront sample

name: Source Generators
shortDescription: Build deterministic incremental generators that replace boilerplate and reflection with inspectable compile-time C#.
overview: C# source generators are compiler components that inspect source, symbols, additional files, and analyzer configuration, then add strongly typed C# to the same compilation. They move repeatable discovery and glue code from runtime or developer maintenance into a deterministic build step.
detail: A production generator is a small compiler extension, not a text-templating shortcut. It runs inside the compiler and IDE, where latency, determinism, compatibility, diagnostics, and failure isolation directly affect every consumer. Modern generators implement IIncrementalGenerator and describe a graph of immutable transformations. Roslyn can cache unchanged values when the pipeline filters early, projects symbols into stable value models, and combines only inputs that actually affect an output. Generation is additive: it can contribute syntax trees but cannot rewrite user code. Good uses include serializers, strongly typed configuration, registration maps, protocol clients, and repetitive partial-type members whose complete inputs are available at compilation. Poor uses include business logic, network-dependent generation, arbitrary file mutation, or tasks better expressed by a normal library, analyzer, code fix, or MSBuild target. A shippable generator also needs intentional packaging, compiler-version compatibility, readable output, stable hint names, actionable diagnostics, snapshot and compilation tests, performance measurements, and a documented escape hatch when generation is unsuitable.
learningObjectives: Explain the compilation lifecycle and distinguish generators from analyzers, code fixes, reflection, templates, and MSBuild tasks.
Design an incremental pipeline that filters syntax cheaply and converts Roslyn symbols into stable immutable value models.
Generate readable, deterministic, collision-safe source without rewriting user syntax or depending on mutable global state.
Report precise diagnostics for invalid consumer declarations and preserve useful locations in compiler output.
Package and consume a generator as an analyzer while keeping compiler dependencies private and compatible.
Test generated text, output compilation, diagnostics, determinism, runtime behavior, and incremental performance.
prerequisites: Strong C# knowledge including attributes, partial types, symbols, nullable reference types, records, and project references.
Familiarity with the .NET build pipeline, NuGet packaging, MSBuild items and properties, and compiler diagnostics.
Basic understanding of syntax trees versus semantic symbols and why IDE-time work must remain fast and cancellation-aware.

use: A repeatable strongly typed API can be derived completely from declarations, attributes, AdditionalFiles, or compiler-visible build configuration.
Runtime reflection, dynamic activation, or handwritten registration creates measurable startup, trimming, AOT, or maintenance costs.
A library must produce compile-time errors and discoverable generated APIs while keeping consumer code concise.
avoid: Inputs require a database, network request, machine-specific state, current time, or writes outside compiler-provided outputs.
A normal generic library, source-generated framework feature, IDE template, analyzer/code fix, or explicit handwritten code is simpler.
Generated behavior would hide important domain decisions or create an API larger and harder to understand than the repetition it removes.

concepts.title: Compiler integration
concepts.description: A generator receives compiler-controlled inputs and contributes syntax trees before emit; it is loaded like an analyzer and does not execute in the application.

concepts.title: Incremental graph
concepts.description: IIncrementalGenerator registers providers and transformations whose values Roslyn can cache and recompute selectively.

concepts.title: Syntax filtering
concepts.description: A cheap predicate eliminates most nodes before semantic work; attribute-driven discovery should normally use ForAttributeWithMetadataName.

concepts.title: Semantic symbols
concepts.description: Symbols provide resolved types, accessibility, namespaces, attributes, and members; syntax alone cannot reliably answer those questions.

concepts.title: Stable value models
concepts.description: Pipeline stages should project Roslyn objects into small equatable records containing only values that influence generation.

concepts.title: Source emission
concepts.description: RegisterSourceOutput turns validated models into deterministic UTF-8 C# with unique stable hint names and nullable-aware declarations.

concepts.title: Diagnostics
concepts.description: ReportDiagnostic gives consumers actionable IDs, severity, messages, and source locations instead of exceptions or silently missing output.

concepts.title: Additional inputs
concepts.description: AdditionalFiles and AnalyzerConfigOptions support controlled non-C# inputs and compiler-visible MSBuild configuration without arbitrary environment access.

concepts.title: Packaging contract
concepts.description: Generator assemblies belong under analyzers/dotnet/cs in a package; Roslyn dependencies usually remain private and consumer runtime assets stay separate.

concepts.title: Compatibility boundary
concepts.description: A generator runs in the host compiler, so target framework, Roslyn API version, language features in emitted code, and consumer SDK support must be tested deliberately.

architecture.description: The compiler turns user declarations and controlled build inputs into a cacheable incremental graph. Validated value models produce diagnostics and generated C# that joins user code in the final compilation.

implementationIntroduction: Start from the consumer contract and the smallest complete set of compile-time inputs. The generator should behave like a pure function from stable values to source and diagnostics.

implementationSteps.title: Define the generated API
implementationSteps.description: Write representative consumer code and generated output first. Decide naming, accessibility, partial-type requirements, nullable behavior, generic constraints, conflicts, and opt-in semantics.

implementationSteps.title: Create the Roslyn component
implementationSteps.description: Use a dedicated analyzer project, target a compiler-compatible framework such as netstandard2.0 when broad tooling support matters, reference Microsoft.CodeAnalysis privately, and enable analyzer rules.

implementationSteps.title: Discover candidates narrowly
implementationSteps.description: Prefer ForAttributeWithMetadataName for attributed targets. Keep the syntax predicate allocation-light and defer symbol inspection to the transform callback.

implementationSteps.title: Project stable models
implementationSteps.description: Extract namespace, type shape, members, configuration, and locations into immutable equatable data. Do not carry Compilation, ISymbol, or SyntaxNode farther than needed.

implementationSteps.title: Validate and diagnose
implementationSteps.description: Detect non-partial targets, duplicate names, unsupported nesting or generic shapes, inaccessible members, and configuration errors; report stable documented diagnostic IDs at useful locations.

implementationSteps.title: Render deterministic source
implementationSteps.description: Order collections ordinally, escape identifiers and literals, use fully qualified framework types where appropriate, emit nullable context, and derive unique hint names from full identities.

implementationSteps.title: Package, consume, and test
implementationSteps.description: Reference the project as an Analyzer with ReferenceOutputAssembly=false, package the DLL under analyzers/dotnet/cs, inspect emitted files, and run snapshot, diagnostic, compilation, runtime, and performance tests.

code.label: TelemetryGenerator.cs
code.introduction: The dedicated sample injects its marker attribute, discovers attributed types through the semantic-aware incremental API, and emits one output per stable target model.

testing.introduction: A generator test suite must verify both sides of the compiler boundary: the source and diagnostics it produces, and the consumer compilation and behavior that result.
items: Run CSharpGeneratorDriver against minimal in-memory compilations and assert every expected diagnostic ID, severity, message argument, and location.
Snapshot or compare normalized generated files so API, formatting, ordering, hint names, and nullable changes are intentional reviews.
Inspect the updated output compilation for errors and test representative consumer calls against the generated API.
Run the same input repeatedly and reorder irrelevant declarations to prove deterministic output and avoid unstable build artifacts.
Use incremental step tracking or benchmarks on large representative projects to detect broad invalidation, excessive allocations, and IDE latency regressions.

security.introduction: Generators execute during builds and design-time compilation, often on developer machines and CI agents. Treat them as supply-chain code with access that must be minimized.
items: Never fetch network content, read secrets, inspect arbitrary machine directories, or execute tools from a generator; use declared AdditionalFiles and compiler-visible configuration only.
Pin, review, scan, and sign generator packages like build infrastructure because a compromised generator runs wherever consumers compile.
Do not embed credentials, absolute paths, environment values, or sensitive AdditionalFiles into generated source, diagnostics, or build logs.
Escape identifiers, strings, namespaces, and file-derived values before emission so untrusted inputs cannot create unintended declarations or directives.
Keep generated APIs least-privileged and do not bypass authorization, validation, or serialization policy simply because code is produced at compile time.

performance.introduction: Generator latency is multiplied across builds and keystrokes. Incremental APIs help only when the pipeline exposes narrow, comparable values instead of invalidating the whole graph.
items: Filter syntax with the cheapest possible predicate and prefer ForAttributeWithMetadataName over scanning every declaration and manually resolving attributes.
Project symbols into small equatable models before combining streams; retaining Compilation or large syntax objects defeats useful caching.
Avoid Collect unless an output truly depends on the complete set, and emit per-item sources so one changed type does not regenerate unrelated files.
Honor cancellation tokens and keep transforms pure, synchronous, and free of locks, mutable static caches, file I/O, and network I/O.
Measure clean build, warm build, single-file edit, allocation, and generated-source size on realistic solutions rather than assuming incremental means fast.

deployment.introduction: A generator is deployed through project references or analyzer assets in NuGet, and its host is the consumer's compiler rather than the consumer application runtime.
items: Package generator assemblies under analyzers/dotnet/cs and verify the nupkg contents; do not place the generator in lib as a normal runtime dependency.
Keep Microsoft.CodeAnalysis references PrivateAssets=all and test against the oldest and newest supported SDK or Visual Studio compiler hosts.
Separate runtime attributes or helper abstractions into a contracts assembly when generated code must reference public runtime types.
Build a sample consumer from the packed package in CI, with warnings as errors, deterministic build checks, and compiler-generated-file inspection.
Version generated public APIs and diagnostic behavior semantically, document breaking changes, and provide migration guidance or opt-outs.

troubleshooting.cause: The project was referenced as a normal assembly or the package placed the DLL outside analyzer assets.
troubleshooting.fix: Use OutputItemType=Analyzer and ReferenceOutputAssembly=false for project references; inspect the nupkg for analyzers/dotnet/cs.

troubleshooting.cause: Candidate filtering, metadata attribute name, namespace, partial declaration, or semantic validation excluded the target.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect generated files and generator diagnostics, reduce to one consumer declaration, and test the discovery pipeline with GeneratorDriver.

troubleshooting.cause: The generator targets an incompatible runtime or references a Roslyn API/dependency unavailable in the host compiler.
troubleshooting.fix: Target a supported framework, minimize dependencies, keep Roslyn assets private, and test the published package against supported compiler hosts.

troubleshooting.cause: The pipeline carries Compilation or symbols too far, calls Collect broadly, or combines unrelated global inputs.
troubleshooting.fix: Project early to equatable values, split independent streams, emit per target, and inspect incremental step reasons in tests.

troubleshooting.cause: Hint names are based only on simple type names or member iteration depends on nondeterministic order.
troubleshooting.fix: Derive hint names from full identities, sanitize consistently, order inputs ordinally, and add repeatability tests.

troubleshooting.problem: IDE succeeds but command-line build fails
troubleshooting.cause: The IDE and CLI use different SDK/compiler versions, configuration, AdditionalFiles, or analyzer assets.
troubleshooting.fix: Pin the SDK with global.json, compare binlogs and generated files, and reproduce with the packed generator in a clean consumer.

productionChecklist: The use case is fully determined by compile-time inputs and is simpler than the runtime or handwritten alternative.
Candidate discovery is narrow, semantic analysis is delayed, and pipeline values are immutable and equatable.
Generated C# is readable, nullable-aware, escaped, deterministically ordered, and uses collision-safe hint names.
Invalid input produces documented diagnostics with stable IDs and precise locations; expected mistakes do not throw exceptions.
Tests cover source snapshots, diagnostics, output compilation, runtime consumption, determinism, and incremental performance.
The package contains correct analyzer assets, private Roslyn dependencies, release tracking, and a clean sample consumer build.
Supported SDK, compiler, language, and target-framework ranges are explicit and exercised in CI.
The generator performs no undeclared file, network, secret, process, clock, or machine-dependent work.
bestPractices: Start with the generated consumer API and keep generation opt-in, predictable, and easy to inspect.
Prefer IIncrementalGenerator and ForAttributeWithMetadataName for modern attribute-driven generators.
Convert Roslyn symbols into minimal stable models before expensive combination or collection steps.
Generate one deterministic file per target with fully qualified framework types and collision-safe hint names.
Report actionable diagnostics for consumer mistakes and track rule releases as part of the public contract.
Package and test the actual analyzer asset rather than proving only a directly referenced generator project.
Benchmark IDE-like incremental edits as well as clean builds and treat latency regressions as product defects.
Keep business policy in normal source code; generation should remove mechanical repetition without hiding important decisions.

interviewQuestions.question: When does a source generator run?
interviewQuestions.answer: It runs inside compiler and IDE compilation processes and adds syntax trees before emit. Its code does not become an application runtime component unless generated source explicitly references a separate runtime library.

interviewQuestions.question: Why prefer IIncrementalGenerator?
interviewQuestions.answer: It expresses generation as composable providers and transformations that Roslyn can cache. The benefit depends on using narrow stable values; carrying the whole compilation through the graph can still invalidate everything.

interviewQuestions.question: Can a generator modify existing source?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Generation is additive. An analyzer can report a problem and a code fix can offer an edit, but a generator cannot replace or mutate a user's syntax tree.

interviewQuestions.question: Syntax node or symbol: which should a generator use?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use syntax for cheap candidate filtering and symbols for resolved meaning such as types, accessibility, attributes, and members. Efficient generators deliberately use both at different stages.

interviewQuestions.question: How do generators differ from reflection?
interviewQuestions.answer: A generator discovers known compile-time structure and emits ordinary typed code, improving diagnostics and often trimming or AOT behavior. Reflection discovers runtime metadata and handles shapes unavailable at compilation but adds runtime cost and dynamism.

interviewQuestions.question: How should invalid consumer input be handled?
interviewQuestions.answer: Emit stable diagnostics with documented IDs, severity, useful arguments, and precise source locations. Expected invalid code should not crash the generator or silently omit output.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes an incremental generator actually incremental?
interviewQuestions.answer: Early filtering, small equatable models, narrow combinations, per-item output, deterministic transforms, and avoiding broad compilation or Collect dependencies allow Roslyn to reuse unaffected pipeline values.

note: Generators add code, analyzers diagnose code, code fixes propose edits, and MSBuild tasks orchestrate build work. A solution may ship several together, but each has a distinct lifecycle and responsibility.
tip: Set EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles in a sample consumer so maintainers can review exactly what downstream developers compile.
warning: A generator executes during typing and builds. Broad syntax scans, unstable models, external I/O, or incompatible dependencies can degrade or break every consuming project.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated incremental generator sample

name: ML.NET
shortDescription: Train and consume classical machine-learning models for classification, regression, recommendation, forecasting, and more in .NET.
overview: ML.NET is an open-source, cross-platform machine-learning framework for training custom models and running predictions inside .NET applications.
detail: ML.NET expresses data preparation and algorithms as a pipeline that is fitted to training data to produce an immutable model. It supports tasks including binary and multiclass classification, regression, clustering, recommendation, anomaly detection, forecasting, and integrations for selected deep-learning scenarios. Models can be trained code-first or with tooling, saved as artifacts, and loaded into applications for local inference.

concepts.title: MLContext
concepts.description: The entry point for loading data, defining pipelines, training models, evaluating results, and saving artifacts.

concepts.title: IDataView
concepts.description: A lazy, schema-aware representation that lets ML.NET process datasets larger than memory through composable transforms.

concepts.title: Estimator pipeline
concepts.description: Data transforms and a trainer are chained, then Fit learns parameters and produces an immutable transformer model.

concepts.title: Evaluation and inference
concepts.description: Task-specific metrics validate a held-out dataset before the saved model is loaded for predictions in an application.

architecture.description: Training data passes through preparation and a trainer to create a versioned model artifact, which an application loads to perform local predictions.

code.label: SentimentModel.cs
code.introduction: A text-featurization and binary-classification pipeline trains a small sentiment model and uses it for a local prediction.

bestPractices: Split training, validation, and test data before experimentation to avoid evaluating a model on examples it learned from.
Choose metrics that match the business cost of false positives and false negatives instead of optimizing accuracy alone.
Version the model together with its input schema, feature pipeline, training data lineage, and evaluation results.
Monitor production data and predictions for drift, and retrain only through a repeatable, reviewed pipeline.

interviewQuestions.question: How is ML.NET different from generative AI libraries?
interviewQuestions.answer: ML.NET primarily trains and runs task-specific predictive models such as classifiers and regressors, while generative AI libraries integrate foundation models that create or transform content.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an estimator and a transformer?
interviewQuestions.answer: An estimator describes a learnable pipeline stage. Calling Fit on data produces a transformer containing the learned parameters that can transform new data.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a held-out test set important?
interviewQuestions.answer: It estimates how the trained model generalizes to unseen data; evaluating on training examples produces overly optimistic metrics and hides overfitting.

note: A model is only as trustworthy as its data, evaluation design, and production monitoring; the training API cannot compensate for biased or unrepresentative examples.
tip: Begin with a simple baseline and one business-relevant metric before experimenting with more complex trainers or AutoML.
warning: PredictionEngine is convenient for simple or single-threaded examples but is not thread-safe; production services should use an appropriate pooled or batch prediction pattern.
latestNote: New guide on classical machine learning and local inference

name: OpenAPI & Scalar
shortDescription: Generate accurate OpenAPI contracts and present an interactive, modern API reference with Scalar.
overview: ASP.NET Core can generate OpenAPI documents from endpoint metadata, while Scalar renders those documents as an interactive API reference for developers.
detail: Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi provides first-party document generation for Minimal APIs and controllers, including runtime endpoints, build-time generation, named documents, and transformers. In .NET 10 the generator emits an OpenAPI 3.1 document from routing, binding, typed results, validation, and explicit endpoint metadata. Scalar.AspNetCore is a separate UI integration that reads that portable document and renders searchable reference documentation and a request client. The UI is not the contract: operation identifiers, request schemas, success and failure responses, security requirements, examples, nullability, and version lifecycle must agree with runtime behavior. Contract tests and reviewed document diffs catch drift before it breaks generated clients, gateways, tests, or partners. Runtime JSON and interactive documentation also enlarge the discovery surface, so production exposure must be an explicit authenticated decision rather than a default copied from development.
learningObjectives: Explain the separate responsibilities of ASP.NET Core OpenAPI generation and Scalar presentation.
Generate OpenAPI 3.1 documents from accurate endpoint metadata.
Stabilize operation identifiers, schemas, responses, and document versions for consumers.
Customize cross-cutting contract details with document, operation, and schema transformers.
Test the generated JSON and interactive reference as deployment artifacts.
Choose a safe production exposure policy for documents and request clients.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core routing, Minimal APIs or controllers, model binding, and HTTP status codes.
JSON schemas and the purpose of a machine-readable API contract.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the dedicated catalog sample.

use: Use first-party generation when ASP.NET Core endpoint metadata is the contract source.
Use Scalar when developers need a searchable interactive reference over an existing OpenAPI document.
Use named documents when versions or audiences have different lifecycle boundaries.
avoid: Do not treat a polished UI as evidence that the underlying contract is accurate.
Do not expose internal operations or browser-stored credentials through an unrestricted production reference.
Do not make accidental operation ID or schema changes without compatibility review.

concepts.title: OpenAPI document
concepts.description: A language-neutral contract describing operations, paths, parameters, request bodies, responses, schemas, and security schemes.

concepts.title: Endpoint metadata
concepts.description: Typed results, attributes, summaries, descriptions, and response declarations feed the generated operation definitions.

concepts.title: Document transformers
concepts.description: Transformers apply cross-cutting changes such as security schemes, branding metadata, or environment-specific server information.

concepts.title: Scalar API reference
concepts.description: Scalar consumes an OpenAPI URL and provides interactive, searchable documentation without generating the contract itself.

concepts.title: Operation identity
concepts.description: Stable endpoint names become operation identifiers used by client generators, tests, gateways, and consumer documentation.

concepts.title: Contract lifecycle
concepts.description: Versioned documents, compatibility review, deprecation, generated artifacts, and consumer communication govern change.

concepts.title: Security descriptions
concepts.description: Security schemes describe how callers authenticate, but runtime authentication and authorization still enforce access.

concepts.title: Exposure boundary
concepts.description: OpenAPI JSON and interactive request clients reveal capabilities and therefore need an intentional environment and access policy.

architecture.description: ASP.NET Core endpoint metadata is assembled into an OpenAPI document, exposed as JSON, and consumed by Scalar or downstream client-generation tools.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated catalog sample generates a .NET 10 OpenAPI 3.1 document, gives each operation a stable name and complete response metadata, and maps Scalar only in Development. Integration tests inspect both the contract JSON and the rendered reference endpoint.

implementationSteps.title: Install deliberate dependencies
implementationSteps.description: Reference Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi, a patched Microsoft.OpenApi version, and Scalar.AspNetCore explicitly.

implementationSteps.title: Register a named document
implementationSteps.description: Call AddOpenApi and decide whether one document or audience-specific documents match the API lifecycle.

implementationSteps.title: Describe operations
implementationSteps.description: Use endpoint names, summaries, descriptions, tags, typed results, and validation metadata to describe behavior.

implementationSteps.title: Describe failures
implementationSteps.description: Include validation, authorization, not-found, conflict, and other meaningful responses rather than documenting only 200.

implementationSteps.title: Apply transformers
implementationSteps.description: Add shared information or security descriptions centrally while keeping business-specific metadata near endpoints.

implementationSteps.title: Control exposure
implementationSteps.description: Map OpenAPI JSON and Scalar in Development or behind approved production authentication and authorization.

implementationSteps.title: Freeze the contract
implementationSteps.description: Test required paths, operation IDs, schemas, and responses, and review document diffs in CI.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: The app generates a first-party OpenAPI document and exposes Scalar only in development, while endpoint metadata improves the contract.

testing.introduction: Contract verification must compare generated metadata with real HTTP behavior.
items: Parse the generated document and assert its OpenAPI version, required paths, methods, and stable operation IDs.
Assert request and response schemas plus every significant status code.
Exercise endpoints with integration tests so documented success and failure outcomes remain executable.
Verify the Scalar route in the environments where it is intended to exist.
Diff a normalized document or run a compatibility checker before publishing breaking changes.

security.introduction: Documentation is part of the API attack and credential-handling surface.
items: Describe authentication schemes accurately without embedding tokens, client secrets, or real examples.
Keep runtime authorization independent from the document and UI.
Disable the document and Scalar in production unless discovery is intended and access is protected.
Apply browser security headers and prevent shared machines from retaining privileged credentials.
Filter internal-only endpoints from public documents and test the filter.

performance.introduction: Generation is usually inexpensive, but large documents and interactive clients still consume startup, bandwidth, and browser resources.
items: Generate once per document and avoid request-dependent expensive transformers.
Split genuinely independent audiences or versions instead of shipping one unbounded contract.
Cache immutable published documents with a versioned URL where appropriate.
Measure generation and UI load time after adding large schemas or examples.

deployment.introduction: The document, UI, gateway import, and generated clients must all refer to the intended release contract.
items: Set the environment explicitly and verify whether document routes exist after deployment.
Publish the generated document as a versioned CI artifact for review and downstream tooling.
Use correct external server URLs when proxies or gateways change the public origin.
Run contract tests against the release build and smoke-test JSON and Scalar routes.
Coordinate breaking changes with version and deprecation policy rather than silently replacing a document.

troubleshooting.symptom: An endpoint is missing from the document.
troubleshooting.cause: It was excluded, lacks discoverable metadata, or belongs to another named document.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect routing and document selection metadata, then assert the expected path in a contract test.

troubleshooting.symptom: A response schema or status is wrong.
troubleshooting.cause: Runtime branches and typed or explicit response metadata disagree.
troubleshooting.fix: Use typed results or Produces metadata for every material outcome and add matching HTTP tests.

troubleshooting.cause: Endpoint names were omitted or renamed during refactoring.
troubleshooting.fix: Assign stable consumer-facing names and test them as compatibility-sensitive identifiers.

troubleshooting.symptom: Scalar loads but cannot fetch the contract.
troubleshooting.cause: The document route, base path, proxy, environment, or authorization policy differs from the UI configuration.
troubleshooting.fix: Open the JSON URL directly and align Scalar's document URL with the deployed route.

troubleshooting.symptom: The production document reveals internal routes.
troubleshooting.cause: Development mapping or audience filtering was copied to production.
troubleshooting.fix: Disable exposure or require authorization and generate a reviewed public document.

troubleshooting.symptom: A dependency audit reports Microsoft.OpenApi risk.
troubleshooting.cause: A vulnerable transitive or direct package version was resolved.
troubleshooting.fix: Pin a patched compatible version, restore, rebuild, and repeat direct and transitive vulnerability audit.

productionChecklist: Every operation has a stable name, summary, inputs, success responses, and failure responses.
Schemas match nullability, validation, formats, and runtime serialization.
Security schemes describe the real authentication contract without containing secrets.
Named documents and versions have owners, lifecycle, and compatibility policy.
Generated JSON is parsed and contract-tested in CI.
Breaking diffs require explicit review and consumer communication.
OpenAPI and Scalar production exposure is disabled or authenticated intentionally.
External URLs, proxy paths, document JSON, and Scalar are smoke-tested after deployment.
bestPractices: Treat the OpenAPI document as a tested contract and fail continuous integration when unintended breaking changes appear.
Use typed results and explicit metadata so status codes, schemas, descriptions, and security requirements match actual behavior.
Give operations stable names because generated clients consume them as identifiers.
Document validation and error responses, not only the happy path.
Version APIs deliberately and publish separate documents when consumers need stable lifecycle boundaries.
Use transformers for coherent cross-cutting metadata rather than ad hoc edits.
Publish a normalized document artifact and review compatibility diffs.
Restrict or secure interactive documentation in production and never prefill real credentials or secrets in a browser-visible client.

interviewQuestions.question: What roles do Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi and Scalar play?
interviewQuestions.answer: The Microsoft package generates the OpenAPI document from ASP.NET Core metadata. Scalar consumes that document and renders an interactive reference; it does not replace accurate contract generation.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can generated documentation still be wrong?
interviewQuestions.answer: Generation reflects available metadata. If response types, status codes, security requirements, or descriptions are missing or differ from runtime behavior, the generated contract will preserve those gaps.

interviewQuestions.question: How should API versioning relate to OpenAPI documents?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each supported public API version should have a clear lifecycle and discoverable contract, commonly through separate named documents that client teams can pin and compare.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are operation IDs compatibility-sensitive?
interviewQuestions.answer: Client generators often turn them into method names, so an accidental rename can break source compatibility even when the path still works.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Scalar be enabled in production?
interviewQuestions.answer: Only when production discovery is intentional and protected. Many services keep both JSON and the interactive client development-only or publish a separately governed public contract.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a document transformer for?
interviewQuestions.answer: It applies cross-cutting document changes such as shared metadata or security scheme descriptions without duplicating edits across endpoints.

note: Scalar is a documentation experience; the OpenAPI document remains the portable source of truth for tools and consumers.
tip: Check the generated JSON into an artifact or compare it in CI so contract changes are reviewed alongside code.
warning: An unrestricted production documentation UI can expose internal operations and make credential misuse easier even when the underlying API still enforces authorization.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated contract-tested catalog sample

name: Feature Flags
shortDescription: Separate deployment from release with runtime flags, targeted rollouts, variants, and operational kill switches.
overview: Feature flags separate deployment from release by making an explicit, observable runtime decision about which behavior a caller receives.
detail: The Microsoft.FeatureManagement libraries give .NET applications consistent APIs for Boolean flags, filters, targeting, time windows, variants, request-aware evaluation, gates, middleware, and evaluation telemetry. Azure App Configuration can store definitions centrally, select them by key and label, authenticate workloads with Microsoft Entra ID, and refresh flags without rebuilding an artifact. A flag is not just a Boolean configuration value: it is temporary operational control with an owner, audience, safe fallback, metrics, expiry condition, and removal change. Good designs evaluate once at stable boundaries, keep a user in a deterministic cohort, avoid using flags as authorization, exercise both branches, and fail safely when configuration is stale or unavailable. Progressive delivery succeeds only when technical and business signals govern expansion, kill switches are rehearsed, and completed flags and dead branches are deleted promptly.
learningObjectives: Explain deployment, release, experimentation, migration, entitlement, and operational kill-switch use cases.
Use Microsoft.FeatureManagement abstractions and Azure App Configuration without coupling business logic to a provider.
Design stable targeting and percentage rollout that avoids users switching cohorts between requests.
Choose safe refresh, caching, fallback, and outage behavior.
Test enabled, disabled, targeted, variant, stale-configuration, and cleanup states.
Observe evaluation and outcome metrics without leaking sensitive targeting attributes.
Own and remove temporary flags before they become permanent architecture.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core routing, dependency injection, configuration, and request context.
Basic continuous delivery and rollback concepts.
Microsoft Entra managed identity and Azure RBAC for an Azure-backed deployment.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the dedicated checkout rollout sample.

use: Use release flags for gradual exposure of already-deployed code.
Use operational flags as tested kill switches for optional risky behavior.
Use variants when named behavior or configuration differs by stable audience.
Use short-lived migration flags when old and new implementations must overlap safely.
avoid: Do not use a feature flag as the only authorization or entitlement control.
Do not flag every refactor or scatter the same decision through many layers.
Do not run an experiment without assignment and outcome telemetry.
Do not keep a temporary flag after the rollout decision is complete.
tradeoffs: Flags improve reversibility but multiply runtime states and test combinations.
Short refresh intervals reduce control latency but increase configuration traffic and fleet inconsistency during propagation.
Targeting enables safe exposure but audience attributes need privacy review and stable identity.
Provider independence improves testability while central App Configuration improves governance and operations.

concepts.title: Deployment versus release
concepts.description: Code can reach production disabled, then be enabled gradually without building and deploying another artifact.

concepts.title: Filters and context
concepts.description: Time-window, targeting, percentage, and custom filters evaluate contextual rules instead of one global value.

concepts.title: Stable cohorts
concepts.description: Deterministic assignment based on a durable subject identifier keeps the same user in the same rollout group.

concepts.title: Variants
concepts.description: A flag can assign named configurations to audiences for experiments, migrations, or tier-specific behavior.

concepts.title: Refresh and consistency
concepts.description: Instances cache definitions and observe changes over time, so rollout propagation is bounded but not globally atomic.

concepts.title: Telemetry
concepts.description: Evaluation reason, allocation, version, technical health, and business outcomes make rollout decisions explainable.

concepts.title: Safe fallback
concepts.description: Every flag defines behavior for disabled, missing, stale, invalid, or unreachable configuration states.

concepts.title: Flag lifecycle
concepts.description: Every flag needs an owner, purpose, creation date, review date, completion condition, and cleanup change.

architecture.description: A central configuration source supplies flag definitions, the feature manager evaluates them against request context, and application code selects the enabled behavior while telemetry records the decision.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: Azure App Configuration loads selected flags using managed identity, while the feature manager evaluates the release decision at one application boundary.

implementationSteps: Classify the flag as release, experiment, migration, entitlement, or operational and define its safe disabled behavior.
Assign an owner, purpose, audience, creation date, review date, completion condition, and removal issue before coding.
Wrap the behavioral choice behind one application service or endpoint boundary and keep authorization independent.
Configure local definitions first, then connect Azure App Configuration with DefaultAzureCredential, narrow selectors, labels, and a deliberate refresh interval.
Choose stable targeting identity, group rules, percentage allocation, variants, and exclusion precedence; document privacy constraints.
Add structured evaluation and outcome telemetry, dashboards, alert thresholds, and a rapid disable runbook.
Test every material state, release to internal users, expand in guarded stages, then delete the definition and dead branch.

testing.introduction: Prove deterministic assignment, both behaviors, provider integration, and failure fallback before changing live exposure.
items: Unit-test globally disabled, globally enabled, targeted, excluded, percentage, and variant outcomes with deterministic subjects.
Test both behavior branches independently rather than only testing the evaluator.
Verify one subject receives stable assignment across processes, restarts, and scale-out.
Exercise missing, malformed, stale, delayed, and unreachable configuration with the documented fallback.
Contract-test selected key prefixes and labels so production does not load the wrong environment.
Run progressive-delivery drills that prove alerts stop expansion and the kill switch restores the safe path.

security.introduction: Treat definition storage, targeting context, administrative changes, and every enabled action as separate security boundaries.
items: Treat flags as release controls, never as the sole authorization check for protected data or actions.
Use managed identity and the App Configuration Data Reader role; disable access keys when operationally possible.
Restrict selected keys, labels, network paths, administrative roles, and change permissions by environment.
Audit definition changes and protect high-impact kill switches with separation of duties and emergency access procedures.
Do not emit raw user identifiers, group membership, secrets, or sensitive business attributes in evaluation telemetry.
Validate custom-filter inputs and bound external calls; evaluation must not become an SSRF, injection, or availability path.

performance.introduction: Keep evaluation local and predictable while controlling refresh traffic, propagation delay, and active flag complexity.
items: Evaluate at stable boundaries and reuse scoped decisions instead of repeatedly evaluating the same flag in a request.
Use provider caching and an intentional refresh interval; do not query a remote store on every decision.
Keep custom filters deterministic, cancellation-aware, bounded, and free of slow network dependencies.
Measure evaluation latency, refresh failures, cache age, provider requests, allocation skew, and downstream impact.
Expect propagation delay across instances and design rollouts that tolerate mixed behavior during the refresh window.
Limit active flags and targeting complexity so startup, refresh, cognition, and test matrices remain manageable.

deployment.introduction: Promote both code paths first, then change exposure through observable, reversible stages and remove temporary state afterward.
items: Provision separate stores or strong key/label boundaries per environment with infrastructure as code.
Grant workload identities read-only data-plane access and release operators only the permissions they require.
Deploy both branches before enabling, verify telemetry, start with staff or a small cohort, then expand by documented gates.
Keep rollout changes auditable and reversible independently from application deployment.
Coordinate flags that affect schemas, messages, or clients with compatibility windows and migration ordering.
After full rollout and soak, remove old code first where safe, remove the flag definition, and verify no references remain.

troubleshooting.symptom: A flag change is not visible
troubleshooting.cause: The key or label was not selected, the refresh interval has not elapsed, middleware is missing, or identity/network access failed.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect selectors, label, endpoint, refresh registration, cache age, managed identity, RBAC, DNS, and provider diagnostics.

troubleshooting.cause: Assignment uses a transient identifier, random evaluation, inconsistent flag names, or different definitions across instances.
troubleshooting.fix: Use one durable subject ID and deterministic hash, then compare definition versions and selectors across the fleet.

troubleshooting.symptom: The flag is enabled but access is denied
troubleshooting.cause: The release decision and authorization policy are separate controls.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep the authorization denial; verify the caller's permissions instead of weakening security because a flag is on.

troubleshooting.symptom: Rollout metrics look worse but aggregate health is green
troubleshooting.cause: Metrics are not segmented by allocation, variant, or evaluation version.
troubleshooting.fix: Correlate evaluation telemetry with errors, latency, and business outcomes for each cohort before expanding.

troubleshooting.cause: Evaluation depends synchronously on the remote provider or has no tested stale/missing fallback.
troubleshooting.fix: Use cached definitions, bounded refresh, and an explicit fail-safe behavior; rehearse provider loss.

troubleshooting.symptom: Nobody knows whether a flag can be removed
troubleshooting.cause: Ownership, completion criteria, references, and cleanup work were not recorded.
troubleshooting.fix: Assign an owner and expiry, search code and telemetry, remove dead behavior in a reviewed change, then delete the definition.

productionChecklist: Flag type, purpose, owner, audience, safe default, creation date, review date, and removal condition are recorded.
Authorization and entitlement controls remain independent and tested.
Target identity and percentage assignment are deterministic and privacy-reviewed.
Key/label selectors, refresh interval, cache, outage fallback, and propagation expectations are documented.
Managed identity, least-privilege RBAC, network access, audit logs, and administrative controls are verified.
Both branches, exclusions, targeting, variants, stale configuration, and kill-switch behavior are tested.
Evaluation, technical health, and business outcome telemetry drive staged rollout gates.
The definition, dead branch, tests, dashboards, and documentation have an explicit cleanup task.
bestPractices: Give every flag a clear owner, creation date, expected removal date, and documented behavior for configuration failure.
Evaluate flags at stable decision points and avoid scattering the same flag through many layers.
Use deterministic subjects for targeting and percentage filters so experiences remain stable.
Test enabled, disabled, targeted, excluded, variant, stale, and provider-outage paths.
Observe errors, latency, allocation, and business metrics while rollout changes.
Use managed identity, least privilege, narrow selectors, and separate environment boundaries.
Remove temporary flags and dead branches promptly after rollout or migration completes.

interviewQuestions.question: How is a feature flag different from application configuration?
interviewQuestions.answer: Both may use configuration infrastructure, but a feature flag represents a managed release decision with targeting, variants, telemetry, ownership, and a lifecycle rather than a general application setting.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a kill switch?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is an operational flag designed to disable risky behavior quickly without redeploying, with a safe and well-tested fallback path.

interviewQuestions.question: Why must percentage rollout be deterministic?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stable hashing keeps one subject in one cohort, making behavior consistent and telemetry attributable; random evaluation can switch experiences on every request.

interviewQuestions.question: What consistency should you expect after a flag change?
interviewQuestions.answer: Instances normally refresh cached definitions independently, so the fleet can temporarily run mixed decisions. The design must tolerate propagation delay rather than assume an atomic global switch.

interviewQuestions.question: Can a feature flag replace authorization?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. A flag controls release exposure; authorization decides whether an authenticated principal may access a resource or action and must be enforced independently.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the main long-term risk of feature flags?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stale flags leave permanent branches and multiply the states developers must understand and test, so cleanup discipline is essential.

note: Feature flags make releases reversible, but they also add runtime states that must be observable and tested.
tip: Start rollout with internal users or a small stable audience and expand only when technical and business metrics remain healthy.
warning: Do not use a feature flag as the only authorization check; release targeting and security policy solve different problems.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated deterministic rollout sample

name: Model Context Protocol
shortDescription: Expose tools, resources, and prompts to AI applications through a standard protocol and the official C# SDK.
overview: Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how AI applications discover and invoke external tools, read contextual resources, and use reusable prompts.
detail: The official C# SDK lets .NET applications act as MCP servers or clients. Servers publish capabilities such as tools, resources, and prompts over transports including standard input/output and HTTP, while clients negotiate capabilities and invoke them through a consistent protocol. MCP improves interoperability, but every exposed capability remains a security boundary that needs validation, authorization, consent, timeouts, and auditability.

concepts.title: Servers and clients
concepts.description: An MCP server publishes capabilities; an MCP client connects, negotiates supported features, and makes those capabilities available to an AI host.

concepts.title: Tools
concepts.description: Model-invocable operations have typed inputs and outputs and can perform actions such as querying an order or creating a support ticket.

concepts.title: Resources and prompts
concepts.description: Resources expose contextual data through URIs, while prompts provide reusable, parameterized interaction templates.

concepts.title: Transports and lifecycle
concepts.description: Stdio suits local process integration, while HTTP supports remote services; initialization, capability negotiation, cancellation, and errors are protocol concerns.

architecture.description: An AI host uses an MCP client to discover server capabilities, then invokes narrowly scoped tools or reads resources through a negotiated transport.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: A small stdio server registers attributed tools from the assembly so compatible clients can discover and call the order-status capability.

bestPractices: Expose small, intention-revealing tools with strict schemas instead of giving a model generic database, shell, or network access.
Authenticate clients, authorize every capability and target resource, and require confirmation for destructive or financially meaningful actions.
Validate inputs and outputs, apply cancellation and timeouts, and return structured errors that do not reveal secrets or internal topology.
Log capability identity, caller, result, latency, and correlation data while redacting prompts, credentials, and sensitive payloads.

interviewQuestions.question: How is MCP different from function calling?
interviewQuestions.answer: Function calling is usually a model-provider feature for requesting a named function. MCP standardizes discovery, schemas, invocation, resources, prompts, transports, and lifecycle between AI hosts and external capability servers.

interviewQuestions.question: When should an MCP server use stdio instead of HTTP?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stdio is a good fit when the host starts and owns a local child process. HTTP is appropriate for independently deployed or remotely shared servers that need network authentication, scaling, and operations.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the main security risk of MCP tools?
interviewQuestions.answer: A model can turn untrusted instructions into real side effects. Tools must enforce the same authentication, authorization, validation, least privilege, and confirmation rules as any other application endpoint.

note: MCP standardizes integration mechanics; it does not decide whether a tool call is safe, permitted, or correct for a particular user.
tip: Start with one read-only tool and test discovery, schema clarity, cancellations, and audit logs before exposing write operations.
warning: Never expose an unrestricted shell, SQL executor, or broad cloud credential as an MCP tool.
latestNote: New guide on MCP servers, clients, tools, resources, and security

name: API Security & OWASP
shortDescription: Design and test ASP.NET Core APIs against common authorization, resource-consumption, configuration, and integration risks.
overview: API security applies identity, authorization, input boundaries, abuse controls, secure configuration, and continuous verification to every exposed operation and object.
detail: The OWASP API Security Top 10 highlights recurring risks including broken object-level authorization, broken authentication, broken object-property authorization, unrestricted resource consumption, broken function authorization, unrestricted access to sensitive business flows, server-side request forgery, security misconfiguration, poor API inventory, and unsafe consumption of upstream APIs. ASP.NET Core supplies authentication, policy authorization, request limits, rate limiting, Problem Details, data protection, output controls, and test hosting, but controls only work when attached to explicit assets, actors, tenants, resources, operations, and trust boundaries. Production API security is continuous: inventory every host and version, validate and minimize input and output contracts, authorize each function and loaded object, bound memory, CPU, time, concurrency, pages, uploads, and downstream calls, restrict outbound destinations, protect secrets, patch dependencies, observe abuse without logging sensitive data, and retire obsolete surfaces. The OWASP list is a prioritization lens rather than a checklist that replaces threat modeling, abuse-case analysis, secure design review, negative tests, dependency auditing, and deployed-environment verification.
learningObjectives: Map OWASP API risks to concrete ASP.NET Core controls and tests.
Threat-model assets, actors, tenants, trust boundaries, entry points, and abuse cases.
Prevent object, property, and function authorization failures.
Bound resource consumption and sensitive business workflows beyond one global rate limit.
Prevent SSRF and unsafe upstream consumption through destination, protocol, response, and timeout controls.
Maintain an accurate API inventory and retire obsolete versions safely.
Verify controls continuously through negative tests, telemetry, dependency audit, and deployment review.
prerequisites: HTTP APIs, JSON contracts, authentication, authorization, and status codes.
ASP.NET Core middleware, routing, dependency injection, and integration testing.
Basic threat-model concepts such as asset, actor, trust boundary, attack surface, and abuse case.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the dedicated secure order API.

use: Use the OWASP API Security Top 10 to structure awareness, design review, testing, and backlog prioritization.
Use system-specific threat modeling to decide which controls and evidence each endpoint needs.
Use defense in depth across edge, application, data, dependency, identity, delivery, and monitoring layers.
avoid: Do not claim an API is secure because a scanner or Top 10 checklist passed.
Do not treat authentication, TLS, CORS, or an API gateway as a replacement for object and function authorization.
Do not use rate limits as the only defense for costly operations or sensitive business workflows.
Do not consume arbitrary client-selected URLs or trust upstream responses because the dependency is internal.

concepts.title: Object-level authorization
concepts.description: Every request for a specific record must verify the caller can access that object; a valid token alone does not prevent identifier-based data exposure.

concepts.title: Abuse and resource controls
concepts.description: Rate limits, request-size limits, pagination, timeouts, quotas, and workflow-specific rules protect compute and sensitive business flows.

concepts.title: Input and output boundaries
concepts.description: Purpose-built request and response models, validation, allowlists, and minimal serialization reduce mass assignment and excessive data exposure.

concepts.title: Inventory and dependencies
concepts.description: Teams must know which API versions and hosts exist, patch them, retire stale endpoints, and treat upstream API responses as untrusted input.

concepts.title: Object-property authorization
concepts.description: Allowlisted request DTOs prevent mass assignment, and minimal response DTOs prevent excessive exposure of internal or caller-forbidden properties.

concepts.title: Function authorization
concepts.description: Every operation enforces server-side policy; a role, route name, HTTP method, or hidden UI is not sufficient permission by itself.

concepts.title: Sensitive business flows
concepts.description: Purchasing, booking, signup, recovery, and other valuable workflows need actor-aware quotas, sequencing, idempotency, fraud controls, and monitoring.

concepts.title: SSRF and unsafe consumption
concepts.description: Outbound calls require allowlisted destinations and schemes, DNS and redirect awareness, timeouts, size bounds, response validation, and restricted egress.

architecture.description: Traffic passes through trusted edge controls, strict protocol and resource bounds, validated identity, function and resource authorization, allowlisted contracts, domain workflow controls, protected data access, and constrained upstream clients while correlated telemetry records security-relevant outcomes.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated order API converts common risks into executable boundaries: tenant and subject authorization, bounded inputs, minimal response DTOs, request limits, rate limiting, an outbound destination allowlist, safe errors, and negative integration tests.

implementationSteps.title: Inventory the surface
implementationSteps.description: Record hosts, routes, versions, owners, data classifications, clients, dependencies, and retirement dates.

implementationSteps.title: Threat-model operations
implementationSteps.description: Identify assets, actors, trust boundaries, object identifiers, privileged functions, costly work, and sensitive workflows.

implementationSteps.title: Constrain contracts
implementationSteps.description: Use allowlisted request and response DTOs, validate shape and semantics, and cap bodies, collections, pages, and files.

implementationSteps.title: Authorize functions and objects
implementationSteps.description: Require server policy, load inside the tenant boundary, and authorize subject, resource, operation, and state.

implementationSteps.title: Bound resource use
implementationSteps.description: Apply actor-aware quotas, concurrency limits, timeouts, cancellation, idempotency, and workflow controls.

implementationSteps.title: Constrain dependencies
implementationSteps.description: Allowlist outbound hosts and schemes, restrict redirects and egress, validate responses, and bound response size and duration.

implementationSteps.title: Test and observe abuse
implementationSteps.description: Automate negative cases, audit dependencies and configuration, monitor denied and anomalous behavior, and rehearse response.

code.label: OrderEndpoints.cs
code.introduction: The endpoint requires authentication and rate limiting, loads the target resource, then performs resource-aware authorization before returning a minimal response.

testing.introduction: Negative tests are executable threat-model evidence, not optional edge cases.
items: Test anonymous, invalid identity, wrong role, wrong tenant, non-owner, and forbidden function access.
Test over-posted properties and assert internal or unauthorized fields never appear in responses.
Test oversized bodies, collections, page sizes, repeated requests, concurrent requests, timeouts, and cancellation.
Test metadata, loopback, private-network, alternate-scheme, redirect, DNS, and oversized upstream-response SSRF cases.
Run dependency, secret, static, dynamic, and configuration scans, then verify findings against the deployed environment.

security.introduction: API security combines prevention, detection, recovery, and continuous inventory across every trust boundary.
items: Authenticate through trusted schemes and authorize every function, tenant, object, and sensitive property.
Validate, normalize, and allowlist input while returning only purpose-built response contracts.
Use least privilege for databases, queues, storage, service identities, and outbound network access.
Protect credentials and keys, patch dependencies, harden production configuration, and remove debug endpoints.
Log security outcomes with correlation and redaction, alert on abuse patterns, and retain evidence according to policy.

performance.introduction: Resource bounds are both capacity engineering and security controls.
items: Cap request and response bodies, uploads, decompression, JSON depth, collection length, and page size before large allocation.
Use per-actor and per-workflow quotas plus global safeguards; include concurrency and cost, not only request count.
Propagate cancellation and set timeouts on databases and outbound calls.
Reject invalid or unauthorized work before expensive queries, file processing, model calls, or downstream effects.
Load-test abusive patterns and monitor CPU, memory, queue depth, rejection rate, and dependency saturation.

deployment.introduction: Security controls must survive the real proxy, network, identity, configuration, and release pipeline.
items: Apply trusted forwarded-header, TLS, host, CORS, request-limit, and security-header configuration at the real edge path.
Run as least privilege, restrict egress, separate environments, and keep secrets in managed stores.
Generate and review an API inventory and dependency inventory for every release.
Deploy compatible contract changes, retire old versions on schedule, and remove abandoned hosts and credentials.
Smoke-test negative cases, telemetry, alerting, rollback, and incident procedures after deployment.

troubleshooting.symptom: Changing an identifier returns another user's data.
troubleshooting.cause: Object-level authorization is absent or occurs after response mapping.
troubleshooting.fix: Scope loading to tenant and subject, authorize the resource, and add cross-owner tests.

troubleshooting.cause: Persistence entities or broad models are bound directly.
troubleshooting.fix: Use allowlisted request DTOs and server-owned values.

troubleshooting.symptom: One request exhausts memory or CPU.
troubleshooting.cause: Bodies, collections, decompression, queries, or downstream work are unbounded.
troubleshooting.fix: Reject early with explicit size, complexity, time, concurrency, and cost limits.

troubleshooting.symptom: An outbound URL reaches internal metadata.
troubleshooting.cause: Client-controlled destinations, redirects, DNS, or egress are unrestricted.
troubleshooting.fix: Use fixed or allowlisted destinations, HTTPS, redirect controls, IP validation, and network egress policy.

troubleshooting.cause: Inventory and decommission ownership are incomplete.
troubleshooting.fix: Discover hosts and gateways, assign owners and retirement dates, remove routes and credentials, and monitor for traffic.

troubleshooting.symptom: Security logs expose tokens or personal data.
troubleshooting.cause: Headers, bodies, or claims are logged without classification and redaction.
troubleshooting.fix: Use allowlisted structured fields, centralized redaction, access controls, and retention rules.

productionChecklist: Every API host, route, version, owner, data class, client, dependency, and retirement date is inventoried.
Threat models cover objects, functions, properties, business flows, resource consumption, SSRF, and dependencies.
Authentication and tenant-aware object and function authorization have negative tests.
Request, response, upload, page, concurrency, duration, retry, and downstream costs are bounded.
Outbound destinations, schemes, redirects, DNS resolution, response size, and egress are constrained.
Secrets, packages, images, configuration, and infrastructure are scanned and patched.
Errors and telemetry are correlated and redacted; abuse alerts and incident runbooks are tested.
The real deployed edge path, old-version retirement, rollback, and recovery are verified.
bestPractices: Threat-model assets, actors, trust boundaries, and abuse cases and convert them into tests.
Authorize every function, tenant, and requested resource on the server.
Use allowlisted request and response contracts instead of persistence entities.
Bound bodies, pages, queries, concurrency, duration, retries, and outbound destinations.
Protect sensitive business flows with actor-aware quotas, sequencing, idempotency, and monitoring.
Treat upstream responses and internal networks as untrusted and constrain egress.
Maintain and retire an owned API inventory and patch all dependencies.
Test controls in the deployed environment and monitor security outcomes without leaking data.

interviewQuestions.question: What is broken object-level authorization (BOLA)?
interviewQuestions.answer: It occurs when an API accepts an object identifier but does not verify that the authenticated caller is allowed to act on that specific object, allowing access by changing identifiers.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is rate limiting not a complete authorization control?
interviewQuestions.answer: Rate limiting controls volume, not permission. A caller below the limit can still access the wrong tenant, object, function, or business workflow unless authorization is enforced separately.

interviewQuestions.question: How should an API consume an upstream API safely?
interviewQuestions.answer: Authenticate the dependency, restrict destinations, set timeouts and size limits, validate responses, avoid blindly following redirects, and treat returned data as untrusted.

interviewQuestions.question: What is broken object-property authorization?
interviewQuestions.answer: It occurs when callers can set properties they should not control or receive properties they should not see; explicit request and response DTOs reduce both risks.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is an API inventory a security control?
interviewQuestions.answer: Unknown or obsolete hosts and versions escape patching, monitoring, ownership, and retirement, leaving unmanaged attack surface.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you defend against SSRF?
interviewQuestions.answer: Avoid arbitrary destinations; allowlist schemes and hosts, control redirects and DNS/IP resolution, restrict egress, set time and size limits, and validate responses.

interviewQuestions.question: What is sensitive business-flow abuse?
interviewQuestions.answer: A legitimate operation such as booking or recovery is automated or repeated for harmful advantage, requiring workflow-specific limits beyond technical authentication.

note: The OWASP list is an awareness and prioritization aid, not a substitute for a system-specific threat model.
tip: For every happy-path integration test, add anonymous, wrong-tenant, wrong-owner, oversized-input, and repeated-request cases.
warning: A globally authenticated API can still be critically vulnerable when object and function authorization are missing.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated OWASP negative-test sample

name: Azure Key Vault & Secrets
shortDescription: Protect application secrets, keys, and certificates with managed identity, Azure RBAC, rotation, and auditable access.
overview: Azure Key Vault protects secrets, cryptographic keys, and certificates behind Microsoft Entra authentication, data-plane authorization, recovery controls, and audit logs.
detail: Key Vault removes sensitive material from source repositories and ordinary application settings, but it does not remove the need to design identity, authorization, retrieval, caching, rotation, recovery, and leakage controls. .NET workloads commonly authenticate with DefaultAzureCredential during development and a managed identity in Azure, then use SecretClient for explicit version-aware retrieval or the ASP.NET Core configuration provider for startup-oriented configuration. Production vaults should use Azure RBAC, least-privilege data roles, separate environment boundaries, soft delete, purge protection, diagnostics, network restrictions where required, and tested rotation with overlapping validity. Applications must decide whether they follow the latest secret version or pin a version, how quickly caches refresh, what happens during vault failure, and how dependent services adopt a new credential without downtime. A retrieved secret becomes ordinary process memory and can still leak through logs, exceptions, telemetry, dumps, responses, or an over-privileged caller.
learningObjectives: Distinguish secrets, keys, certificates, control-plane operations, and data-plane operations.
Authenticate .NET workloads with DefaultAzureCredential and managed identity without a deployed client secret.
Choose Azure RBAC roles, scope, vault boundaries, and network controls using least privilege.
Select explicit SecretClient retrieval or configuration-provider integration by refresh and version needs.
Design cache, version, rotation, overlap, rollback, and outage behavior.
Protect deletion recovery and observe access without logging values.
Test identity, denial, rotation, recovery, and deployed network paths.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core configuration, dependency injection, options, and application startup.
Microsoft Entra identities, OAuth tokens, Azure RBAC scope, and managed identity basics.
Secret rotation and zero-downtime deployment concepts.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the dedicated rotation sample.

use: Use Key Vault for centrally governed application secrets, keys, and certificates that require auditable access and lifecycle controls.
Use managed identity for Azure workloads and approved developer credentials locally.
Use SecretClient when code needs explicit versions, metadata, refresh, writes, or rotation coordination.
Use the configuration provider for secrets that naturally map to startup configuration and whose refresh behavior is acceptable.
avoid: Do not store ordinary non-sensitive configuration in Key Vault by default.
Do not embed a client secret just to retrieve another secret.
Do not grant broad administrator roles to runtime identities.
Do not assume secret rotation automatically refreshes every application instance.
tradeoffs: Centralization improves governance but introduces a runtime dependency that needs caching and outage planning.
Following the latest version simplifies adoption but can cause uncontrolled fleet changes; pinning improves determinism but requires rollout automation.
Private endpoints reduce exposure but add DNS, routing, deployment, and recovery complexity.
Separate vaults improve environment and blast-radius boundaries but increase resource and operational count.

concepts.title: Vault object types
concepts.description: Secrets hold sensitive values, keys support cryptographic operations, and certificates manage certificate material and lifecycle.

concepts.title: Managed identity
concepts.description: An Azure-hosted workload obtains short-lived Entra tokens without storing a client secret in source code or application configuration.

concepts.title: Azure RBAC
concepts.description: Separate control-plane and data-plane roles grant narrowly scoped management or object access and can be audited centrally.

concepts.title: Versions and activation
concepts.description: Updating a secret creates a version; consumers need an intentional latest-versus-pinned policy and controlled adoption.

concepts.title: Caching and availability
concepts.description: Bounded application caches reduce latency and vault load while defining how long an old value can remain active.

concepts.title: Rotation
concepts.description: Zero-downtime rotation usually creates a new credential, overlaps validity, updates dependents, verifies adoption, then revokes the old value.

concepts.title: Recovery protection
concepts.description: Soft delete and purge protection defend vaults and objects against accidental or malicious deletion and require rehearsed recovery.

concepts.title: Network and diagnostics
concepts.description: Firewall or private connectivity constrains reachability while diagnostic logs provide access and change evidence without exposing values.

architecture.description: The .NET workload uses its Entra identity to request narrowly authorized Key Vault data, while diagnostics and rotation processes govern access throughout the secret lifecycle.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: The application adds Key Vault as a configuration source and uses the same credential chain for local development and managed identity in Azure.

implementationSteps: Inventory each secret, owner, producer, consumers, sensitivity, lifetime, rotation capability, and recovery requirement.
Create environment-specific vault boundaries with Azure RBAC, soft delete, purge protection, diagnostics, and the required network path.
Enable a system- or user-assigned managed identity and grant only the required data role at the narrowest practical scope.
Use DefaultAzureCredential and SecretClient for explicit retrieval, or the configuration provider when startup mapping and refresh behavior fit.
Add bounded caching, cancellation, retry/backoff, safe startup or degraded behavior, and redacted health signals.
Implement create-new, overlap, activate, observe, roll back, and revoke stages; never overwrite dependent credentials blindly.
Test denial, expiration, rotation, cache refresh, vault outage, deleted-object recovery, and the deployed DNS/firewall/private-endpoint path.

testing.introduction: Separate application tests from real identity, vault, network, rotation, and recovery verification.
items: Unit-test application behavior with a secret-provider abstraction; never require a real vault for every logic test.
Integration-test DefaultAzureCredential with a dedicated non-production identity and least-privilege role.
Verify unauthorized identities cannot list or read secrets and runtime identities cannot administer the vault.
Run a two-version rotation drill proving old and new values overlap, adoption is observable, rollback works, and old credentials are revoked.
Test missing, disabled, expired, deleted, malformed, throttled, and unreachable secret states with redacted errors.
Recover a deleted object or disposable vault in a rehearsal and record recovery time and permissions.

security.introduction: Protect identity, authorization, network reach, recovery controls, administrators, and every place resolved material can escape.
items: Use managed identity in Azure and approved developer identity or local secret storage; never commit credentials.
Prefer Azure RBAC and separate runtime read roles from secret-management and vault-administration roles.
Use separate vaults or strong boundaries per environment and avoid cross-environment runtime access.
Enable purge protection and diagnostics; restrict public access and use private endpoints when threat and compliance needs justify them.
Never log values, authorization headers, configuration dumps, exception payloads, process dumps, or fingerprints that enable guessing.
Treat the process, operators, deployment system, backups, and downstream service as part of the secret exposure boundary.

performance.introduction: Reuse clients and credentials, cache deliberately, and observe retrieval pressure without weakening rotation objectives.
items: Reuse Azure SDK clients and token credentials; they are designed for concurrent use.
Cache values for a bounded period chosen from rotation objectives and compromise response requirements.
Avoid listing or retrieving secrets per request; fetch only named objects and prevent cache stampedes.
Use bounded retries with jitter for transient throttling and respect service guidance rather than retrying authorization failures.
Measure retrieval latency, failures, throttles, cache age, refresh outcomes, version adoption, and dependency authentication errors.
Estimate startup fan-out across replicas and stagger refresh so a deployment does not overload the vault.

deployment.introduction: Deploy identity, access, recovery, and networking before consumers, then rotate through observable overlapping versions.
items: Provision vault policy, RBAC assignments, diagnostics, recovery, and networking through reviewed infrastructure as code.
Create identities and role assignments before workloads need the secret and allow for RBAC propagation.
Use environment-specific URIs and secret names while keeping values out of templates, outputs, pipeline logs, and source control.
Deploy network and DNS paths before disabling public access; test from the actual hosting environment.
Rotate with overlapping validity, staged consumer refresh, version telemetry, rollback, and final old-credential revocation.
Maintain emergency access, break-glass audit, ownership, expiration alerts, and recovery runbooks.

troubleshooting.symptom: DefaultAzureCredential works locally but fails in Azure
troubleshooting.cause: The deployed identity is missing, the wrong identity is selected, or its data role and scope are incorrect.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the host identity, credential diagnostics, tenant, client ID when user-assigned, role definition, scope, and propagation time.

troubleshooting.symptom: The caller gets forbidden despite a role
troubleshooting.cause: A control-plane role was confused with a data-plane role, scope is wrong, or the vault uses a different permission model.
