troubleshooting.fix: Confirm enableRbacAuthorization, assign the narrow data role, remove conflicting assumptions, and retest after propagation.

troubleshooting.symptom: A rotated value is not used
troubleshooting.cause: The app pins a version, caches longer than expected, or the configuration provider does not refresh automatically as assumed.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect requested version and cache age, invalidate deliberately, restart only when documented, and graph adoption before revoking old credentials.

troubleshooting.cause: DNS resolves the public endpoint, routing or firewall rules block traffic, or deployment agents have no private path.
troubleshooting.fix: Resolve the vault hostname from the workload, inspect private DNS links, routes, endpoint approval, firewall, and deployment topology.

troubleshooting.cause: Clients are recreated, values are fetched per request, replicas refresh together, or retries amplify load.
troubleshooting.fix: Reuse clients, add bounded caches and single-flight refresh, stagger work, honor backoff, and inspect service metrics.

troubleshooting.symptom: A deleted secret cannot be restored
troubleshooting.cause: The recovery window expired, permissions are insufficient, purge occurred, or the runbook was never tested.
troubleshooting.fix: Verify soft-delete state and retention, use authorized recovery procedures, restore dependent configuration, and rehearse before an incident.

productionChecklist: Secret inventory, ownership, consumers, expiration, rotation, recovery, and deletion policy are recorded.
Managed identity and least-privilege Azure RBAC data roles are verified at the intended scope.
Environment separation, network path, private DNS or firewall, and emergency access are tested.
Soft delete, purge protection, diagnostics, alerts, and audit retention are enabled.
Retrieval choice, version policy, cache lifetime, retries, startup behavior, and outage fallback are documented.
Secret values are excluded from logs, errors, telemetry, responses, dumps, templates, and pipeline outputs.
Two-version rotation, staged adoption, rollback, and old-credential revocation are rehearsed.
Deletion recovery and deployed-environment access are verified regularly.
bestPractices: Use managed identity for Azure workloads and developer identity or approved local secret storage during development.
Prefer Azure RBAC data-plane roles, least privilege, separate environment boundaries, and just-in-time administration.
Use explicit version and cache policies rather than assuming every consumer follows rotation automatically.
Design rotation with overlapping validity, adoption telemetry, rollback, and dependency coordination.
Enable diagnostics, purge protection, recovery alerts, and tested restore procedures.
Restrict network access where required and validate DNS and routing from the deployed workload.
Avoid logging resolved values and review every place a retrieved secret can escape process memory.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use managed identity with Key Vault?
interviewQuestions.answer: It removes the need to distribute and rotate an application credential for accessing the vault; Azure issues short-lived tokens to the workload identity.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the Key Vault control plane and data plane?
interviewQuestions.answer: The control plane manages the vault resource and settings, while the data plane operates on secrets, keys, and certificates. Permissions should be scoped separately.

interviewQuestions.question: When should .NET use SecretClient instead of the configuration provider?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use SecretClient when code needs explicit versions, metadata, refresh timing, writes, or fine-grained error handling. The provider fits startup-oriented configuration mapping when its loading and refresh behavior are acceptable.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you rotate a credential without downtime?
interviewQuestions.answer: Create a new credential, allow old and new values to overlap, publish and activate the new version, observe all consumers adopting it, retain rollback, then revoke the old credential.

interviewQuestions.question: Why cache Key Vault secrets?
interviewQuestions.answer: Caching reduces latency, cost, throttling, and outage impact, but the lifetime must be bounded so rotation and compromise response meet objectives.

interviewQuestions.question: Does rotating a Key Vault secret automatically update every running application?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. A new version becomes available, but each integration has its own caching and refresh behavior. Applications need a tested strategy for observing and adopting the new value.

note: Key Vault protects stored secret material, but callers can still leak a retrieved value through logs, exceptions, telemetry, or overly broad process access.
tip: Test rotation in a non-production environment using two valid credential versions before relying on the process during an incident.
warning: Do not replace one embedded application secret with another embedded credential used to access the vault.

name: Internal Developer Platforms
shortDescription: Create product-minded golden paths that give development teams secure, governed, observable self-service delivery.
overview: An internal developer platform (IDP) combines self-service workflows, reusable platform capabilities, and governance to reduce developer cognitive load from idea to production.
detail: Platform engineering treats developers as customers and the platform as a product. An IDP connects templates, source control, CI/CD, infrastructure, secrets, policy, observability, documentation, and service ownership into supported golden paths. For .NET teams, Aspire can standardize local orchestration, service discovery, health checks, telemetry, and deployment models, but it is one building block rather than the entire platform.

concepts.title: Golden paths
concepts.description: Recommended, supported routes encode proven defaults for common workloads while allowing documented escape hatches for genuine exceptions.

concepts.title: Self-service interfaces
concepts.description: Portals, CLIs, APIs, templates, and automation let teams provision and operate services without ticket-driven handoffs.

concepts.title: Platform as a product
concepts.description: A platform team researches developer needs, owns a roadmap and support model, and measures adoption and outcomes rather than mandating tools.

concepts.title: Governance by design
concepts.description: Security, cost, reliability, ownership, and compliance controls are built into reusable workflows with early feedback.

architecture.description: Developers use a portal, CLI, or template to invoke platform APIs that coordinate engineering systems and provision governed runtime capabilities with feedback and telemetry.

code.label: AppHost.cs
code.introduction: A reusable Aspire composition can form part of a .NET golden path by wiring dependencies, health, service discovery, and local orchestration consistently.

bestPractices: Start with a thin, high-friction developer journey and build the smallest viable golden path with teams that will use it.
Provide APIs, automation, documentation, support, and escape hatches; a catalog page alone is not a developer platform.
Encode secure defaults and policy feedback early, while keeping ownership boundaries and failure recovery visible to product teams.
Measure lead time, onboarding time, reliability, adoption, support load, and developer satisfaction instead of output such as template count.

interviewQuestions.question: How is an internal developer platform different from a developer portal?
interviewQuestions.answer: A portal is one possible user interface. An IDP includes the underlying APIs, automation, templates, policies, infrastructure capabilities, ownership model, and operational feedback.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a golden path?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is a supported route for a common workload that packages good defaults and automation to reduce cognitive load without forbidding justified alternatives.

interviewQuestions.question: Where does .NET Aspire fit in platform engineering?
interviewQuestions.answer: Aspire can standardize application composition, local dependencies, service discovery, health, telemetry, and deployment representations for .NET workloads, but CI/CD, cloud provisioning, policy, identity, catalogs, and product ownership still require a broader platform.

note: Successful platforms earn adoption by removing friction; they do not merely centralize control or rename an operations ticket queue.
tip: Interview developers and map one delivery journey before selecting portal or infrastructure products.
warning: A mandatory big-bang platform built without product-team feedback can increase cognitive load and create a new bottleneck.
latestNote: New guide on golden paths, self-service, governance, and Aspire

name: Dapper
shortDescription: Map parameterized SQL to .NET objects with a small, fast API built on standard ADO.NET connections.
overview: Dapper is a small .NET object mapper that executes explicit, parameterized SQL through standard ADO.NET connections and maps result rows to focused application types.
detail: Dapper adds convenient query, command, parameter, multi-mapping, and multiple-result APIs to DbConnection without taking ownership of the relational model. The application still owns SQL text, projections, connection lifetime, transaction boundaries, schema evolution, provider behavior, indexes, query plans, and failure handling. That explicitness makes Dapper a strong fit for read models, reporting, CQRS query paths, stored procedures, and performance-sensitive operations where the team wants precise SQL control. It also means production-ready code must allowlist dynamic identifiers, parameterize every value, bound result sets, propagate cancellation, coordinate transactions deliberately, test against the real database provider, and operate schema changes outside Dapper itself.
learningObjectives: Explain what Dapper adds to ADO.NET and which responsibilities remain with the application and database.
Choose the correct Query, Execute, single-row, scalar, multi-mapping, and multiple-result API for a use case.
Write parameterized SQL while handling dynamic filters, sort columns, directions, and identifiers through trusted allowlists.
Own connection and transaction lifetimes so related commands commit or roll back atomically.
Design bounded projections, stable pagination, indexes, timeouts, and diagnostics for important query paths.
Test mappings, constraints, transactions, and provider-specific SQL against a real relational database.
prerequisites: Comfort with C#, async and await, cancellation tokens, records or DTOs, and dependency injection.
Working knowledge of SQL including joins, grouping, indexes, parameters, transactions, and query plans.
The .NET 10 SDK; the dedicated sample uses SQLite and does not require Docker.

use: Read-heavy features where explicit SQL and narrow result shapes are easier to reason about than ORM query translation.
CQRS query paths, reports, stored procedures, legacy schemas, or hot operations that need precise provider-specific SQL.
Teams with strong SQL ownership that want lightweight row mapping while retaining direct ADO.NET control.
avoid: Aggregate-heavy transactional applications that benefit from identity tracking, relationship fix-up, change detection, and managed migrations; EF Core may remove substantial ceremony.
A team that cannot own SQL review, schema deployment, provider-specific tests, and query-plan analysis as part of normal delivery.
An abstraction intended to make one SQL implementation portable across different database engines without deliberate dialect and behavior work.

concepts.title: Explicit SQL
concepts.description: The application owns query text, joins, projections, indexes, and provider behavior rather than relying on a LINQ translator.

concepts.title: CommandDefinition
concepts.description: A command packages SQL, parameters, transaction, timeout, command type, flags, and a cancellation token for an asynchronous operation.

concepts.title: Parameter binding
concepts.description: Anonymous objects, POCOs, dictionaries, lists, and DynamicParameters bind values without concatenating them into SQL text.

concepts.title: Result cardinality
concepts.description: Query, QueryFirst, QuerySingle, Execute, and ExecuteScalar express different expectations; selecting the right API makes missing or duplicate rows visible.

concepts.title: Row and multi-mapping
concepts.description: Column aliases map rows to typed objects, while splitOn-based multi-mapping folds joined records into object graphs intentionally.

concepts.title: Multiple result sets
concepts.description: QueryMultiple consumes several result grids from one command, reducing round trips when the results belong to one coherent read operation.

concepts.title: Connection and transaction ownership
concepts.description: The application opens and disposes connections and must pass the same connection and transaction to every statement that must be atomic.

concepts.title: Provider reality
concepts.description: Dapper does not normalize SQL syntax, types, locking, stored procedures, or plans; the selected ADO.NET provider and database define behavior.

architecture.description: An application query or command selects reviewed SQL and parameters. Dapper executes through an opened provider connection and optional transaction, the database applies constraints and a query plan, and Dapper materializes explicit result types.

implementationIntroduction: Build the SQL boundary explicitly, then prove mapping, constraints, transaction behavior, and query shape against a relational provider.

implementationSteps.title: Choose the provider and SQL dialect
implementationSteps.description: Install Dapper plus the ADO.NET provider for the production database, and define where provider-specific SQL is allowed to live.

implementationSteps.title: Define result and command models
implementationSteps.description: Create narrow types whose names and nullability match the selected columns and expected cardinality rather than mapping entire tables automatically.

implementationSteps.title: Write parameterized, bounded SQL
implementationSteps.description: Alias columns intentionally, bind every value, apply deterministic ordering, cap page size, and avoid SELECT star on application paths.

implementationSteps.title: Allowlist dynamic structure
implementationSteps.description: Map sort choices, directions, table names, or optional SQL fragments from trusted enums or constants because identifiers cannot be command parameters.

implementationSteps.title: Own connections and transactions
implementationSteps.description: Open connections late, dispose them promptly, and pass one transaction object to every command that forms an atomic unit.

implementationSteps.title: Handle relationships deliberately
implementationSteps.description: Use multi-mapping for joined rows or QueryMultiple for coherent result grids, then de-duplicate parent objects in application code.

implementationSteps.title: Test and measure the database path
implementationSteps.description: Verify mappings, constraints, rollback, cancellation, indexes, plans, row counts, and latency against the target provider with production-shaped data.

code.label: OrderQueries.cs
code.introduction: The dedicated sample binds filter values, caps pagination, propagates cancellation, and selects an ORDER BY clause only from trusted enum-backed constants.

testing.introduction: Dapper tests must execute real SQL because mapping, constraints, transaction behavior, and dialect rules do not exist in an in-memory collection.
items: Create an isolated relational database per test or test collection and apply the same reviewed schema used by the application.
Assert result cardinality, aliases, null handling, numeric and time representations, and multi-mapping boundaries.
Force constraint failures after an earlier write and prove the entire transaction rolls back.
Test allowlisted dynamic sort choices, stable pagination, bounded page sizes, timeouts, and cancellation behavior.
Run critical queries against the production provider and inspect plans with representative row counts; SQLite is valuable but cannot prove PostgreSQL or SQL Server behavior.

security.introduction: Dapper makes value parameters convenient, but application-owned SQL remains a security boundary.
items: Bind all untrusted values; never interpolate or concatenate search text, IDs, dates, or numeric values into SQL.
Map dynamic identifiers, columns, directions, and fragments from strict server-owned allowlists because they cannot be parameters.
Use a least-privilege runtime database identity and a separate controlled identity for schema deployment.
Authorize resource and tenant access before executing a query, and make tenant predicates non-optional in shared data stores.
Do not log secrets or raw personal parameters; record normalized operation names, duration, row count, timeout, and correlation context instead.

performance.introduction: Dapper minimizes mapping overhead, but database work, network round trips, result size, locks, and query plans dominate most production paths.
items: Select only required columns, cap every collection, use deterministic pagination, and stream only when connection lifetime and backpressure are understood.
Measure generated plans, logical reads, row estimates, duration, round trips, and allocation before choosing a micro-ORM for speed.
Create indexes for measured predicates and ordering, while accounting for write amplification and maintenance cost.
Use QueryMultiple only for coherent results and avoid giant joins whose repeated parent columns cause excessive transfer and de-duplication work.
Set realistic command timeouts, propagate cancellation, and keep transactions short so pooled connections and locks are released quickly.

deployment.introduction: Dapper does not create or migrate schemas, so database change delivery needs an explicit operational owner and toolchain.
items: Version schema scripts or use a migration tool, review changes as code, and test them against production-like data volume.
Deploy schema changes from one controlled job rather than allowing every application instance to race at startup.
Use expand-and-contract migrations when old and new application versions overlap, especially for renamed or newly required columns.
Pin and audit Dapper, the ADO.NET provider, native database dependencies, and migration tooling as a compatible set.
Back up data, rehearse forward-fix and rollback procedures, monitor locks and duration, and verify application mappings immediately after deployment.

troubleshooting.symptom: A query returns default values or mapping throws.
troubleshooting.cause: Selected column names, aliases, nullability, or database types do not match the target constructor or properties.
troubleshooting.fix: Select explicit columns, alias them to the model, inspect provider-returned types, and add an integration test for the exact row shape.

troubleshooting.symptom: A dynamic query is vulnerable or fails for some sort choices.
troubleshooting.cause: User input was concatenated into a column, direction, identifier, or SQL fragment that cannot be parameterized.
troubleshooting.fix: Translate a validated enum or fixed key to a server-owned SQL constant and reject every unknown value.

troubleshooting.cause: One command used another connection, omitted the transaction argument, or committed outside the intended unit of work.
troubleshooting.fix: Create one connection and transaction at the service boundary, pass both to every Dapper command, and prove rollback with a forced constraint failure.

troubleshooting.symptom: Multi-mapping creates duplicate parents or empty children.
troubleshooting.cause: The splitOn column is wrong, join rows repeat the parent, or the aggregation callback does not use an identity lookup.
troubleshooting.fix: Alias the split column explicitly, use a parent-key dictionary, add each child once, and test zero, one, and many child rows.

troubleshooting.symptom: A fast local query is slow in production.
troubleshooting.cause: Production data volume, indexes, provider behavior, network latency, blocking, or the selected plan differs from the local environment.
troubleshooting.fix: Capture the production-shaped plan and telemetry, compare parameters and row counts, then correct query shape or indexes based on evidence.

productionChecklist: All values are parameters, and every dynamic identifier or fragment comes from a closed server-owned allowlist.
Queries select explicit columns, enforce bounded results, use stable ordering, and have reviewed indexes and plans.
Connection, transaction, timeout, cancellation, and disposal ownership is visible at each application boundary.
Expected zero, one, and many-row cardinalities use the matching Dapper API and have mapping tests.
Atomic workflows have commit and forced-rollback integration tests against a relational provider.
Schema changes are versioned, reviewed, deployed once, backward-compatible during rollout, and observable.
Critical SQL is tested against the production engine with representative data and safe diagnostic logging.
bestPractices: Always bind changing values as parameters; never concatenate untrusted input into SQL.
Allowlist dynamic identifiers, columns, directions, and fragments with enums or fixed server-owned mappings.
Project only required columns, cap result sizes, use stable ordering, and inspect query plans for important paths.
Choose Query, QuerySingle, QueryFirst, Execute, or ExecuteScalar to match the expected result cardinality.
Open connections late, dispose them promptly, and pass the same explicit transaction to every atomic command.
Use CommandDefinition for cancellation, timeouts, command types, and transaction context where the selected API supports it.
Keep SQL and mapping tests close to the production provider because dialects, types, casing, locking, and plans differ.
Manage schema evolution through reviewed scripts or migration tooling; Dapper is not a schema manager.

interviewQuestions.question: How is Dapper different from EF Core?
interviewQuestions.answer: Dapper maps explicit SQL over ADO.NET and provides little unit-of-work or change-tracking behavior. EF Core supplies LINQ translation, identity and change tracking, relationships, migrations, and a richer ORM model.

interviewQuestions.question: Can Dapper and EF Core be used together?
interviewQuestions.answer: Yes. A common CQRS approach uses EF Core for transactional writes and Dapper for explicit read projections, provided connection and transaction ownership are coordinated when atomicity is required.

interviewQuestions.question: Does using Dapper automatically prevent SQL injection?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Dapper makes parameter binding convenient, but dynamic SQL built by concatenating untrusted input is still vulnerable. Dynamic identifiers and sort choices require allowlists.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use CommandDefinition?
interviewQuestions.answer: It packages SQL with parameters, a transaction, timeout, command type, flags, and cancellation token, making execution policy explicit for supported APIs.

interviewQuestions.question: When should QueryMultiple or multi-mapping be used?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use QueryMultiple for several coherent result grids in one command. Use multi-mapping when one joined row contains columns for multiple objects, then de-duplicate parent objects deliberately.

interviewQuestions.question: Who owns migrations and transactions when using Dapper?
interviewQuestions.answer: The application and its delivery tooling do. Dapper executes against the supplied connection and transaction and does not track a model or generate schema migrations.

note: Dapper reduces mapping ceremony, not the need to understand SQL, transactions, indexes, connection pooling, and provider behavior.
tip: Use dedicated result types whose property names and nullability intentionally match explicit column aliases, then test that shape against the real provider.
warning: A fast mapper cannot rescue unsafe dynamic SQL, an unbounded result, a missing index, a long transaction, or an incorrect production query plan.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated runnable sample

name: Solution Architecture Fundamentals
shortDescription: Turn business outcomes and quality requirements into explicit system boundaries, views, tradeoffs, and evolutionary decisions.
overview: Solution architecture connects business goals, stakeholder concerns, quality requirements, and constraints to a coherent design that teams can build and operate.
detail: A solution architect clarifies the problem before selecting technology. The work includes identifying stakeholders and critical flows, expressing measurable quality attributes, defining system context and boundaries, comparing architecture styles, documenting significant decisions, designing for operations and security, and validating the architecture through prototypes, reviews, tests, and production evidence. Diagrams are communication tools; the architecture is the set of decisions and constraints that shape the system throughout its life.

concepts.title: Drivers and constraints
concepts.description: Business outcomes, critical user journeys, compliance, budget, schedule, existing systems, and team capabilities define the feasible design space.

concepts.title: Quality attributes
concepts.description: Reliability, security, performance, operability, cost, and maintainability become measurable scenarios rather than vague goals.

concepts.title: Boundaries and views
concepts.description: Context, container, component, deployment, data, and runtime views explain different stakeholder concerns without one overloaded diagram.

concepts.title: Tradeoffs and evolution
concepts.description: Styles and technologies are selected against requirements, recorded as decisions, validated early, and revisited as evidence or constraints change.

architecture.description: Stakeholder outcomes and constraints shape measurable requirements, which guide architecture decisions and views that delivery teams validate through implementation and operations.

code.label: QualityScenario.cs
code.introduction: A small quality-scenario record forces an architecture requirement to name its stimulus, operating condition, expected response, and measurable target.

bestPractices: Start with business outcomes, stakeholders, critical flows, constraints, and measurable quality scenarios before choosing services or patterns.
Use a small set of complementary views and keep every diagram scoped, labeled, versioned, and connected to decisions.
Evaluate options against explicit criteria, record material tradeoffs, and prototype the assumptions with the highest cost of being wrong.
Include deployment, observability, security, data ownership, failure recovery, cost, and team ownership in the architecture from the start.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between architecture and design?
interviewQuestions.answer: Architecture focuses on system-shaping structures, constraints, quality attributes, and costly-to-reverse decisions. Design also includes the many local implementation choices made within those boundaries.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose an architecture style?
interviewQuestions.answer: Compare styles against business drivers, quality scenarios, constraints, operational model, data needs, team capabilities, and migration path; then validate the riskiest assumptions.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you know an architecture is working?
interviewQuestions.answer: Define measurable fitness criteria for critical qualities, test them before release, observe them in production, review incidents and costs, and change decisions when evidence no longer supports them.

note: Architecture documentation should make important reasoning discoverable, not attempt to predict every implementation detail.
tip: Write the three most important quality scenarios and use them as evaluation criteria in every architecture review.
warning: A polished diagram without measurable requirements, ownership, tradeoffs, or validation is not an executable architecture.
latestNote: New guide on requirements, views, tradeoffs, and architecture validation

name: Architecture Decision Records
shortDescription: Capture architecturally significant choices with their context, considered options, consequences, ownership, and lifecycle.
overview: An Architecture Decision Record documents why a significant design choice was made and what consequences the team accepts.
detail: An ADR is a short, version-controlled record for a decision that shapes structure, quality attributes, constraints, or future options. It captures the context and forces, the decision, alternatives considered, expected positive and negative consequences, status, owners, and links to evidence. ADRs form a chronological decision log: accepted decisions are not silently rewritten when direction changes; a new record supersedes the old one and preserves the reasoning available at the time.

concepts.title: Architectural significance
concepts.description: Record choices that affect system structure, key qualities, organizational boundaries, or options that are expensive to reverse.

concepts.title: Context and options
concepts.description: State the problem, drivers, constraints, assumptions, and credible alternatives so the decision can be understood independently.

concepts.title: Consequences
concepts.description: Document benefits, costs, risks, operational effects, follow-up work, and the conditions that would trigger reconsideration.

concepts.title: Decision lifecycle
concepts.description: Use proposed, accepted, rejected, deprecated, and superseded states with owners, dates, and links to later decisions.

architecture.description: A significant concern is evaluated against drivers and options, accepted through review, and preserved in a versioned decision log that informs delivery and later reassessment.

code.label: docs/adr/0007-api-gateway.md
code.introduction: A compact template keeps records comparable while leaving room for evidence and explicit tradeoffs.
code.code:
# ADR-0007: Use a managed API gateway

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-08-06
- Owners: Platform Architecture

## Context
Public APIs need consistent authentication, quotas, version routing,
and telemetry across independently deployed services.

## Decision
Use Azure API Management as the external gateway.

## Alternatives
- Application-owned gateway
- Direct exposure through an ingress controller

## Consequences
Central policy and analytics improve consistency, but APIM adds cost,
latency, operational dependencies, and tier-specific constraints.

## Revisit when
Traffic, regions, or gateway availability targets materially change.

bestPractices: Keep ADRs concise, immutable after acceptance except for status and links, and store them beside the code or architecture documentation they govern.
Record only significant decisions and state the context, options, decision, consequences, owners, date, and review trigger.
Use lightweight peer review and include links to prototypes, measurements, threat models, cost estimates, and diagrams that support the choice.
Supersede an obsolete ADR with a new record instead of erasing history, and review the decision log during major changes and incidents.

interviewQuestions.question: Which decisions deserve an ADR?
interviewQuestions.answer: Decisions that materially shape the system, affect important quality attributes or organizational boundaries, impose constraints, or are difficult and expensive to reverse.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should an accepted ADR not simply be edited?
interviewQuestions.answer: Editing destroys the historical reasoning and makes it unclear what teams implemented. A superseding ADR preserves chronology while documenting the new context and decision.

interviewQuestions.question: How do ADRs avoid becoming bureaucracy?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use a short template, record only significant choices, keep review close to normal code workflows, assign ownership, and link each record to delivery or validation evidence.

note: An ADR explains a decision; it does not replace diagrams, API contracts, threat models, runbooks, or implementation documentation.
tip: Start a brownfield decision log by reconstructing only the few choices currently constraining change, then record new decisions as they occur.
warning: A decision log that records only the selected option and omits context, alternatives, and consequences cannot support future reassessment.
latestNote: New guide on concise, versioned architecture decisions

name: API Design Best Practices
shortDescription: Design stable, secure, observable HTTP contracts around resources, standard semantics, compatibility, and predictable failure behavior.
overview: Good API design creates a clear, loosely coupled contract that clients can use correctly and evolve with safely.
detail: An HTTP API should model consumer workflows and durable business resources rather than database tables or implementation methods. Consistent URIs, methods, status codes, representations, Problem Details, pagination, filtering, conditional requests, concurrency controls, idempotency, asynchronous operations, versioning, security, and observability make behavior predictable. Collection work must be bounded and retry behavior must be explicit: a cursor avoids unstable offsets, an idempotency key protects retried creation, and an ETag with If-Match prevents lost updates. Contract-first review and executable compatibility tests help providers and consumers evolve independently. Additive changes are usually safest, while removals and semantic changes need evidence of consumer usage, a published deprecation window, migration instructions, and a controlled version boundary. A good contract also specifies authorization, payload limits, rate-limit signals, cancellation, correlation, privacy, caching, and the difference between a transient failure that can be retried and a permanent client error.
learningObjectives: Model APIs around consumer workflows and resource lifecycles.
Apply HTTP safety, idempotency, status, header, caching, and conditional-request semantics.
Design bounded cursor pagination and predictable validation errors.
Protect retried creation with idempotency keys and concurrent updates with ETags.
Evolve contracts through additive change, compatibility evidence, versioning, and deprecation.
Test the contract and operational behavior from a real client boundary.
prerequisites: HTTP methods, status codes, headers, JSON, and REST resource vocabulary.
ASP.NET Core routing, dependency injection, Problem Details, and integration testing.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the dedicated orders sample.

use: Use resource-oriented HTTP when consumers benefit from standard web semantics and broad tooling.
Use idempotency keys for retryable non-idempotent creation or commands.
Use ETags and If-Match when concurrent writers must not silently overwrite each other.
avoid: Do not expose tables or internal service methods as the public model.
Do not return unbounded collections or ambiguous generic errors.
Do not version every additive field or promise retry safety without a durable idempotency store.

concepts.title: Resource-oriented contracts
concepts.description: Stable nouns, representations, relationships, and workflow resources describe the domain without exposing internal storage or service boundaries.

concepts.title: HTTP semantics
concepts.description: Methods, safety, idempotency, status codes, headers, caching, conditional requests, and content negotiation communicate standard behavior.

concepts.title: Scale and resilience
concepts.description: Pagination, filtering, field selection, rate limits, timeouts, idempotency keys, and asynchronous operations bound work and support retries.

concepts.title: Evolution and governance
concepts.description: OpenAPI review, compatibility checks, explicit versioning, deprecation windows, security defaults, and telemetry protect clients over time.

concepts.title: Cursor pagination
concepts.description: An opaque continuation token gives clients a bounded traversal contract without coupling them to database offsets.

concepts.title: Idempotency records
concepts.description: A client key is stored with request identity and original outcome so safe retries replay but conflicting reuse is rejected.

concepts.title: Optimistic concurrency
concepts.description: ETag and If-Match let a server reject stale writes with 412 rather than silently losing another client's update.

concepts.title: Problem Details
concepts.description: A stable machine-readable error shape carries status, type, title, detail, field errors, and a safe correlation identifier.

architecture.description: Clients use a versioned contract through security and policy controls; resource handlers enforce domain rules while telemetry and compatibility checks govern evolution.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated orders sample turns contract rules into executable behavior: bounded cursor pagination, idempotent creation, Problem Details, ETags, If-Match preconditions, and integration tests for both successful and conflicting requests.

implementationSteps.title: Map consumer workflows
implementationSteps.description: Identify resources, actions, representations, permissions, latency expectations, and failure recovery from the caller's view.

implementationSteps.title: Choose HTTP semantics
implementationSteps.description: Assign methods, routes, status codes, headers, cache rules, and content types according to their standard meaning.

implementationSteps.title: Bound collections and payloads
implementationSteps.description: Set maximum page and body sizes and define opaque continuation tokens, filters, and ordering.

implementationSteps.title: Standardize failures
implementationSteps.description: Return Problem Details with stable types, validation members, safe details, and correlation IDs.

implementationSteps.title: Make retries safe
implementationSteps.description: Store idempotency key, request fingerprint, and original outcome in the same durable boundary as the effect.

implementationSteps.title: Protect concurrent writes
implementationSteps.description: Emit ETags and require If-Match for state replacement where lost updates matter.

implementationSteps.title: Govern evolution
implementationSteps.description: Publish OpenAPI, compatibility tests, version rules, usage telemetry, deprecation dates, and migration guidance.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: A resource endpoint uses a constrained route, typed outcomes, cancellation, and a standard validation problem response.

testing.introduction: API tests should prove semantics that clients depend on, including retries and conflicts.
items: Use an in-memory HTTP host and send real serialized requests through routing and middleware.
Test collection bounds, cursor continuation, deterministic ordering, and invalid cursor handling.
Test same-key replay and different-payload idempotency-key conflict.
Test missing, current, and stale If-Match values and the resulting ETag change.
Assert Problem Details content type, status, validation members, and trace correlation.
Compare OpenAPI or consumer contracts for unintended breaking changes.

security.introduction: Every operation, resource identifier, property, and workload limit is a security boundary.
items: Authenticate the caller and authorize function, tenant, object, and writable properties server-side.
Validate allow-listed request DTOs and minimize response fields.
Bound body, collection, filter, concurrency, and downstream work; add abuse controls by identity and operation.
Never place secrets or sensitive personal data in URLs, logs, idempotency records, or Problem Details.
Use HTTPS and verify proxy, CORS, CSRF, and caching behavior for the actual client type.

performance.introduction: Predictable contracts bound server work and let clients avoid wasteful transfers and retries.
items: Enforce maximum page size and use indexes matching cursor ordering and filters.
Use conditional GET or writes where concurrency and bandwidth justify them.
Avoid offset pagination for large changing collections when stable cursor traversal is required.
Set cancellation, deadlines, connection limits, and downstream timeouts.
Measure latency and errors by normalized operation, status, and consumer without high-cardinality URLs.

deployment.introduction: API compatibility includes the gateway, proxy, persistence, observability, and rollout sequence.
items: Run contract and integration tests against the release artifact.
Use a durable shared idempotency store in multi-instance production and define retention.
Verify proxy forwarding, HTTPS origin, payload limits, rate-limit headers, and cache behavior.
Deploy additive storage and server changes before clients depend on them.
Monitor old-version usage and complete deprecation only after communicated exit criteria.

troubleshooting.symptom: Clients receive duplicate resources after retry.
troubleshooting.cause: Creation has no durable idempotency record or instances do not share it.
troubleshooting.fix: Persist key, request fingerprint, and outcome atomically with the effect and share the store.

troubleshooting.symptom: A retry returns 409 for the same key.
troubleshooting.cause: The client reused a key with a different request payload.
troubleshooting.fix: Generate one key per logical operation and replay exactly the original request.

troubleshooting.cause: The If-Match value is stale because the resource changed.
troubleshooting.fix: Fetch the latest representation, reconcile, and retry with its ETag.

troubleshooting.cause: Page size or filtering is unbounded or the cursor order lacks a supporting index.
troubleshooting.fix: Cap pages, validate filters, use stable indexed cursor columns, and measure the query plan.

troubleshooting.cause: Endpoints return unrelated strings, HTML, or undocumented shapes.
troubleshooting.fix: Adopt Problem Details with stable types and test each status.

troubleshooting.symptom: An additive deployment breaks a generated client.
troubleshooting.cause: A supposedly additive schema change altered requiredness, operation identity, or strict parsing.
troubleshooting.fix: Run compatibility checks and consumer tests, then version genuinely breaking semantics.

productionChecklist: Routes and representations model consumer workflows rather than storage internals.
Methods, status codes, Location, caching, retry, and asynchronous semantics are documented.
Collections, payloads, filters, execution time, and concurrency are bounded.
Problem Details types and validation members are stable and safe.
Idempotency storage is durable, shared, atomic with effects, and has retention policy.
ETag and precondition rules are tested wherever lost updates matter.
Authentication, function, tenant, object, and property authorization are verified negatively.
OpenAPI compatibility, versioning, deprecation, telemetry, and rollback have owners.
bestPractices: Design from consumer workflows and domain resources, publish an OpenAPI contract, and review it before implementation.
Apply standard HTTP semantics consistently and document every status, header, cache, and retry behavior.
Return Problem Details for machine-readable errors with safe correlation data.
Bound collections and work with cursor pagination, filters, payload limits, quotas, timeouts, and cancellation.
Persist idempotency records atomically with business effects and reject conflicting key reuse.
Use ETags and If-Match to prevent lost updates where concurrent writes matter.
Prefer additive evolution and define explicit version and deprecation policy for breaking changes.
Observe normalized operations, latency, status, abuse, and consumer adoption without logging sensitive payloads.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes an HTTP operation idempotent?
interviewQuestions.answer: Repeating the same request has the same intended effect on server state as making it once. GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and safe retry mechanisms should respect that property even if response codes differ.

interviewQuestions.question: When should an API return 202 Accepted?
interviewQuestions.answer: When work has been accepted but will complete asynchronously. The response should identify a status resource or operation URL and document polling, completion, failure, and cancellation behavior.

interviewQuestions.question: How can an API evolve without breaking clients?
interviewQuestions.answer: Prefer additive changes, tolerant readers, contract compatibility tests, explicit policies for breaking versions, usage telemetry, and a communicated deprecation window.

interviewQuestions.question: How do idempotency keys make POST retries safe?
interviewQuestions.answer: The server durably associates a client key with the request fingerprint and original result, replaying an exact retry and rejecting reuse for different input.

interviewQuestions.question: What do ETag and If-Match prevent?
interviewQuestions.answer: They implement optimistic concurrency: a write succeeds only against the version the client read, so a stale client cannot silently overwrite a newer update.

interviewQuestions.question: Why prefer cursor over offset pagination?
interviewQuestions.answer: A cursor can provide stable bounded continuation over changing, indexed data without the increasing scan cost and duplicate or skipped rows common with offsets.

note: REST is one useful interaction style, not a requirement for every internal or event-driven interface; choose the style from consumer and system needs.
tip: Review a proposed API using only its OpenAPI document and example errors; hidden assumptions discovered there are cheaper to fix than deployed contracts.
warning: Exposing database tables directly couples clients to internal storage, expands the attack surface, and makes later redesign unnecessarily breaking.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated retry and concurrency sample

name: Multi-Tenancy Patterns
shortDescription: Balance tenant isolation, scale, cost, customization, and operations across identity, compute, data, messaging, and deployment.
overview: Multitenant architecture serves multiple customers from a solution while deliberately controlling isolation, scale, cost, performance, and customization.
detail: Multitenancy is a component-by-component isolation decision, not one shared-versus-dedicated switch. Identity, compute, data, caches, queues, search, secrets, keys, logs, metrics, backups, networking, deployment, and support access can each be pooled, partitioned into deployment stamps, or dedicated according to sensitivity, residency, performance, recovery, customization, scale, and commercial tier. Tenant identity must come from a validated issuer and authorized membership, become immutable scoped context, and flow through every query, cache key, message, job, file path, telemetry record, and downstream call. Defense in depth combines tenant-filtered repositories, database row policies or separate stores, resource authorization, cryptographic and network boundaries, quotas, fair scheduling, and negative cross-tenant tests. A control plane manages idempotent onboarding, placement, configuration, migrations, metering, suspension, export, deletion, and stamp capacity while the data plane remains simple. Operations need per-tenant and per-stamp health without uncontrolled metric cardinality, plus runbooks for noisy neighbors, migration, regional failure, restore, key compromise, and offboarding proof.
learningObjectives: Build a component tenancy matrix from isolation, residency, scale, recovery, customization, and cost requirements.
Establish immutable tenant context from authenticated and authorized identity.
Enforce tenant boundaries across data, cache, messages, jobs, files, secrets, and telemetry.
Choose pooled, partitioned, stamped, or dedicated models independently per component.
Design an idempotent control plane for the complete tenant lifecycle.
Test cross-tenant denial, noisy-neighbor fairness, migration, restore, and offboarding.
prerequisites: Authentication, authorization, data partitioning, caching, messaging, and cloud deployment basics.
SaaS lifecycle concepts including onboarding, metering, residency, recovery, and deletion.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the tenant-isolated invoice API.

use: Use pooled resources when requirements permit shared blast radius and density is valuable.
Use deployment stamps to bound scale, failure, geography, rollout, and noisy-neighbor impact.
Use dedicated resources where regulation, key ownership, performance, customization, or recovery requires them.
avoid: Do not trust a tenant ID from an unverified header, route, body, or query string.
Do not rely on one ORM filter as the only cross-tenant boundary.
Do not place tenant data in caches, messages, jobs, files, or logs without tenant scope.
Do not create per-tenant infrastructure manually without an idempotent lifecycle control plane.

concepts.title: Isolation models
concepts.description: Shared, partitioned, deployment-stamp, and dedicated models trade cost and density against security, performance, customization, and operational independence.

concepts.title: Tenant context
concepts.description: Trusted identity claims establish tenant context, which authorization, routing, data filters, cache keys, logs, metrics, and messages must propagate safely.

concepts.title: Control plane
concepts.description: Automated onboarding, provisioning, placement, configuration, billing, offboarding, and capacity management keep tenant lifecycle work repeatable.

concepts.title: Scale and fairness
concepts.description: Quotas, rate limits, partition keys, workload isolation, capacity signals, and per-tenant telemetry contain noisy neighbors and support service tiers.

concepts.title: Data isolation
concepts.description: Shared tables, schemas, databases, and accounts trade density against enforcement strength, restore granularity, operations, and cost.

concepts.title: Deployment stamps
concepts.description: Repeatable scale units bound tenants, capacity, geography, rollout, failure, and migration while a control plane manages placement.

concepts.title: Tenant lifecycle
concepts.description: Onboarding, configuration, migration, suspension, export, retention, deletion, and billing are durable idempotent workflows.

concepts.title: Isolation evidence
concepts.description: Negative tests, audits, restore drills, telemetry, and deletion proof demonstrate that boundaries work beyond design intent.

architecture.description: Trusted identity establishes tenant context at the edge, a control plane manages placement and lifecycle, and isolated data-plane stamps serve tenant traffic with per-tenant policy and telemetry.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated invoice API converts a local demonstration identity into a validated tenant claim, creates immutable request context, protects all routes by fallback policy, hides cross-tenant identifiers with 404, scopes repository access and cache keys, applies independent quotas, and verifies isolation with negative HTTP tests.

implementationSteps.title: Define the tenancy matrix
implementationSteps.description: Record isolation, residency, performance, recovery, scale, customization, lifecycle, and cost per component.

implementationSteps.title: Establish trusted context
implementationSteps.description: Validate issuer and tenant membership, normalize the identifier once, and make scoped context immutable.

implementationSteps.title: Enforce data boundaries
implementationSteps.description: Use tenant-scoped repositories plus database enforcement or dedicated stores and non-disclosing resource authorization.

implementationSteps.title: Propagate safely
implementationSteps.description: Include tenant scope in cache keys, messages, jobs, blobs, secrets, downstream calls, and audit records.

implementationSteps.title: Protect fairness
implementationSteps.description: Apply per-tenant quotas, concurrency, rate, storage, and expensive-work limits alongside stamp capacity.

implementationSteps.title: Automate lifecycle
implementationSteps.description: Build idempotent onboarding, placement, migration, suspension, export, deletion, and metering workflows.

implementationSteps.title: Prove isolation
implementationSteps.description: Run negative access, cache, messaging, noisy-neighbor, migration, restore, failover, and offboarding tests.

testing.introduction: Multitenant testing emphasizes denial and isolation, not only tenant-specific happy paths.
items: Test anonymous, invalid membership, tenant mismatch, changed identifiers, and cross-tenant object lookup.
Prove every query and mutation is tenant scoped and inaccessible objects do not disclose existence.
Test cache keys, messages, background jobs, files, search, and telemetry with colliding resource IDs.
Load-test one abusive tenant and prove quotas and fair scheduling protect others.
Exercise tenant migration, stamp failure, backup restore, key rotation, suspension, and deletion.
Run automated isolation suites for every data-access and integration path.

security.introduction: Tenant isolation is an authorization and data-protection boundary with potentially contractual impact.
items: Derive tenant context from validated identity and authorize user-to-tenant membership.
Enforce tenant plus resource plus operation at application and durable data boundaries.
Scope encryption keys, secrets, network rules, caches, queues, blobs, and support access according to requirements.
Prevent tenant identifiers and sensitive data from leaking through errors, logs, URLs, metrics, and exports.
Audit privileged cross-tenant operations and use time-bounded approved support access.

performance.introduction: High density is valuable only when one tenant cannot exhaust shared capacity.
items: Partition and index by tenant plus access pattern and watch skew or hot partitions.
Apply per-tenant rate, concurrency, storage, query, and background-work quotas.
Use deployment stamps and placement policies to bound scale and noisy-neighbor impact.
Measure tenant-level service health through bounded-cardinality top-tenant or drill-down telemetry.
Provide tier-aware capacity and migration before saturation rather than manual emergency moves.

deployment.introduction: Control-plane and data-plane changes must preserve mixed-version tenant lifecycle and placement.
items: Provision stamps from versioned infrastructure and apply policy consistently.
Roll out schema and application changes compatibly across pooled and dedicated tenants.
Use idempotent resumable tenant migrations with reconciliation and rollback.
Test regional routing, residency, backup ownership, restore granularity, and stamp evacuation.
Smoke-test one tenant per isolation tier plus cross-tenant denial after deployment.

troubleshooting.symptom: Changing an ID reveals another tenant's record.
troubleshooting.cause: The load is not tenant scoped or the resource was not authorized.
troubleshooting.fix: Filter by immutable tenant context, authorize the loaded object, and add a negative test.

troubleshooting.symptom: Users intermittently see another tenant's cached value.
troubleshooting.cause: The cache key omits tenant or invalidation is too broad.
troubleshooting.fix: Version and tenant-scope every key and test colliding resource IDs.

troubleshooting.symptom: One customer increases latency for all others.
troubleshooting.cause: Shared compute, database, queue, or dependency lacks fair limits.
troubleshooting.fix: Identify the saturated resource and add tenant quotas, admission control, partitioning, or migration.

troubleshooting.cause: Writes, events, cache, and routing changed without a durable migration state machine.
troubleshooting.fix: Use resumable phases, reconciliation, cutover criteria, and rollback.

troubleshooting.cause: Tenant ID became an unbounded metric dimension.
troubleshooting.fix: Use bounded aggregate metrics, exemplars or logs, and controlled drill-down.

troubleshooting.symptom: Offboarded tenant data remains in backups or caches.
troubleshooting.cause: Retention and deletion were not mapped across every store.
troubleshooting.fix: Maintain a data inventory, expire derived stores, apply retention policy, and record deletion evidence.

productionChecklist: A component-level tenancy matrix defines isolation, residency, recovery, scale, customization, and cost.
Tenant context comes from validated identity and authorized membership and is immutable per operation.
Data, cache, messages, jobs, files, secrets, keys, logs, and downstream calls are tenant scoped.
Cross-tenant object, property, function, cache, queue, and support paths are negative-tested.
Per-tenant quotas and stamp capacity protect fairness and noisy-neighbor boundaries.
Onboarding, placement, migration, suspension, export, deletion, and metering are idempotent workflows.
Backup, restore, key rotation, stamp failure, regional recovery, and offboarding are rehearsed.
Telemetry supports tenant diagnosis without uncontrolled cardinality or sensitive leakage.

code.introduction: Tenant context is derived from an authenticated claim and stored in a scoped service instead of trusting a caller-supplied tenant header.

Derive immutable tenant context from validated identity and authorized membership.
Enforce tenant, resource, and operation boundaries at application and durable data layers.
Tenant-scope every cache key, message, job, file, secret, trace, and downstream call.
Apply per-tenant quotas and deployment-stamp capacity to protect fairness.
Automate onboarding, placement, migration, suspension, export, deletion, and metering idempotently.
Keep per-tenant observability actionable without uncontrolled cardinality.
Test cross-tenant denial, noisy neighbors, stamp failure, migration, restore, and offboarding.

interviewQuestions.question: What are the main multitenancy isolation models?
interviewQuestions.answer: Resources can be fully shared, logically partitioned, grouped into deployment stamps, or dedicated per tenant. Real solutions often mix models by tier and component.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you prevent cross-tenant data leakage?
interviewQuestions.answer: Establish tenant identity from trusted authentication, enforce authorization and tenant filters at multiple layers, partition data deliberately, scope caches and messages, and run automated negative isolation tests.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does a multitenant control plane solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: It automates tenant lifecycle and infrastructure management, including onboarding, provisioning, configuration, placement, scaling, metering, migration, suspension, and deletion.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a global ORM query filter insufficient by itself?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can be bypassed by raw SQL, disabled filters, other stores, caches, jobs, or bugs, so isolation needs defense in depth and negative tests.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a deployment stamp?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is a repeatable scale unit containing a bounded tenant set and resources, used to limit capacity, failure, geography, rollout, and migration blast radius.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle noisy neighbors?
interviewQuestions.answer: Measure the first shared constraint, enforce tenant-aware admission, rate, concurrency, storage, and query limits, then repartition or move tenants when needed.

interviewQuestions.question: How should tenant IDs appear in telemetry?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use them in controlled logs and traces for diagnosis, but avoid unbounded metric labels; aggregate and provide bounded drill-down.

note: A product can be multitenant at the business layer while using a mixture of shared and dedicated infrastructure underneath.
tip: Create a component-by-component tenancy matrix showing isolation, scale unit, data boundary, failure blast radius, and cost owner.
warning: Never authorize a tenant solely from an unverified request header, route value, or query parameter supplied by the caller.

name: Saga Pattern
shortDescription: Coordinate distributed business transactions as local commits with durable progress, idempotent messages, and explicit compensation.
overview: The Saga pattern maintains business consistency across independently owned services by coordinating local transactions and compensating completed work when later steps fail.
detail: A saga decomposes a distributed workflow into local transactions. Each successful step durably records its state and triggers the next action through a command or event. Failures invoke business-specific compensating actions where reversal is possible. Choreography distributes coordination across event handlers; orchestration gives one durable coordinator an explicit state machine. Both require idempotency, duplicate handling, correlation, timeouts, retries, observability, and reconciliation because messages and failures can occur at any boundary.

concepts.title: Local transactions
concepts.description: Each participant commits only its own data and publishes progress reliably, commonly through a transactional outbox.

concepts.title: Compensation and pivot
concepts.description: Compensable steps have semantic undo actions; the pivot is the point after which the remaining retryable steps must complete.

concepts.title: Orchestration or choreography
concepts.description: An orchestrator centralizes workflow state, while choreography reacts to events with less central control but harder end-to-end visibility.

concepts.title: Delivery correctness
concepts.description: Correlation IDs, idempotent handlers, inbox or deduplication state, retries, timeouts, ordering rules, and reconciliation make at-least-once delivery safe.

architecture.description: A durable saga state coordinates commands to service-owned local transactions; replies advance the workflow, while failures trigger compensation and telemetry supports reconciliation.

code.label: PlaceOrderSaga.cs
code.introduction: An explicit state record makes successful steps and compensation progress durable and safe to retry.

bestPractices: Model the workflow, invariants, compensable actions, pivot, retryable actions, timeouts, and terminal states explicitly with domain owners.
Persist saga progress durably and use transactional outbox and inbox or deduplication mechanisms for reliable, idempotent message handling.
Give every saga and message correlation and causation identifiers, structured telemetry, deadlines, and an operator-visible reconciliation path.
Test duplicate, delayed, reordered, lost, and poison messages plus compensation failure and coordinator restart before production.

interviewQuestions.question: How is saga choreography different from orchestration?
interviewQuestions.answer: Choreography has participants react to events without one coordinator. Orchestration uses a central state machine that commands steps and handles replies, improving visibility but concentrating workflow coupling.

interviewQuestions.question: Is a compensating action the same as a database rollback?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Compensation is a new business operation that semantically offsets a committed action; it may be partial, fail independently, require approval, or be impossible after a pivot.

interviewQuestions.question: Why must saga handlers be idempotent?
interviewQuestions.answer: Brokers and retries commonly produce duplicate delivery. Idempotent handlers ensure processing the same message again does not repeat charges, reservations, or other side effects.

learningObjectives: Model local transactions, compensation, pivot, and terminal states.
Choose orchestration or choreography.
Persist workflow state and message deduplication.
Handle retries, timeouts, duplicates, and reordering.
Use outbox and inbox patterns.
Operate reconciliation and manual intervention.

State machines, retries, timeouts, and observability.
Domain owners who can define compensation.

use: A workflow crosses independently owned transactional boundaries.

Durable progress and recovery are required.
avoid: One local transaction suffices.
The steps are only best-effort calls without recovery.
Compensation and intermediate-state semantics are undefined.

concepts.title: Timeouts and deadlines

items: Keep state compact.

items: Evolve messages additively.
Migrate saga state compatibly.

troubleshooting.fix: Inspect timeline and reconcile.

Persist progress durably.

Make every action idempotent.

interviewQuestions.question: Orchestration versus choreography?
interviewQuestions.answer: Central state machine versus distributed event reactions.

interviewQuestions.question: Is compensation rollback?
interviewQuestions.answer: No, it is a new semantic business action.

interviewQuestions.question: Why idempotency?
interviewQuestions.answer: Messages can be delivered more than once.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the pivot?
interviewQuestions.answer: The point after which remaining steps must complete.

interviewQuestions.question: How are timeouts implemented?
interviewQuestions.answer: As durable scheduled messages or deadlines.

interviewQuestions.question: Why outbox and inbox?
interviewQuestions.answer: To coordinate state, sends, and deduplication atomically.

interviewQuestions.question: How repair a stuck saga?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use its timeline and controlled reconciliation commands.

note: A saga provides eventual business consistency, not ACID isolation across services; users and downstream processes may observe intermediate states.
tip: Draw the happy path and every compensation in one state-transition diagram before implementing handlers.
warning: Do not describe a chain of best-effort HTTP calls as a saga unless workflow state, recovery, idempotency, and compensation are durable and explicit.

name: Legacy Modernization
shortDescription: Modernize applications incrementally through portfolio assessment, rationalization, strangler delivery, data transition, and measurable outcomes.
overview: Legacy modernization improves business value and system qualities through evidence-based portfolio decisions and controlled, incremental change.
detail: Modernization begins with business outcomes, portfolio inventory, dependency discovery, risk, cost, and operational evidence. Each workload or capability can be retained, retired, rehosted, replatformed, refactored, or rebuilt rather than receiving one strategy for the entire estate. Incremental patterns such as strangler routing, anti-corruption layers, change-data capture, parallel runs, and reversible cutovers reduce migration risk while automated tests and observability create a safety net.

concepts.title: Assessment and outcomes
concepts.description: Inventory applications, dependencies, ownership, costs, risks, usage, data, and quality gaps, then define measurable business outcomes.

concepts.title: Rationalization strategies
concepts.description: Retain, retire, rehost, replatform, refactor, and rebuild decisions are applied per workload or capability using value, risk, and feasibility.

concepts.title: Incremental replacement
concepts.description: Strangler routing and anti-corruption adapters let new capabilities replace bounded legacy behavior without a single big-bang cutover.

concepts.title: Data and operating transition
concepts.description: Data ownership, synchronization, reconciliation, observability, support, rollback, and team skills are migrated alongside application code.

architecture.description: A routing facade directs selected capabilities to modern services while an anti-corruption layer protects the new model and synchronized data enables gradual, observable cutover.

code.label: LegacyCustomerAdapter.cs
code.introduction: An anti-corruption adapter translates a legacy contract into the new domain vocabulary and prevents old representations from spreading.

bestPractices: Define business outcomes and baseline cost, reliability, security, delivery, performance, and usage before selecting a modernization strategy.
Map dependencies and data ownership, then modernize bounded capabilities in thin, reversible slices with explicit exit and rollback criteria.
Build characterization tests, contract tests, telemetry, reconciliation, and parallel-run evidence before redirecting critical traffic.
Plan operating model, skills, security, compliance, support, decommissioning, and data retention as first-class parts of the program.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose among modernization strategies?
interviewQuestions.answer: Assess business value, urgency, technical health, dependencies, risk, compliance, cost, team skills, target qualities, and migration feasibility per workload or capability.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the Strangler Fig pattern?
interviewQuestions.answer: A facade gradually routes selected capabilities from a legacy system to new implementations until the old behavior can be safely retired.

interviewQuestions.question: Why do modernization programs fail despite new technology?
interviewQuestions.answer: Common causes include unclear outcomes, hidden dependencies, big-bang scope, weak test and telemetry safety nets, ignored data migration, unchanged operating practices, and no funded decommissioning.

note: Modernization can improve the existing system in place; migration to a public cloud is one option, not the definition of modernization.
tip: Choose one valuable, weakly coupled capability and prove the assessment-to-cutover path before scaling the program.
warning: A rewrite that preserves unclear requirements, coupling, data problems, and operating practices can recreate the legacy system on a newer stack.
latestNote: New guide on assessment, 6 Rs, strangler delivery, and safe cutover

name: Azure Resource Manager
shortDescription: Govern Azure infrastructure through a unified management layer — resource groups, subscriptions, RBAC, policies, locks, and deployment modes.
overview: Azure Resource Manager is the control plane for all Azure resources — every portal click, CLI command, Bicep deployment, and SDK call goes through ARM, which enforces identity, policy, and governance before any resource is touched.
detail: ARM provides a consistent management layer across all Azure services. It organises resources into a hierarchy — management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and individual resources — and applies access control, policy, tags, and locks at any level of that hierarchy. Understanding ARM is fundamental to architect-level Azure work because governance decisions made at the ARM layer affect every team and every workload in a tenant. Deployment modes, resource providers, the management plane versus data plane distinction, and the ARM REST API underpin every IaC tool including Bicep, Terraform, and Pulumi.

concepts.title: Resource hierarchy
concepts.description: Resources live in resource groups, resource groups live in subscriptions, and subscriptions live in management groups. Policies and RBAC assignments at a higher scope inherit down, enabling consistent governance across all workloads.

concepts.title: RBAC and role assignments
concepts.description: Azure RBAC controls who can perform which actions on which resources using built-in and custom role definitions assigned to users, groups, service principals, or managed identities at any scope in the hierarchy.

concepts.title: Azure Policy
concepts.description: Policies define rules that ARM evaluates on every resource write — preventing non-compliant resources from being created, auditing existing ones, or automatically remediating drift from the desired configuration baseline.

concepts.title: Deployment modes and resource locks
concepts.description: Incremental mode adds or updates resources without touching others in the group; complete mode deletes any resource not in the template. Resource locks — CanNotDelete and ReadOnly — prevent accidental or unauthorised changes outside the deployment pipeline.

concepts.title: Resource providers and API versions
concepts.description: Each Azure service registers resource types and versioned control-plane schemas that define supported properties, operations, regions, and behavior.

concepts.title: Templates, deployments, and operations
concepts.description: ARM templates create deployment records whose nested operations expose validation, dependency, policy, and provider failures.

concepts.title: What-if and deployment stacks
concepts.description: What-if previews proposed changes while deployment stacks add explicit ownership and controlled handling of resources removed from the declaration.

concepts.title: Management plane and data plane
concepts.description: ARM controls resource lifecycle and configuration, while service-specific data APIs have separate permissions, endpoints, and operational risks.

architecture.description: Every Azure operation — portal, CLI, SDK, or IaC — passes through the ARM API, which authenticates via Entra ID, evaluates RBAC and Policy, and routes to the target resource provider.

code.label: ArmGovernance.cs
code.introduction: The Azure SDK for .NET manages ARM-level resources — creating resource groups, assigning roles, and applying locks — directly in code for automation pipelines or custom governance tooling.

bestPractices: Design the management group and subscription hierarchy before deploying workloads — retrofitting governance scope after resources exist is significantly more complex and disruptive.
Assign Azure roles at the narrowest practical scope—usually a subscription or resource group—and reserve management-group assignments for genuinely shared platform responsibilities.
Use Azure Policy deny effects for non-negotiable standards — allowed locations, required tags, SKU restrictions — and audit effects for visibility before escalating to deny.
Apply CanNotDelete locks to production resource groups containing stateful resources so accidental complete-mode deployments or manual deletions require an explicit lock removal step.
Use managed identities and least-privilege roles for automation instead of long-lived owner credentials.
Preview deployments, retain operation evidence, and use deployment stacks for explicit deletion ownership.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the management plane and the data plane in Azure?
interviewQuestions.answer: The management plane is the ARM API used to create, update, delete, and configure resources — all RBAC and Policy enforcement happens here. The data plane is the resource's own API for working with its content — reading blobs from Storage, sending messages to Service Bus, or querying a database. A user can have ARM RBAC rights to manage a resource without having data plane access to its content, and vice versa.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between incremental and complete deployment mode?
interviewQuestions.answer: Incremental mode, the recommended default, adds or updates resources in the template while leaving unspecified resources in place. Complete mode deletes resources that are absent from the template, but Microsoft is gradually deprecating it for deletion scenarios; use deployment stacks when a declarative deployment must also remove resources.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you enforce a tagging standard across all resources in an Azure tenant?
interviewQuestions.answer: Assign an Azure Policy at the management group scope with a deny effect that requires specified tag keys on all resource writes. For existing untagged resources, use a modify policy with a remediation task to apply default tag values. This ensures compliance for new resources immediately and provides a path to remediate existing ones.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an Azure resource provider?
interviewQuestions.answer: A resource provider implements ARM resource types and operations for a service, publishes API versions, and performs the control-plane work after ARM authorizes and validates a request.

interviewQuestions.question: How are Azure RBAC and Azure Policy different?
interviewQuestions.answer: RBAC decides who may perform an action at a scope; Policy evaluates whether a resource state or requested change complies with organizational rules.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use deployment stacks?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stacks record deployment ownership, can protect managed resources with deny assignments, and define what happens when a resource disappears from the declaration.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you troubleshoot a failed ARM deployment?
interviewQuestions.answer: Start with the deployment and nested operation records, correlation ID, provider error details, activity log, policy evaluation, permissions, quota, and the exact API version and request.

note: ARM governance decisions — hierarchy design, policy scope, RBAC model — are very difficult to change after workloads are deployed. Treat the ARM layer as foundational architecture that deserves the same design rigour as application architecture.
tip: Use the Azure Resource Graph to query the live state of all resources across subscriptions using KQL — it is far faster than iterating through the ARM SDK and essential for compliance reporting and cost visibility at scale.
warning: Complete deployment mode deletes resources that are absent from the template and is not recommended for new deletion workflows. Prefer deployment stacks, and always review a what-if result before any potentially destructive deployment.

troubleshooting.symptom: A dependent resource cannot find its parent.
