name: Azure API Management
shortDescription: Publish, secure, transform, observe, and govern APIs through a managed gateway, control plane, developer experience, and policy model.
overview: Azure API Management is a managed platform for exposing and governing APIs across Azure, on-premises, hybrid, and multicloud environments.
detail: Azure API Management (APIM) is a managed API gateway and governance platform whose runtime gateway is separate from its management plane and developer experience. A production design must cover API import and lifecycle, versions and revisions, products and subscriptions, caller identity, backend identity, policy scope and inheritance, request limits, transformations, caching, observability, networking, certificates, tier capabilities, zones or regions, capacity, recovery, and configuration delivery. APIM can enforce consistent edge policy, but the backend remains responsible for resource authorization, business validation, idempotency, and resilience. Classic, v2, Consumption, workspace, and self-hosted gateways do not have identical capabilities, so architects must validate the current feature matrix rather than assume policy or topology parity.

concepts.title: Gateway and management planes
concepts.description: The gateway processes traffic; the management plane configures APIs, operations, backends, products, subscriptions, users, policies, revisions, versions, workspaces, and diagnostics.

concepts.title: Policy pipeline and scope
concepts.description: Inbound, backend, outbound, and on-error sections execute at global, workspace, product, API, or operation scope with explicit base inheritance.

concepts.title: Identity at both hops
concepts.description: Validate caller tokens at the gateway, authorize domain resources in the backend, and use managed identity or certificates from APIM to protected backends.

concepts.title: Products and subscriptions
concepts.description: Products package APIs for audiences and can use subscriptions for access and metering; subscription keys are not a replacement for user identity.

concepts.title: Versions and revisions
concepts.description: Versions represent breaking public contracts, while revisions support controlled nonbreaking configuration changes and staged release.

concepts.title: Traffic and transformation policy
concepts.description: Quotas, rate limits, caching, routing, validation, and transformations protect dependencies but must preserve correct semantics and useful error contracts.

concepts.title: Gateway choices
concepts.description: Classic, v2, Consumption, self-hosted, and workspace gateways differ in networking, scale, policy, cache, region, and operational responsibility.

concepts.title: Reliability and observability
concepts.description: Tier, units, zones, regions, backend failover, DNS, certificates, capacity, telemetry sampling, and configuration recovery determine end-to-end availability.

architecture.description: Consumers call an APIM gateway that applies identity and traffic policies, routes to protected backend APIs, and exports telemetry while the management plane controls configuration.

code.label: inbound-policy.xml
code.introduction: An inbound policy validates an Entra-issued JWT, limits calls per authenticated subject, and adds a correlation identifier before forwarding the request.
code.code:
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <base />
    <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" failed-validation-httpcode="401">
      <openid-config url="{{entra-openid-config}}" />
      <audiences><audience>{{orders-api-audience}}</audience></audiences>
    </validate-jwt>
    <rate-limit-by-key calls="120" renewal-period="60"
      counter-key="@(context.Principal?.Identity?.Name ?? context.Request.IpAddress)" />
    <set-header name="x-correlation-id" exists-action="skip">
      <value>@(context.RequestId.ToString())</value>
    </set-header>
  </inbound>
  <backend><base /></backend>
  <outbound><base /></outbound>
  <on-error><base /></on-error>
</policies>

bestPractices: Choose tier and gateway type only after mapping required policies, networking, zones, regions, scale, developer portal, and recovery capabilities.
Keep policies small, scoped, source-controlled, reviewed, linted, tested, and promoted through immutable API revisions.
Validate issuer, audience, signature, expiry, and required claims at the gateway, then enforce resource authorization again in the backend.
Use APIM managed identity for Key Vault and backends; keep secrets in Key Vault-backed named values and never log them.
Apply rate limits, quotas, payload limits, timeouts, retry, and circuit behavior from measured backend capacity and idempotency.
Preserve correlation and distributed trace context while redacting sensitive headers and bodies from diagnostics.
Automate OpenAPI import, named values, backends, policies, products, diagnostics, and tests with infrastructure and configuration as code.
Monitor capacity, gateway and backend latency, 4xx and 5xx rates, policy errors, cache behavior, certificates, quotas, and regional health.

interviewQuestions.question: Gateway versus management plane?
interviewQuestions.answer: The gateway is the request data plane. The management plane defines APIs, products, subscriptions, policies, users, revisions, versions, diagnostics, and operational configuration.

interviewQuestions.question: Why must a backend authorize after APIM validates a JWT?
interviewQuestions.answer: Gateway validation establishes an acceptable identity and coarse access, but only the backend understands resource ownership, tenant boundaries, and business permissions.

interviewQuestions.question: Version versus revision?
interviewQuestions.answer: A version exposes a distinct contract, commonly for breaking changes. A revision stages a compatible implementation or policy change before making it current.

interviewQuestions.question: Rate limit versus quota?
interviewQuestions.answer: A rate limit bounds calls in a short renewal window to protect capacity; a quota limits usage over a longer period for entitlement or cost control.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you make APIM highly available?
interviewQuestions.answer: Select a supported production tier, distribute suitable capacity across zones or regions where supported, make backends and DNS resilient, automate configuration recovery, and test dependency failures.

interviewQuestions.question: When use a self-hosted gateway?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use it when traffic must remain near on-premises or multicloud backends while management stays in Azure, accepting responsibility for its hosting, scale, connectivity, upgrades, and availability.

note: API Management governs API exposure; it does not replace careful API contract design, backend authorization, service resilience, or lifecycle ownership.
tip: Treat every APIM policy as production code with source control, review, automated deployment, test calls, and observability.
warning: Tier capabilities and networking behavior differ materially; validate current limits and availability features before committing an architecture.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated APIM policy, Bicep deployment, secured backend, and focused tests
learningObjectives: Explain APIM planes, resources, gateway variants, and policy execution.
Design caller and backend identity without moving domain authorization to the gateway.
Manage contracts with versions, revisions, products, and subscriptions.
Build safe traffic, transformation, cache, and failure policies.
Choose tier, networking, zones, regions, and capacity from requirements.
Test, deploy, observe, recover, and govern APIM configuration as code.
prerequisites: HTTP, REST/OpenAPI, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, JWT, TLS, and DNS.
ASP.NET Core authentication, authorization, resilience, and observability.
Azure identity, RBAC, Key Vault, networking, Bicep, and deployment pipelines.

use: Multiple APIs need consistent exposure, policy, analytics, onboarding, and lifecycle governance.
External or partner APIs need a managed gateway and developer experience.
Hybrid backends need controlled centralized configuration.
avoid: A single private service only needs simple ingress routing.
Required gateway capability is absent from the selected tier or gateway.
The team expects APIM to replace backend authorization or service reliability.

implementationSteps.title: Inventory consumers and APIs
implementationSteps.description: Record contracts, identities, traffic, sensitivity, owners, SLOs, regions, and dependencies.

implementationSteps.title: Choose topology and tier
implementationSteps.description: Validate gateway features, capacity, networking, zones, regions, portal, and recovery requirements.

implementationSteps.title: Define API lifecycle
implementationSteps.description: Import OpenAPI, create stable operation IDs, products, subscriptions, versions, revisions, and ownership.

implementationSteps.title: Secure both hops
implementationSteps.description: Validate caller tokens, configure backend managed identity, restrict networking, and retain backend authorization.

implementationSteps.title: Compose policies
implementationSteps.description: Add correlation, validation, limits, routing, transforms, caching, and safe errors in deliberate scopes.

implementationSteps.title: Automate and test
implementationSteps.description: Deploy with Bicep or Terraform, test policy branches and backends, and promote a revision.

implementationSteps.title: Operate and recover
implementationSteps.description: Load test, alert on capacity and failures, rotate certificates, export configuration, and rehearse recovery.

testing.introduction: Test policies and backends independently, then prove their combined behavior on a deployed gateway.
items: Unit test backend authorization and business rules.
Validate policy XML, expressions, named values, inheritance, and forbidden secrets in CI.
Run gateway tests for missing, invalid, expired, wrong-audience, wrong-scope, and valid tokens.
Verify rate, quota, cache, transformation, timeout, retry, and on-error branches.
Load test gateway capacity and backend saturation with representative payloads.
Inject backend, DNS, certificate, regional, and telemetry failures and rehearse recovery.

security.introduction: Treat APIM as one trust boundary in a defense-in-depth path.
items: Disable anonymous exposure unless deliberate.
Validate tokens strictly and authorize resources in the backend.
Use managed identity and least-privilege roles for backends and Key Vault.
Restrict inbound and outbound network paths and validate certificates.
Redact credentials, tokens, PII, and bodies from logs and traces.
Protect management access with least privilege, change review, and audit.

performance.introduction: Measure gateway and backend together because policy cost and dependency capacity determine useful throughput.
items: Track capacity, request rate, percentiles, policy duration, backend duration, errors, and throttles.
Use caching only for safe responses with correct vary keys and invalidation.
Bound body transforms, validation size, retries, and timeouts.
Scale before sustained saturation and retest after policy changes.
Avoid expensive policy expressions and repeated remote calls.
Model Consumption cost or provisioned units against realistic peaks.

deployment.introduction: Promote declarative configuration and immutable revisions through environments.
items: Pin API versions and infrastructure API versions.
Keep environment values separate from reusable API and policy definitions.
Use federated deployment identity and narrowly scoped management permissions.
Run policy and contract smoke tests before making a revision current.
Roll back by switching revision or forward-fixing compatible configuration.
Retarget DNS and backends only through tested recovery procedures.

troubleshooting.cause: Issuer, audience, claim, token location, subscription, or backend permission differs.
troubleshooting.fix: Trace one safe request, inspect policy scope and JWT metadata, and separate gateway rejection from backend authorization.

troubleshooting.cause: Capacity saturation, expensive policy work, remote validation, retries, or a slow backend.
troubleshooting.fix: Split gateway and backend duration, inspect capacity and policy traces, remove retry amplification, and load test the bottleneck.

troubleshooting.symptom: Policy works at one scope but not another
troubleshooting.cause: Base inheritance is missing or a broader policy overrides behavior.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the effective policy, add deliberate base elements, and test global through operation scopes.

troubleshooting.cause: Tier capability, VNet integration, DNS, route, firewall, identity, or TLS trust is incomplete.
troubleshooting.fix: Verify the selected tier path end to end from gateway subnet and identity, including name resolution and certificate chain.

troubleshooting.cause: Portal edits bypass the declarative delivery path.
troubleshooting.fix: Restrict manual changes, export and compare configuration, restore source control as authority, and redeploy.

productionChecklist: Tier and gateway capabilities match policy, network, availability, region, and recovery needs.
Caller and backend identities use strict validation, least privilege, and no embedded secrets.
Backends retain domain authorization, validation, idempotency, and resilience.
Policies are scoped, inherited, versioned, tested, bounded, and observable.
Versions, revisions, products, subscriptions, owners, and deprecation are governed.
Capacity, latency, errors, certificates, quotas, and regional health have alerts and runbooks.
Infrastructure, configuration, smoke tests, rollback, and disaster recovery are rehearsed.

name: Azure Functions & Serverless
shortDescription: Build event-driven .NET workloads with triggers, bindings, isolated workers, elastic hosting, durable workflows, and production-safe operations.
overview: Azure Functions runs event-driven code on managed, elastic compute and integrates .NET handlers with HTTP, schedules, queues, streams, storage, and other services.
detail: A function app groups functions that share deployment, configuration, scaling, and hosting. Triggers start executions and bindings integrate data, while the .NET isolated worker uses the standard hosting and dependency-injection model outside the Functions host process. Hosting plan, scale behavior, cold starts, concurrency, retries, poison handling, idempotency, networking, identity, observability, package deployment, and execution duration all affect whether a serverless design meets its workload goals.

concepts.title: Function app boundary
concepts.description: Functions in one app deploy, configure, secure, and usually scale together; group only handlers with compatible lifecycle, risk, and load.

concepts.title: Triggers and bindings
concepts.description: One trigger starts an invocation; bindings simplify supported data flow, while SDK clients are clearer for advanced transactions, batching, and control.

concepts.title: Isolated worker model
concepts.description: The .NET worker runs separately from the host and supports modern .NET, dependency injection, middleware, configuration, logging, and testable handler services.

concepts.title: Hosting plans
concepts.description: Flex Consumption, Premium, Dedicated, and container hosting differ in cold start, networking, scale, duration, availability, instance size, and price.

concepts.title: At-least-once processing
concepts.description: Queue and stream events may repeat after retries, locks, crashes, or checkpoint behavior, so durable idempotency and poison handling are mandatory.

concepts.title: Concurrency and scale
concepts.description: Trigger concurrency, batching, prefetch, instance scale, connections, and downstream capacity interact; higher parallelism can reduce reliability.

concepts.title: Durable workflows
concepts.description: Durable Functions persists orchestration history for timers, fan-out, compensation, and human interaction; orchestrator code must remain deterministic.

concepts.title: Operations and delivery
concepts.description: Package deployment, slots or rolling updates, host storage, telemetry, alerts, quotas, replay, and disaster recovery define production behavior.

architecture.description: Events enter through Functions triggers, isolated .NET workers execute stateless handlers and call managed dependencies, while durable state, retries, and telemetry support reliable scale.

code.label: CreateOrderFunction.cs
code.introduction: An isolated-worker HTTP function uses constructor injection, structured logging, cancellation, and an explicit response contract.

bestPractices: Use the .NET isolated worker and supported runtime and extension versions for new C# apps.
Keep functions thin and move business logic into host-independent services.
Make every event-driven side effect idempotent with a durable atomic receipt or state transition.
Configure bounded retries, visibility or lock duration, poison handling, timeout, and cancellation together.
Choose hosting from measured latency, networking, availability, duration, scale, and cost requirements.
Reuse clients and bound trigger concurrency to downstream capacity and connection limits.
Deploy immutable packages with infrastructure as code and production-shaped integration tests.
Alert on failures, retries, poison events, age or lag, saturation, cold starts, host health, and cost.

interviewQuestions.question: Why prefer isolated worker for new .NET functions?
interviewQuestions.answer: It decouples the application process from the Functions host and provides modern framework targeting, dependency injection, middleware, configuration, and worker lifecycle control.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is exactly-once processing not assumed?
interviewQuestions.answer: A crash after a side effect but before acknowledgement causes delivery to repeat; distributed acknowledgement and business state are not one atomic transaction.

interviewQuestions.question: How should functions be grouped into apps?
interviewQuestions.answer: Group handlers that share deployment, configuration, scale profile, security boundary, availability needs, and blast radius; split conflicting workloads.

interviewQuestions.question: Flex Consumption versus Premium?
interviewQuestions.answer: Flex targets dynamic scale with configurable memory, per-function scaling, networking, and always-ready options; Premium provides prewarmed instances and dedicated plan capacity for demanding workloads.

interviewQuestions.question: When use Durable Functions?
interviewQuestions.answer: For stateful coordination such as fan-out, long timers, external events, and compensation where persisted orchestration and replay semantics fit.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can more concurrency make throughput worse?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can exhaust connections, trigger throttling, extend lock times, amplify retries, and overload databases or APIs until useful throughput falls.

interviewQuestions.question: When is Functions the wrong choice?
interviewQuestions.answer: When execution is a continuously running service, requires unsupported host control or protocols, has predictable steady economics elsewhere, or cannot fit hosting, duration, or networking constraints.

note: Serverless transfers server management and scaling responsibilities; it does not remove capacity limits, distributed-systems behavior, security, or operations.
tip: Load test cold and warm executions with real bindings and observe instance scale, dependency pressure, retries, and end-to-end latency.
warning: Do not assume exactly-once event delivery; build handlers and downstream effects to tolerate duplicates and partial failure.
latestNote: Complete guide to isolated workers, triggers, hosting, reliable event processing, scale, delivery, and operations
learningObjectives: Explain function apps, triggers, bindings, isolated workers, hosting plans, scale, and deployment units.
Design reliable queue, stream, HTTP, timer, and durable workflow handlers.
Implement durable idempotency, retries, poison routing, cancellation, and correlation.
Tune batching, concurrency, connection reuse, and instance scale against dependencies.
Secure host storage, identities, endpoints, settings, packages, and networks.
Test and operate cold starts, replays, deployments, outages, recovery, and cost.
prerequisites: C# async programming, dependency injection, configuration, and structured logging.
Queues, streams, HTTP, retries, idempotency, and distributed-system failure basics.
Azure Functions Core Tools and Azurite for the local sample; Azure is optional.

use: Work starts from HTTP, schedules, queues, streams, storage, or other events and benefits from managed elastic execution.
Handlers can be stateless between invocations or coordinate through durable external state.
The selected plan meets latency, networking, availability, duration, scale, and cost needs.
avoid: A continuously running service, unsupported protocol, specialized compute, or deep host control is required.
Predictable steady load is more economical and operationally clearer on another compute service.
The workload cannot tolerate the available cold-start, regional, networking, quota, or execution constraints.

implementationSteps.title: Define event contracts
implementationSteps.description: Version schemas, choose stable event and correlation IDs, document ordering, retention, maximum size, and compatibility.

implementationSteps.title: Choose the app boundary
implementationSteps.description: Group functions by deployment, security, configuration, scaling, availability, and dependency profile.

implementationSteps.title: Create the isolated worker
implementationSteps.description: Pin runtime, worker SDK, and extensions; register services and keep trigger methods as thin adapters.

implementationSteps.title: Make effects idempotent
implementationSteps.description: Use a durable conditional write or state transition keyed by event ID in the same consistency boundary as the effect.

implementationSteps.title: Configure delivery behavior
implementationSteps.description: Set retry, backoff, lock or visibility, poison destination, timeout, cancellation, batching, and concurrency coherently.

implementationSteps.title: Secure connections
implementationSteps.description: Use managed identity and least privilege where supported; protect required host storage and remove public endpoints when justified.

implementationSteps.title: Instrument outcomes
implementationSteps.description: Correlate invocation, event, retry, dependency, business result, poison routing, lag, and cold-start signals.

implementationSteps.title: Deploy and prove
implementationSteps.description: Publish one immutable package, validate settings and infrastructure, load test, inject failures, rehearse replay, and verify regional recovery.

testing.introduction: Separate fast domain tests from worker adapter, trigger integration, deployed platform, load, and recovery evidence.
items: Unit test handlers, validation, idempotency, retry classification, and cancellation without the Functions host.
Run worker integration tests with representative serialized events and local services.
Use isolated Azure resources to verify authoritative trigger, binding, identity, lock, retry, and poison semantics.
Load test cold and warm starts, batching, concurrency, instance scale, and downstream saturation.
Crash after the side effect and before acknowledgement to prove duplicate safety.
Deploy a package, validate telemetry and settings, replay poison events, and execute recovery procedures.

security.introduction: Secure each function endpoint, workload identity, host storage, binding connection, deployment package, network path, and telemetry stream.
items: Use managed identity and least-privilege data-plane roles where triggers and SDKs support it.
Protect the mandatory host storage account and understand its availability dependency.
Require appropriate HTTP authentication and authorization; never rely only on obscurity of a function key.
Keep secrets out of local settings, packages, logs, and source; rotate unavoidable credentials.
Restrict inbound and outbound networking with a complete DNS and dependency design.
Scan and pin worker, extensions, packages, and deployment artifacts.

performance.introduction: Useful throughput depends on the complete trigger-to-dependency path, not invocation count alone.
items: Use async I/O and reuse SDK, HTTP, database, and messaging clients.
Tune batch, prefetch, and concurrency from downstream capacity and lock duration.
Measure event age, lag, useful completions, retries, throttles, connections, and percentile latency.
Use always-ready or Premium capacity when measured cold-start latency violates objectives.
Avoid large payloads; pass durable references when event size and repeated transfer are costly.
Set maximum scale and application backpressure before dependencies collapse.

deployment.introduction: The function app is the deployment unit; ship all its functions as one immutable, observable package.
items: Build, test, audit, and publish a run-from-package artifact.
Provision plan, app, host storage, identity, settings, networking, alerts, and dependencies through code.
Use federated deployment identity and keep application data access separate.
Use supported slots or Flex rolling updates and understand trigger behavior during overlap.
Run HTTP and event smoke tests, verify telemetry, and watch retry and poison signals.
Prefer forward repair; replay only after the defect is fixed and idempotency is proven.

troubleshooting.cause: Worker SDK generation, target framework, Function attribute, extension, or deployment output is incorrect.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect generated metadata and startup logs, pin compatible packages, clean and rebuild, and verify the deployed package layout.

troubleshooting.cause: The handler throws, exceeds visibility, loses a lock, crashes after an effect, or poison handling is absent.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect delivery count and duration, fix idempotency, align timeout and visibility, bound retries, and monitor poison routing.

troubleshooting.symptom: Scaling rises but event age grows
troubleshooting.cause: Per-instance concurrency or a downstream limit is reducing useful throughput.
troubleshooting.fix: Graph age, completions, retries, throttles, connections, and instances; reduce concurrency or increase the actual bottleneck safely.

troubleshooting.symptom: Works locally but trigger is idle in Azure
troubleshooting.cause: Connection configuration, identity RBAC, network path, extension settings, or source name differs.
troubleshooting.fix: Check host logs, exact setting names, token audience, role scope, DNS, firewall, and trigger source configuration.

troubleshooting.cause: Host and worker pipelines, sampling, exporter configuration, or correlation propagation conflict.
troubleshooting.fix: Configure host and worker logging deliberately, retain errors, verify sampling, and trace one event end to end.

troubleshooting.cause: Old and new instances or slots consume the same trigger during rollout.
troubleshooting.fix: Design compatible schemas and idempotency, understand plan deployment behavior, and isolate consumers when strict version ownership is required.

productionChecklist: Function app boundaries match deployment, scale, security, availability, and dependency profiles.
Runtime, worker SDK, extensions, and hosting plan are supported and pinned.
Event contracts, idempotency, retries, poison routing, timeouts, cancellation, and correlation are tested.
Managed identity, host storage, endpoint authorization, secrets, network, and RBAC are verified.
Batching, concurrency, connections, maximum scale, and always-ready capacity come from load tests.
Immutable deployment and infrastructure automation include smoke and telemetry gates.
Alerts cover failures, retries, poison events, age, lag, cold starts, saturation, host health, and cost.
Replay, rollback or forward repair, backup, restore, and regional recovery are rehearsed.

name: Azure Logic Apps
shortDescription: Build secure, observable enterprise integrations with triggers, actions, connectors, workflow state, retries, and source-controlled delivery.
overview: Azure Logic Apps is a cloud platform for building and running automated workflows that integrate applications, data, services, and systems across an enterprise with minimal code.
detail: Azure Logic Apps is a managed workflow and enterprise integration platform. A workflow starts from a trigger and coordinates built-in operations, managed connectors, control flow, transformations, HTTP calls, messaging, B2B artifacts, and custom code. Consumption and Standard have different hosting, billing, networking, deployment, and workflow capabilities; Standard supports multiple stateful or stateless workflows in a single-tenant runtime. Production design must make delivery semantics, retries, run-after behavior, idempotency, timeouts, concurrency, secrets, managed identity, connector limits, run-history sensitivity, observability, resubmission, disaster recovery, and cost explicit. Logic Apps is strongest when orchestration and connectors dominate; complex domain rules still belong in testable application code.

concepts.title: Triggers and actions
concepts.description: A trigger creates a workflow run; actions execute connectors, data operations, conditions, loops, scopes, functions, or HTTP calls.

concepts.title: Built-in and managed connectors
concepts.description: Built-in connectors run with the runtime, while managed connectors use Azure-hosted API connections with distinct authentication, limits, and billing.

concepts.title: Stateful and stateless
concepts.description: Stateful workflows persist execution state and history for durability; stateless Standard workflows favor short low-latency executions with important capability limits.

concepts.title: Consumption and Standard
concepts.description: Consumption is multitenant and execution-metered; Standard is single-tenant, plan-based, hosts multiple workflows, and supports local development and richer networking.

concepts.title: Control flow and scopes
concepts.description: Conditions, switches, loops, parallel branches, scopes, run-after status, terminate actions, and tracked properties express orchestration and error paths.

concepts.title: Delivery and idempotency
concepts.description: Triggers and actions can retry or replay, so external side effects require stable business keys, idempotent APIs, and explicit resubmission rules.

concepts.title: Integration accounts and B2B
concepts.description: Schemas, maps, partners, agreements, certificates, and EDI protocols support governed enterprise document exchange.

concepts.title: Operations and governance
concepts.description: Run history, diagnostics, connector throttles, workflow versions, parameters, identities, private networking, cost, and recovery need ownership.

architecture.description: A trigger fires the workflow; each action calls a connector or runs inline code; the workflow state is persisted between steps for long-running orchestrations and surfaced in the run history for monitoring.

code.label: OrderWorkflowClient.cs
code.introduction: Logic Apps workflows are JSON definitions — this excerpt shows an HTTP trigger, a Service Bus send action, and a conditional branch, the same structure visible in the visual designer.

bestPractices: Choose Logic Apps when connector orchestration and workflow visibility outweigh custom computation.
Choose Consumption versus Standard from hosting, networking, latency, volume, workflow type, deployment, and cost evidence.
Use managed identity for supported connectors and protect unavoidable connection credentials and parameters.
Design every retried side effect to be idempotent and carry stable workflow, correlation, and business identifiers.
Group failure-prone actions in scopes and configure explicit run-after, retry, timeout, compensation, and terminate behavior.
Keep workflow definitions, connections metadata, schemas, maps, and infrastructure in source control and CI/CD.
Minimize sensitive data in trigger inputs, outputs, run history, tracked properties, and diagnostics.
Monitor failures, throttles, duration, backlog, action latency, abandoned runs, connector health, and cost.

interviewQuestions.question: When choose Logic Apps over Functions?
interviewQuestions.answer: Choose Logic Apps for connector-heavy visible orchestration and enterprise integration; choose Functions for compute-heavy custom logic, fine-grained testing, or runtime control.

interviewQuestions.question: Standard versus Consumption?
interviewQuestions.answer: Consumption is multitenant and metered per execution. Standard uses a single-tenant plan, supports multiple workflows, stateful or stateless execution, local development, and richer networking.

interviewQuestions.question: Stateful versus stateless?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stateful persists run state and history for durable long-running work. Stateless keeps execution state in memory for short lower-latency flows and has different connector and action constraints.

interviewQuestions.question: How are failures modeled?
interviewQuestions.answer: Actions expose Succeeded, Failed, Skipped, and TimedOut status. Run-after conditions, scopes, retry policies, compensation actions, and Terminate define the failure path.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you prevent duplicate side effects?
interviewQuestions.answer: Pass a stable business or workflow-run key to an idempotent target, record completion atomically, and define safe retry and resubmission behavior.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you secure connector access?
interviewQuestions.answer: Prefer managed identity where supported, grant least-privilege roles, protect API connections and parameters, restrict networks, and suppress sensitive run data.

note: Logic Apps excels at enterprise integration patterns — it is not a general application platform. Workflows with significant business logic, custom data transformations, or testing requirements are better served by .NET code.
tip: Use the Standard tier with local development tooling for any workflow that will be maintained long-term — it enables debugging in VS Code, source-controlled workflow definitions, and deployment through standard Azure pipelines.
warning: Consumption Logic Apps can accumulate significant costs under high-volume scenarios where thousands of actions execute per minute — model expected execution counts before choosing the consumption tier for frequent event-driven workflows.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a source-controlled workflow, idempotent callback API, Bicep, and focused tests

Required latency, throughput, connector limits, or cost do not fit.
A simple direct API or queue consumer has no meaningful orchestration.

security.introduction: Protect every trigger, connector, identity, parameter, network path, and recorded payload.
items: Authenticate request triggers with Entra ID or a suitable gateway rather than relying only on secret URLs.
Use managed identity and least-privilege roles for supported Azure connectors.
Store secrets outside definitions and protect connection resources and deployment parameters.
Use private endpoints or VNet integration where the selected hosting model supports them.
Enable secure inputs and outputs and avoid PII or secrets in run history and tracked properties.
Restrict workflow editing, resubmission, and run-history access with RBAC and audit.

performance.introduction: Workflow throughput is constrained by runtime capacity, connector limits, action design, and downstream systems.
items: Measure trigger latency, run duration, action latency, throttles, retries, backlog, and cost.
Use stateless workflows only when their execution and connector constraints fit.
Control loop concurrency and avoid unbounded parallel calls to a limited dependency.
Batch or chunk data deliberately and avoid large repeated transformations.
Use asynchronous messaging for long dependency waits instead of holding HTTP calls.
Model managed connector metering even on Standard plans.

deployment.introduction: Treat workflow definitions and connection metadata as application artifacts.
items: Separate reusable definitions from environment parameters and connection resources.
Deploy identities, networking, connections, workflows, diagnostics, and alerts with code.
Use federated pipeline identity and least-privilege deployment roles.
Validate definitions and run smoke workflows before promotion.
Keep compatible target APIs during rollout and preserve idempotency across versions.
Document forward repair, resubmission, rollback, and regional recovery.

troubleshooting.cause: Its run-after condition does not include the prior action status.

troubleshooting.cause: A trigger, action retry, timeout, or resubmission replayed non-idempotent work.

troubleshooting.cause: Loop concurrency or run volume exceeds connector or target limits.

troubleshooting.symptom: Works in designer but deployment fails

troubleshooting.fix: Validate source-controlled definitions and environment mappings and deploy all dependencies in order.

troubleshooting.cause: Inputs, outputs, tracked properties, or diagnostics record payloads.

Triggers, connectors, identities, secrets, and networks use deliberate least-privilege controls.
Retries, timeouts, run-after, compensation, idempotency, and resubmission are designed together.
Workflow, connection metadata, schemas, maps, parameters, and infrastructure are versioned.
Connector limits, concurrency, payload sizes, action count, and cost are load tested.
