name: Azure Event Hubs
shortDescription: Design high-throughput Azure event streams with partitions, consumer groups, checkpoints, replay, Capture, identity, and operational safeguards.
overview: Azure Event Hubs is a fully managed big-data streaming platform that can receive and process millions of events per second with low latency, offering Kafka protocol compatibility and deep Azure ecosystem integration.
detail: Azure Event Hubs is a managed append-only event streaming service for telemetry, logs, clickstreams, IoT signals, and other high-volume ordered streams. Producers publish batches to a hub, optionally selecting a partition key so related events retain order within one partition. Independent consumer groups read the retained log at their own pace. EventProcessorClient coordinates partition ownership across .NET consumer instances and persists checkpoints, commonly in Blob Storage, but checkpointing is not an atomic transaction with business side effects. Production designs therefore require idempotency, poison-event handling, bounded concurrency, stable partition keys, retention and Capture strategy, schema evolution, managed identity, private networking, throughput capacity, lag monitoring, replay runbooks, and downstream backpressure. Event Hubs also exposes Kafka protocol compatibility, but it remains an Azure service with its own tier and feature model.

concepts.title: Namespace, hub, and partitions
concepts.description: A namespace contains event hubs; each hub is an ordered set of fixed partition logs that provide the unit of parallel consumption.

concepts.title: Partition keys and ordering
concepts.description: A stable key routes related events to one partition and preserves their order there; global ordering is not provided across partitions.

concepts.title: Producers and batching
concepts.description: Producers reuse clients and send bounded batches; routing choice, event size, retry, and idempotent semantics affect throughput and hot partitions.

concepts.title: Consumer groups
concepts.description: Each logical application uses its own independent view of the stream, partition ownership, position, and checkpoint namespace.

concepts.title: EventProcessorClient
concepts.description: The .NET processor cooperates with peer instances to claim partitions, rebalance ownership, receive events, and persist progress.

concepts.title: Checkpoints and replay
concepts.description: A checkpoint records the last completed position, reducing recovery replay but never making external side effects exactly once.

concepts.title: Retention, Capture, and schema
concepts.description: Time-based retention supports short replay; Capture archives events for longer recovery and analytics while schemas evolve compatibly.

concepts.title: Capacity and operations
concepts.description: Throughput or processing units, partitions, quotas, throttling, consumer lag, network paths, identity, and disaster recovery define production limits.

architecture.description: Producers send events to Event Hubs partitions; EventProcessorClient instances compete for partition ownership and checkpoint progress to Blob Storage; Capture writes the stream to Data Lake for batch consumers.

code.label: OrderEventProcessor.cs
code.introduction: EventProcessorClient handles partition ownership and checkpoint coordination. This simple handler processes one event at a time and checkpoints only after success; high-throughput applications should checkpoint at a deliberate interval rather than writing a checkpoint for every event.

bestPractices: Choose partition count from long-term peak parallelism and throughput because it is a durable architectural constraint.
Use high-cardinality stable partition keys only when per-key order matters, and monitor for hot partitions.
Reuse producer clients, build bounded batches, handle partial batch sizing, and propagate event IDs, schema versions, and correlation.
Give every logical application its own consumer group and checkpoint store prefix.
Checkpoint only after durable successful side effects at a measured cadence, and make the sink idempotent for replay.
Bound processor concurrency, prefetch, and batches to downstream capacity; quarantine poison events without blocking a partition forever.
Use managed identity, least-privilege data roles, TLS, private networking where required, and disable local authentication when feasible.
Monitor ingress, egress, throttling, partition skew, consumer lag and event age, checkpoint health, errors, retention risk, and Capture.

interviewQuestions.question: Event Hubs versus Service Bus?
interviewQuestions.answer: Event Hubs is a retained partitioned stream for high-throughput telemetry and independent readers. Service Bus is a broker for commands and workflows with queues, topics, locks, dead lettering, sessions, and transactions.

interviewQuestions.question: What ordering does Event Hubs guarantee?
interviewQuestions.answer: Events have a defined sequence within one partition. There is no total order across partitions, so related ordered events must share a partition key.

interviewQuestions.question: What does EventProcessorClient do?
interviewQuestions.answer: It coordinates partition ownership and load balancing across consumer instances, receives events, and uses a checkpoint store to resume progress.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is checkpointing not exactly once?
interviewQuestions.answer: The business side effect and checkpoint are separate operations. A crash after the side effect but before the checkpoint causes replay.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use separate consumer groups?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each logical consumer needs independent partition ownership and progress; sharing a group makes instances cooperate and split events rather than each receive the stream.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Kafka compatibility affect design?
interviewQuestions.answer: Kafka clients can use the Event Hubs Kafka endpoint, but supported features, authentication, capacity, retention, and operational controls remain those of the chosen Event Hubs tier.

note: Event Hubs retention is time-based, not consumption-based — events are deleted after the configured retention period regardless of whether they were consumed. Design consumer catch-up strategies and use Capture for long-term archiving.
tip: Use the Kafka-compatible endpoint when migrating existing Kafka producers from a self-managed cluster to Event Hubs — change only the bootstrap server and credential configuration, validate, then decommission the cluster.
warning: Event Hubs provides at-least-once delivery. A failure after a side effect but before the next checkpoint can replay events, so handlers and downstream writes must be idempotent even though partition ownership is coordinated between processor instances.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated partition, checkpoint, replay, idempotency, Bicep, and test sample

resources.label: Event Hubs authentication with Microsoft Entra ID

learningObjectives: Explain namespaces, hubs, partitions, keys, sequence, offsets, retention, and consumer groups.
Design producer batching, schemas, routing, and client reuse.
Operate EventProcessorClient ownership, checkpoints, replay, and idempotent side effects.
Choose capacity, partitions, concurrency, Capture, and downstream backpressure.
Secure producers, consumers, storage, networks, and deployment identities.
Test lag, throttling, poison events, rebalances, retention loss, and disaster recovery.
prerequisites: Event streaming, async workers, serialization, eventual consistency, and idempotency.
Azure identity, RBAC, Blob Storage, networking, monitoring, and Bicep.
Capacity planning, load testing, schema evolution, and recovery procedures.

use: High-volume append-only events need replay and independent consumers.
Per-key ordering and partitioned scale fit the domain.
Stream analytics or Capture-based data pipelines are required.
avoid: Commands need queue locks, dead lettering, sessions, or transactional broker features.
Strict global ordering is required at high parallelism.
The workload is simple request-response or low-volume task dispatch.

implementationSteps.title: Define stream contracts
implementationSteps.description: Document event IDs, keys, schemas, owners, volume, ordering, retention, sensitivity, and consumers.

implementationSteps.title: Choose tier and partitions
implementationSteps.description: Model event size, ingress, egress, parallelism, retention, Capture, availability, and growth.

implementationSteps.title: Build producers
implementationSteps.description: Reuse clients, batch safely, apply stable keys only when needed, and emit versioned metadata.

implementationSteps.title: Build consumer isolation
implementationSteps.description: Assign one consumer group and checkpoint scope per application and use EventProcessorClient for coordination.

implementationSteps.title: Make effects replay-safe
implementationSteps.description: Validate events, deduplicate atomically, bound retries, quarantine poison records, then checkpoint.

implementationSteps.title: Secure and deploy
implementationSteps.description: Provision identity, RBAC, networking, hub, consumer groups, checkpoint storage, Capture, diagnostics, and alerts with code.

implementationSteps.title: Load and recovery test
implementationSteps.description: Measure skew and lag, kill processors during work, rebalance instances, replay from archive, and test retention-window failure.

testing.introduction: Prove application logic locally and authoritative platform behavior in an isolated Event Hubs environment.
items: Unit test schemas, partition-key selection, idempotency, retry classification, poison routing, and checkpoint decisions.
Integration test serialized events, producer batches, EventProcessorClient, and Blob checkpoint access.
Run multiple processor instances and verify ownership balancing during scale and crashes.
Crash after a durable side effect but before checkpointing to prove replay safety.
Load test event size, batching, key skew, ingress, egress, lag, throttling, and downstream saturation.
Replay from a chosen offset or Capture archive and rehearse retention-loss recovery.

security.introduction: Secure the namespace, hub, checkpoint storage, Capture destination, network, identities, and event data.
items: Use managed identity and least-privilege Event Hubs Data Sender or Receiver roles.
Use separate identities and scopes for producers, each consumer, Capture, and deployment.
Disable local authentication where all clients support Entra ID and rotate unavoidable SAS credentials.
Use TLS and private endpoints with complete DNS and egress design when required.
Do not place secrets or unnecessary PII in event bodies, properties, logs, or partition keys.
Protect checkpoint and archive storage from public access and destructive permissions.

performance.introduction: Throughput depends on event size, batch efficiency, partition distribution, capacity units, consumers, and downstream work.
items: Batch producer sends within service limits and reuse long-lived clients.
Track per-partition ingress and lag to detect hot keys masked by namespace totals.
Tune processor batch, prefetch, and concurrency from downstream capacity.
Scale consumers only up to useful partition parallelism within a consumer group.
Checkpoint at a cadence that balances storage operations and acceptable replay.
Autoscale or increase capacity before sustained throttling, then verify end-to-end useful throughput.

deployment.introduction: Provision the complete streaming path and promote consumers with schema and replay compatibility.
items: Deploy namespace, hub, partitions, retention, consumer groups, storage, Capture, identity, RBAC, network, diagnostics, and alerts with code.
Keep local authentication disabled when identity migration is complete.
Deploy producers before consumers only when schema compatibility permits.
Use separate consumer groups for blue-green validation without stealing partitions.
Smoke publish and consume a uniquely identified event and verify checkpoint and telemetry.
Rollback or replay only with idempotency and schema compatibility proven.

troubleshooting.symptom: Consumer instances run but lag grows
troubleshooting.cause: Hot partitions, insufficient units, downstream saturation, throttling, or excessive per-event work limits useful throughput.
troubleshooting.fix: Graph per-partition age, rate, ownership, throttles, duration, and dependency capacity; tune or repartition future keys deliberately.

troubleshooting.cause: The last side effects occurred after the saved checkpoint or processing crashed before checkpointing.
troubleshooting.fix: Treat replay as normal, make effects idempotent, and choose checkpoint cadence from recovery objectives.

troubleshooting.cause: A consumer group cannot usefully assign more active processors than partitions.
troubleshooting.fix: Compare partition and instance counts and scale only to useful parallelism.

troubleshooting.cause: Checkpoint storage latency, inconsistent configuration, duplicate processor identifiers, or aggressive load balancing destabilizes leases.
troubleshooting.fix: Verify shared checkpoint scope, storage health, processor settings, time synchronization, and version consistency.

troubleshooting.symptom: Authentication succeeds locally but fails in Azure
troubleshooting.cause: Credential source, token audience, RBAC data role scope, DNS, firewall, or private endpoint configuration differs.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the deployed identity, role propagation and scope, fully qualified namespace, token audience, and network path.

troubleshooting.cause: The retention window expired and no suitable Capture archive exists.
troubleshooting.fix: Set retention from outage objectives, enable and monitor Capture, and rehearse archive replay before an incident.

productionChecklist: Event contracts, keys, schemas, ordering, volume, retention, sensitivity, and owners are documented.
Tier, capacity, partitions, consumer groups, and Capture match long-term requirements.
Producers reuse clients, batch safely, and emit event ID, schema version, and correlation.
Consumers are idempotent, bounded, cancellation-aware, poison-safe, and checkpoint after durable success.
Managed identities, least-privilege roles, TLS, storage controls, and network paths are verified.
Per-partition skew, lag, age, throttling, errors, checkpoint health, retention risk, and Capture are monitored.
Scale, crash, rebalance, replay, schema rollback, retention loss, and regional recovery are rehearsed.

name: Azure Data Factory & ETL
shortDescription: Orchestrate secure batch data movement and transformation through pipelines, activities, datasets, linked services, and integration runtimes.
overview: Azure Data Factory is a managed data-integration and orchestration service for moving, transforming, scheduling, and monitoring data across cloud and on-premises systems.
detail: ADF pipelines compose copy, transformation, control-flow, notebook, stored-procedure, and custom activities into parameterized workflows. Linked services describe connection and compute information, datasets describe the data an activity reads or writes, and integration runtimes provide network reach and execution capability through Azure, self-hosted, or Azure-SSIS models. Reliable production pipelines do more than report green activity status: they establish an incremental boundary, persist committed state separately from in-flight work, make sinks idempotent, validate counts, schema, freshness, duplicates, and business rules, reconcile source and target, and advance the watermark only after durable success. Managed identity, Key Vault references, private connectivity, source-controlled deployment, environment parameters, diagnostic logs, lineage, cost controls, and replay runbooks complete the operating model. Copy activity is optimized for movement; complex transformation may belong in mapping data flows or specialized engines that ADF orchestrates. New analytics programs should also evaluate Data Factory capabilities in Microsoft Fabric while matching product choice to existing platform, governance, region, connector, and operational needs.
learningObjectives: Explain pipelines, activities, linked services, datasets, triggers, parameters, and integration runtimes.
Choose Copy activity, mapping data flow, stored procedures, notebooks, or external compute by workload shape.
Design full, incremental, CDC, partitioned, and metadata-driven ingestion.
Build restartable watermark processing with idempotent sinks and reconciliation.
Secure identities, credentials, networks, and self-hosted runtime hosts.
Test data correctness separately from orchestration success.
Deploy, monitor, tune, replay, and recover production pipelines.
prerequisites: Batch data movement, SQL queries, files, object storage, schemas, and ETL versus ELT.
Azure managed identity, RBAC, Key Vault, networking, and private endpoint basics.
Source control, environment promotion, monitoring, and incident response concepts.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the dedicated incremental pipeline model.

use: Use ADF when managed orchestration, broad connectors, hybrid data movement, scheduling, and visual or JSON pipeline operations fit the workload.
Use Copy activity for scalable movement with minimal transformation.
Use mapping data flows or an external analytical engine for distributed transformations.
Use a self-hosted integration runtime only when private or on-premises reach requires customer-managed compute.
avoid: Do not use ADF as a low-latency request/response or event-stream processor.
Do not perform large complex transformations in orchestration expressions.
Do not clone one pipeline per table when metadata-driven parameters can safely reuse behavior.
Do not treat activity success as proof that data is correct and complete.
tradeoffs: Managed orchestration reduces platform code but requires governance for JSON artifacts, parameters, and operational state.
Self-hosted runtime enables private reach but adds patching, capacity, availability, and credential responsibilities.
Watermarks are broadly compatible but require careful boundaries; native CDC can improve fidelity but depends on source capabilities.
Parallelism improves throughput until source, integration runtime, network, or sink limits become the bottleneck.

concepts.title: Pipeline orchestration
concepts.description: Pipelines compose copy, transformation, control-flow, notebook, stored-procedure, and custom activities with dependencies and parameters.

concepts.title: Connections and data
concepts.description: Linked services describe connection information while datasets identify the input and output data used by activities.

concepts.title: Integration runtime
concepts.description: Azure, self-hosted, and Azure-SSIS runtimes provide compute and network reach for data movement, activity dispatch, and package execution.

concepts.title: Incremental boundaries
concepts.description: Watermarks, change tracking, or CDC define a stable source range between committed and captured high-water marks.

concepts.title: Idempotency and replay
concepts.description: Upserts, deduplication keys, immutable partitions, and transactional merges make retries and backfills safe.

concepts.title: Data quality
concepts.description: Counts, schemas, freshness, nulls, duplicates, business rules, quarantine, and reconciliation prove useful output.

concepts.title: Triggers and parameters
concepts.description: Schedules, events, tumbling windows, dependencies, metadata, and parameters drive reusable execution.

concepts.title: Operations and lineage
concepts.description: Run history, metrics, diagnostics, alerts, ownership, lineage, replay, retention, and cost make pipelines supportable.

architecture.description: Triggers start parameterized ADF pipelines, an integration runtime reaches source systems, activities move or transform data, and validated results land in governed analytical storage.

code.label: pipeline-copy-orders.json
code.introduction: A parameterized Copy activity passes a watermark to the source dataset and writes through a configured sink dataset.

implementationSteps: Define source, target, volume, cadence, latency, schema, sensitivity, retention, recovery, and reconciliation objectives.
Choose full load, watermark, source change tracking, CDC, file partition, or event-assisted incremental boundaries.
Select integration runtime and establish identity, connector, DNS, firewall, private endpoint, and credential paths.
Create parameterized linked services, datasets, and pipelines; keep environment values outside reusable definitions.
Capture a high watermark, copy the closed range, transform or merge idempotently, validate output, then commit progress.
Add retry, timeout, cancellation, quarantine, backfill, replay, and failed-run recovery without advancing state early.
Deploy through source control and CI/CD, then monitor orchestration, data quality, lineage, capacity, freshness, and cost.

testing.introduction: Test definitions, data correctness, failure replay, real connectivity, and representative scale as separate concerns.
items: Unit- or contract-test pipeline JSON, required parameters, expressions, dataset references, and environment substitutions.
Use small deterministic fixtures for initial load, no-change run, one delta, update, delete or tombstone, duplicate, and late arrival.
Inject failure before write, during write, after write, during validation, and before watermark commit; reruns must converge safely.
Validate row counts, checksums or aggregates, schema, freshness, duplicates, nullability, business rules, and rejected records.
Test integration-runtime connectivity and least-privilege access from the actual network boundary.
Run scale tests with representative partition skew, file sizes, concurrency, source pressure, sink pressure, and recovery backlog.

security.introduction: Secure source, target, orchestration state, integration runtime, credentials, network paths, and copied data end to end.
items: Prefer managed identity and Key Vault references; keep credentials out of linked-service JSON, parameters, logs, and repository history.
Grant source read, target write, and control-state access separately at the narrowest practical scope.
Use managed virtual network, private endpoints, firewall rules, or self-hosted runtime only according to a documented threat model.
Harden self-hosted runtime hosts with patching, restricted administration, outbound controls, monitoring, capacity, and high availability.
Classify sensitive fields, encrypt transport and storage, minimize copied data, and enforce retention and regional requirements.
Redact pipeline parameters, queries, file paths, errors, and diagnostic payloads that could reveal secrets or personal data.

performance.introduction: Find the constrained stage first, then tune partitioning, files, bulk operations, runtime capacity, and concurrency together.
items: Measure source read, integration-runtime throughput, network, transformation, and sink write separately before scaling concurrency.
Partition large ranges and files by a selective balanced key while preserving source and sink capacity.
Prefer appropriately sized files and bulk writes over many tiny files or row-by-row operations.
Use staged copy, compression, parallel copy, data integration units, and self-hosted nodes only after measurement.
Avoid overlapping runs for the same mutable boundary unless control state and sink semantics support it.
Track throughput, queue time, activity duration, retries, throttling, skew, file count, runtime utilization, freshness, and cost per load.

deployment.introduction: Promote source-controlled definitions and prerequisites safely while preserving triggers, state, replay, and rollback boundaries.
items: Keep factories connected to source control and promote reviewed publish artifacts or infrastructure templates through environments.
Parameterize endpoints, database names, vault references, runtime references, labels, and schedules without parameterizing away governance.
Provision identities, roles, network paths, private DNS, vault access, and runtime capacity before enabling triggers.
Disable production triggers during incompatible migrations and preserve resumable state across deployment.
Canary with a bounded table or partition, compare reconciled output, then expand metadata scope and concurrency.
Maintain backfill, replay, watermark repair, source retention, target rollback, and regional recovery procedures.

troubleshooting.symptom: The pipeline succeeds but data is missing
troubleshooting.cause: The watermark advanced too early, the query boundary excluded rows, late data arrived, or only activity status was checked.
troubleshooting.fix: Compare committed and high watermarks, inspect inclusive/exclusive predicates, reconcile source and sink, replay the affected closed range, and delay commit until validation.

troubleshooting.cause: The sink appends without a deterministic key or the write and progress update are not replay-safe.
troubleshooting.fix: Use merge/upsert, immutable partition replacement, deduplication keys, or transactional staging and rerun the same range.

troubleshooting.cause: Source query, small files, runtime capacity, network, partition skew, throttling, or sink commits limit the path.
troubleshooting.fix: Measure each stage, inspect runtime metrics and throttles, tune query and partitions, batch files, and raise concurrency only where capacity exists.

troubleshooting.cause: The host, service, registration, outbound connectivity, certificate, DNS, proxy, patch, or capacity state failed.
troubleshooting.fix: Check node health and logs, service identity, outbound endpoints, proxy/DNS, version consistency, queue, and high-availability nodes.

troubleshooting.symptom: Authentication works in development but not production
troubleshooting.cause: Identity, RBAC scope, vault access, connector mode, DNS, firewall, or private endpoint differs.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the factory and runtime identity, data roles, linked-service authentication, token audience, secret reference, and deployed network path.

troubleshooting.symptom: Schema drift breaks or silently corrupts a load
troubleshooting.cause: Source changes were neither rejected nor mapped through an explicit compatibility policy.
troubleshooting.fix: Detect schema before write, quarantine incompatible data, version mappings, alert owners, and backfill after a reviewed migration.

productionChecklist: Sources, targets, owners, schemas, sensitivity, volume, cadence, latency, retention, and recovery objectives are documented.
Incremental boundary, committed state, high-watermark capture, late arrivals, deletes, and replay semantics are defined.
Sinks are idempotent and validation occurs before progress is committed.
Managed identity, least-privilege roles, Key Vault, encryption, and network paths are verified.
Integration-runtime type, version, capacity, availability, patching, and monitoring meet requirements.
Pipeline JSON, parameters, expressions, fixtures, failure injection, data quality, and scale are tested.
Runs, freshness, counts, schema, duplicates, rejects, retries, throughput, lineage, and cost are monitored.
Backfill, quarantine, watermark repair, source-retention loss, rollback, and disaster recovery are rehearsed.
bestPractices: Use metadata-driven, parameterized pipelines and reusable datasets or linked services instead of cloning environment-specific workflows.
Prefer managed identity, Key Vault references, private connectivity where required, and least privilege.
Use a self-hosted runtime only when network reach demands it and operate it as production infrastructure.
Design incremental loads with closed ranges, durable committed state, late-data policy, and replay procedures.
Make sinks idempotent and validate counts, schema, freshness, duplicates, and business rules before advancing progress.
Deploy through source control and CI/CD with separate environments and reviewed parameters.
Monitor activity and data-quality outcomes, lineage, throughput, retries, runtime capacity, and cost.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an integration runtime in Azure Data Factory?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is the compute and network bridge used for data movement, dispatching supported activities, transformations, and SSIS execution. Azure, self-hosted, and Azure-SSIS types serve different needs.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
interviewQuestions.answer: ETL transforms data before loading the target. ELT loads data first and uses the target analytical engine for transformation; the best choice depends on scale, governance, latency, and engine capabilities.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you make an incremental pipeline restartable?
interviewQuestions.answer: Persist a committed watermark separately from the captured high watermark, make writes idempotent or transactional, validate and reconcile the closed range, and advance committed state only after durable success.

interviewQuestions.question: When should you use a self-hosted integration runtime?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use it when ADF must reach on-premises or private systems through customer-managed network paths. It adds host patching, availability, capacity, proxy, credential, and monitoring responsibilities.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is pipeline success not enough?
interviewQuestions.answer: Activities can complete while data is incomplete, duplicated, stale, malformed, or semantically wrong. Data-quality validation and reconciliation are separate acceptance signals.

interviewQuestions.question: How do Copy activity and mapping data flow differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: Copy activity specializes in efficient data movement with light mapping. Mapping data flow provides managed distributed transformations; complex workloads may instead use SQL, Spark, notebooks, or another engine orchestrated by ADF.

note: ADF is primarily an orchestration and integration service; complex transformations may be better executed by specialized engines it coordinates.
tip: Track both pipeline success and data correctness—row counts, freshness, schema, duplicates, and reconciliation can fail independently of activity status.
warning: Never advance an incremental watermark before the target write and validation are durably complete, or failed data can be skipped permanently.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated restartable incremental ETL sample

name: Cloud Adoption Framework
shortDescription: Align Azure adoption with business outcomes through strategy, planning, landing zones, workload adoption, governance, security, and management.
overview: Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework provides an organization-wide roadmap for adopting Azure and integrating it into business, platform, governance, security, and operations.
detail: CAF organizes cloud adoption into connected methodologies. Strategy defines motivations and outcomes; Plan prepares people, skills, inventory, costs, and a roadmap; Ready establishes the Azure environment and landing zones; Adopt migrates, modernizes, or builds cloud-native workloads. Govern, Secure, and Manage operate continuously across the estate. CAF complements the workload-focused Well-Architected Framework and implementation patterns in the Azure Architecture Center.

concepts.title: Strategy and Plan
concepts.description: Business outcomes, financial justification, operating model, skills, digital estate, prioritization, and an actionable adoption backlog set direction.

concepts.title: Ready and landing zones
concepts.description: Tenant, identity, management groups, subscriptions, networking, policy, security, and platform automation create a governed environment for workloads.

concepts.title: Adopt workloads
concepts.description: Teams choose migration, modernization, or cloud-native paths and onboard workloads through repeatable application landing zones and delivery practices.

concepts.title: Govern, Secure, and Manage
concepts.description: Continuous controls, security posture, operations, cost, compliance, ownership, and improvement keep the cloud estate aligned as it grows.

architecture.description: Business strategy becomes an adoption plan and landing-zone foundation; workload teams then migrate or build while governance, security, and management operate continuously across the estate.

code.label: application-landing-zone.bicep
code.introduction: A small application landing-zone module exposes ownership and environment metadata as required deployment inputs instead of adding them manually later.

bestPractices: Tie adoption to measurable business outcomes, named owners, funding, risk, and an operating model rather than a technology migration target alone.
Use enterprise-scale landing-zone principles but tailor implementation to organizational size, compliance, connectivity, and platform capabilities.
Automate subscription and application landing-zone vending, policy, identity, networking, budgets, observability, and workload onboarding as platform products.
Run Govern, Secure, and Manage continuously, and assess individual workloads with the Well-Architected Framework throughout their lifecycle.

interviewQuestions.question: How is CAF different from the Azure Well-Architected Framework?
interviewQuestions.answer: CAF guides organization-wide cloud adoption, platform readiness, governance, security, and management. WAF evaluates the design and operation of individual workloads across five quality pillars.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an Azure landing zone?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is a scalable, governed Azure environment and operating foundation covering identity, resource organization, subscriptions, networking, policy, security, management, and automation for workload onboarding.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are Govern, Secure, and Manage continuous?
interviewQuestions.answer: The estate, threats, regulations, costs, services, and workloads keep changing, so controls and operations must evolve throughout adoption rather than occur once at the end.

note: CAF is adaptable guidance, not a mandate to implement every enterprise control before the first workload can learn and deliver value.
tip: Map each CAF methodology to a concrete outcome, accountable team, evidence artifact, and next review date.
warning: A landing zone built without an adoption backlog and workload-team feedback can become an expensive platform with no successful consumers.
latestNote: New guide on cloud strategy, landing zones, adoption, and operations

name: AWS for .NET
shortDescription: Build and operate .NET workloads on AWS with the SDK, dependency injection, identity roles, managed compute, observability, and infrastructure as code.
overview: .NET applications can use AWS SDK clients and managed services across serverless, containers, web hosting, data, messaging, observability, and infrastructure automation.
detail: The AWS SDK for .NET provides service clients, credential and region resolution, retries, pagination, waiters, and dependency-injection integrations. Workloads can run on Lambda, App Runner, Elastic Beanstalk, ECS, EKS, EC2, or other compute selected from latency, scaling, control, networking, and cost needs. IAM roles and temporary credentials, Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry, resilient SDK configuration, infrastructure as code, and multi-account governance form the production foundation.

concepts.title: SDK clients
concepts.description: Service-specific clients expose AWS APIs with asynchronous calls, pagination, retries, region selection, credential resolution, and configurable HTTP behavior.

concepts.title: Compute choices
concepts.description: Lambda, App Runner, Elastic Beanstalk, ECS, EKS, and EC2 trade operational control, scale behavior, startup, portability, networking, and cost.

concepts.title: Identity and configuration
concepts.description: IAM roles, temporary credentials, least privilege, workload identity, Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, and KMS avoid embedded long-lived secrets.

concepts.title: Operations and delivery
concepts.description: CloudWatch, OpenTelemetry, health checks, deployment strategies, CDK or CloudFormation, tagging, budgets, and multi-account boundaries support production.

architecture.description: A .NET workload obtains temporary role credentials, calls AWS services through reusable SDK clients, and emits correlated telemetry while infrastructure and policy are deployed as code.

code.label: DocumentStore.cs
code.introduction: A reusable S3 client relies on the default AWS credential and region chain, allowing local profiles and deployed IAM roles without secrets in code.

bestPractices: Use IAM roles and temporary credentials with least-privilege policies; never embed access keys in source, images, logs, or application settings.
Reuse injected SDK clients, propagate cancellation, configure timeouts and retries deliberately, paginate results, and make retried side effects idempotent.
Choose compute and data services from workload requirements, team capabilities, recovery targets, networking, portability, and measured total cost.
Deploy accounts, networks, policy, alarms, dashboards, budgets, and application infrastructure as code with tags and tested rollback or roll-forward paths.

interviewQuestions.question: How does the AWS SDK for .NET find credentials?
interviewQuestions.answer: It follows a credential provider chain that can use explicit configuration, environment sources, local shared profiles, and workload role credentials. Production workloads should normally use temporary IAM role credentials.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose Lambda versus ECS for a .NET workload?
interviewQuestions.answer: Lambda suits event-driven, bounded executions with elastic demand and minimal host management. ECS suits longer-running services, custom containers, steady processes, and workloads needing more control over runtime and networking.

interviewQuestions.question: How should a .NET service handle AWS API throttling?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use SDK retry behavior with bounded backoff and jitter, respect cancellation and timeouts, reduce concurrency or batch requests, monitor quotas, and ensure retried mutations are idempotent.

note: The AWS SDK for .NET is independent of the compute host; the same application can call AWS services from AWS, on-premises, another cloud, or local development when identity and networking permit.
tip: Test locally with a named profile, but deploy with an IAM role and verify the exact permissions through an integration test in a nonproduction account.
warning: Do not rely on broad managed IAM policies for convenience in production; scope actions and resources and monitor denied access while refining least privilege.
latestNote: New guide on AWS SDK clients, compute, IAM, observability, and delivery

name: Azure Container Apps
shortDescription: Run containerised .NET workloads on serverless infrastructure with built-in scaling, service discovery, Dapr, and .NET Aspire integration.
overview: Azure Container Apps runs containers on fully managed infrastructure, handling scaling, service discovery, ingress, certificates, and revision traffic-splitting without exposing Kubernetes cluster management.
detail: Container Apps sit between Azure Functions and AKS in the control spectrum. The platform abstracts Kubernetes and KEDA, letting teams focus on container configuration, scaling rules, traffic policies, secrets, managed identity, and observability. Each app runs as one or more replicas inside a shared Container Apps Environment, scales to zero when idle, and routes traffic across revisions for safe deployments. Dapr integration adds distributed application runtime capabilities — state, pub/sub, service invocation, and bindings — as a sidecar. .NET Aspire can target Container Apps for cloud deployment directly from the AppHost manifest.

concepts.title: Environment boundary
concepts.description: A Container Apps environment provides shared networking, internal DNS, logs, certificates, Dapr configuration, and workload profiles; choose its ownership deliberately.

concepts.title: Apps, revisions, and replicas
concepts.description: An app is the stable endpoint, a revision is an immutable versioned snapshot, and replicas are runtime instances that scale for each active revision.

concepts.title: Ingress and discovery
concepts.description: Managed HTTP or TCP ingress, internal names, custom domains, certificates, and traffic weights expose only the endpoints the workload requires.

concepts.title: Probes and lifecycle
concepts.description: Startup, liveness, and readiness probes answer different questions; graceful shutdown must stop new work and finish bounded in-flight work.

concepts.title: KEDA scaling
concepts.description: HTTP concurrency and event scalers create replicas from demand; minimum, maximum, polling, cooldown, and authentication shape behavior.

concepts.title: Jobs and services
concepts.description: Continuously running apps serve traffic, while manual, scheduled, and event-driven jobs execute finite tasks with completion and retry semantics.

concepts.title: Identity and secrets
concepts.description: Managed identity supports Azure access, registry pulls, and some scaler authentication; secret references still require rotation and access boundaries.

concepts.title: Releases and observability
concepts.description: Single or multiple revision mode, labels, traffic splitting, logs, metrics, traces, and deployment gates enable controlled rollouts.

architecture.description: External traffic enters through managed ingress, routes to the active revision of a container app inside the environment, which scales with demand and calls dependencies via internal DNS or Dapr.

code.label: AppHost.cs
code.introduction: A .NET Aspire AppHost publishes the Orders API to Azure Container Apps using the Azure Developer CLI publisher — the same local orchestration model extends to the cloud.

bestPractices: Treat each environment as a workload and network boundary with explicit owners.
Use immutable image digests from a private registry and run as a non-root user.
Separate startup, liveness, and readiness probes and test graceful termination.
Keep one minimum replica when user-facing cold-start latency is unacceptable.
Set maximum replicas and concurrency from downstream capacity and quota evidence.
Use managed identity for registry, dependency, and scaler access where supported.
Promote revisions progressively and gate traffic on health and business telemetry.
Monitor replica, restart, ingress, scale, dependency, revision, quota, and cost signals.

interviewQuestions.question: What creates a new revision?
interviewQuestions.answer: Revision-scope changes such as container image, environment variables, resources, probes, and scale rules create an immutable revision; app-scope configuration can change without one.

interviewQuestions.question: Single versus multiple revision mode?
interviewQuestions.answer: Single mode moves traffic to the newest ready revision; multiple mode allows several active revisions and explicit percentage or label routing.

interviewQuestions.question: Why separate liveness and readiness?
interviewQuestions.answer: Liveness decides whether to restart a broken replica; readiness decides whether it should receive traffic, including during startup and graceful drain.

interviewQuestions.question: How does scale-to-zero affect HTTP APIs?
interviewQuestions.answer: The first request after idle waits for replica activation, so startup time becomes user latency and dependencies may receive synchronized reconnects.

interviewQuestions.question: When should a Container Apps job be used?
interviewQuestions.answer: For finite manual, scheduled, or event-triggered executions whose success is completion rather than a continuously addressable service.

interviewQuestions.question: How do managed identity scale rules help?
interviewQuestions.answer: Supported KEDA Azure scalers can authenticate without storing broker secrets, reducing rotation and leakage risk while preserving least privilege.

interviewQuestions.question: What remains your responsibility?
interviewQuestions.answer: Image security, application correctness, identity, data, scaling limits, traffic policy, network design, observability, recovery, cost, and incident response.

note: Container Apps abstracts Kubernetes but still runs on it — understanding replica behaviour, cold starts, revision limits, environment quotas, and networking boundaries matters for production design even though the cluster is not directly managed.
tip: Start with the .NET Aspire Azure Container Apps publisher so the same AppHost that describes your local topology generates the cloud deployment manifest — this keeps local and cloud parity without a separate infrastructure definition.
warning: Scale-to-zero means a first request after idle hits a cold start; measure startup time under real configuration and dependencies before committing to zero minimum replicas for latency-sensitive paths.
latestNote: Complete guide to environments, revisions, ingress, probes, scaling, identity, delivery, and operations
learningObjectives: Model environments, apps, revisions, replicas, jobs, ingress, and internal discovery.
Design probes, lifecycle, scaling, and cold-start behavior for .NET containers.
Operate identity, secrets, registries, networking, and Dapr safely.
Release with revision traffic splitting and measurable promotion gates.
Troubleshoot image, probe, DNS, scaling, quota, and dependency failures.
Decide when Container Apps, Functions, App Service, or AKS is the better compute boundary.
prerequisites: Containers, image registries, HTTP, DNS, and basic distributed systems.
ASP.NET Core health endpoints, configuration, logging, and graceful shutdown.
Azure identity, virtual networking, infrastructure as code, and observability basics.

use: Containerized services or jobs need managed ingress, revisions, internal discovery, and event-driven scaling.
The team wants Kubernetes-backed capabilities without owning cluster operations.
Supported networking, region, quota, workload profile, and protocol capabilities fit.
avoid: The workload requires Kubernetes APIs, custom operators, daemon sets, privileged containers, or cluster-level control.
A simple web app fits App Service better or a trigger-centric handler fits Functions better.
Unsupported protocol, hardware, tenancy, networking, or regional requirements are mandatory.

implementationIntroduction: The revision API is a .NET 10 service with revision metadata, separate probes, graceful readiness transitions, JSON logs, a non-root chiseled image, and Bicep for identity, HTTPS ingress, revision mode, probes, and bounded scaling.

implementationSteps.title: Define the environment
implementationSteps.description: Choose region, network, zone resilience, workload profile, logging destination, ownership, quotas, and isolation boundary.

implementationSteps.title: Build the container
implementationSteps.description: Publish a small non-root image, listen on the configured port, handle termination, scan dependencies, and identify it by digest.

implementationSteps.title: Expose correct health
implementationSteps.description: Implement startup, liveness, and readiness semantics that avoid restart loops and prevent traffic before dependencies are usable.

implementationSteps.title: Configure identity and network
implementationSteps.description: Assign minimal managed identity roles, private registry access, ingress exposure, DNS, egress, and private endpoints.

implementationSteps.title: Model scaling
implementationSteps.description: Select HTTP or event metrics, authenticate scalers, and set minimum, maximum, concurrency, cooldown, and queue behavior from tests.

implementationSteps.title: Create a revision
implementationSteps.description: Deploy immutable configuration and observe provisioning, probe, startup, dependency, and telemetry status before traffic.

implementationSteps.title: Shift traffic safely
implementationSteps.description: Use revision labels or percentages and promote based on latency, errors, saturation, and business results.

implementationSteps.title: Operate and recover
implementationSteps.description: Alert on replicas, restarts, revisions, quotas, and dependencies; rehearse rollback, regional recovery, and job replay.

testing.introduction: Test the application, image, deployment contract, platform lifecycle, and scaling with production-shaped dependencies.
items: Unit test health state, configuration, idempotency, and shutdown behavior.
Build and scan the exact image, run it as non-root, and smoke all endpoints.
Compile and lint infrastructure definitions and inspect deployment previews.
Verify ingress, identity, DNS, registry, secret, and private dependency paths.
Load test cold start, sustained traffic, scale out, scale in, and downstream saturation.
Deploy a canary revision, inject failures, validate traffic gates, rollback, and recovery.

security.introduction: The platform removes cluster management but application, image, identity, network, and supply-chain security remain workload responsibilities.
items: Use trusted minimal base images, digest pinning, scanning, signing, and non-root execution.
Use managed identity and minimal RBAC for dependencies, registry pulls, and scalers.
Keep secrets out of images, command lines, templates, logs, and plain environment values.
Expose only required ingress and design private DNS and controlled egress completely.
Separate application and deployment identities and audit control-plane changes.
Patch and redeploy immutable images promptly; never repair running replicas manually.

performance.introduction: Tune startup, replica resources, concurrency, and scale rules as one system with dependency limits.
items: Minimize image and startup work and reuse outbound clients and pools.
Measure cold and warm percentiles for each workload profile.
Set HTTP concurrency from per-replica testing, not platform defaults.
Cap replicas before downstream quotas and apply application backpressure.
Use event lag and age, not queue depth alone, to judge consumer health.
Track cost per request or job across idle, burst, and sustained profiles.

deployment.introduction: A safe release creates an observable immutable revision and moves traffic only after evidence.
items: Build once, scan and sign, push to a private registry, and deploy by digest.
Preview infrastructure and protect identity, network, scale, and deletion changes.
Wait for provisioning and probes before assigning traffic.
Canary with small traffic or a revision label and compare business and platform metrics.
Promote gradually, then deactivate old revisions according to rollback policy.
Retain deployment evidence and automate forward repair or tested traffic rollback.

troubleshooting.cause: The image, registry authorization, port, resource request, environment setting, or startup command is invalid.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect system logs and revision state, verify digest pull access, target port, architecture, resources, and command locally.

troubleshooting.cause: Liveness begins too early or the process crashes, exhausts memory, or blocks startup.
troubleshooting.fix: Separate startup and liveness probes, inspect exit reason and logs, right-size resources, and remove blocking initialization.

troubleshooting.symptom: App is healthy but receives no traffic
troubleshooting.cause: Readiness fails, ingress target port is wrong, traffic weight is zero, or the revision is inactive.
troubleshooting.fix: Check readiness from inside the replica, ingress configuration, active revision mode, labels, and weights.

troubleshooting.cause: The scaler cannot authenticate, metadata is wrong, or no supported event reaches it.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect scale rule status, identity role and scope, trigger metadata, event lag, min replicas, and platform metrics.

troubleshooting.cause: Replica and per-replica concurrency limits exceed downstream capacity.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower maximum replicas or concurrency, add backpressure and jitter, and coordinate dependency capacity.

troubleshooting.cause: Apps are in different environments or private DNS and network paths are incomplete.
troubleshooting.fix: Verify environment membership, internal FQDN, VNet DNS, routes, firewalls, and private endpoint records.

productionChecklist: Environment ownership, region, network, quotas, resilience, and logging are approved.
Image is minimal, scanned, signed, digest-pinned, and runs non-root.
Startup, liveness, readiness, termination, and health dependencies are tested.
Managed identity and least-privilege registry, scaler, and dependency roles are verified.
Ingress, certificates, DNS, private networking, egress, and secrets are controlled.
Minimum, maximum, concurrency, cooldown, and job retry settings come from load tests.
Revision canary, promotion, rollback, deactivation, and recovery are automated.
Alerts and budgets cover user outcomes, replicas, restarts, scaling, dependencies, quotas, and cost.
