name: Backend for Frontend
shortDescription: Give each frontend its own tailored API layer instead of forcing every client through one general-purpose API.
overview: A Backend for Frontend is a thin API layer built and owned for one specific client—web, mobile, or a partner integration—that aggregates and reshapes calls to backend services into exactly what that client needs.
detail: Instead of one general-purpose API serving every client's differing needs with optional fields and version branches, each frontend gets its own BFF: composing multiple backend calls into one response, hiding backend topology, and evolving independently of other clients' needs. The tradeoff is more services to own and keep consistent, so BFFs work best when client needs have genuinely diverged, not as a default for every project.

concepts.title: Client-owned aggregation
concepts.description: A BFF composes calls to multiple backend services into the single shaped response its one client actually needs.

concepts.title: Reduced client-side complexity
concepts.description: Moving aggregation, retries, and field shaping into the BFF keeps client code focused on presentation instead of backend orchestration.

concepts.title: Independent evolution
concepts.description: Each BFF can change its contract and pace of release without coordinating with unrelated frontends sharing the same backend.

concepts.title: Backend topology hiding
concepts.description: Clients depend on their BFF's contract, not on the internal service boundaries behind it, so backend services can be refactored without breaking clients.

architecture.description: A frontend calls its own BFF, which aggregates and reshapes calls to shared backend services into that client's specific response shape.

code.label: WebBffEndpoints.cs
code.introduction: A BFF endpoint composes two backend calls into the single shape the web client actually renders.

bestPractices: Create a new BFF only once a client's needs have genuinely diverged from others, not preemptively for every frontend.
Keep a BFF thin—composition and shaping, not business logic that belongs in the backend services it calls.
Own each BFF with the team that owns its frontend, so contract changes don't require cross-team coordination.
Apply the same resilience patterns—timeouts, retries, circuit breakers—to a BFF's outbound calls as any other service-to-service call.

interviewQuestions.question: How is a BFF different from an API gateway?
interviewQuestions.answer: A gateway is typically one shared entry point applying cross-cutting concerns like routing, auth, and rate limiting for many clients; a BFF is dedicated to one client, aggregating and shaping backend calls into that client's specific needs—the two are often used together, gateway in front of multiple BFFs.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does a BFF solve that a single shared API doesn't?
interviewQuestions.answer: A shared API serving very different clients accumulates optional fields, version branches, and client-specific logic to satisfy everyone; a BFF lets each client's API evolve and be shaped independently, avoiding that shared complexity.

interviewQuestions.question: What's the main cost of adopting the BFF pattern?
interviewQuestions.answer: More services to build, deploy, and keep consistent—logic like authorization or validation can end up duplicated across BFFs unless it's deliberately kept in shared backend services instead.

note: A BFF is scoped to one client's needs, not a second general-purpose API sitting in front of your services.
tip: Let the frontend team that owns the client also own its BFF; the pattern's main value is removing cross-team coordination from client-specific changes.
warning: Duplicating business rules—not just response shaping—across multiple BFFs recreates the consistency problems the pattern was meant to avoid.
latestNote: New guide on client-owned API aggregation

name: Terraform
shortDescription: Declare cloud infrastructure as versioned, reviewable code that can be planned before it's applied, across any provider.
overview: Terraform describes infrastructure—networks, databases, compute, permissions—as declarative configuration, then plans and applies the changes needed to make real infrastructure match that configuration.
detail: A provider maps Terraform's HCL configuration to versioned platform APIs, so one workflow can manage Azure, AWS, SaaS, and other systems. Terraform refreshes remote objects into protected state, builds a dependency graph, and computes a plan showing creates, updates, replacements, and destroys before any change is applied. Teams use typed variables, validation, modules, outputs, remote backends, locking, imports, and moved blocks to manage infrastructure throughout its lifecycle. Production practice also requires pinned providers, reviewed saved plans, short-lived identity, policy checks, drift ownership, secret-safe state, and recovery procedures.

concepts.title: Providers
concepts.description: A provider translates Terraform configuration into calls against a specific platform's API, letting one tool and workflow target multiple clouds.

concepts.title: State
concepts.description: Terraform records the real infrastructure it manages in a state file, using it to compute the difference between desired and actual on every run.

concepts.title: Plan and apply
concepts.description: Plan shows exactly what will be created, changed, or destroyed before anything happens; apply executes only that reviewed plan.

concepts.title: Modules
concepts.description: Reusable, parameterized configuration packages let teams share a tested infrastructure shape—like a standard app environment—instead of duplicating raw resources.

concepts.title: Resource graph
concepts.description: References between resources create a dependency graph that Terraform evaluates in parallel where safe and in order where required.

concepts.title: Lifecycle and drift
concepts.description: Refresh, import, moved blocks, lifecycle rules, and replacement semantics control how configuration converges with infrastructure that already exists.

concepts.title: Variables and outputs
concepts.description: Typed inputs, validation, locals, and non-sensitive outputs make configuration reusable without hiding important environment decisions.

concepts.title: Backends and locking
concepts.description: A remote backend protects shared state, coordinates locking, controls access, and provides recovery history for team workflows.

architecture.description: Configuration is planned against current state to compute a diff, then applied through the provider to create the real infrastructure.

code.label: main.tf
code.introduction: A module call provisions a standard app environment with parameters instead of duplicating the underlying resources per project.

bestPractices: Store state remotely with locking so two runs can't apply conflicting changes to the same infrastructure at once.
Always review a plan's output before applying it, especially destroy actions—treat plan as a required gate, not a formality.
Package repeated infrastructure shapes as modules with clear inputs and outputs instead of copy-pasting resource blocks.
Keep secrets out of state and configuration; reference them from a secrets manager instead of hardcoding values.
Pin Terraform and provider versions and commit the dependency lock file.
Use workload identity, least-privilege cloud roles, policy checks, and an audited apply pipeline.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Terraform state, and why does losing it matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: State is Terraform's record of the real infrastructure it manages, used to compute what's changed on every run; without it, Terraform has no way to know what already exists and can plan to recreate or orphan real resources.

interviewQuestions.question: Why review a Terraform plan before applying it?
interviewQuestions.answer: The plan shows exactly what will be created, changed, or destroyed as a result of a configuration change, catching unintended consequences—like a destroy triggered by a renamed resource—before they happen against real infrastructure.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem do Terraform modules solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: They let a team package a tested, parameterized shape of infrastructure—like a standard app environment—and reuse it across projects, instead of every project hand-writing and maintaining its own copy of similar resource blocks.

interviewQuestions.question: What is infrastructure drift?
interviewQuestions.answer: Drift is a difference between configuration, recorded state, and real provider state, often caused by manual changes or external automation; refresh and plan reveal its likely reconciliation.

interviewQuestions.question: When should terraform import be used?
interviewQuestions.answer: Import associates an existing remote object with a resource address so it can be brought under management after matching configuration is written and reviewed.

interviewQuestions.question: Why save a plan artifact?
interviewQuestions.answer: Applying the reviewed saved plan ensures the executed change is the same proposal reviewers approved, provided state and provider constraints remain valid.

interviewQuestions.question: How should Terraform state be protected?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use an encrypted remote backend, locking, version history, least-privilege access, audit logs, backups, and careful treatment because state can contain sensitive values.

note: Terraform's plan/apply split exists specifically so infrastructure changes can be reviewed like code changes, before they touch anything real.
tip: Run Terraform in CI with a required plan-review step on every pull request, the same way you'd require a code review.
warning: Manually changing infrastructure that Terraform manages, outside of Terraform, causes state drift that can lead to a later apply silently reverting or fighting your manual change.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with dedicated Azure web platform sample
learningObjectives: Explain providers, configuration, state, graph planning, and apply behavior.
Design protected remote-state and locking boundaries.
Create reusable typed modules without hiding important decisions.
Import, move, replace, and retire resources safely.
Secure provider identity, state, plans, variables, and outputs.
Operate Terraform through reviewed plans, policy gates, drift detection, and recovery.
prerequisites: Basic cloud resource, identity, networking, and CLI concepts.
Familiarity with Git review and environment promotion.
Terraform CLI and provider credentials for optional real plan exercises.

use: One workflow must manage infrastructure across multiple providers or platforms.
Teams need explicit state, plan review, reusable modules, and lifecycle control.
An ecosystem provider supports the required resources and maturity level.
avoid: The target is Azure-only and first-party Bicep coverage and support are the stronger fit.
A service-specific platform already owns provisioning and exposing raw infrastructure adds risk.
State ownership, identity, review, and recovery cannot be operated responsibly.

implementationIntroduction: The Terraform Azure Web Platform provisions a .NET 10 App Service baseline with validated environments, mandatory tags, observability, managed identity, HTTPS, health checks, and a local executable contract inspector.

implementationSteps.title: Define ownership
implementationSteps.description: Choose a state boundary whose resources share lifecycle, access, blast radius, and deployment cadence.

implementationSteps.title: Pin tooling
implementationSteps.description: Constrain Terraform and provider versions, initialize providers, and commit the generated dependency lock file.

implementationSteps.title: Configure the backend
implementationSteps.description: Use encrypted remote state with locking, version history, audit logs, least privilege, and tested recovery.

implementationSteps.title: Model typed inputs
implementationSteps.description: Use descriptions, types, validation, locals, and governance tags so invalid environments fail before planning.

implementationSteps.title: Compose resources and modules
implementationSteps.description: Express real references to build the dependency graph and keep modules cohesive with narrow contracts.

implementationSteps.title: Plan with evidence
implementationSteps.description: Format, validate, refresh, run policy and security checks, and publish a saved plan for review.

implementationSteps.title: Apply through automation
implementationSteps.description: Use short-lived identity, environment approval, concurrency control, the reviewed plan artifact, and retained logs.

implementationSteps.title: Operate lifecycle
implementationSteps.description: Detect drift, import existing objects, use moved blocks for refactoring, rehearse state recovery, and retire resources deliberately.

testing.introduction: Terraform evidence progresses from static configuration checks to plans and ephemeral deployment tests.
items: Run fmt and validate for every change.
Execute module contract and policy tests.
Inspect the full saved plan including replacements and destroys.
Test representative modules in an isolated subscription or account.
Verify outputs, identity, security posture, and observability after apply.
Exercise import, move, rollback, and state recovery procedures.

security.introduction: Configuration, state, plans, providers, and the apply identity are all supply-chain or control-plane assets.
items: Use workload identity and least-privilege provider roles.
Encrypt and tightly restrict remote state and plan artifacts.
Never assume sensitive variables prevent values from entering state.
Pin providers and modules and review their provenance.
Run static, policy, dependency, and cloud-posture checks.
Separate untrusted plan jobs from protected apply credentials.

performance.introduction: Fast predictable plans depend on sensible state boundaries and provider behavior.
items: Split state by lifecycle and blast radius rather than individual resource.
Avoid broad data-source queries and unnecessary cross-state reads.
Allow safe graph parallelism but respect provider throttling.
Cache providers in CI from the lock file.
Measure plan and apply duration and investigate unexpected growth.
Do not use targeted applies as a routine performance shortcut.

deployment.introduction: Promote reviewed configuration and saved-plan evidence through controlled environments.
items: Run speculative plans for pull requests without apply credentials.
Re-plan after merge against current protected state.
Require approval for destroy, replacement, privilege, and network exposure changes.
Serialize applies per state and retain deployment evidence.
Run post-apply security and workload smoke checks.
Prefer forward repair while retaining state-version and provider recovery procedures.

troubleshooting.symptom: State lock remains after a failed run.
troubleshooting.cause: The client exited without releasing the backend lock.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm no apply is active, inspect lock ownership, then use force-unlock with the exact lock ID.

troubleshooting.symptom: Plan wants to recreate an existing resource.
troubleshooting.cause: Its address, identifier, immutable property, or provider interpretation changed.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the replacement reason and use import or moved blocks only when ownership and identity are verified.

troubleshooting.cause: Out-of-band drift conflicts with configuration.
troubleshooting.fix: Decide the authoritative desired state, update configuration or revert drift, and restrict manual writes.

troubleshooting.symptom: A sensitive value appears in state.
troubleshooting.cause: Sensitive affects display, not provider persistence.
troubleshooting.fix: Rotate the value, restrict state, redesign the resource to reference a secret, and remove historical exposure safely.

troubleshooting.cause: Schema, defaults, normalization, or behavior changed.
troubleshooting.fix: Pin versions, read the upgrade guide, test in isolation, and upgrade in a dedicated reviewed change.

troubleshooting.symptom: Apply differs from the reviewed proposal.
troubleshooting.cause: A new plan was generated or state changed after review.
troubleshooting.fix: Apply the reviewed saved plan promptly or regenerate and require a new review.

productionChecklist: State boundary and ownership are explicit.
Remote state is encrypted, locked, versioned, audited, and recoverable.
Terraform, providers, and modules are pinned.
Inputs are typed and validated; outputs exclude credentials.
Plan, policy, security, and cost evidence gate apply.
Apply identity is short-lived and least privilege.
Import, move, drift, and deletion procedures are tested.
Every apply is serialized, observable, attributable, and recoverable.

name: Secrets Management
shortDescription: Keep credentials, keys, and connection strings out of source and configuration, with rotation and least-privilege access built in.
overview: Secrets management is about where credentials live, who and what can read them, and how they get replaced—not just picking a vault product to store them in.
detail: A secret checked into source control or placed in a distributable configuration file must be treated as compromised because Git history, forks, artifacts, backups, logs, telemetry, and developer machines outlive later deletion. The strongest strategy first removes secrets by using workload identity, managed identity, federation, certificates, or platform integration. Remaining passwords, keys, connection strings, and tokens belong in a dedicated store with identity-based access, least-privilege data-plane roles, environment isolation, audit logs, recovery protection, expiration, versioning, and rotation. Applications must retrieve only what they need, avoid copying values into logs or broad process state, cache for a bounded time, refresh without restart, support overlapping credential versions, fail closed when required material is unavailable, and expose metadata rather than values for diagnostics. Operations must cover creation, distribution, use, rotation, revocation, recovery, deletion, incident response, and ownership. A vault is not magic: an overprivileged workload, exported environment dump, unsafe exception, compromised build agent, or unredacted telemetry can still leak every value it can read.
learningObjectives: Classify secrets separately from ordinary configuration and public identifiers.
Eliminate credentials with workload identity or federation before deciding how to store them.
Design least-privilege vault, identity, network, audit, recovery, and environment boundaries.
Retrieve, cache, refresh, and redact secrets safely in .NET applications.
Design rotation with versions, overlap, rollout, verification, rollback, and revocation.
Respond correctly to repository, pipeline, log, host, or runtime secret exposure.
Test secret lifecycle behavior without embedding live credentials in the test suite.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core configuration and dependency injection or .NET console application structure.
Basic identity, role assignment, encryption, TLS, environment, and deployment concepts.
Awareness of Git history, CI/CD artifacts, logs, backups, and process environment exposure.
A .NET 10 SDK to run the dependency-free rotation sample.

use: Use workload identity or federation when a platform can issue short-lived credentials directly to the workload.
Use a managed vault for remaining application secrets that require controlled retrieval, audit, versioning, and rotation.
Use local user-secrets or an approved developer vault only for development values that never enter source.
Use certificates or asymmetric keys when verification can occur without sharing private material.
avoid: Do not store secrets in source, appsettings, container images, client applications, IaC state, pipeline arguments, or generated artifacts.
Do not put ordinary nonsecret configuration into a vault without a security reason.
Do not use one broad master credential or shared vault identity across unrelated workloads and environments.
Do not pin an unversioned secret forever in process memory when rotation is required.

concepts.title: Centralized storage and access control
concepts.description: A dedicated secrets store lets access be granted, audited, and revoked per identity, instead of secrets being copied into every environment's configuration.

concepts.title: Workload identity
concepts.description: Letting a compute resource authenticate to the secrets store using its platform identity removes the need for a bootstrap credential to fetch other credentials.

concepts.title: Rotation
concepts.description: Regularly replacing secrets, ideally automatically, limits how long a leaked or compromised credential remains valid.

concepts.title: Least privilege scoping
concepts.description: An application or service should only be able to read the specific secrets it needs, not every secret in a shared vault.

concepts.title: Secret elimination
concepts.description: Managed identity, workload federation, platform connectors, and asymmetric designs remove long-lived shared values and reduce rotation burden.

concepts.title: Versioning and overlap
concepts.description: New versions allow safe rollout while old and new credentials overlap until every consumer adopts the replacement and rollback risk passes.

concepts.title: Caching and refresh
concepts.description: A bounded cache reduces vault latency and throttling while a refresh policy prevents a running process from holding obsolete credentials indefinitely.

concepts.title: Detection and incident response
concepts.description: Secret scanning, vault audit logs, redaction, anomaly alerts, ownership, revocation, and recovery procedures limit exposure impact.

architecture.description: A workload obtains a short-lived platform identity, passes network and identity policy, retrieves only authorized current secret versions, uses a bounded in-process cache, and refreshes during controlled rotation while audit, scanning, alerting, recovery, and revocation cover the lifecycle.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated sample models the application-side lifecycle without a cloud dependency: versioned lookup, short-lived caching, rotation adoption without restart, deterministic time, redacted diagnostics, and failure when a required secret is absent.

implementationSteps.title: Inventory and classify
implementationSteps.description: Find credentials across code, configuration, repositories, pipelines, artifacts, hosts, and third parties; assign owners and consumers.

implementationSteps.title: Eliminate what you can
implementationSteps.description: Replace shared credentials with managed identity, federation, certificates, or service-native authorization.

implementationSteps.title: Create vault boundaries
implementationSteps.description: Separate environments and applications, configure least-privilege data access, private networking where needed, audit, soft delete, and purge protection.

implementationSteps.title: Integrate through identity
implementationSteps.description: Use the workload's platform credential and inject a narrow provider rather than distributing a bootstrap secret.

implementationSteps.title: Cache and redact
implementationSteps.description: Cache values briefly, keep them out of logs and exceptions, expose only version or age metadata, and clear unnecessary copies.

implementationSteps.title: Rotate safely
implementationSteps.description: Create a new version, overlap validity, refresh consumers, verify adoption, retain rollback briefly, then revoke the old value.

implementationSteps.title: Detect and respond
implementationSteps.description: Scan repositories and pipelines, alert on unusual reads, rotate immediately after exposure, investigate use, and document recovery.

code.label: SecretsSetup.cs
code.introduction: The application authenticates to the vault using its managed identity, with no credential stored in configuration to reach it.

testing.introduction: Tests should prove lifecycle behavior with synthetic values and fake providers, never real production credentials.
items: Use a provider abstraction and deterministic TimeProvider to test cache hit, expiry, refresh, missing value, cancellation, and vault failure.
Prove a new version is adopted without restart after the configured cache interval.
Assert exceptions, ToString, logs, traces, snapshots, and test failure output never contain secret values.
Integration-test identity and vault access in an isolated environment with least-privilege roles and disposable synthetic secrets.
Rehearse rotation overlap, rollback, revocation, deleted-value recovery, and compromised-credential response.

security.introduction: The vault, workload identity, runtime process, administrators, delivery system, and dependent service form one end-to-end secret boundary.
items: Prefer managed identity or federation and narrowly scope data-plane roles per application and environment.
Restrict network access, enable audit, soft delete, purge protection, and alerts for unusual reads or administrative changes.
Never emit values to source, configuration artifacts, command lines, logs, exceptions, traces, crash dumps, support bundles, or client responses.
Separate secret readers, writers, rotators, and administrators and use just-in-time privileged access.
Rotate immediately after suspected exposure and investigate usage; deleting a repository line is not remediation.

performance.introduction: Vault calls are remote and rate-limited, so safe caching improves reliability while overly long caching prevents rotation.
items: Cache with a bounded TTL based on rotation and revocation requirements and add jitter to large-fleet refresh.
Avoid loading entire vaults; request only the values required by the current workload.
Reuse supported clients, propagate cancellation, bound timeouts, and observe throttling without logging names that reveal sensitive architecture unnecessarily.
Use versionless lookup for current credentials when automatic adoption is intended and versioned identifiers where decrypting historic data requires stable material.
Do not place vault access on a hot per-record path when a safe process-level cache is sufficient.

deployment.introduction: Secret management succeeds only when infrastructure, identity, application refresh, dependent systems, and incident operations agree on the lifecycle.
items: Provision vault, identity, roles, network controls, diagnostics, recovery, expiration, and rotation policy through reviewed infrastructure as code.
Keep development, test, staging, and production stores and identities isolated.
Validate configuration contains only vault identifiers and nonsecret metadata, never resolved values.
Roll credentials through overlapping versions, monitor consumer adoption, and revoke the old value after verification.
Include secret scanning, dependency inventory, runtime identity smoke tests, rollback, and emergency rotation in release procedures.

troubleshooting.symptom: The workload cannot read a secret.
troubleshooting.cause: Identity selection, data-plane role, network policy, name mapping, disabled version, or environment configuration is wrong.
troubleshooting.fix: Verify the actual workload principal, narrow role assignment, network path, object state, and safe audit logs.

troubleshooting.symptom: A rotated credential is not adopted.
troubleshooting.cause: The application pinned a version or cached indefinitely.
troubleshooting.fix: Use deliberate versionless lookup, bounded refresh, adoption telemetry, and a rotation integration test.

troubleshooting.cause: The old credential was revoked before every consumer refreshed or the dependency lacked overlap.
troubleshooting.fix: Use two-version overlap, observe fleet adoption, retain rollback, and revoke only after verification.

troubleshooting.symptom: A secret appears in logs or CI.
troubleshooting.cause: Commands, configuration dumps, exception messages, test output, or telemetry captured the value.
troubleshooting.fix: Revoke and rotate immediately, remove and restrict artifacts, investigate access, and add centralized redaction and scanning.

troubleshooting.cause: Every instance refreshes all values simultaneously or retrieves per request.
troubleshooting.fix: Use narrow bounded caches, client reuse, jittered refresh, and capacity-aware rollout.

troubleshooting.cause: Recovery and purge controls or retention were not configured and tested.
troubleshooting.fix: Enable soft delete and purge protection where available and rehearse recovery with owned retention policy.

productionChecklist: Secrets are inventoried with owner, consumers, environment, purpose, expiry, rotation, and revocation procedure.
Long-lived credentials are eliminated through workload identity or federation wherever supported.
Vault data roles, administrative roles, networks, environments, audit, recovery, and purge controls are separated.
No values appear in source, images, IaC state, pipeline logs, arguments, telemetry, dumps, or client artifacts.
Applications retrieve only required values, cache briefly, redact diagnostics, and refresh without restart.
Rotation supports version overlap, adoption evidence, rollback, and old-value revocation.
Repository and pipeline secret scanning plus unusual-access alerts are enabled and owned.
Exposure, vault outage, throttling, deletion recovery, compromised identity, and emergency rotation runbooks are rehearsed.
bestPractices: Eliminate secrets with workload identity or federation before storing them.
Never commit a secret; rotate immediately after any suspected exposure.
Separate vaults or strong boundaries by application, region, and environment.
Grant each workload only the data operations and objects it needs.
Retrieve only required values and cache them for a bounded rotation-aware duration.
Redact values from logs, exceptions, telemetry, dumps, commands, and diagnostics.
Automate rotation with overlap, adoption verification, rollback, and revocation.
Enable scanning, audit, anomaly alerts, recovery protection, and owned incident runbooks.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is committing a secret to source control dangerous even if you delete it in the next commit?
interviewQuestions.answer: Git history retains every prior version by default, and the secret may already be in forks, backups, CI logs, or cached clones, so deleting it from the latest commit doesn't remove it from anywhere it's already been.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does workload identity solve for secrets management?
interviewQuestions.answer: Without it, an application needs some credential to authenticate to the secrets store in the first place, which just relocates the original problem; workload identity lets the platform vouch for the application's identity directly, removing that bootstrap credential entirely.

interviewQuestions.question: Why rotate secrets that haven't been confirmed as leaked?
interviewQuestions.answer: You can't always know a secret has leaked—rotation limits the value and window of a leak you don't yet know about, the same way changing a lock periodically doesn't require proof a key was copied.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between configuration and a secret?
interviewQuestions.answer: Configuration controls behavior and is not necessarily confidential; a secret grants access or proves identity and requires restricted storage, use, rotation, and incident handling.

interviewQuestions.question: How can an application adopt rotation without restart?
interviewQuestions.answer: Resolve the current version through a provider, cache it for a bounded time, refresh safely, support overlapping credentials, and observe which version is in use without logging the value.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does a vault not prevent every leak?
interviewQuestions.answer: Authorized workloads and administrators can retrieve values, and those values can still escape through logs, exceptions, dumps, process access, or overbroad permissions.

interviewQuestions.question: What should happen after a secret is committed to Git?
interviewQuestions.answer: Revoke and rotate it immediately, investigate where it propagated and whether it was used, restrict or remove exposed artifacts, then improve scanning and process controls.

note: Secrets management is as much about identity and access design as it is about which product stores the values.
tip: Design for rotation from day one—retrofitting a rotation-tolerant application after every secret is hardcoded at startup is much harder than building it in from the start.
warning: A single shared master credential granting broad access to a whole vault defeats much of the purpose of centralizing secrets in the first place.
latestNote: Gold-standard guide with a dedicated rotation and redaction sample

name: Infrastructure as Code (Bicep)
shortDescription: Define, version, and deploy Azure infrastructure declaratively using Bicep modules, parameter files, deployment stacks, and CI/CD pipelines.
overview: Bicep is Microsoft's domain-specific language for declaring Azure infrastructure as code — compiled to ARM templates, reviewed like application code, and deployed repeatably across environments.
detail: Bicep replaces raw ARM JSON with a clean declarative syntax, strong typing, native module support, and first-class IDE tooling. Infrastructure defined in Bicep is committed to source control, reviewed in pull requests, promoted through environments with parameter files, and deployed by CI/CD pipelines using the Azure CLI or Azure Developer CLI. Deployment stacks extend this model by tracking which resources a deployment owns and cleaning up orphaned resources when the stack is updated or deleted. For .NET teams, Bicep pairs naturally with the azd CLI that Aspire uses for cloud deployments.

concepts.title: Declarative resource definitions
concepts.description: A Bicep file describes the desired state of Azure resources — their type, SKU, location, properties, and dependencies. The platform reconciles current state to match the declaration on each deployment.

concepts.title: Modules
concepts.description: A module is a reusable Bicep file that accepts parameters and encapsulates one cohesive set of resources — a module for a Container App, a module for a Key Vault, a module for a SQL server — composable into larger deployments.

concepts.title: Parameter files and environments
concepts.description: Bicepparam files supply environment-specific values — SKUs, capacities, feature flags, connection strings — keeping the template logic environment-neutral and the differences version-controlled and reviewable.

concepts.title: Deployment stacks
concepts.description: A deployment stack tracks all resources deployed as a unit and applies a deny-assignment to prevent out-of-band changes. Updating or deleting the stack reconciles or removes managed resources automatically.

concepts.title: Scopes and symbolic dependencies
concepts.description: Target scope, existing resources, symbolic names, and module outputs express ownership and ordering without manually writing dependsOn arrays.

concepts.title: Type system and diagnostics
concepts.description: Resource schemas, decorators, compile-time validation, lint rules, and editor completion catch many deployment mistakes before Azure is contacted.

concepts.title: Registries and versioning
concepts.description: Private module registries and template specs distribute approved modules with immutable versions across teams and subscriptions.

concepts.title: What-if and deployment history
concepts.description: What-if previews control-plane changes while ARM deployment records provide operation status, correlation, and audit evidence.

architecture.description: Bicep source is compiled and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline, promoting one validated template with environment-specific parameters from dev through staging to production.

code.label: container-app.bicep
code.introduction: A focused Bicep module deploys a Container App with managed identity, Key Vault secret reference, and environment-linked configuration — accepting only the values that change per environment.

bestPractices: Treat Bicep files as production code — review them in pull requests, lint with the Bicep linter, and enforce no-hardcoded-secrets and explicit API versions as CI checks.
Use modules to encapsulate cohesive resource groups — a Container App module, a networking module — and compose them in a main.bicep rather than putting everything in one large file.
Separate environment-specific values into Bicepparam files and keep template logic environment-neutral so the same compiled template is promoted from dev to prod without modification.
Run what-if deployments in CI before applying to staging or production so reviewers can see exactly which resource properties will change before approving the pipeline run.
Pin module versions and API versions, and update them through reviewed compatibility tests.
Use workload identity with least-privilege deployment roles and keep secrets out of source, outputs, and logs.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an ARM template and a Bicep file?
interviewQuestions.answer: A Bicep file is a higher-level declarative language that compiles to an ARM JSON template. Bicep provides cleaner syntax, type safety, native modules, string interpolation, conditional expressions, and IDE tooling, while ARM JSON is verbose and error-prone to write by hand. The compiled output is identical — Bicep is a transparent abstraction over ARM.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a Bicep deployment stack and when would you use it?
interviewQuestions.answer: A deployment stack tracks all resources deployed as a unit and can apply deny-assignments to prevent out-of-band changes to managed resources. When the stack is updated, resources removed from the template can be detached, deleted, or left in place according to the configured cleanup policy. It is useful when you want the infrastructure definition to be the authoritative source and prevent drift from manual portal changes.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you pass secrets into a Bicep deployment without hardcoding them?
interviewQuestions.answer: Reference secrets from Azure Key Vault using a Bicepparam file with a getSecret() call — this injects the secret value at deployment time from Key Vault without it appearing in source control, pipeline logs, or the compiled template. The deployment identity needs Key Vault Secrets User access on the vault.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Bicep determine deployment order?
interviewQuestions.answer: Symbolic resource references and module outputs create implicit dependencies; use explicit dependsOn only when no data reference expresses the real ordering.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an existing resource in Bicep?
interviewQuestions.answer: The existing keyword references a resource managed elsewhere without redeploying it, allowing modules to read identifiers and properties at the correct scope.

interviewQuestions.question: How should reusable Bicep modules be distributed?
interviewQuestions.answer: Publish versioned modules to a private Bicep registry or template specs, document contracts, test compiled output, and upgrade consumers deliberately.

interviewQuestions.question: What can make what-if incomplete?
interviewQuestions.answer: Runtime values, provider behavior, policy, permissions, quota, extension resources, and unsupported change analysis can produce noise or unknown results, so what-if is evidence rather than a guarantee.

note: Bicep defines desired infrastructure state — it does not replace application configuration, secrets management, identity assignment, or monitoring setup, all of which need their own deliberate design.

name: Health Checks
shortDescription: Expose meaningful liveness, readiness, and startup signals from .NET applications so orchestrators, load balancers, and dashboards can act on real dependency health.
overview: Health checks expose signals that tell orchestrators, load balancers, and monitoring systems whether an application is alive, ready to serve traffic, and has access to its dependencies.
detail: Health endpoints are control-plane contracts, not generic diagnostics. Liveness answers whether the process is irrecoverably stuck and should restart; it must not fail merely because a dependency is unavailable. Readiness answers whether this instance should receive new traffic and may include only dependencies required for serving that traffic. Startup protects slow initialization from premature liveness failures. ASP.NET Core registers IHealthCheck implementations and uses tags and predicates to expose separate endpoints. Checks need short cancellation-aware timeouts, bounded concurrency, stable sanitized output, and failure status chosen from operational consequences. Cache expensive results where appropriate, secure detailed dashboards, and test probe timings against deployment grace periods. A misdesigned probe can create restart loops or synchronized dependency load during the incident it was meant to diagnose.

concepts.title: Liveness
concepts.description: A lightweight process signal whose failure asks the orchestrator to restart this instance.

concepts.title: Readiness
concepts.description: A traffic-admission signal that reflects whether the instance can serve its required workload.

concepts.title: Startup
concepts.description: An initialization gate that delays normal liveness and readiness evaluation for slow-starting applications.

concepts.title: IHealthCheck
concepts.description: A cancellation-aware component reports Healthy, Degraded, or Unhealthy plus controlled diagnostic data.

concepts.title: Tags and predicates
concepts.description: Registration tags let separate endpoints select only the checks appropriate for each consumer.

concepts.title: Dependency criticality
concepts.description: Required and optional dependencies map to different aggregate statuses and routing consequences.

concepts.title: Probe budgets
concepts.description: Timeout, period, and failure threshold together define how quickly infrastructure reacts.

concepts.title: Operational output
concepts.description: Machine-readable status supports automation while detailed diagnostics remain protected and sanitized.

architecture.description: Kubernetes probes call dedicated health endpoints filtered by tag; the readiness endpoint checks real dependencies while the liveness endpoint stays lightweight, and the UI dashboard polls all endpoints for operator visibility.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: Checks are registered with tags, exposed on separate endpoints filtered by tag, and a custom database check demonstrates how to surface a real dependency result with diagnostic data.

bestPractices: Separate probe semantics.
Keep liveness local.
Tag checks by consumer.
Classify dependency criticality.
Honor cancellation.
Sanitize public output.
Bound probe cost.
Rehearse deployment transitions.

interviewQuestions.question: Liveness versus readiness?
interviewQuestions.answer: Liveness decides restart; readiness decides whether this instance receives traffic.

interviewQuestions.question: Why not put database checks in liveness?
interviewQuestions.answer: A shared outage would restart every healthy process and can worsen recovery.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a startup probe for?
interviewQuestions.answer: It grants initialization time before normal liveness and readiness thresholds apply.

interviewQuestions.question: How do tags help?
interviewQuestions.answer: They let endpoints select different registered checks for different consumers.

interviewQuestions.question: When should a check return Degraded?
interviewQuestions.answer: When an optional capability is impaired but core traffic can still be served.

interviewQuestions.question: Why must checks honor cancellation?
interviewQuestions.answer: Probe infrastructure has a deadline and abandoned dependency calls consume resources.

interviewQuestions.question: Should health checks repair systems?
interviewQuestions.answer: No; checks should observe and report, while controlled operators perform remediation.

note: A health check that always returns Healthy is worse than no health check — it builds false confidence. Check the actual dependency, return meaningful status, and include data that helps an on-call engineer act without additional investigation.
tip: Add a dead-letter message count check to your Service Bus or RabbitMQ health check — a rising dead-letter count is one of the earliest signals of a processing problem and is nearly free to surface from the broker's management API.
warning: Health check endpoints should never require authentication from the orchestrator — Kubernetes and load balancers call them without credentials — but restrict them from the public internet using network policy or path-based ingress rules.

name: Orleans
shortDescription: Model distributed state and behavior as virtual actors that the runtime activates, places, and recovers automatically.
overview: Orleans lets you write distributed systems as single-threaded objects called grains, while the runtime handles where each grain runs, how it's activated on demand, and how it recovers after a failure.
detail: A grain is addressed by stable identity rather than location. Orleans activates it on a silo when called, routes later calls to that activation, deactivates idle activations, and recreates them after loss. Its turn-based execution simplifies ownership of mutable entity state, but distributed calls can still fail, duplicate work, interleave when reentrancy is enabled, and lose unpersisted activation state. Production design therefore includes clustering, persistence, serializers, timeouts, idempotency, reminders, placement, telemetry, upgrades, and recovery.
learningObjectives: Recognize domains that fit virtual actors and stable single-owner identities.
Define grain contracts, keys, serialized messages, implementations, and client calls.
Reason about activation lifecycle, turn-based execution, reentrancy, and call cycles.
Choose clustering, membership, placement, gateway, and silo configuration for each environment.
Persist recoverable state with provider-aware consistency and schema evolution.
Use timers, reminders, streams, and observers according to durability and delivery requirements.
Test grains, multi-silo behavior, failure, recovery, serialization, and rolling upgrades.
Secure, observe, scale, deploy, and operate Orleans clusters in production.
prerequisites: C# async programming, dependency injection, hosted services, and serialization.
Distributed-system basics: partial failure, retries, idempotency, partitioning, and eventual consistency.

use: Use Orleans for large numbers of addressable entities with clear single-owner state and behavior.
Use it for devices, accounts, carts, games, sessions, workflows, or tenants that map naturally to stable keys.
Use reminders when work must survive activation loss and streams when event flows fit actor processing.
Use stateless workers or placement strategies when work is computational rather than entity-state ownership.
avoid: Do not model every repository row or stateless request as a grain.
Do not use grains as a general analytical query store or hide unbounded collections inside one hot actor.
Do not depend on in-memory fields when state must survive deactivation or silo loss.
Do not enable reentrancy or build cyclic grain call graphs without explicit interleaving and deadlock analysis.
tradeoffs: Virtual actors remove manual activation and location code while requiring the Orleans runtime, clustering, and provider operations.
Turn-based execution simplifies local state but hot identities serialize throughput and can become bottlenecks.
Persistent grain state improves recovery while adding provider latency, concurrency, schema, and failure considerations.
Transparent routing simplifies clients, but network calls still need timeouts, idempotency, compatibility, and observability.

concepts.title: Grains
concepts.description: A grain is a single-threaded, addressable unit of distributed state and behavior, identified by a stable key rather than a physical location.

concepts.title: Virtual actors
concepts.description: Grains always logically exist; the runtime activates them on demand and deactivates them when idle, so callers never manage a grain's lifecycle directly.

concepts.title: Silos and placement
concepts.description: A cluster of silos hosts grains; Orleans decides where to activate each grain and can reactivate it elsewhere automatically if a silo fails.

concepts.title: Turn-based execution
concepts.description: A grain normally processes one turn at a time; awaits and reentrancy rules determine when other calls can interleave.

concepts.title: Persistence
concepts.description: Storage providers recover selected grain state across activation loss; writes, versioning, concurrency, and provider failure remain application concerns.

concepts.title: Timers and reminders
concepts.description: Timers are activation-scoped scheduling; reminders are durable registrations that can reactivate a grain after failure or idleness.

concepts.title: Streams
concepts.description: Orleans streams connect producers and grain consumers with provider-specific delivery, ordering, persistence, and replay behavior.

concepts.title: Contracts and serialization
concepts.description: Version-tolerant grain interfaces and generated serializers allow clients and silos from compatible versions to coexist during upgrades.

architecture.description: A client calls a grain by its identity; the runtime activates it on an available silo, and that grain processes messages one at a time, persisting state as needed.

code.label: OrderGrain.cs
code.introduction: A grain interface and implementation define addressable, single-threaded state; Orleans handles activation and placement.

implementationSteps: Identify domain entities with stable keys, cohesive behavior, single-writer ownership, and enough activity to justify an actor boundary.
Define small asynchronous grain interfaces and version-tolerant serialized contracts before choosing implementations or providers.
Implement grain turns without blocking threads, unbounded work, accidental reentrancy, or long cyclic call chains.
Configure localhost clustering for development and a shared membership, gateway, and clustering provider for production.
Choose persistent state, timers, reminders, streams, and stateless workers according to durability and delivery semantics.
Add workload identity, provider access, call filters, validation, timeouts, telemetry, health, dashboards, and runbooks.
Test multi-silo placement and failure, then deploy compatible mixed versions with graceful silo shutdown and verified recovery.

testing.introduction: Test domain behavior quickly, then prove the runtime semantics that only appear with real activations, silos, storage, and failure.
items: Unit-test pure policies extracted from grains, including validation, state transitions, idempotency, and message compatibility.
Use the Orleans test cluster to call real grains through IGrainFactory and reset state between tests.
Run multi-silo tests for placement, concurrent callers, activation loss, silo shutdown, and recovery from persisted state.
Verify serializers and contracts across old and new versions used during rolling deployment.
Exercise storage outage, slow calls, duplicate commands, reminder recovery, stream redelivery, and cancellation.
Load-test hot keys, activation count, memory, storage calls, queueing, latency percentiles, and cluster rebalance.

security.introduction: Orleans simplifies location and lifecycle, not trust; protect gateways, APIs, providers, contracts, and administrative surfaces independently.
items: Authenticate external callers at the application edge and authorize grain operations using trusted tenant and subject context.
Restrict silo and gateway networking, use encrypted transport where required, and never expose cluster internals directly to untrusted clients.
Give cluster identities least-privilege access to membership, grain storage, reminders, streams, secrets, and telemetry.
Validate grain keys, arguments, collection sizes, payload types, and tenant ownership before allocating work or state.
Treat grain call filters and serializers as security-sensitive extension points; pin and audit packages and generated contracts.
Redact state and identifiers in logs, encrypt sensitive persisted state, rotate credentials, and audit operator changes.

performance.introduction: Scale across identities while detecting hot grains, slow turns, excess activation churn, and provider bottlenecks.
items: Choose keys that distribute naturally; split or redesign identities that concentrate unrelated work in one grain.
Keep turns short, asynchronous, bounded, and free of blocking I/O or CPU-heavy loops.
Batch persistence deliberately, but define acceptable state-loss and consistency behavior before reducing writes.
Avoid chatty grain call chains; colocate cohesive behavior, use fan-out carefully, and measure serialization overhead.
Track activation count, working-set memory, turn queue time, call latency, timeouts, rejects, storage latency, and silo load.
Capacity-test rebalancing and failure because surviving silos must absorb activations and replay without collapse.

deployment.introduction: Deploy Orleans as a coordinated cluster while keeping application contracts and state compatible across mixed silo versions.
items: Provision a shared production membership provider, durable grain storage where needed, reminder and stream providers, identity, networking, and telemetry with IaC.
Use stable cluster and service IDs per environment and prevent accidental cross-environment membership.
Ship additive interfaces, serializers, and state schema changes before removing fields or methods.
Roll silos gradually with readiness, graceful shutdown, activation migration, capacity headroom, and rollback criteria.
Back up and restore durable providers, test regional or zone failure, and document how reminders, streams, and clients recover.
Monitor cluster membership, silo restarts, activation churn, provider errors, hot grains, latency, and version distribution throughout release.

troubleshooting.cause: No gateway is reachable, cluster and service IDs differ, membership is unhealthy, or network rules block discovery.
troubleshooting.fix: Compare client and silo clustering configuration, inspect membership, gateway endpoints, DNS, identity, ports, and cluster logs.

troubleshooting.cause: The grain has a long or blocked turn, a call cycle, a slow dependency, a hot identity, or a failed silo is being detected.
troubleshooting.fix: Trace the call chain, inspect turn queue and silo load, remove blocking work, break cycles, bound dependencies, and review placement.

troubleshooting.cause: The grain used activation memory, wrote to the wrong provider, failed before WriteStateAsync completed, or storage configuration differs.
troubleshooting.fix: Use the intended persistent state provider, verify write success and keys, test reactivation, and inspect provider access and errors.

troubleshooting.symptom: A reminder or stream handler runs twice
troubleshooting.cause: Delivery is retried after failure or ownership changes and the handler is not idempotent.
troubleshooting.fix: Use stable operation identity, store completion with the business effect, and test redelivery and recovery semantics.

troubleshooting.symptom: One grain becomes a throughput bottleneck
troubleshooting.cause: Its key owns too much unrelated state or all callers serialize through one activation.
troubleshooting.fix: Measure queue time, partition the domain by stable child keys, move stateless work out, or redesign aggregation consistency.

troubleshooting.cause: Grain contracts, serializer field IDs, or state types changed incompatibly while versions coexist.
troubleshooting.fix: Restore compatibility, use additive contracts and stable field IDs, migrate state deliberately, and test the mixed-version window.

productionChecklist: Grain candidates have stable keys, cohesive behavior, bounded state, and a documented reason for actor ownership.
Interfaces, serializer field IDs, state schemas, reminders, streams, and deprecation rules are version-compatible.
Production cluster membership, gateways, cluster and service IDs, placement, storage, reminders, and stream providers are configured and tested.
External authorization, workload identity, least privilege, network restrictions, encryption, validation, redaction, and audits are enforced.
Grain turns are async, bounded, nonblocking, cycle-aware, and explicit about reentrancy and idempotency.
Metrics, traces, logs, health, membership, provider telemetry, hot-grain detection, dashboards, alerts, and runbooks are operational.
Multi-silo load, failure, recovery, provider outage, duplicate delivery, rolling upgrade, backup, and restore tests pass.
Deployments preserve capacity headroom, compatibility, graceful shutdown, rollback, and disaster-recovery objectives.
bestPractices: Keep grain calls single-purpose and short-lived; a grain is a unit of state and behavior, not a place for long synchronous blocking work.
Persist only the state a grain actually needs to recover, and choose a storage provider that matches your durability requirements.
Design grain identities deliberately—they determine how work and state are partitioned across the cluster.
Avoid grain-to-grain call chains that form cycles; they can deadlock or time out under turn-based execution.
Treat every grain call as a fallible distributed call and make retryable operations idempotent.
Use durable reminders only when scheduling must survive activation loss; use timers for activation-local work.
Keep serializer field IDs stable and evolve contracts additively across rolling upgrades.
Observe hot identities and provider latency before adding silos or changing placement.

interviewQuestions.question: What does 'virtual actor' mean in Orleans, and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: A grain logically always exists at its identity, whether or not it's currently activated in memory; callers never create or destroy it explicitly, and the runtime transparently activates, deactivates, and relocates it, which removes a whole class of lifecycle and placement code the application would otherwise have to write.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Orleans avoid the need for locks inside a grain?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each grain processes incoming calls one at a time, single-threaded, so there's never concurrent access to a grain's own state from within—concurrency exists between grains, not within one.

interviewQuestions.question: What happens to a grain's in-memory state if the silo hosting it fails?
interviewQuestions.answer: The in-memory activation is lost, but if the grain persists its state through a storage provider, Orleans can reactivate it—with that persisted state restored—on another silo when the next call arrives.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an Orleans timer and reminder?
interviewQuestions.answer: A timer belongs to the current activation and disappears with it. A reminder is a durable registration that can trigger future work and reactivate the grain.

interviewQuestions.question: Can a grain process more than one call at a time?
interviewQuestions.answer: Normally it executes one turn at a time. Reentrancy and interleaving controls can allow other calls during awaits, so invariants must be reviewed before enabling them.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you scale a hot grain?
interviewQuestions.answer: First reduce or bound its work. If one identity owns too much state, partition the domain into stable child grains or move stateless computation out; adding silos alone does not parallelize one single-activation key.

note: Orleans trades explicit distributed-systems plumbing for a programming model where distribution is mostly the runtime's problem, not the application's.
tip: Start by modeling your domain's natural single-owner entities—one order, one device, one session—as grains; that mapping is usually where Orleans fits most naturally.
warning: A grain is not a substitute for a database; treat its persisted state as what that one entity needs to recover, not as your system's queryable source of truth.

name: Event Sourcing
shortDescription: Store state as an immutable sequence of domain events and derive current state by replaying them.
overview: Event Sourcing persists the history of what happened to a domain object rather than just its current state, making every change first-class and queryable.
detail: Instead of storing the current row in a database table, an event-sourced system appends a new immutable event every time something meaningful happens to an aggregate. Current state is derived by replaying those events in order. This gives a complete audit trail for free, enables temporal queries, supports event replay into new projections, and makes debugging production incidents far easier. The trade-offs are query complexity, event versioning discipline, and the need for snapshot strategies when event streams grow long.

concepts.title: Event store
concepts.description: An append-only log that persists domain events for each aggregate stream. Events are never updated or deleted — only new events are written.

concepts.title: Aggregate reconstitution
concepts.description: An aggregate is loaded by reading its event stream and applying each event in order, rebuilding current state from history rather than from a snapshot column.

concepts.title: Projections and read models
concepts.description: Read models are built by subscribing to the event stream and projecting events into query-optimised shapes — separate from the write model and rebuildable at any time.

concepts.title: Snapshots
concepts.description: When an aggregate stream grows long, a snapshot captures state at a checkpoint so reconstitution loads the snapshot plus only the events after it.

architecture.description: Commands produce domain events appended to an event store; projections subscribe to the store and populate read models that queries use.

code.label: Order.cs
code.introduction: The aggregate applies events to change its own state; the command handler appends those events to the store rather than saving a mutated entity.

bestPractices: Name events in past tense after meaningful business facts — OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed — not technical operations like OrderUpdated.
Treat event schemas as public contracts; use upcasting or versioned event types to handle schema evolution without rewriting history.
Introduce snapshots only when reconstitution is measurably slow — start without them and add them at a measured stream length threshold.
Keep projections idempotent and rebuildable so a new read model can be populated by replaying the full event history at any time.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the key difference between event sourcing and storing domain events alongside a state record?
interviewQuestions.answer: Event sourcing makes the event stream the source of truth — there is no separate state column to keep in sync. Current state is always derived by replaying events. Storing events alongside a state record is an audit log, not event sourcing, because the state record can diverge from the events.

interviewQuestions.question: How does event sourcing relate to CQRS?
interviewQuestions.answer: They are complementary but independent. CQRS separates read and write models; event sourcing is a write-side persistence strategy. Together, the event store is the authoritative write side and projections populate the read side, but you can use either pattern without the other.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the main challenge of event versioning and how do you handle it?
interviewQuestions.answer: Events are immutable, so when a schema needs to change, old events in the store still use the old shape. Upcasting transforms old events to the current schema during loading so the aggregate always sees a consistent version, without rewriting the store.

note: Event sourcing solves the audit and temporal query problem well, but adds complexity around versioning, projection rebuilds, and eventually consistent reads — apply it where that trade-off is genuinely worth making.
tip: Use Marten with PostgreSQL as an event store for a pragmatic .NET start — it gives you append-only streams, snapshots, projections, and async subscriptions without running a separate event store infrastructure.
warning: Do not use event sourcing as a default persistence strategy for every aggregate; apply it where auditability, temporal queries, or event replay provide concrete business value that justifies the operational cost.
