name: Redis & Distributed Caching
shortDescription: Speed up .NET applications and reduce database load with Redis for distributed caching, pub/sub, rate limiting, and distributed locks.
overview: Redis is an in-memory data structure store used in .NET applications for distributed caching, session storage, pub/sub messaging, rate limiting, and distributed coordination.
detail: A process-local cache is fastest but each application instance holds different state and loses it on restart. A Redis-backed distributed cache gives nodes a shared L2 store, while .NET HybridCache can add a local L1, serialization, and same-process stampede protection behind one API. Cache-aside reads the cache, loads the authoritative source on a miss, and stores a bounded value with explicit expiration; writes must choose invalidate, update, versioned keys, or event-driven invalidation according to the accepted consistency window. Production design defines ownership, key namespace and tenant scope, TTL and jitter, negative caching, payload limits, hot-key behavior, eviction policy, memory headroom, connection reuse, failure fallback, observability, encryption, authentication, network isolation, and regional topology. Cache data is disposable acceleration rather than the only system of record. Redis pub/sub is not durable messaging, distributed locking has lease and fencing hazards, and sharing one instance across cache, sessions, rate limits, backplanes, and coordination couples failure and eviction blast radius. Managed Redis products, clustering, replicas, and persistence still require workload-specific recovery and capacity tests.
learningObjectives: Choose process, distributed, and hybrid cache layers from topology and consistency needs.
Implement cache-aside with bounded values, versioned tenant-aware keys, expiration, and invalidation.
Prevent stampedes and hot-key overload while preserving source-of-truth fallback.
Configure Redis connections, memory, eviction, security, high availability, and observability.
Distinguish caching, output caching, sessions, pub/sub, streams, counters, and locks.
Test hit, miss, concurrency, invalidation, staleness, outage, and multi-instance behavior.
prerequisites: ASP.NET Core dependency injection, JSON serialization, async data access, and distributed systems basics.
Expiration, consistency, replication, memory limits, and network security concepts.
A .NET 10 SDK; Redis is optional for Development but required for a production-shaped run.

use: Use HybridCache when L1 plus distributed L2 and same-process stampede protection fit the workload.
Use Redis for shared low-latency disposable data across multiple instances.
Use output caching for safe repeatable HTTP responses with explicit vary and invalidation policy.
avoid: Do not cache low-reuse, unbounded, sensitive, or correctness-critical data without a precise policy.
Do not make Redis the only durable record for business state.
Do not use pub/sub where offline consumers, replay, acknowledgement, or dead-lettering is required.
Do not treat a time-limited distributed lock as proof that stale holders cannot write; use fencing or a stronger consistency design.

concepts.title: Cache-aside pattern
concepts.description: The application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads from the source of truth, populates the cache with a TTL, and returns the value. Eviction and expiry keep the cache from growing unbounded.

concepts.title: IDistributedCache and output caching
concepts.description: IDistributedCache is the ASP.NET Core abstraction for distributed string or byte caches. Output caching middleware caches full HTTP responses at the framework level with Redis as the backing store.

concepts.title: Pub/sub and streams
concepts.description: Redis pub/sub broadcasts messages to all subscribers on a channel, powering SignalR backplanes and lightweight event fan-out. Redis Streams provide a durable, consumer-group-aware alternative.

concepts.title: Distributed locks and rate limiting
concepts.description: The Redlock algorithm uses atomic SET NX EX commands to acquire time-bounded locks across processes. Sliding window and token bucket counters built on INCR and EXPIRE enable per-key rate limiting without a dedicated service.

concepts.title: Hybrid L1 and L2
concepts.description: HybridCache combines fast per-process memory with an optional shared distributed cache and coalesces concurrent misses in one process.

concepts.title: Invalidation and versioning
concepts.description: Remove, update, tag, event, and versioned-key strategies trade write complexity, stale windows, and multi-node coherence.

concepts.title: Memory and eviction
concepts.description: Maximum memory, eviction policy, payload size, TTL distribution, hot keys, and headroom determine behavior under pressure.

concepts.title: Failure semantics
concepts.description: Timeouts, circuit behavior, stale serving, source fallback, and recovery load define whether cache outage becomes application outage.

architecture.description: Application instances share one Redis cluster; cache hits return data without touching the database, while pub/sub channels and lock keys coordinate distributed behaviour across all nodes.

implementationIntroduction: The dedicated product API configures Redis as HybridCache L2 when a connection string exists and a clearly labeled process-local provider only in Development or Testing. It applies bounded payloads, versioned keys, expiration, same-process miss coalescing, explicit invalidation after writes, and tests source-read counts to prove behavior.

implementationSteps.title: Define the cache contract
implementationSteps.description: Record source of truth, consumers, consistency window, miss behavior, outage behavior, and ownership.

implementationSteps.title: Design keys and values
implementationSteps.description: Namespace by environment, domain, version, tenant, and stable identifier and bound serialized payload size.

implementationSteps.title: Configure the provider
implementationSteps.description: Reuse Redis connections, protect credentials, set instance namespace, topology, timeouts, and network access.

implementationSteps.title: Implement cache-aside
implementationSteps.description: Use HybridCache GetOrCreateAsync with cancellation and a source loader that remains correct on misses.

implementationSteps.title: Control freshness
implementationSteps.description: Set L1 and L2 expiration, jitter or refresh policy, negative caching, and explicit write invalidation.

implementationSteps.title: Test failure and concurrency
implementationSteps.description: Prove hit, miss, stampede, invalidation, stale window, corrupt value, timeout, outage, and recovery behavior.

implementationSteps.title: Operate capacity
implementationSteps.description: Monitor hit ratio, latency, errors, connections, memory, eviction, hot keys, source fallback, and recovery load.

testing.introduction: Caching tests assert source-of-truth calls and concurrency, not merely returned values.
items: Count source reads to prove a second request is a cache hit.
Issue concurrent same-key misses and prove they are coalesced as designed.
Mutate the source and prove invalidation or versioning returns the new value.
Test missing, negative-cached, oversized, corrupt, and serialization-incompatible values.
Inject Redis timeout or outage and verify the documented fallback and recovery-load behavior.
Run multiple app instances against Redis to verify shared L2 and cross-node invalidation assumptions.

security.introduction: Redis contains application data and coordination state and must be treated as a protected network data service.
items: Use private networking, TLS, supported identity or rotated credentials, and least-privilege administration.
Tenant-scope keys and never allow caller-controlled raw cache keys.
Avoid caching secrets, authorization decisions, or sensitive personal data unless encryption, lifetime, and revocation are designed.
Bound key, payload, decompression, deserialization, and command work to prevent resource abuse.
Redact values and credentials from logs, traces, diagnostics, and benchmark artifacts.

performance.introduction: A cache helps only when reuse and saved source work exceed network, serialization, memory, and invalidation cost.
items: Measure hit ratio, miss penalty, Redis latency, serialization, payload bytes, and source load by cache family.
Reuse multiplexer or framework-managed connections and avoid synchronous network calls.
Use L1 for very hot safe data and account for cross-node invalidation lag.
Distribute TTLs and prewarm selectively to avoid synchronized expiry and recovery stampedes.
Find hot keys, large values, memory fragmentation, evictions, connection saturation, and slow commands before scaling.

deployment.introduction: Cache topology and application rollout determine compatibility and recovery behavior.
items: Provision managed Redis or equivalent with private access, TLS, identity, capacity, replicas, maintenance, and recovery policy.
Use versioned keys when old and new application versions serialize differently.
Deploy source-compatible readers before changing writers and avoid fleet-wide cold starts.
Verify memory and eviction policy do not mix workloads with incompatible durability needs.
Smoke-test hit, miss, invalidation, outage fallback, failover, and restart through the deployed route.

troubleshooting.cause: Keys vary unexpectedly, TTL is too short, reuse is low, values are evicted, or invalidation is excessive.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect normalized key families, TTL distribution, evictions, access frequency, and invalidation events.

troubleshooting.symptom: Database load spikes when entries expire.
troubleshooting.cause: Many callers or keys rebuild simultaneously.
troubleshooting.fix: Use miss coalescing, TTL jitter, bounded refresh, stale-while-revalidate where safe, and source admission control.

troubleshooting.cause: Tenant scope is missing from a key or caller input controls the namespace.
troubleshooting.fix: Build typed server-side tenant-aware keys and add colliding-ID isolation tests.

troubleshooting.symptom: Redis outage takes down the API.
troubleshooting.cause: Cache calls have long waits or no documented source fallback and circuit behavior.
troubleshooting.fix: Set bounded timeouts, degrade deliberately, protect the source, and test recovery.

troubleshooting.cause: Values are large, TTLs are long, traffic exceeds capacity, fragmentation grows, or eviction policy is wrong.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect memory by key family, payload limits, expiration, eviction, fragmentation, and headroom.

troubleshooting.symptom: New deployment cannot deserialize old entries.
troubleshooting.cause: The value contract changed under the same key version.
troubleshooting.fix: Use versioned keys or backward-compatible serialization and allow old entries to expire.

productionChecklist: Source of truth, consistency window, ownership, miss, outage, and recovery behavior are documented.
Keys include environment, domain, version, tenant, and stable identifier and cannot collide.
Payload, key, TTL, negative cache, L1, L2, invalidation, and serialization policies are bounded.
Connections are reused and Redis uses private networking, TLS, identity or rotated credentials.
Stampede, hot key, eviction, memory pressure, failover, outage, and cold-start behavior are tested.
Cache data is disposable and no business record depends only on Redis.
Pub/sub, locks, sessions, counters, and cache workloads have compatible failure and eviction requirements or are separated.
Hit ratio, latency, errors, memory, evictions, connections, hot keys, and source fallback have dashboards and alerts.

code.label: ProductCache.cs
code.introduction: A typed cache service wraps IDistributedCache with JSON serialisation, a configurable TTL, and safe cache-aside logic — the database is only called on a miss.

bestPractices: Cache only measured high-reuse data with a documented source of truth and stale window.
Use versioned collision-safe environment, domain, tenant, and identifier key namespaces.
Set bounded L1 and L2 expiration, payload size, negative caching, and serialization policy.
Use HybridCache or another proven coalescing strategy to protect the source from stampedes.
Invalidate or version entries deliberately when authoritative data changes.
Reuse Redis connections and design bounded timeout, outage fallback, and recovery load.
Separate cache, durable messaging, locks, sessions, and counters when failure requirements differ.
Monitor hit ratio, latency, errors, memory, eviction, hot keys, connections, and source fallback.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the cache stampede problem and how do you prevent it?
interviewQuestions.answer: A stampede happens when many requests simultaneously find a cache miss for the same key and all race to load from the database at once, multiplying load. Prevention strategies include probabilistic early expiry, a short-lived Redis lock so only one request rebuilds the entry while others wait or serve the slightly stale value, or background refresh before expiry.

interviewQuestions.question: When should you use Redis pub/sub versus Service Bus or Event Grid?
interviewQuestions.answer: Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget with no durability — if a subscriber is offline it misses messages. It suits low-latency fan-out within a trusted environment, such as a SignalR backplane or cache invalidation broadcast. Service Bus and Event Grid provide delivery guarantees, dead-lettering, and durable storage, which are essential for business-critical events.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between IDistributedCache and IMemoryCache in ASP.NET Core?
interviewQuestions.answer: IMemoryCache is in-process, fast, and invisible to other application instances — suitable for single-server or read-heavy non-critical data. IDistributedCache abstracts a shared external store such as Redis, so all instances behind a load balancer share the same data and eviction, at the cost of network latency per cache operation.

interviewQuestions.question: What does HybridCache add?
interviewQuestions.answer: It provides a unified L1 and optional distributed L2 API, serialization, and same-process stampede protection around GetOrCreateAsync.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use versioned cache keys?
interviewQuestions.answer: They prevent new application versions from interpreting incompatible old value shapes and allow safe coexistence during rollout.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is Redis pub/sub not a durable event bus?
interviewQuestions.answer: Messages are delivered only to current subscribers and have no built-in replay, acknowledgement, or dead-lettering.

interviewQuestions.question: What should happen when Redis is unavailable?
interviewQuestions.answer: Follow an explicit bounded policy: fail closed for security state, or bypass and protect the source for disposable cache data, while avoiding a recovery stampede.

note: Redis improves read performance and reduces database load, but it introduces a distributed dependency, consistency trade-offs, memory limits, and connection overhead that must be designed for explicitly.
tip: Use .NET Aspire's AddRedis resource in the AppHost for local development so every developer gets a consistent Redis container without manual setup, and switch to Azure Cache for Redis in production through the same Aspire integration.
warning: Never cache sensitive personal data or security tokens without encryption, short TTLs, and careful key scoping — a cache key collision or overly broad invalidation can expose one user's data to another.

name: YARP — Reverse Proxy
shortDescription: Build a programmable .NET reverse proxy and API gateway using YARP with route-based forwarding, transforms, load balancing, and middleware integration.
overview: YARP (Yet Another Reverse Proxy) is a Microsoft library for building high-performance, programmable reverse proxies and API gateways directly in .NET using ASP.NET Core middleware.
detail: Unlike infrastructure proxies such as NGINX or managed services such as Azure API Management, YARP runs inside a .NET application and integrates with the full ASP.NET Core pipeline — dependency injection, authentication, rate limiting, OpenTelemetry, and custom middleware all apply. Routes and clusters are configured in appsettings.json or loaded dynamically from a database or service registry. Request and response transforms allow header manipulation, path rewriting, query modifications, and claim forwarding. YARP is an excellent fit for the Backend for Frontend pattern, internal API gateways in Modular Monolith decomposition, and migration facades in Legacy Modernisation.

concepts.title: Routes and clusters
concepts.description: A route matches an incoming request by path, host, or header and maps it to a cluster — a named group of destination backends with load balancing, health checks, and session affinity settings.

concepts.title: Transforms
concepts.description: Request and response transforms modify headers, paths, query strings, and the request body before forwarding or after receiving the upstream response — configurable in JSON or code.

concepts.title: Load balancing and health checks
concepts.description: YARP distributes traffic across cluster destinations using round-robin, least-requests, power-of-two, or random strategies and actively or passively monitors destination availability.

concepts.title: Dynamic configuration
concepts.description: Routes and clusters can be reloaded at runtime from any IProxyConfigProvider implementation — a database, Consul, or a custom control plane — without restarting the proxy process.

architecture.description: Inbound traffic hits the YARP middleware pipeline, which matches a route, applies transforms, forwards to the selected cluster destination, and returns the upstream response through the response transform chain.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: YARP is registered as middleware, routes are declared in configuration, and a custom transform forwards the authenticated user's claims to the upstream service as a trusted header.

bestPractices: Centralise cross-cutting concerns — authentication, rate limiting, correlation ID injection, and request logging — in the YARP middleware pipeline rather than duplicating them in every upstream service.
Use the dynamic configuration provider pattern to reload routes and clusters from a database or service registry at runtime, enabling zero-downtime topology changes without a proxy restart.
Apply path-strip transforms at the proxy rather than requiring upstream services to understand gateway-prefixed paths — each service should be independently addressable without the proxy prefix.
Monitor YARP's built-in metrics for request rate, error rate, and destination health alongside upstream service telemetry so the proxy itself is not a blind spot in the observability picture.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose YARP over Azure API Management?
interviewQuestions.answer: YARP is a good fit when the gateway logic is complex enough to need code, when deep ASP.NET Core middleware integration is required — custom auth, claim transforms, feature flags — or when a managed gateway's cost, latency, or networking constraints are not acceptable. APIM is better when a managed service, a developer portal, a built-in policy engine, and multi-region capabilities are needed without writing and operating gateway code.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the Backend for Frontend pattern and how does YARP support it?
interviewQuestions.answer: Backend for Frontend creates a dedicated gateway per client type — web, mobile, third-party — each exposing the exact API shape that client needs, aggregating and transforming upstream responses. YARP supports this by letting each BFF be a .NET application with its own route configuration, transforms, and authentication policy, all sharing common middleware through the ASP.NET Core pipeline.

interviewQuestions.question: How does YARP handle upstream service discovery in a dynamic environment?
interviewQuestions.answer: A custom IProxyConfigProvider implementation reads destination addresses from any source — a database, Consul, Kubernetes endpoints, or an Azure App Configuration store — and returns a new configuration on each poll. YARP watches for configuration changes and reloads routes and clusters without restarting, enabling dynamic registration and deregistration of upstream services.

note: YARP is a programmable proxy library, not a fully managed API gateway product — teams own its deployment, scaling, observability, and upgrades alongside the rest of the application.
tip: Use YARP as the strangler facade in a Legacy Modernisation — route new paths to modern services and old paths to the legacy system, then gradually shift routes as capabilities are migrated with no client-visible change.
warning: Placing authentication and authorisation exclusively in the YARP layer creates a single trust boundary — upstream services must still validate the forwarded identity header rather than treating an internal network call as implicitly trusted.
